body:
Li-Nica-Roy Proposition A.6 conditional drift and diffusion moment checks, in a precise conditional-moment specialization. Fix d,p,delta,h_n and the Markov transition increment Delta_n(y)=h_n*B_n(y)+sqrt(h_n)*sigma_n(y)*xi_n+h_n*n^(-delta)*R_n(y). Assume the companion small-jump hypotheses with q=4, uniformly on each compact set. Conditional on each current state y assume E[B_n(y)|y]=b_n(y), E[xi_n|y]=0, and E[xi_n*xi_n^T|y]=I_d. Within-step B_n,xi_n,R_n may be correlated. Suppose the deterministic b_n and sigma_n converge uniformly on compact sets to b and sigma. Let Pi_n(y,dz) be the law of y+Delta_n(y). Define the truncated characteristics beta_n(y)=h_n^(-1)*integral_{||z-y||<=1}(z-y)Pi_n(y,dz) and alpha_n(y)=h_n^(-1)*integral_{||z-y||<=1}(z-y)(z-y)^T Pi_n(y,dz). Then beta_n converges uniformly on compact sets to b, alpha_n converges uniformly on compact sets to sigma*sigma^T, and h_n^(-1)*Pi_n(y,{z:||z-y||>epsilon}) converges uniformly on compact sets to zero for every epsilon>0. These are the transition-characteristic conditions used in source equationsA.6-A.7 and checked in A.12-A.14. Path convergence additionally needs the appropriate tightness/compact-containment and well-posed diffusion/martingale-problem hypotheses; the displayed moment conclusions alone do not assert stopped or unstopped path convergence.
Fixed dimension and p,delta>0; conditional one-step moments uniformly bounded on each compact set as stated.
Additional conditional mean/covariance and coefficient convergence assumptions appear explicitly in the characteristics lemma.

The cross term between h_n*B_n and sqrt(h_n)*sigma_n*xi_n is O_R(sqrt(h_n)) by conditional Cauchy-Schwarz; it need not vanish if the terms are correlated. Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and scope audits pending. Let N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,F=K-r,gcd(r,F)=1. One unknown A/S context pair has an arbitrary r-truth support in A and all K truths in S; N-2 other contexts are known S. The source chooses a context uniformly then a true candidate uniformly. Observe n iid untagged facts and independent uniform ell-subsets of truths in BOTH variable contexts, including S, 0<=ell<=r. Every realized generator of a randomized learning policy must satisfy source Mis_infinity<=c in all data-compatible worlds, where 0<=c<1/(2NrK), and source coarsening is uniform in exact generator-score bins. For sample counts u,v and truth-union sizes a,b in actual A,S coordinates, set h=min(a,b), kappa=F/K, A_h=F/(2(K-h))*((2-h/r-h/K)/N-c), O_a=F/(K-a)*max((r-a)/(Nr)-c,0), L(u,j)=(K/r)^u*binom(K-j,r-j)/binom(K-ell,r-ell) if j<=r and zero otherwise. For b<=r let pi=max(L(u,a),L(v,b))/(L(u,a)+L(v,b)). Set f=O_a when b>r, f=A_h when b<=r,h>=1, and f=kappa/N-kappa*c*pi when b<=r,h=0. Define P_m(j|u)=binom(m-ell,j-ell)/m^u * sum_{i=0}^{j-ell}(-1)^i binom(j-ell,i)(j-i)^u, with 0^0=1. The exact global expected robust minimax false mass is Gamma=sum_{u+v+w=n} n!/(u!v!w!)*(N-2)^w/N^n *sum_{a=ell}^r sum_{b=ell}^K P_r(a|u)P_K(b|v)f. The same-data known-partition oracle replaces f by O_a; the difference is the exact experiment-specific learning penalty. For ell>=1 the posterior whole-context correction vanishes; for ell=r, Gamma=(kappa/(2N)-c/2)*(1-kappa/N)^n. The efficient causal policy pools uncertified residuals when h>=1, reduces the posterior-more-likely-A whole context when h=0, and uses the residual oracle when resolved. Policy symmetrization, not averaging output laws, supplies global matching. This does not establish an arbitrary-VC or classical labeled-sample ERM/PAC result.
N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,gcd(r,K-r)=1; one variable A/S pair, all other contexts known S
Actual untagged iid factual samples, independent uniform ell truth sets from BOTH variable contexts including S
Pathwise robust source exact-score calibration in every data-compatible world; randomized learning policies allowed

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9375fcf0a1718154957e1a719a3358fe277573b347014e444e326701c54c3478","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/93/9375fcf0a1718154957e1a719a3358fe277573b347014e444e326701c54c3478.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8b3757a4682a8c1e4745843f9a28870a8148db2cd9aaae666f9ae3368e652eaa","bundle_entry_key":"global-coprime-single-pair-frontier","bundle_id":"population.t379-global-single-pair-coprime-all-n-verifier-20261020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"calibrated generation; global minimax; Bayesian occupancy","draft":"w709/bundle_013.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.calibration:kalai-vempala-global-coprime-single-pair-occupancy-verifier-frontier","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Global coprime single-pair frontier: working candidate

T379-C021 v2, proof (unaudited); exact checks PASS. Target 1, secondary target 2.
General multi-pair/VC frontier remains open.

Model: N>=3 contexts, K>=2 atoms per context, 1<=r<K, F=K-r,
gcd(r,F)=1. One variable A/S pair; A has arbitrary r truths, S all K.
N-2 other contexts are known S. The source chooses a context uniformly,
then a true atom uniformly. Observe n iid facts without orientation tags,
plus independent uniform ell-subsets of truths from BOTH variable contexts,
including S, with 0<=ell<=r. Every realized generator of a randomized
learning policy must have source Mis_infinity<=c in every compatible world.
Let 0<=c<1/(2NrK). Gamma(c)=inf_policy sup_fixed_world E[false mass].

In actual A/S coordinates let u,v be sample counts, a,b known union sizes,
h=min(a,b), kappa=F/K. Define

 A_h(c)=F/(2(K-h))*((2-h/r-h/K)/N-c),
 O_a(c)=F/(K-a)*max((r-a)/(Nr)-c,0),
 L(u,j)=(K/r)^u*binom(K-j,r-j)/binom(K-ell,r-ell) for j<=r,
         zero for j>r.

For unresolved data b<=r set pi_max=max(L(u,a),L(v,b))/(L(u,a)+L(v,b)).
Define f=O_a if b>r; f=A_h if b<=r and h>=1;
f=kappa/N-kappa*c*pi_max if b<=r and h=0.

For m>=ell, let

 P_m(j|u)=binom(m-ell,j-ell)/m^u
             *sum_{i=0}^{j-ell}(-1)^i binom(j-ell,i)(j-i)^u.

Use 0^0=1. The proposed exact global frontier is

 Gamma(c)=sum_{u+v+w=n} n!/(u!v!w!)*(N-2)^w/N^n
                *sum_{a=ell}^r sum_{b=ell}^K
                    P_r(a|u)*P_K(b|v)*f(u,v,a,b;c).          (1)

The same-data known-partition oracle is the same sum replacing f by O_a.
Their difference is the exact learning penalty in this VC-one family.

## Hardest step: conditional BAYES all-generator lower bound

This is the decisive analytic step; finite exact checks support it below,
and independent review remains necessary. A conditional minimax bound cannot
simply be averaged into a global expected minimax bound.

Source bin masses are integer multiples of 1/(NrK). Robustness gives
pairwise coarsened-source TV<=2c<1/(NrK); thus all score-bin source masses
are invariant across compatible worlds. This is a BIN-MASS lattice,
not a coarsened-atom-probability lattice.

Support swaps force each unsaturated outside-known set into one bin.
If one context is saturated, coprimality forces its outside-known set
into one bin too: F divides r*v, hence F divides v, and 0<=v<=F.
This is C019's already saved structural step.

Unless both contexts are saturated, outside-known bins either differ or
agree. If they differ, each contains an ENTIRE context and none of its
sibling. If common, the bin contains K-k atoms from EACH sibling, with
the same k known truths omitted from each, 0<=k<=h, plus possible fixed-S
safe atoms. Every false atom belongs to this bin. Its source score is
at least b_k=[1/K+(r-k)/(r(K-k))]/(2N), since fixed-S atoms have density
lambda=1/(NK)>=b_k. With w safe atoms, its false fraction is at most
tau_k=F/(2(K-k)). Its actual false mass in either orientation is at least
F*b_k-tau_k*c. This decreases with k, hence is at least A_h(c).
Pooling after selecting h known truths in each sibling, then transferring
c residual mass to fixed S, attains A_h in every world.

In whole-context mode, baseline posterior false mass is kappa/N. Every
bin's posterior false fraction is <=kappa*pi_max, even with safe mixing.
TV c therefore permits reduction at most kappa*pi_max*c. Removing c mass
from the more-likely-A context and adding it to fixed S attains
B_pi(c)=kappa/N-kappa*c*pi_max.

If both unions have size r, an invariant bin satisfies
F*(u_L-u_R)=r*(v_L-v_R), with u known counts, v outside counts.
Coprimality implies either balanced counts u_L=u_R,v_L=v_R, or the bin
contains an entire context and none of its sibling. One whole-context
bin forces the rest of the sibling into its own whole-context bin.
Otherwise all bins are balanced. For balanced bins, posterior false
fraction is <=1/2 and independent of orientation. Artificial fair mean
density is lambda/2 on outside atoms, while all safe densities are
>=lambda. Coarsening cannot lower mass on the outside set; TV c implies
false mass >=F*lambda/2-c/2=A_r(c). Pooling attains this.
Thus conditional Bayes optimum is min(A_h,B_pi) in every unresolved case.

For h>=1, A_h always wins on this c interval. Indeed
D_h=kappa/N-F*b_h=h*F^2/(2NrK(K-h)) and
B_pi-A_h>=D_h-c*(kappa-tau_h).
If kappa-tau_h>0, positivity at c*=1/(2NrK) reduces to
2K*h*F>K-2h, true for h>=1,F>=1. For h=0, B_pi<=A_0 since pi_max>=1/2.

Resolved data b>r identify the A context. Swaps force its outside atoms
into one bin if a<r. Safe mixing raises baseline density, and the exact
known-partition value is O_a(c). If a=r, it is zero, not an oracle slope
inferred from a zero-mass group.

## Actual posterior and global matching

Use the uniform prior on orientations and A supports. The verifier-set
marginal is identical in A and S. Conditional A supports are uniform
r-subsets containing the certificate. Relative to S, the factual sample
sequence likelihood in a context is exactly L(u,j) above. Thus pi is
the TRUE posterior, not a surrogate fair bit. With ell=0, u repeated
copies of one fact have likelihood ratio (K/r)^(u-1), not (K/r)^u.

The finite group generated by sibling swaps and within-context atom
permutations is transitive on worlds and equivariant on the experiment.
Symmetrize LEARNING POLICIES, retaining each separately realized generator.
Never average generator laws: exact-score calibration is not convex in g.
The symmetrized policy remains feasible pathwise and has constant-world
risk equal to original uniform-prior risk. Worst risk is always at least
prior-average risk. Conditional Bayes minima above are attained, so global
minimax equals their uniform-prior average. This is standard finite-group
minimax methodology, not a new minimax theorem.

Condition on sample context counts u,v. Their multinomial distribution is
the coefficient in (1). Choose j-ell new truths and use inclusion-exclusion
to require each chosen new truth to appear: this gives P_m(j|u), with
samples allowed to hit the ell original verifier truths. The two context
occupancy experiments are independent given context counts and a fixed
world. The conditional Bayes value is symmetric, hence averaging in ANY
fixed world's actual A/S coordinates yields (1).

Equivalently let V_cond=O_a on resolved data, A_h otherwise. Then

 Gamma(c)=E[V_cond]-kappa*c*
      E[(pi_max-1/2)*1_{unresolved and h=0}].                (2)

The correction vanishes for ell>=1. It must not be applied on resolved
data. At ell=r, (1) reduces to
(kappa/(2N)-c/2)*(1-kappa/N)^n. At c=0, Gamma=E[V_cond] for ONE pair.
C020's zero-budget averaging failure uses TWO pairs and is consistent.

Primary source statistic: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3, Definitions 1--2,
pp.8--9. Structural inputs: C017/C019, unaudited. Standard minimax card:
recall/walk005.txt. Independent mathematical, priority, scope audit pending.

## Efficient policy and target scope

The policy uses sample multiplicities and observed truth unions. If the
partition is identified, use the A residual group with its native density,
remove min(c,residual source mass), and transfer this mass to fixed S.
For unresolved h>=1, choose an h-subset of known truths uniformly in each
sibling, pool their 2(K-h) remaining atoms at the common source density,
and move c mass to fixed S. Other selected-known atoms have their common
paired source score. For h=0, choose the posterior-more-likely A context
(uniform tie break), lower its entire context mass by c, and add it to
fixed S. All these operations use observed quantities only. Selected known
subsets and ties randomize policies, never averages of output laws.

The output law and the required likelihood comparison have polynomial
arithmetic complexity in n and the explicit alphabet size NK. The finite
sum (1) is also polynomial-time evaluable in n,K by precomputing the
occupancy tables. This is an expected minimax result under a pathwise
compatible-world robustness requirement, not a high-probability PAC result.
The two orientation functions form a VC-one partition class. Factual
observations do not provide labeled partition examples; this does not prove
a classical labeled-sample ERM rate or the unrestricted arbitrary-VC target.
The exact difference of sums is an experiment-specific estimation penalty,
not an assertion that it equals ordinary classification error. A MAP
orientation can be used as a data-dependent tie break among feasible
partitions, but the optimal pooled output need not be an oracle plug-in
using that single orientation. These distinctions require scope review.

## Exact independent finite checks

logs/global_single_pair_check.json records 237 conditional Bayes games and
588969 exhaustive invariant score partitions, 621 actual all-world
generator calibration checks, 237 full-world likelihood-posterior checks,
330 direct sequence/occupancy comparisons, 720 global occupancy-sum checks,
252 full-verifier closed-form checks, 24 two-sample closed-form checks, and
seven genuine repeated-fact wrong-exponent controls. Exhaustive partition
checks have NK<=9; larger parameter checks concern occupancy and algebra.

Separately logs/global_single_pair_policy_check.json sums the explicit
causal policy under all six fixed N=3,K=3,r=2 worlds, ell=0..2, n=0..4,
at zero and positive budgets: 59400 actual data/verifier histograms and
180 exact fixed-world expectations and normalizations. These equal (1)
and are constant across fixed worlds, without substituting posterior risk
for an actual-world loss. Both scripts use only integers and Fraction.
Finite checks are not an independent mathematical audit of the general proof.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:81ee50e127bfb14a5f03a78a3a06c0e51e589b42410a5a1f204312b1a99439c9","revision_digest":"sha256:39f359fca3402a1a696a1fc6c481b0860225853def9331d81be2cb29ae5ee267","source_id":"owner:w709:T379-C021:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20T13:57:38.168701+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 7 (Paralinearization of the transformed fractional flux operator) of arXiv:2608.29726, '\LARGE A Priori Estimates for Singular Fractional Stochastic Burgers Equations'] Let \(1<\gamma<2\), \(0<\beta<1\), and let
\(\Psi\in C^{1+\beta}(\T)\) be an orientation-preserving bi-Lipschitz map
with Jacobian satisfying \eqref{eq:J-bounds}.
The operator \(\Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}\) defined in
\eqref{eq:Dflux} admits the paralinearization
\begin{equation}
  \Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}f
  =(J^\gamma)^\Phi\prec\Rcal_\gamma f
  +\mathcal S_\Psi f,
\end{equation}
where \(\prec\) is the spatial Bony paraproduct.  For every
\(f\in H^{\gamma/2}\) and every
\begin{equation}
 \sigma<\min\{\gamma/2,1-\gamma/2+\beta\},
\end{equation}
the remainder satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \norm{\mathcal S_\Psi f}_{H^\sigma}
  \lesssim\norm f_{H^{\gamma/2}}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\mathcal S_\Psi\) has order at most
\(\max\{0,\gamma-1-\beta\}+\).  Consequently,
\begin{align}
  \norm{\Dcal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}f}_{H^{1-\gamma/2}}
  &\lesssim\norm f_{H^{\gamma/2}},
  \\
  \norm{\Acal_{\Psi}^{\gamma}f}_{H^{-\gamma/2}}
  &\lesssim\norm f_{H^{\gamma/2}}.
  
\end{align}
The map
\[
 \Psi\longmapsto\Acal_\Psi^\gamma
 \quad\text{with values in}\quad
 \mathcal L(H^{\gamma/2},H^{-\gamma/2})
\]
is continuous on bounded subsets of \(C^{1+\beta}\) with fixed
bi-Lipschitz constants.  After any loss from \(\beta\) to
\(\beta_0<\beta\), this dependence has a local H\"older modulus.  All
displayed bounds are locally uniform under these assumptions.

Let $N_*=K\lceil N/K\rceil$. Then, for all $t>0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\frac{U-\mathbb{E}U}{N_*}>t\Bigr)\leq  \exp\biggl\{ -\frac{N_*t^2}{2(d_{\max}+1)(\sigma^2 +bt/3)}\biggr\}.
\]

[campaign result 2026-09-14; values computed exactly from the intersection-array identity tau_0 = k sum_{i=1}^d (k_i+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i). That identity was checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, among them the cubic graphs K_{3,3}, Q_3, Petersen, Heawood, Pappus, Desargues and the dodecahedron, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls.] This is the cubic case of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For a finite connected simple distance-regular graph G with n vertices, let tau_0 = max_{x,y} E_x[T_y] for simple random walk. By the known classification, there are exactly thirteen cubic (valency-three) distance-regular graphs. Their (n, tau_0) values are: K_4 (4, 3); K_{3,3} (6, 6); cube Q_3 (8, 10); Petersen (10, 12); Heawood (14, 19); Pappus (18, 27); Desargues (20, 65/2); dodecahedron (20, 35); Coxeter (28, 45); Tutte-Coxeter (30, 48); Foster (90, 675/4); Biggs-Smith (102, 195); Tutte 12-cage (126, 234). Hence, given the classification, the maximum of tau_0/(n-1) over all cubic distance-regular graphs is 195/101 (about 1.9307), attained uniquely by the Biggs-Smith graph. This reproduces exactly the value Aldous and Fill attribute to Biggs and settles, for valency three, Biggs's outlined claim that it is the largest. The general O(n) conjecture over non-cycle distance-regular graphs is not settled by this computation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.

body:
[Lemma 27 of arXiv:2608.29157, 'Dilator-based analysis of $\KP$'] For each $n\in\bbN$, let $A$ be the leading formula of $[\ttX_n]\vdash \Gamma_n$. 
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item If $A \equiv B\land C$, then either $B$ or $C$ is in $\Gamma_{n+1}$.
            \item If $A \equiv B\lor C$, then both $B$ and $C$ are in $\Gamma_{n+1}$.
            \item If $A \equiv \forall^\tau x B(x)$ for $\tau\neq \ord$, then there is a free variable $x$ of type $\tau$ such that $B(x)$ is in $\Gamma_{n+1}$.
            \item If $A \equiv \exists^\tau x B(x)$ for $\tau\neq \ord$, then for every term $t$ of type $\tau$, there is $m>n$ such that $B(t)$ occurs in $\Gamma_m$.
            \item If $A\equiv \forall^\ord x B(x)$, then there is $v\in \ttX$ such that $B(v)$ is in $\Gamma_{n+1}$.
            \item If $A\equiv \exists^\ord x B(x)$, then for every $v\in \ttX$ there is $m>n$ such that $B(v)$ occurs in $\Gamma_m$.
        \end{enumerate}

\]

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We can talk about ellipses, in several possible ways, as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item As the curves appearing via $d(z,p)+d(z,q)=l$, with $p,q\in\mathbb R^2$, and $l>0$.

\item Up to a translation and rotation, as the curves given by $(x/a)^2+(y/b)^2=1$.

\item Or equivalently, in polar coordinates, given by $x=a\cos t$, $y=b\sin t$.

\item As the conics, that is, the plane curves of degree $2$, which are compact. 

\item As the compact curves obtained by cutting a 3D cone with a plane.

\item As the pictures of a circle, taken from various 3D perspectives.

\item As the trajectories of the planets around the Sun.
\end{enumerate}

[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Let $(\bm{X}_{n})_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of \iid random vectors in $\R_{+}^{d}$, 
  such that the tail distribution function $\widebar{F}_{j}$ of each marginal $X_{1, j}$ 
   belongs to $\SRV{\alpha}{\rho_{j}}$ with auxiliary function~$A_{j}$, for a common $\alpha > 0$
  and possibly different $\rho_{j} < 0$,
  $j=1,\ldots , d$. Then,
  for some $C > 0$ and every $n \geq 1$ we have 
\[
\prob\big(\exists j \in \lbra 1, d \rbra,\ \exists i' \neq i \in \lbra 1,n \rbra,\ X_{i, j} = X_{i', j}\quad \mathrm{and} \quad X_{i, j} \ge X_{1, j}, \dots, X_{n, j} \big) \leq C\Big(\frac{1}{n} + A_{j_{0}}(a_{n, j_{0}})\Big),
\]
where $a_{n, j} = F_{j}^{\leftarrow}(1 - n^{-1})$ and $j_{0}$ is such that $\rho_{j_{0}} \geq \rho_{j}$ for every $j \in \lbra 1, d \rbra$.
title: Corollary 9 of arXiv:2608.17562

[Theorem fredi of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $n$ be a fixed integer. Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume
  that for every finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N} \log
    \mathbb{E}[H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A),
    \ldots, \lambda_n (A))] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum_{i = 0}^r
    \frac{1}{N^{j \varepsilon}} \Psi_j (x_i) \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi_n
    (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi_0, \ldots, \Psi_n$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of
  $0$, the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$ and $0 <
  \varepsilon < n^{- 1}$. Then the $1 / N^{n \varepsilon}$ correction of the
  average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} A$ is given by
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
    \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{1}{N^{j
    \varepsilon}} \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k^{(n)},
    
  \end{equation}
  where for every $j \in \{0, \ldots, n\}$
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k := \sum_{b_1 + 2 b_2 + \cdots + j \text{} b_j
     = j} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k - m
     - b_1 - \cdots - b_j) !b_1 ! \ldots b_j !} \text{{\hspace{8em}}} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{14em}}} \times \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'_0
    (x))^{k - m - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} (\Psi'_1 (x))^{b_1} \ldots (\Psi'_j
    (x))^{b_j}) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation}
title: Theorem fredi of arXiv:2412.09290

\(m(\alpha+\eta)<1\). Define
\[
\theta(x):=x_1+\cdots+x_m,
\qquad
G_\eta(x)
:=
\frac{1}{1+|\theta(x)|^2}
\prod_{j=1}^m
\left(
|x_j|^{\alpha-1-\eta}
+
|x_j|^{\alpha-1+\eta}
\right).
\]
Then \(G_\eta\in L^1(\mathbb R^m)\).

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.31070, 'Sub-Laplacians on Compact Lie Groups: Heat Kernels, Distance, and Zeta Determinants'] If $\pLie$ generates $\gLie$ as a Lie algebra, that is, $\Lie(\pLie)=\gLie$, then, for $g\in G$ and $t>0$,
		\[
		p_t(g)=e^{-t|\rho_L|^2}
		\int_{\lLie}q_t^{\C}(ge^{iY})j_L^{\nc}(Y)^{1/2}
		\frac{e^{-|Y|^2/(4t)}}{(4\pi t)^{\dim L/2}}\,\mathrm dY.
		\]
		The integral is absolutely convergent. The holomorphic kernel has the signed affine lattice formula of \Cref{thm:heat-kernel-image}, and \Cref{thm:cartan-general} reduces the integral to the Cartan subalgebra $\tLie$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.31070

[Theorem 11 (Boundedness on the infinite chain) of arXiv:2608.30991, 'A block-Toeplitz approach to the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincaré operator on self-similar'] Let $p\in(1,\infty)$ and $s\in(-1,1)$, and define the geometric scaling exponent
	\[
	\alpha=\frac{d-1}{p}-s.
	\]
	If $0<\alpha<d$, then the rescaled sequence-space operators $\widetilde{\mathbb{S}}_\alpha$, $\widetilde{\mathbb{K}}^*_\alpha$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb{K}}_\alpha$ are bounded linear operators on $\ell^p\bigl(\mathbb{N},W_0^{s,p}(\Gamma_0)\bigr)$.
	
	Consequently, through the isomorphisms established above, the layer potentials on the infinite chain are bounded operators on the global mean-zero space:
	\[
	\widetilde{S}_\Gamma,\,\widetilde{K}^*_\Gamma,\,\widetilde{K}_\Gamma
	\in
	\mathcal{L}\bigl(W_0^{s,p}(\Gamma)\bigr),
	\]
	where $s$ and $p$ are determined by $0<\alpha<d$.

[Lemma lem:dgt4-linearization-from-survival of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Suppose that the scenery variables are independent and identically
	distributed, atomless, centered, and have finite positive variance.
	Fix $T>0$, let $n_R\coloneqq\lfloor R^2T\rfloor$, and let
	$q_{R,j}\in[0,1]$ be deterministic for $0\leq j<n_R$. Suppose that
	as $R\to\infty$,
	\[
		R^{-2}\sum_{j=0}^{n_R-1}
		\mathbf E_0\left|
		\mathbb{P}(S_{n_R,j}(X)=1\mid X)-q_{R,j}
		\right|
		\longrightarrow0,
	\]
	and that there is $C<\infty$ such that, for every $\delta\in(0,T)$, there are
	deterministic numbers $\varepsilon_R(\delta)\geq0$ with
	$\varepsilon_R(\delta)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$ and, uniformly over
	$0\leq i,j\leq n_R-\delta R^2$ and all deterministic nearest-neighbor paths
	$X=(X_0,\ldots,X_i)$ and $Y=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$,
	\[
		\left|
		\Cov(S_{n_R,i}(X),S_{n_R,j}(Y)\mid X,Y)
		\right|
		\leq
		\frac{C}{\delta R^2}
		\sum_{r=0}^i\sum_{h=0}^j\mathbf{1}_{\{X_r=Y_h\}}
		+\varepsilon_R(\delta)\, .
	\]
	Then, for every
	$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$,
	\begin{equation}
		\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\Biggl(R^{(d-4)/2}\Biggl(
		u_{n_R}-\mathbb{E} u_{n_R}(0)
		-\sum_{j=0}^{n_R-1}q_{R,j}P^j\zeta
		\Biggr)^{(R)}(\varphi)\Biggr)^2\Biggr]
		\longrightarrow0\, .
	\end{equation}
	Consequently, for every $s>(d-4)/2$,
	\[
		R^{(d-4)/2}
		\left(u_{n_R}-\mathbb{E} u_{n_R}(0)
		-\sum_{j=0}^{n_R-1}q_{R,j}P^j\zeta\right)^{(R)}
		\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0
		\quad\text{in }H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\, .
	\]

body:
[Proposition 1 (Full-space reduction and its interior equality case) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] For $p\in[0,1-\delta]$, let $P_{n,k,t,\delta}(p)$ be the PCS for $k-t$ probabilities equal to $p$ and $t$ probabilities equal to $p+\delta$. For each $\boldsymbol\theta\in\ThetaPZ$, define
\[
 p(\boldsymbol\theta)=\theta_{[k-t+1]}-\delta\in[0,1-\delta].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \PCS_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
 \ge P_{n,k,t,\delta}\bigl(p(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr).
 
\end{equation}
If $p(\boldsymbol\theta)\in(0,1-\delta)$, equality holds if and only if
\[
 \theta_{[1]}=\cdots=\theta_{[k-t]}=p(\boldsymbol\theta),
 \qquad
 \theta_{[k-t+1]}=\cdots=\theta_{[k]}
 =p(\boldsymbol\theta)+\delta.
\]
Consequently, for every $n,k,t$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}
 \inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\ThetaPZ}\PCS_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
 =\min_{0\le p\le1-\delta}P_{n,k,t,\delta}(p).
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Full-space reduction and its interior equality case

[Corollary 5 (Regret under the logarithmic buffer) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] For each $t$ choose \(\beta_t = \frac{\tau} {\log(\mathrm e + t)},\) and define \(K_\tau \coloneqq \left\lceil \exp\!\left(\frac{\tau}{\rho_\tau}\right)-\mathrm e \right\rceil\). Then, under the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:UCB-BQRL-finite}, with probability at least \(1-2\delta\), $\Reg_\tau(T)\le\;2H K_\tau+ \allowbreak \frac{c\log(\mathrm e+T-1)}{\tau}\sqrt{SA TH^4\log\!\frac{2SATH}{\delta}} + \allowbreak\frac{c\log(\mathrm e+T-1)}{\tau}\sqrt{\frac{TH^4}{2}\log\!\frac{2SATH}{\delta}\log\!\frac{1}{\delta}} \allowbreak$. Consequently,
\(\Reg_\tau(T) = \widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(
\frac{1}{\tau}\sqrt{SATH^4}
\right) + O(K_\tau H)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Regret under the logarithmic buffer

body:
[Theor thm:c4-finite-subgraph of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] There exists a universal constant
$C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}\ge1$ such that the following holds.
Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a real $\rho\in(0,1]$, and positive integers $k,r,n$ with  
 $$2 \le \rho k \le r\le k\le n.$$

Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be $C_4$-free with $|I|=k$, $|J|=n$, and right degrees satisfying
\[
2\le |N_G(j)|\le d
\qquad\forall j\in J.
\]

Define
\[
K_\star:=
\max\left\{
K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:
K\log K\le \Lambda 
\right\}, \quad \mbox{ where } \Lambda :=\min\left(\frac r2,\frac nk\right). 
\]
and let $m_\star$ be a positive integer satisfying
\[
\left(\frac{C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}d^4m_\star}{\rho}\right)^{C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}d^3m_\star}
\le K_\star.
\]
Assume such an $m_\star$ exists.
If $\Omega\subseteq J$ is chosen uniformly from $\binom Jr$, then
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(\text{$G[\Omega]$ contains a \hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m_\star$-matching rooted tree}}}}\bigr)
\ge
1-\exp(-\sqrt{K_\star})-\frac{32d}{\log K_\star}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finite $C_4$-free sampling theorem

[Prop mom-dbm of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For any $C_1>0$, there exists $C=C(C_1)>0$ such that the following holds.
For any $N\in\mathbb N$, $0\le \boldsymbol{\tau}_1<\boldsymbol{\tau}_2 \le C_1$, $C_1^{-1}N^{2/3}<k<C_1N^{2/3}$, we have
\[
\mathbb E \left[  \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \left(1+N^{-2/3}\mathbf Y_i^{(N)}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_1)/2 \right)^k - \sum_{i=1}^N \left( 1+N^{-2/3}\mathbf Y_i^{(N)}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_2)/2\right)^k\right)^4  \right] < C (\boldsymbol{\tau}_2-\boldsymbol{\tau}_1)^2.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop mom-dbm of arXiv:2411.10829

body:
[Lemma lem:OnejVolumeAnalysis of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] There exists a real number $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds. Consider any $\lambda \in (0,\lambda_0)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ such that $p_0=1$ and, for all $i \ge 1$, $W_i \le (4/\lambda)^i$. Suppose that $\overline{p}$ has finitely many bins which are strongly exposed. 
Let $j_0$ be a sufficiently large positive integer
where  all strongly-exposed bins are in $[j_0-1]$.
Let $\tau_0$ be a non-negative integer. Let $\Psi_0$ be the   initialising high-level state with  $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper).  
Let $V$ be a volume process from $\Psi_0$ with transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$, 
 send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and birth rate~$\lambda$  (Definition~(def:volume-process of the paper)).
For any
$t \ge \tau_0$, 
let   $T(t) = \{\tau_0,\ldots,t\}$.
Then  the following statement holds  for
every $t > \tau_0$ and
every tuple
$ 
\overline{\psi}_{T(t-1)} = (\psi_{\tau_0},\dots,\psi_{t-1})$  of high-level states 
such that  
$\mathbb{P}( \overline{\Psi}_{T(t-1)} = \overline{\psi}_{T(t-1)}) > 0$, 
$\psi_{t-1}$ is a $j$-filling state, 
$\tau^{\psi_{t-1}} = t-1$, and $z_j^{\psi_{t-1}} = 0$.
Conditioned on $\overline{\Psi}_{T(t-1)} = \overline{\psi}_{T(t-1)} $,
with 
probability at least $1-
\exp(-\lambda j/1000) $,  
the following events occur, where  
\[
\tau_{j,\mathrm{full}} = \min\{t'  \geq t \colon \textup{type}^{\Psi(t')} = \textup{failure} \mbox{ or }j^{\Psi(t')} = j+1\}.\]
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\Psi(\tau_{j,\mathrm{full}})$ is $(j+1)$-filling or $(j+1)$-advancing
and $z_{j+1}^{\Psi(\tau_{j,\mathrm{full}})}=0$.

\item $\tau_{j,\mathrm{full}} \leq t+
\lceil 4(4 j)^{\phi} W_j\rceil
$.

[Lemma lem6.11 of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] Suppose $\phi: [1,\infty) \to (-\infty, 0]$ is a function
that satisfies the following conditions: \hfil\break
(a) $\phi$ is continuous, strictly decreasing, and convex 
on $[1, \infty)$; \hfil\break
(b) $\phi$ is continuously differentiable on the open 
half line $(1, \infty)$; and \hfil\break 
(c) one has that
\begin{equation}

\lim_{x \to \infty} \phi(x)\ =\ -\infty 
\indent {\rm and} \indent
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac {\phi(x)} {x}\ =\ 0.
\end{equation}

   For each $y \in (1, \infty)$ (the open half line), let 
$L^{(y)}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ denote the affine function whose graph is tangent to that 
of $\phi$ at the point $(y, \phi(y))$ --- that is, the affine function that satisfies
\begin{equation}

L^{(y)}(y)\ =\ \phi(y) \indent {\rm and} \indent 
L^{(y)}(x)\ \leq\ \phi(x)\ \ {\rm for\ all}\ x \in [1, \infty). 
\end{equation}
 
   Then the following statements (I), (II), and (III) hold:
\medskip

   (I) The following statements hold: \hfil\break
(i) For each $x \in (1, \infty)$,
$\phi(x) < \phi(1) \leq 0$ and $\phi'(x) < 0$.  \hfil\break  
(ii) The function $x \mapsto \phi'(x)$ for $x \in (1, \infty)$, 
is nondecreasing. \hfil\break  
(iii) One has that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \phi'(x) = 0$. \hfil\break
(iv) For each $y \in (1, \infty)$,  
$[{\rm slope\ of}\ L^{(y)}] = \phi'(y) < 0$. \hfil\break 
(v) For each $y \in (1, \infty)$, 
$L^{(y)}(0) = \phi(y) + y \cdot (-\phi'(y)) > \phi(y)$.
\medskip

   (II) For any negative number $D$ and any positive number 
$s$, there exists a number    
$T = T(\phi, D, s) > 1$ with the following property:

   For each $y \geq T$, the affine function 
$L^{(y)}$ in (the entire sentence of) eq.\ ((eq6.112 of the paper))
satisfies 
\begin{equation}

-s\ \leq\ [{\rm slope\ of}\ L^{(y)}]\ =\ \phi'(y)\ <\ 0 
\indent {\rm and} \indent
L^{(y)}(0)\ \leq\ D. 
\end{equation}
  
   (III) Suppose also that $\psi: [1, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ is a  
function such that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \psi(x) = \infty$.
 
Then for any negative number $D$ and any positive numbers
$B$ and $s$, there there exists a real number 
$T^* := T^*(\phi, \psi, B, D, s) > 1$ with the following 
property:
\smallskip

For each $y \geq T^*$, the affine function 
$L^{(y)}$ in (the entire sentence of) eq.\ ((eq6.112 of the paper))
satisfies ((eq6.113 of the paper)) and also 
[strengthening part of ((eq6.113 of the paper))] satisfies  
\begin{equation}
  
L^{(y)}(0) + B\ \leq\ D \indent {\rm and} \indent
L^{(y)}(x) + B\ \leq\ \phi(x) + \psi(x)\ \ 
{\rm for\ all}\ x \geq 1.    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem6.11 of arXiv:2508.12951

body:
[Proposition prop:moment_R_ex1 of arXiv:2510.21186, 'Weingarten Calculus with Virtual Isometries'] Let $m$, $l$, $q$ be nonnegative integers, and consider four sequences:
\[
\bm{i}=(i_1,\dots, i_m), \qquad \bm{j} =(j_1,\dots, j_m), \qquad
\bm{i}'=(i_1',\dots, i_l'), \qquad \bm{j}' =(j_1',\dots, j_l')
\]
 of positive integers in $\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$
Then, for each $1 \le s \le n$ the moment
\[
\mathbb{E} \bigl[p_{i_1 j_1} \cdots p_{i_m j_m} \overline{p_{i_1' j_1'} \cdots p_{i_l' j_l'}} r_{ss}^q\bigr]
\]
 vanishes unless $\bm{i} \sqcup \bm{j}'$ is a permutation of $\bm{j} \sqcup \bm{i}'$.
In this case, the moment is equal to
\[
\alpha_1 ! \cdots \alpha_{n-1}! \, \frac{n^{\uparrow \alpha_n}}{n^{\uparrow (m+q)} n^{\uparrow l}}
\times
\begin{cases}
(n+m-\alpha_s-1)^{\uparrow q} & \text{if $s<n$}, \\
(m-\alpha_n)^{\uparrow q} & \text{if $s=n$},
\end{cases}
\]
where $\alpha_k:=\mathsf{m}_{k}(\bm{i}\sqcup \bm{j}') = \mathsf{m}_{k}(\bm{j}\sqcup\bm{i}')$
for all $k=1,2,\dots, n$.
Note that the last factor may be zero.
title: Proposition prop:moment_R_ex1 of arXiv:2510.21186

[Lemma lem:rationalize-prefix-free-ball-code of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] For every prefix-free ball code \(\varphi\), there is a prefix-free ball code
\(\varphi'\) whose values are rational closed balls such that
\[
K_{\varphi'}(x;r)
\le
K_\varphi(x;r+1)
\]
for all \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\in\omega\).  In particular, in the
prefix-free ball-code characterizations of Hausdorff and packing dimensions in
Theorems~(thm:prefix-free-ball-code-hausdorff of the paper)
and~(thm:packing-ball-code-dimension of the paper), it is enough to consider ball codes
whose ranges consist of rational closed balls.

[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $\mathcal L\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and assume $\mathrm{(A_{an})}$. Then $\lambda_p(L)=\Lp(\cA_L)$ is real analytic on $\mathcal L$. More precisely, if $v_L(\xi)=\phi_L(L\xi),\qquad -1\le\xi\le1$,
and $v_L(0)=1$, then $L\mapsto v_L$ is real analytic from $\mathcal L$ into $C^1([-1,1])$. After pull-back and a fixed nonzero normalization, the adjoint eigenfunction depends real analytically on $L$ as well.

At every $L_0\in\mathcal L$, writing $h=L-L_0$, one has convergent expansions
\[
\mathscr A_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\mathscr A_n,\qquad
\lambda_p(L_0+h)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\lambda_n,\qquad
v_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^nv_n
\]
in $\mathcal L(C^1,C)$, $\R$ and $C^1([-1,1])$, respectively. The coefficients are determined recursively by
\[
(\mathscr A_0+\lambda_0)v_n+\lambda_nv_0
=-\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k},
\qquad v_n(0)=0,
\]
for $n\ge1$. If $v_0^*$ is the adjoint eigenfunction normalized by $\int_{-1}^{1}v_0v_0^*=1$, then
\[
\lambda_n=-\int_{-1}^{1}v_0^*(\xi)
\left(
\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k}
\right)(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]

[Corollary cor:tailrl-binary-recovery of arXiv:2609.02987, 'Tail Likelihood Reinforcement Learning'] Suppose $r_i\in\{0,1\}$ and let
$M:=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf 1\{r_i=1\}$. If $M>0$, then every successful
rollout receives weight $1/M$ and every unsuccessful rollout receives weight
zero. Hence the uncentered TailRL{} estimator reduces to
\begin{equation}
g_{\mathrm{TailRL}}^{(N)}(x)
=
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{i:r_i=1}S_i,

\end{equation}
which is the MaxRL estimator. After mean-centering, successful rollouts have
weight $1/M-1/N$ and unsuccessful rollouts have weight $-1/N$. If $M=0$,
all uncentered and centered weights are zero.

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2506.10817, 'On the Weak Error for Local Stochastic Volatility Models'] For $h$ such that $\frac Th\in \mathbb{N}$ and $j\in \{0,\dots,\frac Th\}$ let $(\hX_{jh}^{h,\delta},\xi_{jh})_{0\le j\le T/h}$ be defined in \eqref{eq_Xhdelta} and $(\tiX_{jh}^{h,\delta},\xi_{jh})_{0\le j\le T/h}$ be defined in \eqref{Eq:Half_step}. 
    
    Then $\mathcal{L}\bigl((\hX^{h,\delta}_{jh})_{j\le T/h},(B_t)_{t\le T}\bigr)=\mathcal{L}\bigl((\tiX_{jh}^{h,\delta})_{j\le T/h},(B_t)_{t\le T}\bigr)$.
    In particular their joint laws are equal, i.e.\ it holds that $\mathcal{L}\bigl( (\hX_{jh}^{h,\delta},\xi_{jh})_{j\le T/h}\bigr) =\mathcal{L}\bigl((\tiX_{jh}^{h,\delta},\xi_{jh})_{j\le T/h}\bigr)$.

[Prop w0exist3 of arXiv:2608.30777, 'Inhomogeneous nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \\ in Fourier-Lebesgue and modulation space'] Let $\phi_{0} \in L^2, \psi\in \widehat{L}^{r}$ and $X_{1}(T)$ be as in  (equation X1(T) of the paper). Denote by  $v_{0}$  the $L^2-$global solution  (as in (equation gwpl2 of the paper)) for initial value $\phi_{0}$.
Then  there exists  a constant $C=C(\alpha,b)>0$ such that  integral equation $$w_{0}= i \mu \int_{0}^{t} e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}|x|^{-b} G(v_{0} + e^{i\tau\partial_x^2}\psi_{0}, w_{0},0) \, d\tau +  i \mu \int_{0}^{t} e^{i(t-\tau)\partial_x^2}|x|^{-b} G(v_{0}, e^{i\tau\partial_x^2}\psi_{0},0) \, d\tau$$ has a unique solution  $w_{0} \in X_{1}(T)$   provided $T$ satisfying
\begin{align}
    T &\leq 1 \\
    T &\leq C \left( \|\phi_{0}\|_{L^{2}} + \|\psi_{0}\|_{{\widehat{L}^{r}}} \right)^{-\frac{\alpha-1}{\frac{5-\alpha}{4} - \frac{1}{\nu}}} \\
   T &\leq C \left( \|\psi_{0}\|_{\widehat{L}^{r}} \right)^{-\frac{\alpha-1}{\frac{5-\alpha}{4} - \frac{1}{\nu} + \frac{\alpha-1}{q(r)}}}.
\end{align}

body:
[Theorem thm.scfc of arXiv:2606.30517, '\textsc{Convergence towards Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations with a focus on Diestel--'] Let $(E,\mathbf{o},\mu)$ be a proper pointed measured metric space and, for $\lambda >0$, let $X^{(\lambda)}$ be a Poisson point process with intensity measure $\lambda\mu$. Then, $X^{(\lambda)}$ converges weakly (after a suitable shift) to a nontrivial point process $(\Theta_i,\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ in the extended boundary if and only if:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  the volume function $F$ is log-regularly-varying with positive index (say $b$), and
			\item  the probability measure $F(r)^{-1} \restrict{\mu}{B_r(\mathbf{o})}$, regarded as a probability measure on $\bar E$, converges weakly to a probability measure on $\partial E$ (say $\nu_0$) as $r\to\infty$. 
		\end{enumerate}  
		
		If these conditions hold, then $(\Theta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ are i.i.d.~points on $\partial E$ with distribution $\nu_0$ and $(\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$ is an independent Poisson point process on $\mathbb R$ with intensity measure proportional to the measure $\beta$ defined by $\beta((-\infty,r])\coloneqq e^{br}$. If, in addition, the nondegeneracy condition provided just after (def:voronoi of the paper) holds a.s., then the corresponding Poisson--Voronoi diagrams also converge to the Poisson--Voronoi diagram of $(\Theta_i,\Delta_i)_{i\geq 1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:sector of arXiv:2605.03896, 'Dimer models on astroidal zig-zag graphs'] Let $e\in E(N)$, $\mathsf b\in B(\mathsf G_{c, \mathsf f_0})$ and $\mathsf w\in W(\mathsf G_{c, \mathsf f_0})$.
Assume that one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf b}(e)=+$ and $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf w}(e)=-$.
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf w}(e)=-$ and $\mathsf b$ lies on $\beta_e$.
\item $\operatorname{sign}_{{\mathsf{R}}_\mathsf b}(e)=+$ and $\mathsf w$ lies on $\beta_e$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $e\subset \mathfrak{N}_{\mathsf b,\mathsf w}$.

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(a_n\to\infty\) be any deterministic sequence of positive real numbers.
There exist deterministic dyadic numbers \(h_n\downarrow0\), with
\(h_n\leq a_n\), such that, with
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_n:=\frac{h_n}{a_n},\qquad
  M_n:=\left\lfloor\frac{a_n}{h_n}\right\rfloor,
  \qquad
  \mathcal G_n:=\{j\Delta_n:0\leq j\leq M_n\},
  
\end{equation}
the following holds.  If \(K_n\) is the maximising index of \(B\) on
\(\mathcal G_n\), \(\tau_n=K_n\Delta_n\), and
\begin{equation}
  \Xi_n^{\mathrm{grid}}(t)
  :=a_n^H\bigl(B_{\tau_n+t/a_n}-B_{\tau_n}\bigr),
  
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
  d_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Xi_n^{\mathrm{grid}},\Xi_{a_n})\longrightarrow0
  \quad\text{almost surely}.
  
\end{equation}
Moreover, writing \(T_n=M_n\Delta_n\),
\begin{equation}
  a_n\tau_n\longrightarrow\infty,
  \qquad
  a_n(T_n-\tau_n)\longrightarrow\infty
  \quad\text{almost surely}.
  
\end{equation}

[Definition 40 (Full-support and coefficient-pure response) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] A Rees response kernel is \emph{full-support} in order $r$ if its left
support is $G_r$.  Relative to declared native readers, it is
\emph{coefficient-pure} if the total pushed-forward kernel lies in
\[
 G_r\otimes E_r\otimes\mathbf k\tau_r
\]
for a finite-dimensional label space $E_r$.  A window-pure family is defined
by replacing $D_\infty$ by finite truncations which reproduce the same
singular values on every prescribed finite output window.

[Lemma equivalence des normes of arXiv:2412.00865, 'On the spectral problem and fractional diffusion limit for Fokker-Planck with(-out) drift '] The two norms $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_0}$ and $\|\cdot\|_*$ defined by
$$ \| \psi \|_{{\mathcal{H}}_0}^2 := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \bigg|\nabla_v\bigg(\frac{\psi}{M}\bigg) M \bigg|^2 + \frac{|\psi|^2}{\langle v \rangle^2} \ \mathrm{d} v   \quad \mbox{ and } \quad   \|\psi\|_*^2 := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \bigg|\nabla_v\bigg(\frac{\psi}{M}\bigg) M \bigg|^2 + V|\psi|^2 \ \mathrm{d} v$$
are equivalent, i.e., there are two positive constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that
$$ C_1 \| \psi \|_{\mathcal{H}_0} \leqslant \| \psi \|_* \leqslant C_2 \| \psi \|_{\mathcal{H}_0} , \quad \forall \psi \in \mathcal{H}_0 . $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]
if $\dimh E\geq u$.

body:
For $u_t+Lu\le0$ with $Lu=-a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu$, the identity $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u=\max_{\Gamma_T}u$ requires $c\equiv0$; with $c\ge0$ only the weaker $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u\le\max_{\Gamma_T}u^+$ survives; with $c$ of arbitrary sign even that fails. (a) $c<0$ destroys everything: on $U=(0,\pi)$, $u(x,t)=e^t\sin x$ satisfies $u_t-u_{xx}-2u=0$ (so $c=-2$), has $u=0$ on the lateral sides and $u=\sin x\le1$ at $t=0$, hence $\max_{\Gamma_T}u=1$, yet $u(\pi/2,T)=e^T$ is arbitrarily large. (b) $c\ge0$ genuinely needs the positive part: on $U=(0,\pi)$ let $u$ solve $u_t-u_{xx}+u=0$ with $u\equiv-1$ on $\Gamma_T$ (initial and lateral data $-1$). Then $w=u+1$ solves $w_t-w_{xx}+w=1$ with $w=0$ on $\Gamma_T$, so $w\ge0$ by the $c\ge0$ principle and $w\not\equiv0$; hence $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u>-1=\max_{\Gamma_T}u$, while indeed $\max u\le0=\max_{\Gamma_T}u^+$. (c) What always survives for bounded $c$ of any sign is the comparison principle: $u_t+Lu\le0$ and $u\le0$ on $\Gamma_T$ imply $u\le0$, because $v=e^{-\gamma t}u$ solves an inequality with zeroth-order coefficient $c+\gamma\ge0$ for $\gamma\ge\|c^-\|_\infty$. Uniqueness for the initial-boundary value problem therefore holds for any bounded $c$; it is only the location of extrema that needs the sign condition. Auditor's check: whenever a proof cites 'the maximum principle' for an equation with a reaction term, ask which of (a), (b), (c) is actually being used, and note that the sign convention depends on whether the operator is written $u_t-\Delta u+cu$ or $u_t-\Delta u-cu$.
Sign convention: L u = -a^{ij} u_{x_i x_j} + b^i u_{x_i} + c u, subsolution means u_t + Lu <= 0
c identically zero for the full maximum principle
c >= 0 for the version with the positive part
bounded c of any sign for the comparison (sign) principle only
title: Pitfall: The Parabolic Maximum Principle needs a sign condition on the zeroth-order coefficient

[Lemma lb spread of arXiv:2509.02432, 'A threshold for online balancing of sparse i.i.d. vectors'] Let $C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}} := 3$. Fix any choice of online algorithm $\sigma$, let $1\leq q\leq \frac{\log\log n}{2\log C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}}}$, and define
$$
k:=\sum_{u=1}^q \Big\lceil\frac{n}{(\log n)^{e^u}}\Big\rceil.
$$
Then with probability at least $1-\frac{q}{\log n}$ there are
$\ell\leq 0\leq r$ with $r-\ell\geq q$ such that 
$(A,\sigma)$ contains an $(\ell,r)$--spread
of size at least $\frac{n}{(\log n)^{C_{\text{\tiny{(lemma:lb spread of the paper)}}}^q}}$ at time $k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:barrier-hull of arXiv:2608.30700, 'Convex hulls and area minimizing currents in asymptotically locally hyperbolic manifolds'] Let $(M^{n+1}, g)$ be $C^2$ conformally compact asymptotically locally hyperbolic. For every closed $S\subseteq \partial M$, there exists a closed totally convex set $\mathcal{H}(S) \subseteq M$ such that
    \[
        \partial_\infty \mathcal{H}(S) = S.
    \]
    If $V$ is a stationary rectifiable $p$-varifold in $M$, for $1 \leq p \leq n$, and $\partial_\infty \spt V \subseteq S$, then
    \[
        \spt V \subseteq \mathcal{H}(S).
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$t\in\left[  0,T\right]  $, to the solution $x^{\alpha}\left(  t\right)  $ of
the stochastic equation in Stratonovich form (see Section 2.1)
\[\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\ds{dx^{\alpha}\left(  t\right)    =\overline{u}\left(  x^{\alpha}\left(
t\right)  \right)  dt+\sum_{k\in K}\xi_{k}\left(  x^{\alpha}\left(  t\right)

t\right)  \right)  dt}\\[10pt]
\ds{x^{\alpha}\left(  0\right)     =x_{0}}
\end{array}\right.\]
where
\begin{equation}
b_{\alpha}\left(  x\right)  =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\alpha}{c_{0}k_{T}\left(
x\right)  +\alpha}\left(\,  \sum_{k\in K}D\xi_{k}\left(  x\right)  \xi
_{k}\left(  x\right)  +C\left(  x\right)  c_{0}^{-1}\nabla\log k_{T}\left(
x\right)  \right)  
\end{equation}
and where the matrix $C\left(  x\right)  $ is given by 
\[C\left(  x\right)
=\sum_{k\in K}\xi_{k}\left(  x\right)  \otimes\xi_{k}\left(  x\right).\]

[Lemma Lem E eps 1 eps 2 bound v of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $z_1\neq z_2\in D$
and $r_0>0$ such that the disks
$\overline{\mathbb{D}(z_1,r_0)}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{D}(z_2,r_0)}$
are disjoint and contained in $D$.
There is a constant
$c=c(D,z_1,z_2,r_0)>0$ 
(depending on $D$, $z_1$, $z_2$ and $r_0$),
such that for every $v\in\mathbb{R}$,
and for every $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in (0,r_0]$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^v)
\leq
\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^0)
e^{-c v^2}.
$$

In particular, let $\mathcal{V}$ be a countable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ and 
$a:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$.
Then assuming that for every $b>0$,
$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}
\vert a(v)\vert e^{-b v^2}
<+\infty,
$$
we have that as $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$,
$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}
a(v)\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^v)
=
\varepsilon_1^{1/8}
\varepsilon_2^{1/8}
(\mathbf{C}_{\rm{SLE}4}^{\rm loop})^2
\,
\sigma_{\rm tw}^D(z_1,z_2)
\,
\Big(
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}a(v)
e^{-v^2 \mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)}
\Big)
(1+o(1)).
$$
title: Lemma Lem E eps 1 eps 2 bound v of arXiv:2604.15146

[Definition 17 (T-chain) of arXiv:2607.20838, 'Long-memory Markov chains with power-law intensities'] Let $a$ be a sampling distribution over the non-negative integers $\mathbb{Z}_+$
	and there exists a substochastic transition kernel $T$ such that
	$$
	K_a(x, B) := \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a(k) P^k(x, B) \geq T(x, B), \quad x \in \mathcal X, B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal X)
	$$
	where $T(\cdot, B)$ is a lower semicontinuous for any $B \in \mathcal B(\mathcal X)$.
	Then $T$ is called a continuous component of $K_a$.
	If $\{X_n\}$ is a Markov chain for which there exists a sampling distribution $a$ such that $K_a$ possesses a continuous component $T$ with $T(x, \mathcal X) > 0$ for all $x$, then $\{X_n\}$ is called a T-chain.
title: T-chain

Method: Weak concentration of nearest-unvisited walks under exponential edge noise structural calculation Result: A standard bounded-difference proof faces a real discontinuity. On the line with vertices A=0,B=1,D=3,C=-1-epsilon, start at A. For epsilon>0 small, the NUV order is A,B,D,C and length7+epsilon. With C=-1+epsilon, the order is A,C,B,D and length5-2epsilon. An arbitrarily small point perturbation changes the route length by nearly2. Thus NUV length lacks the elementary geometric Lipschitz property available for optimized MST or TSP costs. Check: Both examples use true Euclidean shortest-path distances and strict choices for positive epsilon. The discontinuity comes from a tie limit, not a violation of the triangle inequality. It is a deterministic methodological obstruction, not a random-exponential concentration counterexample. Obstruction: One needs probabilistic control of near-tie cascades or stabilization, rather than a uniform deterministic one-coordinate Lipschitz estimate. The no-macroscopic-edge hypothesis alone has not been shown sufficient here.

$$\mu=\sum_{x\in X}P(x)\delta_{f(x)}$$

Let (X_{n, k}, \mathcal{F}_{n, k})_{1 \le k \le k_n} be a martingale difference array with \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{n, k-1}] \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} \eta^2, where \eta^2 is an almost surely positive random variable. If for every \epsilon > 0, \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2 \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n, k}| > \epsilon\}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n, k-1}] \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} 0, then \sum_{k=1}^{k_n} X_{n, k}^2 \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} \eta^2 as well.

[Corollary 2 (Rectangular matrices) of arXiv:2606.25204, 'Exponential Rank Bounds for Random Matrices'] Fix \(b\in(0,1)\).  Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) random matrix with
independent real entries such that
\[
   \sup_{x\in\R}\PP\{A_{ij}=x\}\leq b<1
   \qquad (1\leq i\leq m,\ 1\leq j\leq n),
\]
and set \(d=\min(m,n)\).  Then for all \(1\leq k\leq d\),
\begin{equation}
   \PP\{\rank A\leq d-k\}\leq \exp(-c_{1.1}dk).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Rectangular matrices

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-SENS v2; no novelty claim]. Let a connected d-regular graph have simple ordinary SRW gap gamma=lambda_2(L)/d, with unit Euclidean Fiedler vector phi. Add absent edge uv with weight t. The gap derivative at t=0 is [(phi_u-phi_v)^2-gamma(phi_u^2+phi_v^2)]/d; the half-lazy derivative is half this expression. With b=e_u-e_v, C=e_u e_u^T+e_v e_v^T and U=[e_u,e_v], for g outside the spectrum of L/d the exact determinant is det(L+tbb^T-g(dI+tC))=det(L-gdI)det(I_2+tH(g)U^T(L-gdI)^(-1)U), H(g)=[[1-g,-1],[-1,1-g]]. Excluded poles require checks in the original pencil. This unadjusted edge variant changes stationary law and differs from Diaconis's stationary-preserving Metropolis variation.

body: In number theory, the Chevalley–Warning theorem implies that certain polynomial equations in sufficiently many variables over a finite field have solutions. It was proved by Ewald Warning and a slightly weaker form of the theorem, known as Chevalley's theorem, was proved by Chevalley. Chevalley's theorem implied Artin's and Dickson's conjecture that finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed fields.
title: Chevalley–Warning theorem

body: [Lemma superposition_intensity of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] If $\Phi = \sum_i \Phi_i$ is the superposition process, then $\mathcal{F}_t$ is a history of $\Phi$. Furthermore, the total stochastic intensity of $\Phi$ is simply $\lambda(t) = \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i(t)$. Moreover, $\lambda_i(t)$ is a stochastic intensity for process $i$ with respect to the enlarged history $\mathcal{F}_t$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.12853, 'Coupling Markov Chains \\with a Common Image Chain'] Let $k \ge 0$ and $(a_0,b_0), \dots, (a_k,b_k) \in \Delta$ with $c_i = f(a_i) = g(b_i)$ for $0 \le i \le k$. Suppose $\upalpha_Z(c_0) > 0$. Then for each $m \ge k$, 
    \begin{align}
    \begin{split}
    
    \mathbb{P}&(W^m_0 = (a_0,b_0), \dots, W^m_k = (a_k,b_k)) \\  
        &   
         = \mathbb{E}\bigl[
        \mathbb{P}(X^m_{\le k} = (a_0, \dots, a_k) \mid Z)\, \mathbb{P}(Y^m_{\le k} = (b_0, \dots, b_k) \mid Z)
        \bigr] 
        \\
        & = 
        \mathbb{E}\bigl[
        \mathbb{P}(X^m_{\le k} = (a_0, \dots, a_k) \mid Z_{\le m})\, \mathbb{P}(Y^m_{\le k} = (b_0, \dots, b_k) \mid Z_{\le m})
        \bigr]
        \\
        & = 
        \frac{\upalpha_X(a_0)\upalpha_Y(b_0)}{\upalpha_Z(c_0)}\biggl(\prod_{i= 1}^{k}R((a_{i-1},b_{i-1}),(a_i,b_i))\bigg)\,\varphi_{m-k}(a_k,b_k)\,.
    \end{split}
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 1 of arXiv:2604.12853

body: Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. Two facts to keep straight: this is the semigroup for the standard Gaussian, and other normalisations of the generator (for example Laplacian/2 minus x . grad/2) rescale time and change the constants in the associated Poincare and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. As t -> infinity, P_t f -> integral f dgamma, and the exponential rate of that convergence in L^2 is exactly 1, the spectral gap, which is the Gaussian Poincare inequality. [standard; e.g. Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Section 2.7]

[Proposition 61 of arXiv:2608.12947, 'Branch-stationary max-stable fields on rooted trees'] The field
\begin{equation}
  U_v^\psi
  =
  \psi\left(
    \frac{\eta_v^{-\alpha}}{S_\psi}
  \right),
  \qquad v\in\mathcal T,
  
\end{equation}
has standard uniform margins and finite-dimensional copulas
\((C_K^\psi)\). In particular, these copulas extend continuously to
\([0,1]^K\) and form a projectively consistent family of Archimax
copulas.
 
The following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item \(\eta\) is branch-stationary;
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\begin{equation}
  \ell_{aK}(x^a)=\ell_K(x),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad x\in[0,\infty)^K;
  
\end{equation}
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\[
  C_{aK}(u^a)=C_K(u),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad u\in(0,1]^K;
\]
\item for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\),
\[
  C_{aK}^\psi(u^a)=C_K^\psi(u),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad u\in(0,1]^K;
\]
\item \(U^\psi\) is branch-stationary.
\end{enumerate}
 
If \(Z\) satisfies (equation 17 of the paper) and
\(\Theta=\Theta^{[\varnothing]}\), then
\begin{equation}
  \ell_K(x)
  =
  \E*{
    \max_{v\in K}x_v\Theta_v^\alpha
  },
  \qquad x\in[0,\infty)^K.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 61 of arXiv:2608.12947

DRAFT proof-audit material, independent referee check pending. For every integer d>=1 and epsilon>0 there exists a stationary finite-dependent {0,1} field on Z^d with probability of good at each vertex at least 1-epsilon and all nearest-neighbour good components finite. Construct it from iid Bernoulli(q) seeds. L(v) is a nearest seed in the l-infinity ball B_R(v), with lexicographic tie-breaking, or bottom if the ball is empty. A vertex is good exactly when its non-bottom label agrees with every nearest neighbour's label. Its indicator uses seeds in B_(R+1)(v), so index sets at l-infinity distance greater than 2(R+1) are independent. Each good component has one seed label s and lies in B_R(s). For a finite dimension-dependent constant K_d, P(v bad)<=exp(-q(2R-1)^d) +K_d q^(1/d); choosing q small then R large gives the claimed density. The dependence range varies with epsilon. This is correlated site percolation and does not refute iid critical bond percolation or a fixed-range domination theorem.
d is an integer>=1
iid seeds with 0<q<1
R is an integer>=1
Good connectivity is nearest-neighbour
title: High density with a growing dependence range need not percolate

body:
[Defn 13 of arXiv:2506.19123, 'The longest increasing subsequence of Brownian separable permutons'] Let $n \geq 0, k \geq 1$ be integers, let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k>0$ and $\alpha_0=\sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i$. 
    \begin{itemize}
    \item 
    The Dirichlet distribution $\Dir \left( \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$ is the law on $k$-tuples of non-negative real numbers $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ which sum up to $1$ given by the probability density function
     \[\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\Gamma(\alpha_1)\cdots \Gamma(\alpha_k)} \prod_{i=1}^k x_i^{\alpha_i - 1}.\]

    
    \item The Dirichlet-multinomial distribution $\DirM \left( n; \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$ is the law on $k$-tuples of non-negative integers $(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ which sum up to $n$ given by the probability mass function
        \[ \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0) \Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(n+\alpha_0)} \prod_{i=1}^k \frac{\Gamma(n_i+\alpha_i)}{\Gamma(\alpha_i) \Gamma(n_i+1)}. \]
    In other words, a $\DirM \left( n; \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$-distributed random variable $\mathbf{N}=\left( N_1, \dots, N_k \right)$ can be obtained as follows: let $\mathbf{D}=(D_1, \dots, D_k)$ follow the Dirichlet distribution $\Dir \left( \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k \right)$; then, conditionally on $\mathbf{D}$, sample the vector $\mathbf{N}$ as a multinomial vector with parameters $(n;\mathbf{D})$.
    \end{itemize}

[Df equiv_collar of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] We say that two $k$-collars
  \[
  \delta\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \delta'\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \]
  based at the same discrete $(k-1)$-sphere $S$ are \emph{equivalent} if there exists a continuous map
  \[
  H\colon\bigl(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\bigr)\times[0,1]\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|
  \]
  such that
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $H(\cdot,0)=\delta$ and $H(\cdot,1)=\delta'$, that is, $H$ is a homotopy between $\delta$ and $\delta'$;
    \item the map $H(\cdot,t)\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times I_\varepsilon\to|\mathcal{K}_k^d|$ is a $k$-collar based at $S$ for every $t\in[0,1]$~(in particular, each $H(\cdot,t)$ is injective).
  \end{itemize}

  We denote by $[\delta]$ the equivalence class of a $k$-collar $\delta$.
  For an equivalence class $\Delta=[\delta]$, we set $S_\Delta:=S_\delta$ and refer to it as the \emph{base sphere} of $\Delta$.
  (See Figure~(fig:collars of the paper).)
title: Equivalence class of $k$-collars

body:
[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2511.09930, 'Martingale dimensions for a class of metric measure spaces'] Let $m\le n$. For each $f\in l(V_m)$ there exists a unique $h\in l(V_n)$ such that $h|_{V_m}=f$ and
\[
\cE^{(n)}(h,h)=\inf\{\cE^{(n)}(g,g)\mid g\in l(V_n)\text{ and }g|_{V_m}=f\}.
\]
Moreover, for any $w\in\tilde W_m$ and $x\in V_n\cap \tilde K_w$,
\[
\min_{\psi_w(V_0)}f\le h(x)\le \max_{\psi_w(V_0)}f.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 19 of arXiv:2511.09930

body:
Let A be a complex m by n matrix and sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_n >= 0 the square roots of the eigenvalues of A*A, so that sigma_k = 0 for k > rank A. For 1 <= k <= n, sigma_k = max over k-dimensional subspaces S of C^n of min over nonzero x in S of ||Ax|| / ||x||, and sigma_k = min over (n - k + 1)-dimensional subspaces T of max over nonzero x in T of ||Ax|| / ||x||. The maximum is attained at S = span(v_1, ..., v_k) and the minimum at T = span(v_k, ..., v_n), where v_1, ..., v_n is an orthonormal eigenbasis of A*A with eigenvalues in decreasing order.

body:
[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2609.03403, 'Hyperpositive functions, sector bounded functions and a trace formula'] Let $F\in \mathcal{ HP}_{T,t}$. Then for every $z\in\mathbb C_r$, the matrix-valued function $F(z)$
      belongs to the closed matrix ball with center $T^{-1}$, left radius $(T^{-1}+tT)^{1/2}$ and right
      radius $T^{-1/2}$. When $m=1$ and using the notation $T=\beta$ in that case (to be consistent with our
      previous works \cite{MR4255499,MR4756530}), $F(z)$ belongs to the closed disk with center
      \[
        C(\beta)=\frac{1}{\beta}
      \]
      and radius
      \[
R(\beta)=\sqrt{t+\frac{1}{\beta^2}}.
\]
In that case it holds that
\[
(C(\beta))^2-(R(\beta))^2=-t.
  \]

If $C$ is not hyperelliptic, only the first case occurs.

body:
[Prop of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'] The Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t)$ satisfy the following properties:

\begin{enumerate}[left=0pt]
\item They are monic and have the form
$$P_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n;t) = x_1^{\lambda_1}x_2^{\lambda_2}\cdots x_n^{\lambda_n} + \text{(lower-order monomials in the lexicographic order)};$$

\item When $\lambda\in\Sig_n^+$ ranges over all nonnegative integer signatures of length $n$, the Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\cdots,x_n;t)$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[t]$-basis of $\Lambda_n[t]$, where $\Lambda_n[t]:=\mathbb{Z}[t][x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{S_n}$ is the ring of symmetric polynomials in $n$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[t]$;

\item When $\lambda\in\Sig_n$ ranges over all integer signatures of length $n$, the Hall-Littlewood polynomials $P_\lambda(x_1,\cdots,x_n;t)$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[t]$ basis of $\mathbb{Z}[t][x_1^{\pm 1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm 1}]^{S_n}$, the ring of symmetric Laurent polynomials in $n$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[t]$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered prop of arXiv:2412.05999, 'Non-Archimedean GUE corners and Hecke modules'

body:
[Proposition 5 (Generalized predictable Euler-Maruyama ``SDEs'' universally approximate SDEs in $\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$) of arXiv:2607.14361, 'NeuralChaos: Optimal Adapted Approximation of Square Integrable Predictable Processes'] For measurable functions
\[
b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^{d_X}\to \mathbb R^{d_X},
\qquad
\Sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^{d_X}\to \mathbb R^{d_X\times D},
\]
that are Lipschitz and of linear growth, and $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal{F}_0;\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$, we consider the process\footnote{Since the solution process has $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.\ continuous paths and is adapted, it is predictable.} $X_{\cdot} \in \mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb R^{d_X})$
solving the induced (Markovian) SDE
$$
X_t = \xi +\int_0^t\, b(s,X_s)\,ds + \int_0^t\, \Sigma(s,X_s)\,\ud W_s, \qquad \mbox{ for } t \in [0,T].
$$
For every approximation error $\varepsilon>0$, there exists some $\hat{X}_{\cdot}\in \mathfrak{B}$ satisfying
$
    \big\|
        \hat{X}-X
    \big\|_{\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb R^{d_X})}
    <
    \varepsilon
$.
title: Generalized predictable Euler-Maruyama ``SDEs'' universally approximate SDEs in $\mathcal{H}_T^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_X})$

body: [Lemma lem:reduction_overall of arXiv:2609.01745, 'The Directional Localization Game on Graphs'] Let $G$ be the incidence graph of a finite projective plane of order $q$, and consider the partial-feedback game on $G$.  Suppose that at the end of a probing phase, all contaminated vertices are contained within $N(x) \cup N(y)$ for some non-adjacent $x \in \mathcal{P}$ and $y \in \mathcal{L}$, and let $i$ denote the number of contaminated line vertices.  If $i > 2$, then the cops can either win or ensure that at the end of some subsequent probing phase, the contamination will be contained in $N(u) \cup N(v)$ for some non-adjacent point vertex $u$ and line vertex $v$, and one partite set will contain at most $i-1$ contaminated vertices.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] A map $f\colon X\to Y$ is called a \emph{$G$-equivariant fibration} if it is a $G$-equivariant level fibration and for all closed subgroups $H\subset G$ and $H$-representations $V,W$, the naturality square
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}
            X(V)\arrow[r,"\tilde\sigma"]\arrow[d,"f(V)"'] & \Omega^WX(V\oplus W)\arrow[d,"\Omega^Wf(V\oplus W)"]\\
            Y(V)\arrow[r,"\tilde\sigma"'] & \Omega^WY(V\oplus W)
        \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    for the adjunct structure maps is a homotopy pullback in $\textbf{\textup{$\bm H$-Top}}_*$.

    An orthogonal $G$-spectrum $X$ is called a \emph{$G$-$\Omega$-spectrum} if the unique map $X\to 0$ is a $G$-equivariant fibration, i.e.\ the adjunct structure map $X(V)\to \Omega^WX(V\oplus W)$ is an $H$-equivariant weak equivalence for each closed subgroup $H\subset G$ and all $H$-representations $V,W$.

[Corollary cor:universal-principal-skeleton of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R^{[0]}(h,k)=\{M_{h,k}\},
 \qquad
 \mathcal R^{[1]}(h,k)
 =\{M_{h,k}-M_{h-r,k}:2\leq r\leq h\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, exactly $h$ attainable cardinalities have minimum active
rank at most one.  They are exactly the values whose realization-frequency
quasipolynomial has degree greater than $k-2$: the maximum has degree $k$,
the other $h-1$ values have degree $k-1$, and every remaining attainable
cardinality has degree at most $k-2$.

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a stably triangulated category with coproducts and $E \in \mathcal{T}$. An object $X$ is $E$-acyclic if $E \otimes X = 0$. An object $Y$ is $E$-local if $\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y) = 0$ for all $E$-acyclic $X$. A Bousfield localization with respect to $E$ is an exact functor $L_E: \mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}$ equipped with a natural transformation $\eta: \operatorname{id} \to L_E$ such that for every $X$, $L_E X$ is $E$-local and the fiber of $\eta_X$ is $E$-acyclic.
\mathcal{T} is a tensor-triangulated category with coproducts
E \in \mathcal{T} is a fixed object
title: Bousfield Localization Functor in Triangulated Categories

body: In mathematics, the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma is a result named after William B. Johnson and Joram Lindenstrauss concerning low-distortion embeddings of points from high-dimensional into low-dimensional Euclidean space. The lemma states that a set of points in a high-dimensional space can be embedded into a space of much lower dimension in such a way that distances between the points are nearly preserved. In the classical proof of the lemma, the embedding is a random orthogonal projection.
title: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma

body:
[Proposition prop:root-sweep-dictionary of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$ and $k\geq2$.  One has the exact difference identity
\begin{equation}
 E_{h,k}-E_{h,k}=h\mathsf R_{k-1}\cap\mathsf A_{k-1}.
\end{equation}
For an ordered real tuple $a=(a_1<\cdots<a_k)$, write
\({\bf1}=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^k\) and let
$a^\circ=a-k^{-1}(\sum_i a_i){\bf1}$ be its centered representative.  Let
$F_h(a)$ be the face of $\mathfrak Z_{h,k}$ exposed by $a^\circ$.  The
following data determine one another:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item the total preorder on $E_{h,k}$ induced by $u\mapsto u\cdot a$
      (equivalently, its ordered weak partition into level sets);
\item the complete ordered $h$-addition table of $a$, including ties;
\item the face $F_h(a)$.
\end{enumerate}
The dimension of $F_h(a)$ is the active relation rank $r_h(a)$.  In the
ambient space ${\bf1}^{\perp}$, its normal cone has dimension
$k-1-r_h(a)$, and the relative interior of that cone consists precisely of
the centered weights inducing the same complete table.  Moreover, the same
face determines every ordered addition table in degrees $1\leq j\leq h$.

Fix any field $K$.  If $a\in\mathbb Z^k$, put
$A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and define
\[
 \varphi_a:K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\longrightarrow K[u,t,t^{-1}],
 \qquad x_i\longmapsto u t^{a_i},
 \qquad I_a=\ker\varphi_a,
\]
where $\deg u=1$ and $\deg t=0$.  Then the number of blocks in the face
label is the Hilbert value
\begin{equation}
 |hA|=\dim_K\bigl(K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/I_a\bigr)_h.
\end{equation}
Thus the face records the equality rank and Hilbert/block label, while its
normal cone encodes the normalized shape, realization frequency, and integer
compression developed below.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2607.06428, 'Impact of spinning on the early-warning signs in non-Markovian stochastic systems'] A stochastic process $(\mathbf{x}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is called strictly stationary or strongly stationary if for all $k\ge0$ and all sequences $(t_1,\dots, t_m)\in\R^m_+$ we have
    $$(\mathbf{x}_{t_1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t_m})\overset{d}{=}(\mathbf{x}_{t_1+k},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t_m+k}).$$
   The process $(\mathbf{x}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is called second order stationary or weakly stationary, if we have for all $t\in\R$ $\E[|\mathbf{x}_t|]<\infty,~\E[|\mathbf{x}_t|^2]<\infty$ and for all $s,t,\tau\ge0$
    $$V_t(\tau)=V_s(\tau).$$
    As the autocovariance only depends on $\tau$, we drop the subscript and write $V(\tau)$ whenever we consider a stationary process.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2607.06428

Pourkamali-Macris Proposition3, independent-spectra version of the source coupling. Fix positive integers N<=M and lambda>0. Let sigma,sigma_tilde in[0,infinity)^N be independent random singular-value vectors, each with finite second moment. Let U in O(N),V in O(M) be independent normalized Haar matrices, independent of both vectors. Define S=U*diag_{N by M}(sigma)*V^T and S_tilde=U*diag_{N by M}(sigma_tilde)*V^T, so the pair shares its singular vectors. Let P_1,P_2 be the respective marginal signal priors. For j=1,2, take Y_j=sqrt(lambda)*S_j+G_j with iid N(0,1/N) Gaussian entries independent of the signal. Define Z_j(y)=E_{X~P_j} exp(N*sqrt(lambda)*Tr(X^T*y)-(N*lambda/2)*||X||_F^2), where the inner X is an independent prior draw, and F_j(lambda)=-(N*M)^(-1)*E log Z_j(Y_j) with expectation under the matching planted model. Then |F_1(lambda)-F_2(lambda)| <= (lambda/(2*N))*(sqrt(E||sigma||_2^2)+sqrt(E||sigma_tilde||_2^2))*sqrt(E||sigma-sigma_tilde||_2^2). The last expectation is over the independent spectral pair specified above, with its chosen coordinate ordering. The result is finite-dimensional; it does not by itself justify a limiting spectral-atom extension or convergence in expectation from mere weak convergence.

body:
Consider testing a simple null hypothesis H0: X has density f0 against a simple alternative H1: X has density f1 (with respect to a common dominating measure), at a fixed significance level alpha in (0,1). Define a test with rejection rule: reject H0 when f1(x) > k f0(x); accept H0 when f1(x) < k f0(x); and reject with some probability gamma in [0,1] when f1(x) = k f0(x); where the constant k >= 0 and the randomization probability gamma are chosen so that the test has size exactly alpha, i.e. Pr(reject H0 | H0) = alpha. Then this likelihood-ratio test is most powerful at level alpha: for every other test phi with size at most alpha, the power of phi under H1 is no greater than the power of the likelihood-ratio test.
H0 and H1 are simple hypotheses with densities f0, f1 with respect to a common dominating measure
significance level alpha lies strictly between 0 and 1

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $f:X \longrightarrow Y$ be an almost covering map, where $X$ is a closed topological manifold and $Y$ is a closed topological pseudomanifold. Suppose the fibered set $R = \bigsqcup_{\beta} T_{\beta} \subset Y$ is equipped with a suitable decomposition. Assume that $R$ is a closed topologically stratified space of codimension greater than or equal to $2$. Let $R = \bigsqcup_{\alpha} S_{\alpha}$, $T_{\beta} = \bigsqcup_{\gamma} V^{\beta}_{\gamma}\ \text{for each } \beta$, and 
	$Y = \bigsqcup_{\eta} W_{\eta}$
	be intrinsic stratifications. Furthermore, assume that the inclusion $R \xhookrightarrow[]{\phantom{.} i \phantom{.} } Y$ is locally flat. Then the decomposition
	\begin{align}
	Y = \bigl( W_{\eta_{\text{top}}} \setminus (R \cap W_{\eta_{\text{top}}}) \bigr) \;\bigsqcup_{\alpha,\eta,\beta,\gamma}\; \bigl( W_{\eta} \cap V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \cap S_{\alpha}\bigr)
	\end{align}
	is a refined stratification on $Y$, where $W_{\eta_{\text{top}}}$ denotes the top stratum of $Y$.
title: Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.30875

[Lemma lemlocalex of arXiv:2606.29036, 'The limit law of the largest interpoint distance in a $d$-dimensional ellipsoid'] Let $x=x(e,\delta,w)$ and $y=x(-g,\delta',w')$, where
$e,g\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$ and $\langle e,g\rangle=\cos\theta$.
Then, as $\delta,\delta',\theta,\|w\|,\|w'\|\to 0$, we have
\[
 2-\|x-y\| = \frac{\delta+\delta'}{2} + \frac{\theta^2}{4}
- \frac{1}{4} \|A(w-w')\|^2 + r(\delta,\delta',\theta,w,w'),
\]
where
\[
r(\delta,\delta',\theta,w,w') = o\!\left(\delta+\delta'+\theta^2+\|w\|^2+\|w'\|^2
\right).
\]
The remainder is uniform in $e,g\in \mathbb{S}^{k-1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let H and K be Hilbert spaces. A bounded operator T: H -> K is Hilbert-Schmidt if sum_{i in I} ||T e_i||^2 < infinity for some orthonormal basis (e_i)_{i in I} of H. The sum is then the same for every orthonormal basis of H, and ||T||_2 = (sum_i ||T e_i||^2)^{1/2} is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Equivalently, T is compact and sum_n s_n(T)^2 < infinity, with ||T||_2^2 = sum_n s_n(T)^2. Properties: ||T|| <= ||T||_2; ||T*||_2 = ||T||_2; every Hilbert-Schmidt operator is compact (it is the ||.||_2-limit, hence operator-norm limit, of finite-rank operators); the Hilbert-Schmidt operators S_2(H,K) form a Hilbert space under <A,B>_2 = sum_i <A e_i, B e_i> = tr(B*A), independent of the basis; and they form an ideal: ||A T B||_2 <= ||A|| ||T||_2 ||B|| for bounded A, B. Basis independence follows from sum_i ||T e_i||^2 = sum_i sum_j |<T e_i, f_j>|^2 = sum_j ||T* f_j||^2 for any orthonormal basis (f_j) of K.
H and K are Hilbert spaces
T: H -> K is a bounded linear operator

[Proposition classification_halfplane of arXiv:2603.05491, '\textbf{Local limits of uniform triangulations with boundaries in high genus}'] \begin{enumerate}
\item  For any $0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c$, there exists a unique random triangulation of the half-plane\footnote{Here $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ is the analogue of $H_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha \le \frac{2}{3}$, and $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}$ is the analogue of $H_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha \ge \frac{2}{3}$.} $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ characterized by the probabilities
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset \widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}) = \big(32h+4\big)^{|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|}\lambda^{v_{\mathrm{in}}}.
\]
In particular, we have $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda_c} = \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_c}$.
\item  Let $H$ be a strongly Markovian random triangulation of the half-plane. Then $H$ is either of the form $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}$ for some $0 < \lambda \le \lambda_c$ or $\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}$ for some $0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c$.

\item  Let $H$ be a weakly Markovian random triangulation of the half-plane. Then $H$ is a mixture of $\{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda}\}_{0 < \lambda \le \lambda_c} \cup \{\widetilde{\mathbb{H}}_{\lambda}\}_{0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_c}$.

\end{enumerate}

body: [Defi Closed walk of arXiv:2607.28817, 'Limiting spectral distribution for the adjacency matrix of the Watts--Strogatz random grap'] For any rooted graph $(G,o)$ and any $k\ge1$, a closed walk of length $k$ is a sequence of vertices $v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}$ such that $v_1=v_{k+1}$ and, for every $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$, the edge $\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}$ is an edge of $G$. If, moreover, $v_1=o$, then the walk is called a closed rooted walk. The number of closed rooted walks of length $k$ in $(G,o)$ is denoted by $c_k(G,o)$.

[Lemma slice-over-fibrant of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $\textbf{\textup{C}}$ be a model category with collection of weak equivalences ${\mathcal{W}}$, and let $Y\in\textbf{\textup{C}}$ fibrant. If $\textbf{\textup{C}}$ is right proper, the claim holds without the fibrancy assumption on $Y$.

For the second claim, it will then suffice that for right proper $\textbf{\textup{C}}$ and any weak equivalence $Y\to Y'$ to a fibrant $Y'$, the induced map $\textbf{\textup{C}}_{/Y}\to\textbf{\textup{C}}_{/Y'}$ becomes an equivalence after localization, which is in turn a direct consequence of [rezk-proper]*{Proposition~2.5}.
