{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4bd7b04b5b7a94864afcf30d797a4508ad77fe7cff0f25ee6d83ed613ba54a6c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4b/4bd7b04b5b7a94864afcf30d797a4508ad77fe7cff0f25ee6d83ed613ba54a6c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f6b4890dd126bcfeabf4a399dd0cc6cf569fd2631c0bd9d1daa25d0484fe1d01","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion-019","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_019.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C053: a uniform tanh double expansion, through the first logarithmic width term

20 October 2026. Target 3. Proof draft, unaudited. No novelty asserted.
This proves a first finite-width correction and arbitrary finite small-t
Taylor order. It does NOT prove the all-orders inverse-width expansion
available for the exactly multiplicative ReLU chain in C019.

## Statement

Use the exact unshaped critical tanh chain
K_(j+1)=n^(-1)sum_i tanh(sqrt(K_j)Z_(j,i))^2, K_0>0 fixed,
with independent Gaussian rows/layers, zero bias and weight variance 1/n.
Fix an integer k>=1 and c<infinity. For integers 1<=L<=cn put t=L/n,
Y=2L K_L, and, using ONE Brownian path B,

    A_t=integral_0^1 exp(tr+sqrt(2t)B_r)dr,
    H_t=exp(t+sqrt(2t)B_1),
    m_j(t)=E A_t^(-j),
    J_j(t)=E[H_t A_t^(-j-1)],             m_0=1.

There exist finite C=C(k,K_0,c) and n_0 such that, for every n>=n_0,
uniformly over all those L,

    |E Y^j - m_j(t) -(5j/12)J_j(t)log(L)/L| <= C/L,
                                                 1<=j<=k.       (1)

In particular the logarithm is log L, not a log n term asserted uniformly
down to L=1. At fixed t>0 this is a log n/n correction with O_t(1/n)
remainder. The unspecified finite constant in (1) is uniform; no numerical
closed form for it has been optimized or supplied here.

Let P_k(x_1,...,x_k)=sum_(pi in Pi_k) (|pi|-1)!(-1)^(|pi|-1)
product_(D in pi) x_|D| be the moment-cumulant polynomial. Define

    F_k(t)=P_k(m_1(t),...,m_k(t)),
    G_k(t)=sum_(j=1)^k j J_j(t) (partial_j P_k)(m_1(t),...,m_k(t)).

Then

    |kappa_k(Y)-F_k(t)-(5/12)G_k(t)log(L)/L| <= C'/L.        (2)

For an independent final Gaussian readout R=sqrt(2L)z_out, its conditional
variance is Y and
kappa_(2k)(R)=[(2k)!/(2^k k!)]kappa_k(Y); multiply (2) by this factor.
Odd cumulants vanish by conditional Gaussian symmetry.

For every integer M>=0 these functions have computable Taylor coefficients
f_(k,r),g_(k,r) at zero, with an explicit finite Gaussian-integral bound
C_(k,M,c) described below, such that

 |kappa_k(Y)-sum_(r=0)^M f_(k,r)t^r
              -(5/12)(log L/L)sum_(r=0)^M g_(k,r)t^r|
 <= C_(k,M,c)t^(M+1)(1+log L/L)+C'/L.                    (3)

First coefficients are

    m_j(t)=1+j(j-2)t/3+O(t^2),
    J_j(t)=1+(j-1)(j-2)t/3+O(t^2).

Consequently F_2(t)=2t/3+O(t^2), G_2(t)=2t/3+O(t^2).
Thus Var(Y)=2t/3+(5/18)t log(L)/L
+O_(K0,c)(t^2(1+log L/L)+1/L). This is an absolute uniform
remainder, not a relative error in a regime where 1/L dominates t.

## 1. Rescaling keeps the entrance uniform in L/n

Let epsilon=1/L and W_j=1/(L K_j). The diffusion reference, on the unit
time interval, is

    dW=(2tW+2)ds+sqrt(2t)W dB_s,        W(0)=0,
    A^(t)=(2tw+2)D+tw^2 D^2.

Its terminal value is 2 A_t in law, jointly with its affine initial-state
slope H_t. Write P_s^(t) for its semigroup, f(w)=(2/w)^j and
g_s(w)=P_(1-s)^(t) f(w). The true starting state is W_0=1/(LK_0).
In particular P_1^(t)f(0)=m_j(t) and

    D_j(t):=(P_1^(t)f)'(0)=-(j/2)J_j(t).                  (4)

The joint identity in (4) uses time reversal of the Brownian increments
and preserves the endpoint B_1: H and A are not made independent.

## 2. Backward tests and the terminal singularity

The reference transition is affine, W_s(w)=H_s w+I_s, with
H_s=exp(ts+sqrt(2t)B_s), I_s=2int_0^s exp(t(s-r)+sqrt(2t)(B_s-B_r))dr.
For M_B=sup_(0<=r<=1)|B_r|, these give, uniformly 0<=t<=c,
H_s and its inverse <=exp(c+sqrt(2c)M_B), and
I_s>=2s exp(-c-2sqrt(2c)M_B). Differentiation in w and Gaussian
integrability of exp(a M_B) therefore give, for each fixed derivative r,

 |g_s^(r)(w)|<=C_r(1+w)^(-j-r),             s<=1/2,
 |g_s^(r)(w)|<=C_r w^(-j-r),               s>=1/2.         (5)

All needed time derivatives on s<=1/2 satisfy analogous bounds by applying
A^(t). In particular |g_s'(w)-D_j(t)|<=C(s+w) there. Constants depend
only on j,r,c. The Gaussian supremum bounds below make them finite
and computable; no differentiation at a singular initial value is used.

C027, now reviewer PASS, implies for every fixed p,

    E W_j^(-p)=L^p E K_j^p<=C_p[L/(j+1)]^p,              (6)

including j=0 with a K_0-dependent constant. Thus every derivative bound
in (5), even at the terminal test s=1, is integrable along the second
half of the exact chain, uniformly in L,n. This is the terminal-tail
control missing from a bare application of weak convergence.

## 3. The next one-step operator

Conditionally on K_j=q, W_j=w, put S=n^(-1)sum_i Y_q(Z_i),
Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q. Then W'=w/S, q=epsilon/w, n^(-1)=t epsilon.
The scalar expansions needed are

 E Y_q=1-2q+(17/3)q^2+O(q^3),
 Var(Y_q)=2-16q+O(q^2),  kappa_3(Y_q)=8+O(q).

Writing delta=S-1, the retained terms, in powers of (q,h), h=1/n, are

 E delta=-2q+(17/3)q^2,
 E delta^2=2h+4q^2-16qh,
 E delta^3=-12qh+8h^2,
 E delta^4=12h^2.

Each omitted term is bounded by C(q^3+q^2 h+q h^2+h^(5/2)) on a fixed
small interval q<=eta. This follows from the centered iid sample moment
identities and their fifth/sixth moment bounds. Taylor expansion of
(S^-1-1)^r, for 1<=r<=4, yields respectively

 2q+2h-(5/3)q^2-4qh+4h^2;
 2h+4q^2+8qh+20h^2;
 12qh+28h^2;
 12h^2.

C044 removes the inverse-sample tails at exponentially small cost,
uniformly in q<=max(1,K_0), for n above a fixed threshold depending
on the derivative/moment orders. The positive sample tails are bounded
using Y_q<=Z^2. Thus the expansion applies to these unbounded tests.

For Q_n the exact one-step kernel this identifies

 Q_n g = g+epsilon A^(t)g+epsilon^2 B^(t)g+remainder,

 B^(t)g=(4t^2w-4t-5/(3w))g'
       +(10t^2w^2+4tw+2)g''
       +((14/3)t^2w^3+2tw^2)g'''+(t^2w^4/2)g''''.

Subtract the reference semigroup expansion. The defect operator is

 C^(t)=B^(t)-(A^(t))^2/2
      =(2t^2w-6t-5/(3w))D
        +(3t^2w^2-2tw)D^2+(2/3)t^2w^3 D^3.             (7)

Only the 1/w coefficient is singular at the entrance.

## 4. Summed remainder bound (the uniformity step)

For q<=eta and s<=1/2, (5) and the previous moment estimates bound the
one-step remainder after subtracting epsilon^2 C^(t) by

 C[epsilon^3(w^-2+w^-1+1)+epsilon^(5/2)+exp(-a n)].      (8)

For example the worst q^3 term is w q^3=epsilon^3/w^2;
h^(5/2)w^r |g^(r)|<=C epsilon^(5/2), since t<=c. The fifth Taylor
remainder has the same bound. The third semigroup remainder is bounded
by C epsilon^3 through A^3 g. For s>=1/2 the counterpart of (8) is
bounded by a finite sum of these quantities multiplied by powers of
w^-1, which are integrable uniformly by (6).

In the first half, summing the worst term uses

 epsilon^3 sum E W_j^-2 =epsilon sum E K_j^2<=C epsilon,
 epsilon^3 sum E W_j^-1 =epsilon^2 sum E K_j<=C epsilon.

Both follow from C027; the remaining sums in (8) are O(epsilon).
In the second half, (6) bounds the sum by O(epsilon^(3/2)+epsilon^2).
Exponential tails sum to O(1/L), since L<=cn; constants may depend on c.

On q>eta do not use the small-q series. In the first half, w<=epsilon/eta
and C044 gives E W'<=C w, so the bounded Lipschitz test changes by
O(epsilon); the reference step and epsilon^2 Cg have the same bound.
The expected number of these visits is bounded by
eta^-2 sum E K_j^2<=C. In the second half, (5)-(6), with two additional
positive K moments, bound each such visit's expected defect by
O(epsilon^2): use 1_(q>eta)<= (epsilon/(eta w))^p, p sufficiently large.
Its sum is O(epsilon). This establishes, with no unstated localization,

 sum_(j=0)^(L-1) E |Q_n g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)
             -P_epsilon^(t)g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)
             -epsilon^2 C^(t)g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)| <= C/L.    (9)

The nonsingular terms of (7), summed with epsilon^2, are also O(1/L),
using (5) before the midpoint and (6) after it.

## 5. Entrance occupation gives the logarithm

C046 gives, uniformly L<=cn,

    sum_(j=0)^(L-1) E K_j=(1/2)log L+O_(K0,c)(1).         (10)

Indeed its error divided by j sums as j^-3/2+(nj)^-1/2, whose sum is
bounded by C(1+sqrt(L/n)). For the weighted version, before the midpoint
use (5), E K_j<=C/(j+1), and the EXACT identity K_j W_j=1/L:

 sum E[K_j |g_((j+1)/L)'(W_j)-D_j(t)|] <= C.

After the midpoint |g'|<=C W^-j-1, so (6) bounds each summand by C/L.
(The exponent j in this sentence denotes the fixed test moment order,
not the summation index.) Thus

 sum E[K_i g_((i+1)/L)'(W_i)]
       =(D_j(t)/2)log L+O(1).                            (11)

The singular part of (7) contributes -(5/(3L)) times (11). By (4) this
is +(5j/12)J_j(t)log L/L+O(1/L). Exact backward-semigroup telescoping,
(9), and |P_1f(W_0)-P_1f(0)|<=C/(LK_0) prove (1).
No independent products of conditional bounds have been used.

## 6. Cumulants and small-t remainders

Apply the finite polynomial P_k to the k moment estimates (1). Its
linear correction is exactly G_k. Moments and coefficients are bounded
for t<=c by Brownian supremum exponential moments. Quadratic correction
terms are O((log L/L)^2)=O(1/L), because sup_(L>=1)(log L)^2/L<infinity.
This proves (2), including k=1.

For explicit small-t remainder construction put z=sqrt(t),
a(z)=int_0^1 exp(z^2r+sqrt(2)zB_r)dr and h(z)=exp(z^2+sqrt(2)zB_1).
The expectations of a(z)^(-j) and h(z)a(z)^(-j-1) are even smooth
functions of real z, by B -> -B. Their derivatives can be passed under
the expectation: with M_B=sup|B|, they are bounded by a polynomial in
M_B times exp(C sqrt(c)M_B+C c).

More explicitly let Z_c=2(2sqrt(c)+sqrt(2)M_B+1), D_0(j)=1 and

 D_N(j)=sum_(r=1)^N ((j)_r/r!) binom(N-1,r-1), N>=1.

Normalized derivatives of a satisfy |a^(r)|/r!<=a Z_c^r. The reciprocal
power composition formula therefore gives

 |(a^-j)^(N)|/N! <= D_N(j) Z_c^N exp(j sqrt(2c)M_B),
 |(h a^-j-1)^(N)|/N!
   <= [sum_(r=0)^N D_r(j+1)] Z_c^N exp(c+(j+2)sqrt(2c)M_B).

These expectations are explicit finite Gaussian-integral constants.
For a fully numerical bound use P(M_B>x)<=min(1,4exp(-x^2/2)) and
E F(M_B)=F(0)+int_0^infinity F'(x)P(M_B>x)dx for increasing F.
Taylor at z=0 through degree 2M+1, with N=2M+2, gives the stated
O(t^(M+1)) remainders. The coefficients are finite Gaussian polynomial
moments, computable by Wick pairings and integrals of min(r,s), hence
rational. Finite polynomial substitution gives (3) with an explicit
finite sum of these bounds and derivatives of P_k on the bounded
moment box.

Finally E int B=0, E(int B)^2=1/3, and E[B_1 int B]=1/2 give the first
coefficients displayed in the statement. In particular the small-t
limiting variance is 2t/3. This is a check on the model normalization;
it is NOT a transfer to a non-Gaussian weight universality class.

## Limits and remaining scope

For the bounded depths L<=4, enlarge the constant directly using
K_L<=1, the finite diffusion inverse moments, and bounded J_j on [0,c];
the midpoint arguments above are needed only for L>=5.
All finite-chain estimates above are simultaneous for n>=n0 and
1<=L<=cn; no L->infinity limit is hidden in the O(1/L) statement.
At fixed t, log L/L=log n/(nt)+log t/(nt). The last term belongs to
the unknown order-1/n coefficient. Determining that coefficient, or
arbitrary powers of 1/n and their boundary logarithms, requires a
finer entrance matching calculation and is NOT proved here.

## Exact coefficient artifact and source discrepancy

scripts/tanh_series_exact.py computes the Taylor coefficients by exact
rational integration over ordered Gaussian times. For j>=0,

 E A_t^j = j! int_(0<=r1<=...<=rj<=1)
                 exp(2t sum_i (j-i+1)r_i) dr,
 E[H_t A_t^j] = exp(2t) j! int_ordered
                 exp(2t sum_i (j-i+2)r_i) dr.

Expanding (A-1)^r by binomial inversion, for 0<=r<=2M, gives all
Taylor coefficients through t^M of the required inverse moments.
The script is finite exact Fraction arithmetic; it checks coefficients,
not the analytic finite-width remainder. Through t^3 it gives

 F_1=1-t/3+t^2/15-4t^3/315,
 F_2=2t/3-14t^2/45+2t^3/21,
 F_3=16t^2/15-568t^3/945,
 F_4=96t^3/35,
 G_1=1-t^2/15+8t^3/315,
 G_2=2t/3-2t^3/21, G_3=16t^2/15, G_4=96t^3/35,

each with its own O(t^4) Taylor remainder. These F_k are cumulants of
the normalized VARIANCE mixture variable Y, not ordinary cumulants of
the final Gaussian-mixture output.

The 2/3 variance coefficient agrees with Roberts-Yaida-Hanin, book
arXiv:2106.10165, printed p.142 (PDF p.150), Eq.(5.131), and Hanin
arXiv:2204.01058, Corollary4.1, Eq.(4.12), C4=2/3. However that latter
source prints C6=28/15 and C8=8756/315, which do NOT equal our F3 and
F4 leading coefficients after the apparent normalization Eq.(3.12).
This higher-order source/normalization discrepancy is OPEN FOR REVIEW;
neither printed number is used in this proof. An independent Wick
check of our F3 coefficient is:

 a=sqrt(2)int_0^1 B_r dr, b=int_0^1(r+B_r^2)dr,
 Y=1-sqrt(t)a+t(a^2-b)+O_in_moments(t^(3/2)),
 [t^2]kappa_3(Y)=3[Var(a^2)-Cov(a^2,b)]
                 =3[8/9-4 int_0^1(r-r^2/2)^2dr]=16/15.

We have checked the covariance and joint-cumulant definitions in
Hanin Eq.(3.12); a referee should inspect the remaining large-depth
coefficient derivation before declaring the source wrong. No claim
of a universality transfer is being made.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:264fa0bbae6ae6bec60290e4dcbc49d7f357d91989213f1c1fa3d50aa536ab4d","revision_digest":"sha256:412e5279d1e420d9da6610ad5affaf7fa0d62280c0a63506abfb3b20c914f221","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C053:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T14:12:29.483033","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The measurable functions $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $f_n$ are measurable, so are $g=\sup_nf_n$, and $h=\limsup_nf_n$.

\item If $f_n$ are measurable, so are $k=\inf_nf_n$, and $l=\liminf_nf_n$.

\item If $f_n\to f$ and $f_n$ are measurable, then $f$ is measurable.

\item If $f,g$ are measurable, so are $h=\min(f,g)$ and $k=\max(f,g)$.

\item If $f$ is measurable, so are $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-=-\min(f,0)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 19 (Main partial coloring of Bansal--Jiang--Meka ---  slightly adapted) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] There are universal constants \(c,\eta,C>0\) with the following property. Let
\(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be self-adjoint matrices satisfying
\[
\|L_i\|\le 1,
\qquad
\|L_i\|_F^2\le \frac{n}{\log^3(en)}
\]
for every \(i\in[n]\). Let \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(s:=|S|\) be arbitrary and let $t_L(s):=
C\left(\sqrt{s}+n^{1/4}s^{1/4}\right)$.
Then there exist a subspace $H_S\subseteq \mathbb R^S$ with $\dim H_S\ge (1-\eta)s$ such that the  discrepancy body   $K_L(S):=\{z\in H_S:\left\|
\sum_{i\in S}z_iL_i
\right\|
\le
t_L(s)\}$  relative to this subspace satisfies
\[
\gamma_{H_S}\bigl(K_L(S)\bigr)\ge \exp(-\eta s).
\]
Consequently, for every point \(y\in(-1,1)^S\), there exists a partial coloring increment \(z\in\mathbb R^S\) such that $y+z\in[-1,1]^S$ and $|\{i\in S: |y_i+z_i|=1\}|\ge cs$ satisfying

\[
\left\|
\sum_{i\in S}z_iL_i
\right\|
\le
C\,t_L(s).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition Projective separator of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] For a $2\times2$ matrix $X$ and $t>0$, let $\xi_t=(1,-t)$.  We say
that $t$ \emph{separates} $X$ if
\[
 \xi_tX\le0
\]
componentwise.  If $c>0$ and $d=Xc=(d_1,d_2)^\top$, separation implies
$d_1-td_2\le0$.  In particular,
\[
 d_2<0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_1<0.
\]
Thus a separator is exactly the kind of certificate that rules out the
endpoint sign pattern $d_2<0<d_1$ corresponding to an upward crossing
of an affine word-cost difference.
title: Projective separator

[Definition D_Bs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $T$ be a TWG with root $H^{(e)}$. 
We call $B\subset T$ a {\it branch}
of $T$ if $B$ is a TWG. 
Inductively, $B$ is a branch of $T$ if $B=T$ or if $B$ is
a branch of one of its primal branches $T_f$. 
A branch $L$ of order $\vartheta(L)=1$ is 
called a {\it leaf} of $T$.
title: Branches and leaves of TWGs

body: A family {X_i : i in I} of random variables on a probability space is uniformly integrable if sup_{i in I} E[|X_i| 1(|X_i| > K)] tends to 0 as K tends to infinity; equivalently, for every epsilon > 0 there exists K such that E[|X_i| 1(|X_i| > K)] < epsilon for every i in I simultaneously. Uniform integrability of a family bounded in L^1 is the exact extra condition needed to upgrade almost-sure or in-probability convergence to convergence in L^1. [standard, e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales]
title: Uniformly Integrable Family of Random Variables

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] [Liquid and frozen region, arctic boundary]
  Given any open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, we call a function $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ \emph{admissible} if $F$ is $1$-Lipschitz and satisfies $\nabla F (z) \in \overline{\mathcal{T}}$ for Lebesgue almost every $z \in \Omega$. Let $\Adm (\Omega)$ denote the set of admissible functions $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and, for any function $f : \partial \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, let $\Adm (\Omega; f)$ denote the set of $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ satisfying $F |_{\partial \Omega} = f$.  Define the \emph{liquid region} $\mathfrak{L}_F \subseteq \Omega$ associated with an admissible height function $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ by 
         \begin{flalign*}
         	\mathfrak{L}_F = \big\{ z \in \Omega : \nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T} \big\},
         \end{flalign*}
         where the condition $\nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T}$ in particular implies that $\nabla F(z)$ exists.

         In particular, we define the liquid region of $\cH_{q;a,b,c}$ as
         \[\mL_{q;a,b,c}:=\mL_{\cH_{q;a,b,c}}.\] The  boundary
        $\mathfrak A_{q;a,b,c}:=\partial\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the
        \emph{arctic boundary} and the interior of
        $\mX_{a,b,c}\setminus\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the \emph{frozen
        region}.
title: Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664

[Cor 7 of arXiv:2606.24584, '2606.24584'] Let $D\in\ds$ be an irreducible doubly stochastic matrix and let $P$ be a permutation matrix such that
\[
P^{\intercal} D P = \left( \bigoplus_{i=1}^{h} D_{i}  \right) \!\left( K_{h} \otimes I_{n'} \right),
\]
where $h:=h(D)$ and $D_{i} \in \Omega_{n'}$, $1\leq i \leq h$ and $n'=n/h$. Then
\[
P^{\intercal} D^{m} P
=
\left( \bigoplus_{i=1}^{h} D_{i,m}  \right) \!\left( K_{h}^m \otimes I_{n'} \right)
\]
and
\[
\|D_{i,m+1}-J_{n'}\|_2 \leq \|D_{i,m}-J_{n'}\|_2, \qquad 1\leq i \leq h,
\]
where $\|\cdot\|_2$ denotes the spectral norm.

[Lem 4 of arXiv:2608.28355, 'About the contractibility of the walking coinductive equivalence'] For all $\ell>0$, the cone $\Cone\cC[\ell]$ can be expressed as an iterated pushout of the form
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
  
  \partial\cC[\ell-1]
  \arrow[rr]
  \arrow[d,hook]
  \arrow[drr, phantom, "\pushout", very near end,
  yshift=0.2cm, xshift=0.1cm]
  &
  &
  \Cone\cC[\ell-1]\arrow[d]
  &
  &
  \\
  
  \cC[\ell-1]
  \arrow[r,hookrightarrow]
  &
  \partial\cC[\ell]
  \arrow[d,hook]
  \arrow[r]
  \arrow[dr, phantom, "\pushout",
  very near end, yshift=0.2cm, xshift=0.1cm]
  &
  \cA[\ell]\arrow[d]
  &
  &
  \\
  
  &
  \cC[\ell]\arrow[r]
  &
  \cA'[\ell]
  \arrow[d]
  
  &
  &
  \partial\cC[\ell]\arrow[ll]
  \arrow[d,hook]
  \arrow[dll, phantom, "\text{\reflectbox{$\pushout$}}",
  very near end, yshift=0.2cm, xshift=-0.1cm]
  \\
  
  &
  &
  \cA''[\ell]\arrow[d]
  &
  \partial\cC[\ell+1]
  \arrow[l]
  \arrow[d,hook]
  &
  \cC[\ell]
  \arrow[l,hookrightarrow]
  \arrow[dll, phantom, "\text{\reflectbox{$\pushout$}}",
  very near end, yshift=0.2cm, xshift=-0.1cm]
  \\
  
  &
  &
  \Cone\cC[\ell]
  &
  \cC[\ell+1]\arrow[l]
  &
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Moreover, the vertical composite
\[
\Cone\cC[\ell-1]\to\cA[\ell]\to\cA'[\ell]\to\cA''[\ell]\to\Cone\cC[\ell]
\]
is induced by the cotarget map $\cC[\ell-1]\to\cC[\ell]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 4 (Uniform subcritical occupancy lower tail) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(N\ge2\) and \(m\ge N\).  If
\[
        \Lambda_{N,m}:=N\left(1-\frac1N\right)^m,
\]
then
\[
        \frac{N!S(m,N)}{N^m}
        \le \exp\{-\Lambda_{N,m}\}.
\]
Consequently, in any range where \(N\le m\le 2N\log N\) and
\(\Lambda_{N,m}\to\infty\), the onto probability is at most
\(\exp\{-c\Lambda_{N,m}\}\) for any fixed \(0<c<1\), for all sufficiently large \(N\).

Moreover, if \(M\le n\log n\), then
\[
        (n-1)\left(1-\frac1{n-1}\right)^{M-1}
        \asymp
        n\left(1-\frac1n\right)^M ,
\]
and hence the same exponential lower-tail bound may be applied to the
\((n-1,M-1)\) occupancy probability appearing in the flux formula.

Let $\Phi(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ and $e^{t\Delta}g=\Phi(\cdot,t)*g$ for $t>0$. For $1\le p\le q\le\infty$ and $g\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$: $\|e^{t\Delta}g\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^n)}\le(4\pi t)^{-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\|g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$, and $\|\nabla e^{t\Delta}g\|_{L^p}\le C_nt^{-1/2}\|g\|_{L^p}$ with $C_n=\|\nabla\Phi(\cdot,1)\|_{L^1}$. In particular $e^{t\Delta}$ is a contraction on every $L^p$ ($p=q$), maps $L^1$ into $L^\infty$ with norm $(4\pi t)^{-n/2}$, and $e^{t\Delta}g\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ for $t>0$ with all derivatives bounded: the heat semigroup is instantaneously smoothing and has infinite propagation speed ($e^{t\Delta}g>0$ everywhere for $t>0$ whenever $g\ge0$, $g\not\equiv0$). The restriction $p\le q$ is essential.
1 <= p <= q <= infinity
g in L^p(R^n)
t > 0

\[
\int_0^t (K_1(t,s) - K_2(t,s))^2\,d\mu_s = 0 \quad \text{for all } t\in[0,T].
\]
Hence $K_1(t,s) = K_2(t,s)$ for $\mu$-a.e.\ $s\in[0,t]$, for each $t$. The Cameron--Martin spaces $\mathcal{H}_{K_1}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{K_2}$ are therefore isometrically identical (their defining inner products coincide on a dense set). Consequently, $D^{K_1} = D^{K_2}$, $\Pi^{K_1} = \Pi^{K_2}$, and $\norm{\Pi^{K_1}D^{K_1}X_s}^2 = \norm{\Pi^{K_2}D^{K_2}X_s}^2$ for a.e.\ $s$. body:
[Proposition uniformly-Skorohod of arXiv:2603.01823, 'on a fractional stochastic heat equation arising from the disordered pinning model'] Let $U=(u_1, u_2,\dots)$ be an $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$-valued random vector such that $u_k\in L^1$ for all $k\in\mathbb N$. Denote $H_n:=\mathbb E[\mathcal{P}_n U|\mathcal{F}_n]$. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $n$, $S_n:=\int{\raisebox{-.33em}{\hspace{-.87em}\scriptsize \bf o}}\hspace{.5em} H_n\xi$ exists and  $\{S_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is  uniformly integrable.

\item $U$ is $L^1$-Skorohod integrable.

\end{enumerate}
If any of these conditions holds, then 
$S_n$ is a martingale that converges almost surely and in $L^1$ to $\int{\raisebox{-.33em}{\hspace{-.87em}\scriptsize \bf o}}\hspace{.5em} U{\mathrm d} \xi$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition uniformly-Skorohod of arXiv:2603.01823

[Corollary 5 (Matrix Freedman) of arXiv:2606.24323, 'Conditioning of incoherent sub-dictionaries sampled from a coherent dictionary'] Let $(Y_\ell)_{\ell}$ with $Y_0=0$ be a matrix martingale adapted to the filtration $(\mathcal F_\ell)_\ell$, whose values are symmetric (self-adjoint) $d\times d$ matrices.
Assume that the difference sequence $X_\ell = Y_\ell-Y_{\ell-1}$ is almost surely bounded by $R$ and that the quadratic variation process is almost surely bounded by $\sigma^2$, meaning 
\begin{align*}
    \|X_\ell\| \leq R \quad  \mbox{and} \quad & \| \sum_{\ell=1}^L \E[X_\ell^2\mid \mathcal F_{\ell-1}]\| \leq \sigma^2 \quad \mbox{(a.s.), then}\\
\P(\| Y_L \|\geq t) = \P\Big(\| \sum_{\ell=1}^L X_\ell \| &\geq t \Big)\leq d \cdot \exp\left(\frac{-t^2/2}{\sigma^2+ Rt/3}\right)\leq d \cdot \exp\left(\frac{-t^2}{2\sigma^2+ Rt}\right).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Matrix Freedman

\[

 =\C(\u,g_1,g_2)=\C(g_1,g_2),

 (Z_1+Z_2)(Z_1+Z_2+2)Z_1^2Z_2^2 \\

It has genus $4$.

body: Stokes' theorem, also known as the Kelvin–Stokes theorem, is a theorem in vector calculus that relates the behavior of a vector field along the edge of a surface to the behavior of its curl on the surface itself. [Theorem 7 of arXiv:2609.02381, '\bfseries Viscosity Supersolution Barriers to a\\ Non-local Free Boundary Problem'] Let $\nu(dz)$ be a L\'evy measure on $\mathbb{R}_0$ with finite
large-jump intensity
$\lambda:=\nu(\{|z|>1\})<\infty.$
Let for given constant $M>0$ holds
\[
r+\rho<\sqrt{\lambda}\,M,
\;\;
\text{and set}
\;\;
\beta:=\sqrt{\lambda}\,M-(r+\rho)>0.
\]
Fix a uniform linear-growth ceiling constant $C_{\max}>0$. Suppose that
there exist $\tau\in(0,T)$ and $\alpha_*>0$ such that
$\alpha(t)\geq\alpha_*,\;\; t\in[0,\tau].$
Then whenever $\tau$ satisfies
\[
\tau>T_{\mathrm{crit}}
:=
\frac{1}{\beta}
\log\left(\frac{C_{\max}}{\alpha_*}\right),
\]
there exists an admissible jump amplitude $\gamma_*$, with
$L^2(\nu)$-Lipschitz constant $M$, for which there is no
nonnegative lower semicontinuous function
$v^T:\mathbb{R}\times[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$
satisfying the uniform linear-growth bound
\begin{equation}
v^T(g,t)
\leq
C_{\max}(1+|g|),
\qquad
(g,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times[0,T],
\end{equation}
that simultaneously satisfies the obstacle inequality
\begin{equation}
v^T(g,t)-v^T(-g,t)
\geq
\alpha(t)g-c,
\qquad
(g,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,T),
\end{equation}
and the viscosity supersolution inequality for the
integro-differential operator on
$\mathbb{R}\times(0,T)$.

[Lemma 17 (Lower bound for $\|B\|_{HS}$, uniform over choices of $A_l$) of arXiv:2608.30722, 'Intermediate Singular Values of Random Matrices\\ under Second-Moment and Anti-Concentrati'] There exist constants $c,C>0$, depending only on $a$ and $b$, such that
\[
  \bbP\!\left(\sum_{k=m_l+1}^n\dist(A^k,H_{m_l,k})^{-2}
    < c\,\frac{n}{l}\right)
  \;\le\;e^{-Cl}.
\]
In particular,
\[
  \bbP\!\left(\|B\|_{HS} < \sqrt{\frac{cn}{l}}\right)
  \;\le\;\exp(-C l),
\]
and this bound holds for every choice of $S\subseteq[m_l]$ with $|S|=l$.

[Proposition 3 (Uniform-in-time weak expansion) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth}, \ref{ass:flow-smothness} and
\ref{ass:coeff-level-new} hold. Let $\varphi \in C_b^7\left(\R^d\right)$ and let
$\Phi_1,\Phi_2\colon\Ptwo\to\R$ be defined above. Then,
there exist measurable functions $\beta_\ell \colon \left[ 0,\infty
\right) \to \R$, $\ell \in \left\{ 1,2 \right\}$, and constants $ C_\ell, C_\ell' > 0 $ such that, for every $ t \ge 0 $ and every $ N \ge 1 $,
\begin{equation}

\E\left( \Phi_\ell\left( \mu_t^N \right) \right)
=
\Phi_\ell\left( \mu_t \right)
+
\frac{\beta_\ell\left( t \right)}{N}
+
\frac{1}{N}
\int_0^t \Gamma P_{t-s}\Phi_\ell \left( \mu_s \right) ds
+
R_{\ell,N}\left( t \right),
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}

\abs{\beta_\ell\left( t \right)} \le C_\ell e^{-\omega t}\quad\mbox{and}\quad
\abs{\Gamma P_r\Phi_\ell \left( \mu \right)} \le C_\ell e^{-\omega r},
\end{equation}
for all $ t,r \ge 0 $ and $ \mu \in \Ptwo $, and with
\begin{equation}

\sup_{t \ge 0} \abs{R_{\ell,N}\left( t \right)} \le \frac{C_\ell'}{N^2}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition defn:c-convolution of arXiv:2412.01015, 'Classical beta ensembles and related eigenvalues processes at high temperature and the Mar'] The probability measure $\mu$ is the $c$-convolution of two probability measures $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ if 
\[
	{\mathcal M}_{c}(\mu) = {\mathcal M}_{c}(\mu_1) * {\mathcal M}_{c}(\mu_2).
\]
Here `$*$' denotes the (classical) convolution of two probability measures.
We write $\mu = \mu_1 \boxplus_c \mu_2$. Note that we have implicitly assumed that all the MKTs exist.

Let $W_T \subsetneq W_C$ be nested attribution time windows such that $Y^{W_T} \le Y^{W_C}$ almost surely for non-negative cumulative consumption. Then the na"ive difference estimator $\hat{\tau}_{mismatch}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y^{W_T} \mid T=1, X=x] - \mathbb{E}[Y^{W_C} \mid T=0, X=x]$ has asymptotic bias given by $\operatorname{Bias}(x) = -\mathbb{E}[Y^{W_C}(1) - Y^{W_T}(1) \mid X=x]$, which is strictly negative whenever treated consumption accumulates beyond window $W_T$.
W_T is strictly smaller than W_C
Outcome Y is cumulative non-negative consumption
Treatment assignment is unconfounded

[Thm 27 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] There exists a unique strict étale sheaf $L\mathcal{W}\uomega^*_{-/\sR}$ of $p$-complete $W(k)$-modules on $\mathrm{lSch}^{qcoh}_{(k,N)}$ such that for each $\sX$ and each étale local chart $(A,L)\in \PreLog_{(k,N)}$ of $\sX$, the natural map  $L\mathcal{W}\uomega^*_{(A,L)/\sR} \to \Gamma(U, L\mathcal{W}\uomega^*_{/\sR})$ is an equivalence, where $U\in \mathrm{lSch}^{qcoh}_{(k,N)}$ is associated to the pre-log scheme $(\Spec(A),L)$. 
    \begin{proof}
By definition,
$L\mathcal W\uomega^*_{-/\sR}$ is a sifted left Kan extension. It
therefore preserves sifted colimits, and in particular filtered
colimits. This verifies condition~\textup{(i)} of
Proposition~\ref{prop_global}. Condition~\textup{(ii)} is
Lemma~\ref{lem:descent}, and condition~\textup{(iii)} follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:log_inv}. Proposition~\ref{prop_global} now gives the
claimed strict-\'etale sheaf and its uniqueness.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

  If the torus action on \(N\) is slice-maximal then the action of \(\pi_1(M)\) on \(\pi_2(M)\) is \(C(m)\)-trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let M be a smooth manifold and p a point of M. The tangent space T_pM is the real vector space of derivations at p: linear maps v from the algebra of smooth real-valued functions defined near p to R that satisfy the Leibniz rule v(fg) = f(p)v(g) + g(p)v(f) for all smooth f, g. Equivalently, in a coordinate chart (U, phi) around p with coordinates x^1,...,x^n, T_pM is the n-dimensional real vector space spanned by the partial derivative operators d/dx^1|_p ,..., d/dx^n|_p, and a tangent vector may also be identified with an equivalence class of smooth curves through p under the relation of having equal velocity at p.
title: Tangent Space

Agresti and Veraar (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 5 asks: if u_0^n tends to u_0 in L^2(Omega; H), does u^n tend to u in L^2(Omega; L^2(0,T;V) intersect C([0,T];H))? Our result (id P0267, 2026-09-08): NO, from the same critical Allen-Cahn example as P0266. Take u_0^n = 1/n tending to 0; the limit solution is identically zero, and convergence in L^2(Omega; C([0,T];H)) would require E sup ||u^n||^2 to tend to 0, but that quantity is infinite for every n by the P0266 result (the constant-data solution's supremum has tail index one, coming from a four-dimensional Bessel process's capacity estimate). Verification as the source words it: uses the same construction and checks as Problem 4; of the six problems attacked in that session the memo states these two have the best odds of being genuinely new, since the source is a year old. Let n, m ≥ 1 and T > 0. Consider ∂_t u + Σ_{j=1}^n A_j(t,x) ∂_j u + B(t,x) u = F(t,x) for u : [0,T]×R^n → C^m, where each A_j is Hermitian (real symmetric in the real case) at every (t,x), A_j ∈ C¹ with A_j and ∂_{x_j}A_j bounded on [0,T]×R^n, B continuous and bounded, and F ∈ C([0,T];L²). Let u ∈ C¹([0,T]×R^n;C^m) be a solution with u(t,·) supported in a fixed compact set for all t (or u ∈ C([0,T];H¹) ∩ C¹([0,T];L²)). Put K = (1/2) sup |Σ_j ∂_j A_j| + sup |B| (matrix operator norms). Then for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≤ e^{Kt} ( ‖u(0)‖_{L²} + ∫_0^t ‖F(s)‖_{L²} ds ). In particular the Cauchy problem has at most one such solution, and the solution depends continuously on the data in L². The wave equation fits this framework via the first-order system for U = (∂_t u, ∇u).
each coefficient matrix A_j(t,x) is Hermitian/symmetric at every point (symmetric hyperbolicity)
A_j ∈ C¹ with A_j and its first x-derivatives bounded; B bounded
the solution is C¹ (or H¹-regular in x) and compactly supported in x for each t, so boundary terms vanish

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2605.31471, 'Convergence Rates of Continuous-Time Random Walks to Time-Fractional Diffusions with Unbou'] Consider the SDE \eqref{eq:SDE-flow}.  
    Let Assumption~\ref{asm:classical} (items \emph{(1)}–\emph{(2)}) hold.  
    Assume that $\nabla \sigma_j(x)$ is well-defined and (globally) $\alpha$-H\"older continuous for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and all $j = 0, \dots, d$.
    Then the process $\nabla X_t(x)$ is well-defined and is locally $\beta$-H\"older continuous in $x$, almost surely, for any $\beta < \alpha$. Furthermore, it is the unique strong solution of the SDE
    \begin{equation}
        
        \nabla X_t(x)
        =
        e
        + \int_0^t \bigl(\nabla b\bigl(X_s(x)\bigr)\bigr)\,\nabla X_s(x)\,ds
        + \sum_{l=1}^d \int_0^t
            \bigl(\nabla \sigma_l\bigl(X_s(x)\bigr)\bigr)\,\nabla X_s(x)\,dW_s^l,
    \end{equation}
    where $e[u] = u$ is the identity mapping on $X$.  
    Moreover, for every $u \in X$ and $p \ge 2$ we have
    $\nabla X_t(x)[u] \in L^p$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 19 of arXiv:2605.21638, 'Markov renewal theory for transfer operators and point processes on the line'] Suppose that $(\tilde M_n)_{n\in \Z}$ is a stationary Markov chain with transition kernel $P=P_p= P_{\beta,p}$. 
    Then $(Z_n)_{n\in \Z}$ satisfies the DLR equations at $\beta,p$, i.e., 
	\[
		\P\Bigl( (Z_j)_{j\in \Gamma} \in A\, \Big|\, (Z_j)_{j\in \Z\setminus \Gamma}\Bigr) 
		 = \pi_{\Gamma;p}\bigl( A\mid (Z_j)_{j\in \Z}\bigr)
	\] 
	almost surely, for all finite non-empty subsets $\Gamma \subset \Z$ and all measurable $A\subset \R_+^\Gamma$.

Let $(\bar{M}, \bar{g})$ be a 4-dimensional vacuum spacetime and $\Sigma \subset \bar{M}$ a spacelike hypersurface with induced metric $g$, second fundamental form $h$, and timelike unit normal $e_0$. Then: (1) The Gauss equation implies $R_{ijkl} = W_{ijkl} + h_{ik}h_{jl} - h_{il}h_{jk}$; contracting yields $R + H^2 - |h|^2 = 0$. (2) The Codazzi equation implies $\nabla_i h_{jk} - \nabla_j h_{ik} = W(e_0, e_k, e_i, e_j)$; contracting yields $\operatorname{div}_g h - \nabla_g H = 0$.
Spacetime is vacuum Einstein Ric(g_bar) = 0
\Sigma is an embedded spacelike hypersurface
e_0 is the unit normal vector field

body:
[Definition def:rw_reset of arXiv:2603.24803, 'Critical Spectral Invariants in Random Walks with Geometric Resetting'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. 
Fix $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and $z \in \{1,\dots,a-1\}$. 
Let $\{X_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a discrete-time stochastic process on 
$\{0,1,\dots,a\}$ with initial condition $X_0=z$.

Let $\{\xi_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables, independent of 
everything else, with
\[
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=+1)=p, 
\qquad 
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=-1)=q=1-p.
\]

Let $\{\sigma_i\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ geometric random variables with 
parameter $\gamma\in(0,1)$, supported on $\{1,2,\dots\}$:
\[
\mathbb{P}(\sigma_i=k)=\gamma(1-\gamma)^{k-1}, 
\qquad k\ge1,
\]
independent of $\{\xi_n\}$. Define reset times recursively by
\[
\mathbf{t}_0:=0,
\qquad
\mathbf{t}_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} \sigma_j,
\quad i\ge1.
\]

Then the process evolves according to
\[
X_n =
\begin{cases}
z, & \text{if } n \in \{\mathbf{t}_i\}_{i\ge1}, \\[6pt]
X_{n-1}+\xi_n, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
and is absorbed upon first hitting $0$ or $a$. Equivalently, at each 
step the walker resets to $z$ with probability $\gamma$ or performs a 
standard biased step with probability $1-\gamma$, independently of its 
current position.
title: Random walk with geometric resetting

\([0,1)^2\times[0,1]\).  After the continuous extension, we define $\F,\G,\HF$ on $[0,1)^2$ such that
   \BGE \F =F(\cdot,\cdot,1),\quad \G =G(\cdot,\cdot,1) ,\quad \HF =F_3(\cdot,\cdot,1).\EDE
 Then  for $j\in [2]$, the following hold in $(0,1)^2$:
 \BGE \L_{r_j}\F=0 ;\EDE

    \BGE  |
        \partial_{r_1}^{n_1}\partial_{r_2}^{n_2}\F
         | \lesssim t_1^{(\gamma-n_1)\wedge 0} t_2^{(\gamma-n_2)\wedge 0} \quad \text{for any }n_1,n_2\in\N_0\text{ with }n_1\vee n_2\le 2; \EDE

          |
        \partial_{r_1}^{n_1}\partial_{r_2}^{n_2}\HF
         |
        \lesssim t_1^{\gamma-1-n_1}t_2^{\gamma-1-n_2}  \quad \text{for any }n_1,n_2\in\N_0\text{ with }n_1+n_2\le 2;

\end{equation}
\BGE 2( \beta-1)\HF -\beta(1-\beta) \F =t_1t_2\G.\EDE

(ii) If $\beta\in (1/3,2/3]$, then $F$, $r_1F_1$, $r_2F_2 $, $r_1r_2 F_{12}$ and $\beta F_3+t_1t_2 G$  extend continuously to $[0,1)^2\times [0,1]$, and (\ref{F-bdry-hyper})   still holds. If $\beta\in [1/2,2/3]$, we also have (\ref{F1&N*}).

Under the assumptions, let f_t=f(.;z_t), x_(t+1)=x_t-eta_t*grad f_t(x_t), and fix 0<v_0<=v_1<=...<=v_T. Define c_t=eta_t*v_t^2-(v_t-v_(t-1))*sum_(s=t)^T eta_s*v_s. Then sum_t c_t*E[f_t(x_t)-f_t(x_star)] <= (v_0^2/2)*||x_1-x_star||^2+(1/2)*sum_t eta_t^2*v_t^2*E||grad f_t(x_t)||^2 -(1/(2*beta))*sum_t eta_t*v_t*[sum_(s=1)^t (v_s-v_(s-1))*E||grad f_t(x_t)-grad f_t(x_s)||^2+v_0*E||grad f_t(x_t)-grad f_t(x_star)||^2]. The coefficients c_t need not be positive. Interpolation and independence of the whole sample sequence are not assumed.
Each f(.;z):R^d->R is convex and beta-smooth, beta>0; Euclidean norms.
For every s<=t, conditional on z_1,...,z_(s-1), z_s and z_t have the same distribution. This is conditional equality of marginal laws, not conditional independence.
Fixed comparator x_star and initialization x_1 in R^d; deterministic positive step sizes eta_1,...,eta_T. All displayed expectations are finite.
Positive nondecreasing deterministic weights v_0,...,v_T.

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2605.31471, 'Convergence Rates of Continuous-Time Random Walks to Time-Fractional Diffusions with Unbou'] Consider the SDE \eqref{eq:SDE-flow} under Assumption \ref{asm:classical}.
    Fix $m \in \mathbb N$ and $p \ge 2$. Then there exist functions
    $A_m(\cdot,p) : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ such that, for all
    $v_1,\dots,v_m \in \cX$,
    \begin{equation}
        \E \bigl\| \DD^m X_t(x)[v_1,\dots,v_m] \bigr\|^p
        \;\le\; A_m(t,p) \prod_{j=1}^m \|v_j\|^p,
        \qquad t \ge 0.
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, there exist constants $\mu_{m,p}>0$ and $\lambda_{m,p}>0$
    depending only on $K,d,m,p$ such that
    \begin{align}
        A_1(t,p) &\le e^{\mu_{1,p} t}, \\
        A_m(t,p) &\le \lambda_{m,p} \bigl( e^{\mu_{m,p} t } - 1 \bigr),
        \qquad m \ge 2.

body:
[Proposition p:exp.mu.n of arXiv:2601.12677, 'Stable and Fréchet limit theorem for subgraph functionals in the hyperbolic random geometr'] Let $\gamma\in \big(\frac{1}{2\alpha},1\big)$. \\
$(i)$ We have, uniformly for $u \in (0,{\gamma R_n})$, 
$$
\mu_{k,n}(u) \le \big( 1+o_n(1) \big) B_{k,\alpha} \bigg( 1+ \sum_{\ell=0}^{k-2}\binom{k-1}{\ell} (e^{\frac{1}{2} (d-1)(1-2\alpha)u} +s_n)^{k-1-\ell} \bigg) e^{\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(k-1)u}, 
$$
where $s_n:= B_\alpha^{-1} n^{-(2\alpha-1)(1-\gamma)} e^{\alpha(d-1)\omega_n}$. \\
$(ii)$ We have, uniformly for $u \in (0,{\gamma R_n})$, 
$$
\mu_{k,n}(u) \ge \big( 1+o_n(1) \big) B_{k,\alpha} \big( 1- e^{\frac{1}{2} (d-1)(1-2\alpha)u} \big)^{k-1} e^{\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(k-1)u}. 
$$
$(iii)$ There exists $C\in (0,\infty)$, independent of $n$ and $u$, such that for all $n\ge1$ and $u\in (0,R_n)$,  
$$
\mu_{k,n} (u) \le C e^{\alpha(d-1)(k-1)\omega_n}\cdot e^{\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(k-1)u}, 
$$ 
where $\omega_n :=\log \log R_n$.

body:
[Theorem t:main square-integrable of arXiv:2605.22803, 'Persistence of asymptotic variance under transport:\\ from hyperfluctuation to stealthy hy'] Suppose that $\Phi$ is a locally absolutely square-integrable invariant random complex measure, and that $K$ is an invariant transport kernel. Further, assume that either Condition~(c:condition square-integrable general of the paper) or Condition~(c:condition square-integrable Markov of the paper) holds.
Then $K\Phi$ is locally absolutely square-integrable.
\begin{proof}
If Condition~(c:condition square-integrable general of the paper) holds, the assertion follows from Lemma~(l:remainder2case1 of the paper). If Condition~(c:condition square-integrable Markov of the paper) holds, the assertion follows from Lemma~(l:remainder2case2 of the paper). In both cases, we apply the lemmas with $p=0$. The lemmas each actually include a stronger statement, which we do not need here but in the following subsection. Also, while Lemmas~(l:remainder2case1 of the paper) and~(l:remainder2case2 of the paper) make the same statements under different conditions, the proofs differ completely. The proof of Lemma~(l:remainder2case2 of the paper) follows a technique that is adapted from a proof in~[Dereudre_Flimmel_Huesmann_Leblé_2024].
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem t:main square-integrable of arXiv:2605.22803

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Consider the symbol defined on $[0,1] \times \T$
\[
a(x,z) = d(x) z^{-1} + b(x) + c(x) z,
\]
where $b,c,d$ are continuous complex-valued functions on $[0,1]$. Let $\mu_n$ be the sequence of eigenvalue-counting measures
\[
\mu_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{\lambda \in \mathrm{sp}(\mathcal{T}_n(a))} \delta_{\lambda}.
\]
Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly to the measure $\mu$ defined by
\[
\mu=\int_0^1 \alpha_x~dx,
\]
where $\alpha_x$ denotes the arcsine measure on the complex interval
\[
\bigl[b(x)-2\sqrt{d(x)c(x)},\, b(x)+2\sqrt{d(x)c(x)}\bigr].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2604.20617

[Thm 2 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Assume that the function $g:[0,1] \to \rr$ is differentiable and its derivative $g'$ is $\beta$-H\"{o}lder
continuous for some $\beta \in (0,1]$. Let
\beq
\sigma^2_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{n,i}\left(g'\left( p_{n,i}\right)\right)^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{n,i}g'\left( p_{n,i}\right)\right)^2
\deq
and
\beq
\gamma=
\begin{cases}
\beta/2 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0,0.5]\\
\beta-0.5 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0.5,1]
\end{cases}.
\deq
If
\begin{enumerate}[$(1)$]
\item $\beta\in (0.5,1]$ or
\item $\beta\in (0,0.5]$ and
\beq
\sup_{n}\sum_{i=1}^\infty p_{n,i}^{(\beta+1)/2}<\infty,
\deq
\end{enumerate}
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma_n}(\hat \theta_n-\theta_n)\le x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|\le\frac{C}{n^{\gamma/2} \sigma_n^{1/2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    r(x,a)=r(x_{\mathcal K},a)$,
    $
    \pi(a\mid x)=\pi(a\mid x_{\mathcal K})$,
    and the transition of the active state satisfies
    $p(x'_{\mathcal K}\mid x,a)
    =
    p(x'_{\mathcal K}\mid x_{\mathcal K},a)$.}
\end{itemize}
Under either condition,
$
Q^\pi(x,a)=Q^\pi(x_{\mathcal K},a)$,
so that $\mathcal K$ can serve as an active feature set in
Assumption~\ref{sparseQ}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defi 3 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] For each $h>0$,  the space 
  $D_h ( \R^{2 n })$  stands for the set of   functions $F$ on $\R^{2 n }$ such that there exists an analytic  function $ (X,Y)\rightarrow F^{\rm ext} (X , Y)$ on   $\C^{2n }$ 
  having the following properties.
  
  i)  $F^{\rm ext}$ satisfies for any $(X,Y)\in\R^{4n}$,

    \be   (\partial _{x_j } + i \partial _{\xi_j }) 
   F^{\rm ext} (X , Y) = 0 ,\quad
     (\partial _{y_j } - i \partial _{\eta_j })
      F^{\rm ext}    (X , Y) = 0,\ee 
      
  ii) We have $$F^{\rm ext}(X , X) = F(X).$$ 
  
 iii) There is 
a function $\psi_F \in L^1(\R^{2n}) \cap L^{\infty}(\R^{2n})$ verifying the estimate for all $(X,Y)\in\R^{4n}$,
       
       $$ | F^{\rm ext}(X , Y)| \leq e^{ \frac { 1 }  { 4h } |X-Y|^2  } 
       \psi_F (X - Y) .$$
       
When the conditions i) ii) and iii) are fulfilled, we set,

$$ \Vert F \Vert _{D_h( \R^{2n})}  =  \Vert \Psi_F  \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})} + 
 \Vert \Psi_F \Vert _{L^{\infty } (\R^{2n})}.  $$

[Lem AnaLem of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $N\geqslant2$ be a given fixed integer. Suppose
that $S_{n}(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})=0$ for all $n\leqslant N-1$ and
all non-degenerate sequences $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})$ with $a_{j}\in2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$.
Let $(b_{1}^{*},\cdots,b_{N}^{*})$ be a fixed non-degenerate sequence
with $b_{j}\in2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$. Given $w\in\mathbb{C}$, we define
the path development $F_{w}:\mathbb{C}^{2}\rightarrow\mathfrak{sl}_{N+1}(\mathbb{C})$
by 
\begin{equation}
F_{w}({\rm e}_{1})\triangleq A_{w},\ F_{w}({\rm e}_{2})\triangleq E_{12}+\cdots+E_{N,N+1},
\end{equation}
where $A_{w}\in\mathfrak{h}$ is chosen to satisfy 
\begin{equation}
[A_{w},E_{k,k+1}]=(b_{k}^{*}+w)E_{k,k+1}\ \ \ (k=1,\cdots,N).
\end{equation}
Then for any vector $K=(k_{1},\cdots,k_{n})$ satisfying $|K|=N,n\geqslant2$ or $|K|\leqslant N-1,n\geqslant1$ and any $j=1,\cdots,N,$ there exists a meromorphic function $\Psi_{K,j}:\mathbb{C}^{|K|}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$
(i.e. the quotient of two holomorphic functions) in $|K|$ complex variables,
such that 
\[
\hat{F}_{w}(H_{K})=\sum_{j}\Psi_{K,j}(b_{j}^{*}+w,\cdots,b_{j+|K|-1}^{*}+w)E_{j,j+|K|}
\]
and the function $w\mapsto\Psi_{K,j}(b_{j}^{*}+w,\cdots,b_{j+|K|-1}^{*}+w)$
is analytic in a neighbourhood of $w=0$ for all $(K,j)$. Here $\hat{F}_{w}$
is the induced Lie homomorphism on ${\cal L}((\mathbb{C}^{2}))$ (cf.
((eq:HatF of the paper))). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.14802, 'Dynamical Gibbs-non-Gibbs transitions for finite-alphabet models on trees'] Let $(U,d)$ be a metric space, $(G_a)_{a\in A}$ a family of $s$-tree contractions with corresponding contraction constants $\lambda_a$ satisfying
\begin{equation*}
  \lambda:=\sup_{a\in A}\lambda_a<1.
\end{equation*}
Furthermore, let $U_0\subset U$ satisfy $D:=\mathrm{diam}(U_0)=\sup_{x,y\in U_0}d(x,y)<\infty$
and $G_a\big((U_0)^s\big)\subset U_0$ for every $a\in A$.
Then, large distance behavior of any tree-indexed sequence of initial boundary data $U_0$ under any tree-indexed composition of maps $(G_a)_{a\in A}$ becomes asymptotically independent of the intial boundary data $U_0$. 

More precisely, let $(G^{(i)})_{i\in\N_0}$
be a tree-indexed sequence of maps from the family $(G_a)_{a\in A}$, where $G^{(i)}_j$
is attached to the $j$-th vertex in the $i$-th annulus and $G_j^{(i)}=G_{a(i,j)}$ for arbitrary $a(i,j)\in A$. Let
\begin{equation*}
    u^{(n)}=\left(u^{(n)}_1,\dots,u^{(n)}_{s^n}\right),~~\text{and}~~v^{(n)}=\left(v^{(n)}_1,\dots,v^{(n)}_{s^n}\right)
\end{equation*}
be arbitrary boundary data in $U_0^{s^n}$ for each $n\in\N$.
Let $x_n$ and $y_n$ denote the output of the same depth-$n$ tree composition with boundary data
$u^{(n)}$ and $v^{(n)}$, respectively.
Then
\begin{equation*}
     d(x_n,y_n)\leq \lambda^n D
\end{equation*}
for all $n\in \N$.
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.14802

[Lemma 23 (Uniform moment bounds for the shifted process) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let $p\ge 1$ and define the shifted process $\widetilde Y_n := (1-\eta_n)Y_n' + \eta_n \widehat X_n$ for $n\ge0$. Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:P-moment-drift} (with constants $q, C > 0$), and assuming $\widehat M_p := \sup_{n\ge 0} \E\|\widehat X_n\|^p < \infty$, we have
\[
  \E\|\widetilde Y_n\|^p \le e^{-q\lambda n}\E\|\widetilde Y_0\|^p + \frac{C\lambda+\widehat M_p}{1-e^{-q\lambda}},
\]
yielding the uniform bound $\sup_{n\ge 0} \E\|\widetilde Y_n\|^p \le \E\|\widetilde Y_0\|^p + \frac{C\lambda+\widehat M_p}{1-e^{-q\lambda}} < \infty$.

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2609.02755, 'The Sharp Rate of Probabilistically Strong Convergence to the KPZ Equation'] Given a rooted tree $\tau$, we say that $C \subset E_+(\tau)$ is a cut of $\tau$ if any path in $E(\tau)$ with the root of $\tau$ as an endpoint contains at most one edge in $C$. We denote by $\mathbb{C}[\tau]$ the set of all cuts of $\tau$.
	We recall that for a rooted tree $\tau$, there is a natural partial ordering on $E(\tau)$ in which $e \ge e^\prime$ iff $e^\prime$ lies on the unique path from $e$ to the root.
	
	 We write $\tau_{\ng C}$ for the subgraph consisting of those edges $e \in E(\tau)$ such that there does not exist $\tilde{e} \in C$ with $e \ge \tilde{e}$.

body: [Lemma lem:cox_J of arXiv:2412.04589, 'Inverting the Markovian projection for pure jump processes'] Let $\lambda$, $\Lambda$, $E$ and $\tau$ be given by Lemma~(lem:cox of the paper). Furthermore, suppose that $\Omega$ supports a non-vanishing integrable random variable $J$ which is independent of $\mathcal{F}_\infty \lor \sigma(E)$. Define the filtration $\widetilde{\mathbb{A}} = (\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_t)_{t \geq 0}$ by $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_t \coloneqq \sigma(J\bm{1}_{\{\tau \leq s\}}; s \leq t)$. Let $\widetilde{\mathbb{G}} \coloneqq \mathbb{F} \newtriangledown \widetilde{\mathbb{A}}$. Then, the process $(J\bm{1}_{\{\tau \leq t\}} - \mathbb{E}[J]\Lambda_{\tau \land t})_{t \geq 0}$ is a $\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}$-martingale, and we have $\mathbb{F} \hookrightarrow \widetilde{\mathbb{G}}$.

body:
[Proposition 21 (Strong local error) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Let Assumptions~\hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}--\hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}} hold.
Let \(X_t\) denote the solution of \eqref{eq:LSDE} started from \(X_0=x\), and
\(\widehat X_t\) the one-step interpolation associated with \eqref{eq:kTULA} started from \(\widehat X_0=x\).
Set \(M := \max\{3(\ell+1),\,2\ell'+4\ell\}\).
Then there exists a constant \(C>0\), independent of \(x\in\R^d\), \(d\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1]\), such that for every \(x\in\R^d\),
\[
  \|\widehat X_\lambda - X_\lambda\|_{L^2}
  \;\le\;
  C\bigl(1+d^{M/2}+\|x\|^{M}\bigr)\,\lambda^{3/2}.
\]
In particular,
\[
  E_{\mathrm{strong}}(x)
  :=

    \Prob(Z_t>\beta_0 r)

\end{equation}

[Theorem thm:max_lh of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$. There exists a constant $C_{\mu}>0$ such that the following holds. Set
$$k^*_{n} =  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})}\log n +  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log\bigl((1-\mu_1)C_{\mu}\bigr).$$
Then for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ we have
\[
\P\bigl(\lambda(\mathcal{T}^n) \leq \lfloor k^*_{n} + t\rfloor\bigr) - \exp\bigl(-\mu_1^{t+1 - \{k^*_{n} + t\}}\bigr) \to 0.
\]
\item[(ii)] Assume that $\mu_{1}=0$. Set $\kappa = \min\{i \geq 2 : \mu_i > 0\}$. There exists a constant $D_{\mu} \in (0,1)$ such that the following holds. Set
$$
k_{n}^{**} \coloneqq  \log_\kappa \log n - \log_\kappa \log(1/D_{\mu}).
$$
 Write $m_n=\lfloor k_n^{**}\rfloor$ and
$\theta_n=\{k_n^{**}\}$, and define
$$
  J_n=
  \begin{cases}
    \{m_n-1,m_n\},&\theta_n\le\tfrac12,\\
    \{m_n,m_n+1\},&\theta_n>\tfrac12.
  \end{cases}
$$
Then $\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)\in J_n)\longrightarrow1$. In addition, if $\liminf_n\min(\theta_n,1-\theta_n)>0$, then
$\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)=m_n)\to1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] For $h \in \sH$, the vector space $U_k(\fn_h)^*$ is a subspace of $J^k_h$ by the exact sequence in Definition \ref{d.contact} (iii). By Theorem \ref{t.Taylor}, it can be identified with the vector space of polynomials of the form   $$ \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I $$ with coefficients $c_I \in \C$.  
  For each $1 \leq a \leq m$, define the  homomorphism  $\delta_{\sX_a,h}$ (resp. $\delta_{\sY_a,h}$)  from $U_k(\fn_h)^*$ to $U_{k-1}(\fn_h)^*$
 as follows. 
\begin{eqnarray*} 
\delta_{\sX_a,h} \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big) & := & (\frac{\p}{\p x_a} + \frac{y_a}{2} \frac{\p}{\p t}) \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big)
 \\
\delta_{\sY_a,h} \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big) & := & (\frac{\p}{\p y_a} - \frac{x_a}{2} \frac{\p}{\p t}) \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big),
\end{eqnarray*}
where on the righthand side, the vector fields act on the polynomial functions on $\sH$ as derivative. 
Also define the homomorphism $\delta_{T,h}: U_k(\fn_h)^* \to U_{k-2}(\fn_h)^*$ by
\begin{eqnarray*} 
\delta_{T,h} \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big) & := &  \frac{\p}{\p t} \big( \sum_{|I|= k} c_I \ h^*(xyt)^I \big).
\end{eqnarray*}
They define vector bundle homomorphisms $$\delta_{\sX_a}, \delta_{\sY_a}: U_k(\fn)^* \to U_{k-1}(\fn)^*, \ \delta_T: U_k(\fn)^* \to U_{k-2}(\fn)^*$$ and corresponding sheaf homomorphisms, which we denote by the same symbols,
$$\delta_{\sX_a}, \delta_{\sY_a}: \sO(U_k(\fn)^*) \to \sO(U_{k-1}(\fn)^*), \ \delta_T: \sO(U_k(\fn)^*) \to \sO(U_{k-2}(\fn)^*).$$

[Proposition prop:endpoint-deconvolution of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Fix \(E\subset V\) and nonempty \(S\subset E\), and put
\(B=E\setminus S\).  There are numbers
\(\boldsymbol{\nu}_S(C)\ge0\), \(\varnothing\ne C\subset B\), such that, for every
\(W\subset B\),
\begin{equation}
        \mathbf H_S(W)d_W=
        \sum_{\varnothing\ne C\subset W}\boldsymbol{\nu}_S(C)d_{W\setminus C} .
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
        \boldsymbol{\rho}_S^1(C)=\frac{d_{B\setminus C}}{d_B}\boldsymbol{\nu}_S(C)\ge0,
        \qquad C\ne\varnothing .
\end{equation}
Moreover \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_S(C)\), and hence \(\boldsymbol{\rho}_S^1(C)\), vanishes unless \(C\) is
\(S\)-attached.

body: A graph G = (V, E) is a finite set V of vertices together with a set E of edges, each an unordered pair of vertices; G is simple if it has no loops or repeated edges. A subgraph uses a subset of the vertices and edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges, and the handshake lemma gives sum of degrees = 2|E|. A walk is a vertex-edge alternation; a path has distinct vertices, a cycle is a closed path, and G is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path. Standard families: the complete graph K_n (all pairs adjacent), a tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges), and a bipartite graph (vertices two-colorable so every edge crosses, equivalently no odd cycle). The vertex connectivity kappa(G) and edge connectivity lambda(G) are the least numbers of vertices, respectively edges, whose deletion disconnects G (or reduces it to a single vertex), and kappa(G) <= lambda(G) <= min-degree.
title: Graph, Subgraph, and Basic Invariants

		where here $q_*\in [0,q]$ is any point such that $\zeta([0,q_*])=1$. It is easily verified that $\mathcal{P}_{\beta}(q,\zeta)$ is independent of the choice of $q_*$.

body:
Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.
X and Y are Banach spaces
T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X
title: Closed Operator, Closable Operator, and Core

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.03122, 'Propagation of support for super-Brownian motion with general branching mechanism'] Given a super-Brownian motion $X$ with a branching mechanism $\Psi$ satisfying Condition \ref{con_localize}, for any $\mu\in M_c$, $0<R_1<R$ and $0<t<\dfrac{R_1^2}{d}$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{P}_\mu\left\{X_u\left((S(\mu)^R)^c\right) > 0 \text{ for some } u \leq t\right\} \\
&\quad \leq \mu(1) \cdot u_{R,\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}}(R_1) \cdot C(d) \left(\frac{R_1}{\sqrt{t}}\right)^{d-2} \exp\left(-\frac{R_1^2}{2t}\right) \\
&\quad \leq \mu(1) \cdot G_{\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}}^{-1}(R-R_1) \cdot C(d) \left(\frac{R_1}{\sqrt{t}}\right)^{d-2} \exp\left(-\frac{R_1^2}{2t}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$
where $C(d)$ is a constant depending only on dimension $d$, and $u_{R,\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}}$ denotes the unique radial classical solution of singular boundary value problem \eqref{SBVP} in $B(0,R)$ with $\Phi$ replaced by $\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}$. If $\Psi$ satisfies Condition \ref{con_general} with lower bound $\Phi$, then this estimate reduces to the same bound with $u_{R,\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}}$ and $G_{\Phi_{\rho(\mu)+R}}^{-1}$ replaced by $u_{R,\Phi}$ and $G_\Phi^{-1}$, respectively. In particular, the spatially constant case is obtained by taking $\Psi(x,u)=\Phi(u)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.03122

body: For a convex problem (convex objective and inequality constraints, affine equalities), Slater's condition - the existence of a strictly feasible point where every inequality holds strictly - implies strong duality: the primal and dual optimal values coincide and the dual optimum is attained. Without convexity or a constraint qualification, a duality gap can exist.

Planar last-passage percolation with geometric weights is noise sensitive in the sense that, for every $p\in(0,1)$ and $t>0$,

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Free multiplicative convolution and log-unimodality: three questions of Hasebe, Ueda and Wang (2026) answers Problems 4.3, 4.7 and 4.11 of T. Hasebe, Y. Ueda and J.-C. Wang, Log-unimodality for free positive multiplicative Brownian motion (Colloq. Math. 169, 2022, 209-226; arXiv:2009.13848), sigma_t denoting that Brownian motion. Theorem A: the free multiplicative convolution of two multiplicatively symmetric log-unimodal laws need not be log-unimodal; for L >= 6 the log-uniform law on [e^-L, e^L] convolved with itself has a log-density with a strict local minimum at 0. Theorem B: for nu = (delta_{1/10} + delta_{10})/2, sigma_t ⊠ nu is not log-unimodal for any t > 0. Proposition D: if nu is log-unimodal and supported in [alpha, beta], then sigma_t ⊠ nu is log-unimodal for all t >= (pi/2)(beta/alpha + alpha/beta). Theorem C: sigma_t is not ⊠-strongly log-unimodal for any t > 0. Paper and a Lean 4 check of the inequalities: https://github.com/yspennstate/free-multiplicative-log-unimodality (commit 8f7665f177d6). Not refereed.
title: Hasebe-Ueda-Wang Problems 4.3, 4.7 and 4.11 answered: free multiplicative convolution and log-unimodality of free positive multiplicative Brownian motion (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/free-multiplicative-log-unimodality)

body:
[Proposition 42 (Coxeter orbit of the monomial physical contour) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] In the adjacent basis of
\cref{cor:monomial-Gaussian-Betti-row}, let \(M_m\) be the positive
Coxeter monodromy of the \(A_{m-1}\) sector fan, fixed by
\[
 M_m\Gamma_0=-\sum_{j=0}^{m-2}\Gamma_j,
 \qquad
 M_m\Gamma_j=\Gamma_{j-1}
 \quad(1\leq j\leq m-2).
\]
Then
\[
 \chi_{M_m}(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^m-1}{\lambda-1}.
\]
For the physical class
\[
 r_m=[\R]=-\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\Gamma_j,
 \qquad \ell=\lfloor m/2\rfloor,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
 \dim_\C\Span\{M_m^kr_m:k\in\mathbb Z\}
 =
 \begin{cases}
  m-1,&m\ \mathrm{odd},\\[1mm]
  m/2,&m\ \mathrm{even}.
 \end{cases}
 
\end{equation}
For even \(m\), the missing dimension equals the dimension of the
parity-odd Jacobi sector.  Thus the Betti orbit rank agrees numerically
with \eqref{eq:monomial-observable-rank}; this rank count alone does not
assert a canonical identification of the two sectors.  The rank in
\eqref{eq:monomial-Betti-orbit-rank} is the rank of the monodromy orbit
ledger; the single physical row \(C_\R\) itself, of course, has matrix
rank one.

[Corollary cor:finite-SE-bins of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1/3)$. Let $\overline{p}$ be a send sequence with $p_0=1$ such that, for all positive integers~$x$, $W_x \le (6/\lambda)^x$. 
 If $\overline{p}$ has
 infinitely many   strongly exposed bins
 then the under-backoff process 
 with birth rate~$3\lambda$ and send sequence~$\overline{p}$
is not positive recurrent (specifically, the empty state is not positive recurrent).

[Theorem thm:int-3_one-dim_version of arXiv:2510.06891, 'Multivariate CLT for L\'evy processes: convergence rates without moment assumptions'] Let $Y=(Y_t)_{t\geqslant0}$ be a real-valued symmetric L\'evy process, and let $Z$ be a standard Gaussian random variable. Assume there exists a measurable function $B:[1,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
t \mapsto t^{-1}d_{\mathscr{K}}(B(t)^{-1}Y_t,  Z )\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(+\infty),
\]
where $B(t)$ is non-zero for all sufficiently large $t$ and $ B(t) \to \infty$ and $B(t)^{-1} B(f(t))\to 1$ as $t \to \infty$ for any non-decreasing $f$ with $f(t)/t\to 1$. Then $\mathds{E}[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $d_{\mathscr{K}}( B(t)^{-1}Y_t,  Z )\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:int-3_one-dim_version of arXiv:2510.06891

body:
[Theorem 7 (Error bound for the slope change classifier) of arXiv:2609.00402, '2609.00402'] Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:slope} holds. Let \(T\geq5\), \(\mathcal I=\{3,\ldots,T-2\}\), and \(m_T=\lvert\mathcal I\rvert=T-4\). For \(\tau\in\mathcal I\), define \(v_\tau=1/D_L(\tau)+1/D_R(\tau)\), \(v_T^{\max}=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal I}v_\tau\), and, for \(\alpha_S\in(0,1)\), \(\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}=\sigma_S\sqrt{2v_T^{\max}\log(2m_T/\alpha_S)}\). Then \(h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=\mathbb I\{S(\bm X)>\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}\}\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=1\mid Y=0\}\leq\alpha_S\) and
\[
\mathbb P\{h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=0\mid Y=1\}
\leq
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\kappa_S-\lambda_{S,\alpha_S})_+^2}{2\sigma_S^2v_T^{\max}}\right\},
\]
where \(x_+=\max\{x,0\}\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{err}(h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}})
\leq\pi_0\alpha_S+
\pi_1\exp\left\{-\frac{(\kappa_S-\lambda_{S,\alpha_S})_+^2}{2\sigma_S^2v_T^{\max}}\right\}
=:\mathfrak B_S(\alpha_S).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Error bound for the slope change classifier

[Prop nonzero-imag-bispectrum of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Let $0<m<1$, let $h$ be a probability density supported on $(0,\infty)$, and consider the stationary one-sided linear Hawkes, equivalently Poisson branching-cluster, process with immigrant rate $\nu$ and offspring density $mh$. Let $B$ denote its reduced third factorial-cumulant bispectrum. Suppose either
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\[
\int_x^\infty h(u)\,du\sim x^{-\alpha}L(x),\qquad x\to\infty,
\]
for some $0<\alpha\le2$ and slowly varying $L$; or
\item $h$ is nonincreasing on $(0,\infty)$, $\int_0^\infty u^2h(u)\,du<\infty$, and $h$ is not of the form $a^{-1}\1_{(0,a)}$ for some $a>0$.
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists $t_0>0$ such that
\[
\mathrm{Im} B(t_0,t_0)\neq0.
\]
Consequently, this one-sided process is separated at third order from every reversible process whose reduced third factorial cumulant has an $L^1$ density. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Non-vacuity of the imaginary bispectrum

[Lem 8 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] {\rm (\cite{ChF1}, Theorem 1.1)} Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional forward complete Finsler measure space. Assume that ${\rm Ric}_{\infty}\geq -K$  for some $K\geq 0$.  Then, for any $0< r_{1} < r_{2}$, we have
\be
\frac{m(B_{r_{2}}(x_0))}{m(B_{r_{1}}(x_0))}\leq \left(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}\right)^{n+1}e^{\frac{K+ \vartheta_{0}^{2}}{6}r_{2}^2}, 
\ee
where  $x_{0}\in M$ is an arbitrary fixed point and $\vartheta_{0}$ is defined by (\ref{supS}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Existence of finite FPP geodesics without distributional assumptions structural argument Result: If all edge times are at least a>0, a fixed connecting path of cost M bounds any competing path length by M/a; only finitely many simple paths of that length start at a fixed vertex, so a minimum exists. Without a positive lower bound, a deterministic ladder can fail: give each vertical edge from height j-1 to j on both rails weight2^(-j), and the rung at height k weight3*2^(-k). A route across at height k costs2+2^(-k), with infimum2 unattained. Check: For a finite ladder route attaining maximum height k, vertical cost is at least2(1-2^(-k)) and at least one rung has cost at least3*2^(-k); this gives the same strict lower bound. Embed the ladder into Z^d with all other edges cost100 to preserve failure. Obstruction: The ladder environment is deterministic and spatially inhomogeneous, so it is only a counterexample to a general compactness inference. The iid critical case requires additional probabilistic structure.

u(F)}$. Moreover, if $|V(F)| - 
u(F) < rb-b$, then
    $$|\sS_{\varepsilon, k, b}(F)| \lesssim_{r,b,\lambda} \varepsilon c_n^{|V(F)| - 
u(F)} . $$

,

[Lem 5 of arXiv:2607.03360, 'Smoluchowski-Kramers Approximation Meets Khasminskii Averaging Principles in Nonequilibriu'] Suppose that \assmref{ass:mom-bdd} and \assmref{ass:gd-lip} hold. For each $t\in [0,T]$, the quantity $\sqrt{m} |v_t^m|$ is bounded in $L^2(\Omega)$. More precisely, there exists a constant $C_{T,\la_0,|v_0|}>0$, independent of $m$, such that 
\beq{bdd-mvs}
\EE\Big[m|v_t^m|^2\Big] \leq C_{T,\la_0,|v_0|}.
\eeq
Consequently,
\beq{0-mvs}
\EE\Big[|mv_t^m|^2\Big] \leq C_{T,\la_0,|v_0|}m.
\eeq
and hence $m|v_t^m| \to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$, thus in probability. Moreover, we also have
\beq{4-mv}
\EE|mv_t^m|^4 \leq C_{T,\la_0,|v_0|}.
\eeq

[Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let indices $a(q_d),a^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}, and let
indices $i(q_d),i^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand.Ising}. 
For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]} 
	\bigg|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^\sigma(q_\ell,a(q_{\ell+1}))
	\bigg|^8
	\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_t-q_s)^4
	\]
for all $0\le s\le t\le \dmax$.
The same bound holds
	with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
	or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\sigma}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
	in place of $\Delta X^\sigma(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.
We also have
	\[
	\E \left[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]}
	\left|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))
	\right|^8
	\right]
	\le L^{O(1)}(q_t-q_s)^4\,,
	\]
and likewise with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$ or $\Delta X^{\Isplus}(q_\ell,i^\frozen(q_{\ell+1}))$ in place of $\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
This follows by a very similar argument as for Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}. We will describe the proof for $X^\RomII$. A key difference is that in Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} we considered $X^\RomII(q_d,a)$ as a process indexed by time $q_d$ for a fixed index $a\in[M]$, with respect to the filtration $\cG(t)$. Here, we instead consider the process $X^\RomII(q_d,a(q_d))$, with respect to the filtration $\cFt(t)$ defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt.plus}. With this change, repeating the argument of
Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} gives the conclusion for $X^\RomII$ (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.X.holder.estimate}). The conclusions for $X^\RomIII$ and $X^\Ising$ follow similarly. It is straightforward to verify that the same bounds hold for the modified processes 
$X^{\trunc,\sigma}$ and $X^{\frozen,\sigma}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] There exist constants \(C>0\) and \(\kappa>0\) such that, for every
		\(\bm f\in \mathcal L^2((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\),
		\[
		\|T_t\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2}
		\le
		Ce^{-\kappa t}\|\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2},
		\qquad t\ge0.
		\]
		Consequently, the adjoint semigroup also satisfies
		\[
		\|S_t\bm f\|_{\mathcal  L^2}
		\le
		Ce^{-\kappa t}\|\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2},
		\qquad t\ge0.
		\]
		In particular,
		\[
		\lim_{t\to\infty}T_t\bm f=0,
		\qquad
		\lim_{t\to\infty}S_t\bm f=0
		\]
		in \(\mathcal  L^2((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\).

[Thm conv-DL-zero of arXiv:2411.16376, 'Higher order approximations in arcsine laws for subordinators'] Under the assumption of Theorem $(Thm:potential-zero of the paper)$ with $\beta_0=\beta\in(0,1]$,  let us define a function $\varepsilon_2:(0,+\infty)\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ by 
\begin{align}
    \Pi((x,+\infty))=
    \frac{c_0 x^{-\beta}}{\Gamma(1-\beta)}+\varepsilon_2(x),
    \quad
   0<x<+\infty.	
\end{align}
Set 
\begin{align}
 \varepsilon_3(s,x)
   =
   s\Pi((s-sx,+\infty))\varepsilon_1(sx),
   \quad 0<s, x<+\infty.	
\end{align}
Then, for $s\in(0,+\infty)$, the finite measure 
\begin{align}
\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}\in dx,\; 0<\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}<1\bigg),
\quad 0<x<1,
\end{align}
 admits a density expressed in the form
\begin{align}
   s\Pi((s-sx,&+\infty))u(sx)
   \\
   =\,&
   \frac{\sin(\pi\beta)}{\pi}x^{-1+\beta}(1-x)^{-\beta}
   +
   \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{c_0 s^{\beta_k-\beta}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)\Gamma(1-\beta)}
   x^{-1+\beta_k}(1-x)^{-\beta}
   \\
   &+
   \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{s^{\beta_k}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)}
   x^{-1+\beta_k}\varepsilon_2(s-sx)
   +
   O(\varepsilon_3(s,x)),
   \quad
   \text{as $s\to0+$,}	
\end{align}
uniformly in $x\in I$ for any closed interval $I\subset (0,1)$. 
Therefore, for any closed interval $I\subset (0,1)$,
\begin{align}
	&\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}\in I\bigg)
	\\
	=\,&
	 \frac{\sin(\pi\beta)}{\pi}
	 \int_I x^{-1+\beta}(1-x)^{-\beta}\,dx
	 +
	 \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{c_0 s^{\beta_k-\beta}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)\Gamma(1-\beta)}
   \int_I x^{-1+\beta_k}(1-x)^{-\beta}\,dx 
   \\	
   &+
   \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{s^{\beta_k}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)}
   \int_I
   x^{-1+\beta_k}\varepsilon_2(s-sx)\,dx
   + 
   O\bigg(\sup_{x\in I}\varepsilon_3(s,x)\bigg),
   \quad
   \text{as $s\to0+$}.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: higher order approximation in short-range Dynkin--Lamperti theorem

body:
[Thm unstable-equiv-main of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The global $\infty$-category $\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}$ is equivariantly presentable, and the unique equivariantly cocontinuous functor $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}\to\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}$ preserving the terminal object is an equivalence.
    \begin{proof}
        The topological functor $\ensuremath{c}$ induces a global functor $\smash{{N_\textup{top}}(\textbf{\textup{Top}}^\flat)}\to\smash{{N_\textup{top}}(\cat{$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}^\flat)}$, which by Proposition~(prop:triv-ff of the paper) descends to a fully faithful and levelwise left adjoint functor $\ensuremath{c}\colon\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}\to\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}$. To complete the proof, it will now suffice to show that the essential image of the composite
        \[
            \Psi\colon\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}\xrightarrow{\;\ensuremath{c}\;}\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_\textup{gl}\xrightarrow[\smash{\raise3.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}]{\;\,\Phi\,\;}\ul\Spc_{\textup{Glo}}
        \]
        agrees with $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}\subset\ul\Spc_{\textup{Glo}}$, where $\Phi$ denotes the unique equivalence.

        To see that $\Psi$ factors through $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}$, it suffices by Elmendorf's Theorem to show that the left adjoint $\Psi_G\colon{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_G\to\ul\Spc_{\textup{Glo}}(G)$ maps $G/H$ into $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}}(G)$ for any compact Lie group $G$ and any closed subgroup $H\subset G$. To this end, let us write $i\colon H\hookrightarrow G$ for the inclusion, so that $\ensuremath{c}(G/H)\simeq\textbf{\textup{L}}i_!\ensuremath{c}(1_H)$ by Proposition~(prop:quotient-we-global of the paper) and hence $\Psi_G(G/H)=\Phi_G\textbf{\textup{L}}i_!\ensuremath{c}(1_H)=i_!\Phi_H\ensuremath{c}(1)=i_!1\in\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}(G)$.

        For the converse, note that $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}}(\mathbb B{G})\simeq\PSh({\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}_{/\mathbb B{G}})$ is generated under ordinary colimits by the objects $(i\colon H\hookrightarrow G)=i_!1_H$ for closed subgroups $H\subset G$, so that also $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}(\mathbb B{G})$ is generated by the objects $i_!1_H$. We have just seen that $\Psi_G(G/H)\simeq i_!1_H$; thus, the essential image of the fully faithful left adjoint $\Psi_G$ contains a set of generators of $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}(\mathbb B{G})$, so it already has to be all of $\ul\Spc_{{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\triangleright\textup{Glo}}(\mathbb B{G})$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm unstable-equiv-main of arXiv:2608.28504

 Suppose that  the function $\Phi_1 $ is the symbol of a bounded operator in  $L^{\infty } (\R^{4n} )$  commuting with  translations. 
Assume that the function $\Phi_2 \in C^{\infty } (\R^{4n} )$ and that, for any $\alpha\in \N^{4n}$,
   there exists a real number $A_{\alpha }$ such that, for every  $u\in\R^{4n}$,
  
   \be | \partial ^{\alpha }\Phi_2 (u) | \leq A_{\alpha } (|u|^2 +1).
  \ee
  
Also suppose that there exists $m  \in \R$  such that,  for any $u\in\R^{4n}$ large enough,
  
      \be  {\rm Re} \,\Phi_2 (u) \leq  m |u|^2 .\ee

   \be   m < \lambda,\quad 
   0 < \mu <  4 ( \lambda -m) . \ee 
   
Then, there exists an operator  $T$ bounded from $ D_{\lambda h}(\R^{4n})$ 
  into $ D_{\mu h}(\R^{4n})$ which is commuting with  translations and with  symbol equals to

[Corollary 9 (Poisson-type concentration of roots) of arXiv:2607.13210, 'Punctured Wilson--Evolving Sets and Root Identities for Massive Kirchhoff Forests'] For $U\subset V$, let $\mu_q(U):=\sum_{x\in U}\beta_q(x).$\\
For every family $(s_x)_{x\in U}$ of non-negative numbers, we have:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee\left[
    \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+s_x\1_{\{x\in\Root\}}\right)
  \right]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}(1+s_x\beta_q(x)).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, for every $\theta\geq0$, it results:
\begin{equation}
  \Ee[e^{\theta N_q(U)}]
  \leq
  \prod_{x\in U}\left(1+\beta_q(x)(e^\theta-1)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left(\mu_q(U)(e^\theta-1)\right).
\end{equation}
For every $\delta>0$, one finds:
\begin{equation}
  \Pp\left(N_q(U)\geq(1+\delta)\mu_q(U)\right)
  \leq
  \exp\left[-\mu_q(U)
  \bigl((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta\bigr)\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover, one gets:
\begin{equation*}
  \Ee[(N_q(U))_k]
  \leq
  k!\,e_k\bigl((\beta_q(x))_{x\in U}\bigr)
  \leq\mu_q(U)^k.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:reverse of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $(X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ solve (equation eq:forward of the paper) and let $\varepsilon\in(0,T)$. On
$[0,T-\varepsilon]$ set $Y_{s}:=X_{T-s}$. Then there exists a free Brownian motion
$(\bar S_{s})$, adapted to the filtration generated by $(Y_{r})_{r\le s}$, such that
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d} Y_{s}=\Big(\tfrac12\beta(T-s)\,Y_{s}-\beta(T-s)\,\xi_{\mu_{T-s}}(Y_{s})\Big)\mathrm{d} s
  +\sqrt{\beta(T-s)}\;\mathrm{d}\bar S_{s},
\end{equation}
where $\xi_{\mu_{t}}=2H\mu_{t}$ is well defined in $L^{2}$ for $t\ge\varepsilon$ by
Lemma~(lem:regularise of the paper). The spectral law of $Y_{s}$ is $\mu_{T-s}$; in particular
$\mu_{Y_{T-\varepsilon}}=\mu_{\varepsilon}\to\mu_{0}$ weakly as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

[Theorem th:ERA of arXiv:2510.10299, '\Large Sparse graphs and their Benjamini-Schramm limits: a spectral tour'] Let $d > 0$, $G$ be an Erd\H{o}s–Rényi graph on $n$ vertices and edge probability $\min(1,d/n)$. Let $\mu_1 \geq  \mu_2  \ldots   \geq \mu_n$ be the eigenvalues of its adjacency operator $A$. Then, for any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, with probability tending to one as $n \to \infty$, for all $1 \leq k \leq n^{1-\epsilon}$, we have
$$
 \ABS{ \mu_k - \sqrt{d_k} } \leq  \epsilon \sqrt{d_1} \quad \hbox{ and } \quad   \ABS{ \mu_{n+1-k} + \sqrt{d_k} }  \leq \epsilon \sqrt{d_1},
$$ 
where $d_1 \geq d_2 \geq \cdots$ is the ordered degree sequence of $G$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]

For every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.
X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed
for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable
Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case

body: Every n by n complex matrix A can be written as A = U P, where U is unitary and P is positive semidefinite Hermitian, specifically P = (A* A)^{1/2}. \[
