[Proposition prop:anchor-inputs of arXiv:2608.26765, 'Beyond Client Averaging: A Client-Independent Second-Order Stationary-Bias Component in St'] Under the matched assumptions summarized in (tab:imported-interface of the paper) and sufficiently small step size, [mangold2025scaffold] establish the following facts.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(L\arabic*)}]
  \item \textbf{Stationarity.} The joint global/control process is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with a unique stationary distribution and geometric convergence in $W_2$; see [mangold2025scaffold].
  \item \textbf{Coarse moments.} The stationary global/local iterates have coarse second moments of order $O_H(\gamma)$, the control second moments are $O_H(1)$, and Appendix~B of [mangold2025scaffold] provides coarse fourth/sixth-moment estimates for the global/local iterates. We use those iterate moment bounds, but we do \emph{not} rely on an imported control sixth-moment bound.
  \item \textbf{Control second moment.} In the one-dimensional homogeneous additive-noise specialization of [mangold2025scaffold],
  \begin{equation}
  
    Q_{\gamma,N,H}:=\frac1N\sum_{c=1}^N\mathbb{E}[\xi_c^2]
    =\frac{\sigma^2}{H}\left(1-\frac1N\right)+O_H(\gamma).
  \end{equation}
  In this homogeneous setting, the ideal controls satisfy $\xi_c^\star=-f'(0)=0$, so the squared deviation from the ideal control is the raw second moment displayed above.
  \item \textbf{Known first bias layer.} [mangold2025scaffold] prove a leading stationary bias of order $\gamma/N$ and leaves a higher-order remainder $O(\gamma^2H+\gamma^{3/2})$. In the present scalar homogeneous specialization, the leading coefficient is
  \begin{equation}
  
    -\frac{\tau\sigma^2}{4a^2}\frac{\gamma}{N}.
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 6 (Multi-group non-degenerate limit) of arXiv:2605.21155, 'Asymptotic Probabilities of Attaining the Maximum in Heterogeneous Gaussian Samples'] Assume that $n_k\to\infty$ for every $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. Then \(\boldsymbol p_n\) converges to a non-degenerate limit \(\boldsymbol p=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)\in(0,1)^K\) if and only if
\[
\boldsymbol\beta_n\to\boldsymbol C=(C_1,\ldots,C_K)\in(0,\infty)^K.
\]
Under this condition, for each \(k=1,\ldots,K\),
\[
p_k
=
\mathbb P\!\left(\sigma_k^2(\Lambda_k-\kappa(C_k,\sigma_k)) > \sigma_j^2(\Lambda_j-\kappa(C_j,\sigma_j)),\ \forall j\neq k\right),
\]
where \(\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_K\) are independent Gumbel random variables, and  \(C_1=1\) and \(\kappa(C_1,\sigma_1)=0\). Equivalently,
\[
p_k
=
\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\kappa(C_k,\sigma_k)}}{\sigma_k^2} x^{1/\sigma_k^2 - 1} \exp\left( - \sum_{j=1}^K e^{-\kappa(C_j, \sigma_j)} x^{1/\sigma_j^2} \right) \mathrm{d} x,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.
\]

[Lemma uppbdd of arXiv:2608.09465, 'Balancing fractional Brownian motion'] Let $B(t) = (B_1(t), B_2(t))^\top$ be a planar Brownian motion started from the origin with constant correlation $\rho\in (-1, 1)$. Let $\lambda_1(\rho)>0$ be the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of the negative Laplacian $(-\Delta)$ on $\mathcal R(\rho)$, where $\mathcal R(\rho)$ is defined in (equation Rrho of the paper). For $0<\varepsilon<1$,   
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}\left\{B(t)\in [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]^2, \forall t\in [0, 1]\right\} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}(1-\rho^2)^{1/4}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\lambda_1(\rho)}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}-1\right)\right\}. 
\end{align}
\begin{proof}
Let $T = \varepsilon^{-2}$. 
Denote by $W(t)$ the standard planar Brownian motion started from the origin and killed on $\partial\mathcal R(\rho)$ (see (equation Rrho of the paper) for the definition of $\mathcal R(\rho)$), and $p_t(x, y)$ the corresponding transition kernel. Let $P_t: f\mapsto \int_{\mathcal R(\rho)}f(y)p_t(x, y) \mathrm{d} y$ be the semigroup of $W_t$. Following a similar argument as in the proof of (lm:corB of the paper) and the semigroup property, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\left\{B(t)\in [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]^2, \forall t\in [0, 1]\right\}=(P_T1)(0) &= (P_1P_{T-1}1)(0)\\
&= \int_{\mathcal R(\rho)}p_1(0, y) (P_{T-1}1)(y) \mathrm{d} y\\
&\leq \|p_1(0, \cdot)\|_{L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))}\|P_{T-1}1\|_{L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))}\\
&\leq \|p_1(0, \cdot)\|_{L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))}\|P_{T-1}\|_{L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))\to L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))}|\mathcal R(\rho)|^{1/2}\\
&\leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}e^{-\lambda_1(\rho)(T-1)/2}|\mathcal R(\rho)|^{1/2}, 
\end{align*}
where the last step follows from the last inequality in (equation 2toinfty of the paper) and $\|P_{t}\|_{L^2(\mathcal R(\rho))} = e^{-\lambda_1(\rho)t/2}$ for $t>0$. 
The proof is finished by noting $|\mathcal R(\rho)|=4/\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

On one uniform bit x in {-1, 1}, let 1 < p < q < infinity, rho in [-1, 1], T_rho the noise operator (T_rho x = rho x) and f_eps = 1 + eps x. Then log(||T_rho f_eps||_q/||f_eps||_p) = ((q - 1) rho^2 - (p - 1)) eps^2/2 + ((p - 1)(p^2 + p - 3) - (q - 1)(q^2 + q - 3) rho^4) eps^4/12 + O(eps^6) as eps -> 0. So if rho^2 > (p - 1)/(q - 1), small eps != 0 give ||T_rho f||_q > ||f||_p; if rho^2 < (p - 1)/(q - 1) the ratio is below 1 to second order; and at rho^2 = (p - 1)/(q - 1) the quartic coefficient equals (p - 1)(p - q)(pq - p - q + 2)/(12 (q - 1)) < 0, a strict local contraction.

body:
Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set, d = d_TV(p, q), A = {x : p(x) > q(x)} and B = {x : q(x) > p(x)}. The maximal coupling, a coupling with P(X != Y) = d, is unique if and only if d = 0, or d > 0 and |A| = 1 or |B| = 1. When d > 0 and both A and B have at least two points there are infinitely many maximal couplings.

Method: Transform asymptotics, exact special case, coupling reduction or identifiability check Result: Consider iid job marks taking two values with equal probability. A job has first-node service requirement B=1 or B=3. In model A only the B=3 jobs are routed downstream; in model B only B=1 jobs are routed downstream. Both models have the same marginal service distribution and the same routing probability 1/2. But E[B*R] is 3/2 in A and 1/2 in B, and Cov(B,R) is respectively 1/2 and -1/2. Marginal service and routing data thus do not identify the marked flow dependence entering a downstream approximation. Check: E B=2 and E R=1/2 in both examples, so subtracting their product one gives the two covariance signs. The examples use legal iid per-job marks; no independence between B and R was assumed. Obstruction: Need a marked or class-resolved closure and bounds for its error. The scalar marginal primitives alone cannot recover this cross moment.

body: [Corollary 5 of arXiv:2504.16254, 'New bounds on the modularity of $G(n,p)$'] Let n ∈N, p = p(n) ∈(0, 1] and let G(n, p) be a binomial random graph. Set d = d(n) = np and assume that d ≫(ln n)2. Then with high probability mod(G(n, p)) ≤(1 + o(1)) 4 √ d . The 1/ √ d growth rate of mod(G(n, p)) when d is above 1 and not too big was first conjectured in 2006 by Reichardt and Bornholdt [25]. In 2020 McDiarmid and Skerman formally confirmed it proving the following result.
title: Corollary 5 of arXiv:2504.16254: New bounds on the modularity of $G(n,p)$

[Theorem thm:finite of arXiv:2608.09368, 'A proof of Ross's conjecture for two-site moving-target search'] Under the strict-interior positive-determinant assumptions, for every
$n\ge1$ the first-stage minimiser for $V_n$ admits a monotone threshold
stage selector.  Choosing such a selector $\mu_m$ whenever $m$ searches
remain gives an optimal finite-horizon policy whose decision at every
stage is threshold in the current belief.  Equivalently, the first-stage
action differential satisfies
\begin{equation}
 p<p',
 \qquad D_n(p)<0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 D_n(p')\le0.
 
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:burning-inf of arXiv:2605.19419, 'Tail exponents of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree and Abelian sandpile'] Assume $d\ge3$. For every $R\ge1$ and every integer $n\ge2$,
\begin{align}
\mathbf{P}\bigl(\mathrm{diam}_{\mathrm{ext}}(W_{1}(H))\ge R\bigr)
&=G(0,0)\,\mathbb{P}_{0}\bigl(\mathrm{diam}_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathfrak{T})\ge R\bigr),\\
\mathbf{P}\bigl(|W_{1}(H)|\ge n\bigr)
&=G(0,0)\,\mathbb{P}_{0}\bigl(|\mathfrak{T}|\ge n\bigr).
\end{align}
More generally, the same identity holds for every continuity event $\mathcal{A}$ of finite vertex sets such that every set in $\mathcal{A}$ contains a nearest neighbour of $0$.

body:
[Theorem thm:arbitrary-proper-blowup of arXiv:2608.20480, 'When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone \\ Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification'] Let $F:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)$ be nondecreasing.  There exist a universal constant $\varepsilon_0>0$ and a countable, closed class $\mathcal{H}_F$ of finite coordinatewise range such that
\[
    N^{\mathrm{prop}}_{\mathrm{iid}}(\varepsilon_0,\delta;\mathcal{H}_F)
    =
    \Theta\!\left(\log\frac1\delta\right),
    \qquad
    N^{\mathrm{imp}}_{\mathrm{ad}}(\varepsilon_0,\delta;\mathcal{H}_F)
    =
    \Theta\!\left(\log\frac1\delta\right),
\]
whereas $N^{\mathrm{prop}}_{\mathrm{obl}}(\varepsilon_0,\delta;\mathcal{H}_F)\geq F(1/\delta)$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$.  Nevertheless, $\mathcal{H}_F$ remains properly PAC learnable against arbitrary adaptive additions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

 =1.77629988\ldots .

Method: Invariant ergodicity does not imply component indistinguishability Result: Construct a periodic forest on Z^2 using blocks of four horizontal rows. The first row is a bi-infinite horizontal path. The next three rows form a comb: the middle row is a horizontal spine, with each vertex in the two outer rows attached vertically to that spine. Repeat and choose a uniformly random vertical phase. The law is translation invariant and ergodic on its finite phase orbit, yet its components are distinguishable as lines and combs by the existence of degree-four vertices. Check: Every vertex belongs to exactly one component and there are no cycles. If full square-lattice automorphism invariance is desired, also choose a uniform horizontal/vertical orientation; the full automorphism group is transitive on the resulting finite orbit. Obstruction: This is not a minimal-spanning-forest construction. It disproves only the shortcut from invariance and ergodicity to indistinguishability.

[Theorem 14 (Strict radial maximum at uniform) of arXiv:2606.29635, 'Extremality and Limit Laws for the Siblings of the Coupon Collector'] Fix $N\ge2$ and $j\ge2$. Let
\[
        \Phi_j(p)=\E_pU_j^N,
        \qquad u=(1/N,\ldots,1/N).
\]
For every nonuniform probability vector $p$, the map
\[
        \theta\mapsto \Phi_j(u+\theta(p-u))
\]
is strictly decreasing on $(0,1]$. Consequently,
\[
        \Phi_j(p)<\Phi_j(u)
\]
for every nonuniform $p$.

body:
[Proposition 37 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ with $\alpha + \beta/2>1$. Suppose for some $K \geq 1$ and
        \[0 \leq \lambda < \frac{\beta}{2-\alpha} \land \Big( 1- \frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}\Big),\]
    we have that for all $j \in \N, n \in \{0,1,2\}, p \geq 1$,
    \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \mathcal{C}^0_{t,x}} \leq K p^\lambda 2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]   
    Then there exists $\delta(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)>0$ and  $C(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)>0$ such that for all $N \in \N$, there exists a random field $M^N : \T^d \to [0,\infty)$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
         For all $p \geq 1$ and $t \geq 2,$
        $\P(\|M^N\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_y} \geq t) \leq  C e^{C p^C K^C} (\log t)^{-p}$,
        \item 
        for all $p \geq 1$, $\|M^N\|_{L^p_\omega L^p_y} \leq C e^{Cp^C K^C}$,
        \item 
        
        and for any $y,z \in \T^d$, any $w \in \mathcal{C}^{1/2 + \delta}([0,1])$ with $w_0 =0$, if we let $X_t = \Phi^N_t(y)$, and take the solution $\tilde X$ to 
          \begin{equation}
         
         \tilde X_t=z+\int_0^t U^N(s,\tilde X_s)\,ds+w_t,\qquad t\in[0,1],
         \end{equation}
         then we have the stability estimate on the time interval $[0,1]$,
         \[\|X - \tilde X\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1/2 +\delta}_t} \leq M^N(y)\big(|y-z| + \|w\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1/2+\delta}_t}\big),\]
         and the expansion/compression estimate for all $t\in[0,1]$
         \[ \frac{1}{M^N(y)}|y-z|-\|w\|_{C^{1/2+\delta}_t}\leq |X_t-\tilde X_t|\leq M^N(y)\big(|y-z|+\|w\|_{C^{1/2+\delta}_t}\big).\]
    \end{enumerate}

body:
[Lemma L:bernstein-conditional-complex of arXiv:2607.15966, 'Canonical Mandelbrot Cascades on Curves Are Rajchman'] Let
\(
        \mathcal{G}\subset\mathcal{F}
\)
be a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra, and let
\(
        X_1,\ldots,X_N
\)
be square-integrable complex-valued random variables which are conditionally independent given \(\mathcal{G}\).  
Suppose that
\[
        \mathbb{E}
        \left(
        X_k
        \,\middle|\,
        \mathcal{G}
        \right)
        =
        0
        \qquad\text{almost surely}
\]
for every \(1\leq k\leq N\).

Assume that there exist finite nonnegative \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variables \(R\) and \(V\) such that
\[
        |X_k|\leq R
        \qquad\text{almost surely for every }1\leq k\leq N,
\]
and
\[
        \sum_{k=1}^{N}
        \mathbb{E}
        \left(
        |X_k|^2
        \,\middle|\,
        \mathcal{G}
        \right)
        \leq V
        \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Then there exist absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(t>0\),
\[
        \mathbb{P}
        \left(
        \left|
        \sum_{k=1}^{N}X_k
        \right|
        \geq t
        \,\middle|\,
        \mathcal{G}
        \right)
        \leq
        C
        \exp
        \left(
        -\frac{ct^2}{V+Rt}
        \right)
        \qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] Let $A\in\mathcal M_+$.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item
		If $A$ has a zero entry, then 
		\[
		A\in\T\Longleftrightarrow G(A)\geq0.
		\]
		In that case $A\in R_5$, and $G(A)=0$ implies $A\in R_4$.
		
		\item
		If $A>0$, then $A\in\V$ if and only if $\max_{i,j}V_{ij}(A)\geq0$.
		More generally, if $A\in \mathcal M_+$, then
		\[
		A\in\T\cup\V
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\max_{i,j}V_{ij}(A)\geq0.
		\]
		
		\item
		If $A\notin\T\cup\V$, then $A\in\NH$ if and only if, for some
		ordered pair $(i,j)$ with $i\neq j$, the quadratic $q_{ij}^A$
		has a root in $[0,C_{ij}(A)]$.
	
		
		\item
		One has
		\[
		R_6=\T\cup\V\cup\NH.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}

		\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition DPP of arXiv:2605.12777, 'Mesoscopic Rates of Convergence for Complex Wishart Matrices at the Leftmost Spectrum Edge'] A point process (PP) $\mathfrak{X}$ in a locally compact Polish space $\Lambda$ is a random discrete subset of $\Lambda$. For any $A\subset\Lambda$,  $\mathcal{N}_\mathfrak{X}(A)$ denotes the number of points of $\mathfrak{X}$ in $A$. The integer-valued random function: $A\rightarrow\mathcal{N}_\mathfrak{X}(A)$
is called the \textbf{counting function} of $\mathfrak{X}$.
title: Definition DPP of arXiv:2605.12777

body: Intermediate value theorem: Let f be a real-valued function that is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] with a < b, and let u be any number between f(a) and f(b). Then there exists a point c in [a, b] with f(c) = u; if u lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then c may be taken in the open interval (a, b). Equivalently, the image f([a, b]) of an interval under a continuous real function is again an interval, and it contains every value between f(a) and f(b).
title: Intermediate value theorem

[Defn 12 of arXiv:2605.30779, '2605.30779'] Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb C\) be an open set, and let \( \{ f_N \}^{\infty}_{N = 1} \) and \(f\) be meromorphic functions on \(\Omega\). We write
  \[
    f_N\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mer}} f
    \qquad\text{on }\Omega
  \]
  if, for every compact set \(K\subset\Omega\) containing no pole of \(f\), there exists \(N_0=N_0(K)\) such that \(K\) contains no pole of \(f_N\) for all \(N\ge N_0\), and
\[
\sup_{z\in K}|f_N(z)-f(z)|\to0
\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty .
\]
title: Definition 12 of arXiv:2605.30779

For a = (alpha,beta) in F_2^t x F_2^t the Walsh transform factors as (Hv)_a = prod_{i=1}^t sum_{u,w in F_2} (-1)^{uw + alpha_i u + beta_i w}, which lies in {+-2^t} (41). [Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.30030, 'Critical exponents for planar random-cluster model with cluster-weight~$q=4$'] There exists~$c >0$ such that the following holds. 
	For any~$R > r > \delta$ and
	any events~$A$ and~$B$ depending on the edges in~$\Lambda^\delta_{r}$ and outside~$\Lambda^\delta_{R}$, respectively, 
	\begin{align}
	\big|\tfrac{\rcP[A \cap B]}{\rcP[A]\rcP[B]}-1\big| \le c \Delta^\delta(r,R).
	\end{align}
	For any~$r_1,r_2 > \delta$ with~$r_1 + r_2 \leq |x|/2$, 
	and any events~$A$ and~$B$ depending on the edges in~$\Lambda^\delta_{r_1}$ and~$\Lambda^\delta_{r_2}(x)$, respectively, 
	\begin{align}
	\big|\tfrac{\rcP[A \cap B]}{\rcP[A]\rcP[B]}-1\big|\le c \Delta^\delta(r_1,|x|) \Delta^\delta(r_2,|x|).
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 10 of arXiv:2609.01851, 'Minimum Weakly Saturated Graphs and Bootstrap Percolation in General Host Graphs'] Suppose that $n$ and $m$ are integers with $1\leq n \leq m$. If $S(n,m)\not\in \{S(1,1), S(1,2)\}$, then $S(n,m)$ self-percolates to $K_{m+n+2+q}$ if and only if $n\leq2$ and $q>0$. The $S(n,m)$-percolation is accomplished in $k\leq 4$ rounds.

[Prop censor of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Fix $t\geqslant0$. On $\{\tau_{\mathrm{col}}>t\}$, the following statements hold.
\begin{enumeratei}
\item $\mathcal{A}_1(t)\cap\mathcal{A}_2(t)=\varnothing$.
\item If $u\in\mathcal{A}_1(t)$, $v\in\mathcal{A}_2(t)$, and
$\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}$, then the edge $\{u,v\}$ lies on no geodesic
from $0$ to a vertex of $\mathcal{A}_1(t)$ and on no geodesic from $U_n$ to a
vertex of $\mathcal{A}_2(t)$.
\item For $i=1,2$,
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q)=\mathcal{A}_i(q),
 \qquad 0\leqslant q\leqslant t.
\end{align*}
Consequently, $\widehat \mathsf{T}_i(v)=\mathsf{T}_i(v)$ for every $v\in\mathcal{A}_i(t)$.
\end{enumeratei}

Let $\mathbb Q_{\mathfrak h}^{(-)}$ be the sub-probability measure on $\Phi^-$

We similarly denote by $\widehat{\mathbb Q}_{\mathfrak h}^{(+)}$
the law of $\{\Phi^-(-\,\cdot)\}$, and define the product measure
\[
\widecheck \mathbb Q_{\mathfrak h}(\widecheck\Phi):=\widehat{\mathbb Q}_{\mathfrak h}^{(-)}(\Phi^-)\widehat{\mathbb Q}_{\mathfrak h}^{(+)}(\Phi^+)\mathbb Q_\star(\Phi^o) \,.
\]

[Prop 75 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Let $\phi \in \B(\A,\rmM_k)_+$ be positive definite.
\begin{itemize}
\item[a.] We have $\rmh^\ann_{\bspi}(\phi) \le \log \det \phi(1)$. In particular, if $\phi(1)$ is singular, then $\rmh^\ann_{\bspi}(\phi) = -\infty$.
\item[b.] If $Q$ is an invertible $k$-by-$k$ matrix and
\[\psi(a) := (Q^\rm{T})^\ast \phi(a) Q^\rm{T} \qquad (a \in \A),\]
then
\[\rmh^\ann_{\bspi}(\psi) = 2\log|\det Q| + \rmh^\ann_{\bspi}(\phi).\]
The analogous formula holds if $\rmh^\ann_{\bspi}$ is replaced by $\ul{\rmh}^\ann_{\bspi}$ on both sides.
\end{itemize}

[Theorem thm:N-symmetrisation of arXiv:2607.14266, 'The Swapping Mechanism for Interacting Diffusions: Framework, Comparison with Switching, a'] Let $(\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_t,\Lambda_t)$ be the switching process with
		generator (equation eq:gen-sw-N-final of the paper) and initial condition
		$(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathrm{id})$. Then
		$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_t:=\Lambda_t^{-1}\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_t$ is the
		unique $N$-particle swapping process with generator $\mathcal{L}_N$ and
		initial value $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}_0=\mathbf{x}_0$; in particular
		$\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}$ has the same law as $\mathbf{X}$.
		Consequently, if $p(t,\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y})$ denotes the transition
		density of the swapping process and
		$p_\theta(t,\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y})$, $\theta\in\mathfrak{S}_N$, the
		density of the switching process conditioned on starting in regime
		$\theta_0=\mathrm{id}$ and being in regime $\theta$ at time $t$, then
		for every $t>0$ and $\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y}\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^N$,
		\begin{equation}
			p(t,\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y})
			= \sum_{\theta\in\mathfrak{S}_N}
			p_\theta\bigl(t,\mathbf{x}_0,\theta^{-1}\mathbf{y}\bigr),
		\end{equation}
		where $(\theta^{-1}\mathbf{y})^i=y^{\theta(i)}$.

[Lemma lemq of arXiv:2411.03942, 'Asymptotic expansions relating to the distribution of the product of correlated normal ran'] Let $a,A,z>0$ and $b,m\in\mathbb{R}$. Let $g:(0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $g(x)=O(x^{-1/2})$ as $x\rightarrow\infty$.  Consider the equation
\begin{equation}Ax^m\mathrm{e}^{-ax+b\sqrt{x}}\big(1+g(x)\big)=z,
\end{equation}
and notice that there is a unique solution $x$ provided $z$ is sufficiently small. Then, as $z\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}x&=\frac{1}{a}\ln(1/z)+\frac{b}{a^{3/2}}\sqrt{\ln(1/z)}+\frac{m}{a}\ln(\ln(1/z))+\frac{b^2}{4a^2}+\frac{\ln(A/a^m)}{a}\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{bm}{2a^{3/2}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/z))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/z)}}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/z)}}\bigg).
\end{align}
In the case $b=0$ and $g(x)=O(x^{-1})$ as $x\rightarrow\infty$, the error in the asymptotic approximation ((lemqeqn of the paper)) is of the smaller order $O(1/\ln(1/z))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lemq of arXiv:2411.03942

body:
[Proposition 1 (Standard asymptotic characterization) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Assume the rows $\bx_i\in\C^{p}$ are i.i.d., centered (i.e., $\E[\bx_i] =\bzero$), and isotropic
(i.e., $\E[\bx_i\bx_i^*] = \bI_p$). Assume further that there exists 
$\sfK \in (0,\infty)$
such that, for each $i\in[n]$, all deterministic $\bA\in \C^{p\times p}$, and all $t>0$,

\begin{equation}

   \P\Big( \big|\bx_i^*\bA \bx_i - \Tr(\bA)\big| \ge t \Big)
   \le
   2 \exp\bigg\{-c \min\bigg(\frac{t^2}{\sfK^4 \|\bA\|_\Fnorm^2},\, 
   \frac{t}{\sfK^2 \|\bA\|_\op}\bigg)\bigg\}\, ,
\end{equation}
for some universal constant $c>0$, where $\|\bA\|_\Fnorm$ and $\|\bA\|_\op$ denote 
the Frobenius and operator norms of $\bA$, respectively.
Fix integer $k\ge 1$, $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ and
let $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
Define
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) := \int  \bT(\bI + \bS\bT)^{-1} \nu(\de \bT) - \frac1\alpha\bS^{-1},\quad\quad \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}:\C^{k\times k} \to\C^{k\times k}.
\end{equation}

For any $z \in\bbH_+$, there exists a unique 
solution 
$\bS_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z)$
to
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) = z\bI,\quad\quad \bS\in\bbH_+^k := \{\bB\in \C^{k\times k}: \Im(\bB) \succ\bzero\}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
    \begin{equation}
        s_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z) := 
         \frac{\alpha}{k} \Tr(\bS_\up{\alpha,\nu}(z))\quad\quad\textrm{for}\quad z\in\bbH_+
    \end{equation}
is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure 
$\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu}\in\cuP(\R)$ such that, almost surely
\begin{equation}
    \hmu_{\bW_k} \Rightarrow \mu_\up{\alpha,\nu} \quad\quad \textrm{almost surely, as} \quad\quad n\to\infty,\;\frac{n}{p} \to\alpha,
\end{equation}
where $\hmu_{\bW_k}$ is the empirical spectral distribution of $\bW_k$ and $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence of probability measures.

Finally, if $\dist(\{\bT_i:i\le n\},\supp(\nu))\to 0$ (with $\dist$ denoting
Hausdorff distance between sets in $(\reals^k,\|\,\cdot\,\|$), then,
almost surely,

\begin{align}
\dist\big(\supp(\hmu_{\bW_k}),\supp (\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu})\big) \to 0\, .
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Standard asymptotic characterization

body:
[Proposition 38 (MTP for the marked Poisson point process) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}$ be the marked Poisson point process on $X$ with intensity $\lambda \, {\rm vol}$ for some $\lambda>0$.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}_o={\bf Y}^{(\lambda)} \cup \{\mathbf o\}$, where~$\mathbf o$ is equipped with an independent ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$-mark.
Then
\begin{equation*} 
\mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(o,Y^{(\lambda)}_i,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg] = \mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(Y^{(\lambda)}_i,o,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg]
\end{equation*}
for every measurable $F : X\times X\times \mathbf M(X\times[0,1]) \to [0,\infty]$ such that 
$$
F(\tau(x),\tau(y),\tau \circ \overline \eta) = F(x,y, \overline \eta)
$$
for every $\overline\eta \in\mathbf M(X\times[0,1])$ and every $x,y\in X$ and $\tau\in{\rm Isom}(X)$ which interchanges $x$ and $y$.

body:
[Lemma omega-oo-both-adjoints of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The evaluation functor $\Omega^\infty\coloneqq\ev_0\colon{\mathpalette\ulhelper{{\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{lvl}\to\ul{{\mathfrak S\kern-.4pt}}_{\textup{gl},*}$ admits both a fully faithful left adjoint $\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty$ as well as a fully faithful right adjoint.
    \begin{proof}
        The existence of the right adjoint is a special case of Lemma~(lemma:ev-V-param-la of the paper). For the existence of the left adjoint, observe that $\ev_0\colon\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}_*$ is right Quillen by Lemma~(lemma:ev-RA of the paper), with left adjoint given by the usual suspension spectrum functor. It then only remains to verify the Beck--Chevalley condition. Unravelling definitions, this amounts to showing that for any $\alpha\colon G\to G'$, any cofibrant $X\in\cat{$\bm{G'}$-$\textbf{\textup{ L}}$-Top}_*$ and any cofibrant replacement $f\colon Y\to \alpha^*X$, the induced map $\Sigma^\infty f\colon \Sigma^\infty Y\to \Sigma^\infty \alpha^*X$ is a $G$-global level weak equivalence, i.e.\ for every $V$ the map $S^V\smashp f$ is an $(O(V)\times G)$-global weak equivalence. This is however simply an instance of Corollary~(cor:global-smash-well-based of the paper).

        Finally, it is clear that the ordinary unit $X\to\Omega^\infty \Sigma^\infty X$ is an isomorphism for every (cofibrant) $X$; thus, the derived unit $\textup{id}\to\Omega^\infty\,\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty$ is invertible, i.e.\ $\textbf{\textup{L}}\Sigma^\infty$ is fully faithful. 
        It follows formally (see e.g.~[haine2025fullyfaithfulfunctorspushouts]*{Lemma 1.2}) that the right adjoint of $\Omega^\infty$ is also fully faithful.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:prefix-free-ball-code-dimension of arXiv:2608.29561, 'Ball codes: A coding characterization of Hausdorff and packing dimensions'] Let \(\varphi\) be a prefix-free ball code.
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\in\omega\), define
\[
K_\varphi(x;r)
=
\min
\left\{
|p|
:
p\in\dom(\varphi),
x\in \varphi(p),
\ \diam(\varphi(p))\le 2^{-r}
\right\},
\]
with the convention that \(K_\varphi(x;r)=\infty\) if no such \(p\) exists.
Define
\[
\dim_\varphi(x)
=
\liminf_{r\to\infty}
\frac{K_\varphi(x;r)}{r}.
\]
Finally, for nonempty \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\dim_\varphi(E)
=
\sup_{x\in E}\dim_\varphi(x).
\]

body: In mathematics, a self-avoiding walk (SAW) is a sequence of moves on a lattice that does not visit the same point more than once. This is a special case of the graph theoretical notion of a path. A self-avoiding polygon (SAP) is a closed self-avoiding walk on a lattice. Very little is known rigorously about the self-avoiding walk from a mathematical perspective, although physicists have provided numerous conjectures that are believed to be true and are strongly supported by numerical simulations.

Let tau be uniform on [T,2T], T>0, and let A and B be products of at most r prime factors each, all primes <=y, y>=2. For A=B, E exp(-i tau log(A/B))=1. For A!=B its modulus is at most min(1,2/(T |log(A/B)|))<=min(1,2 y^r/T). Independent Haar phases at the primes have the same expectation 1 when A=B and 0 otherwise. Thus for a finite polynomial in these phases and their conjugates with such monomials and coefficient absolute sum M, the time-average versus Haar moment error is at most 2 M y^r/T. This is a sufficient fixed-moment approximation window, not a necessary condition and not a decomposition theorem for log|zeta|.

body:
[Lemma lem:internalcutpoint of arXiv:2608.23135, 'Graph distance and effective resistance of the random walk trace in four and five dimensio'] Let $(j,k)\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{RW}}$.  Suppose that
\[
   [u_{j-1},u_{j+2}]\subset I_a,
   \qquad [u_{k-2},u_{k+1}]\subset I_b.
\]
Let $\widetilde A_{j,k}$ be the event that there exist times
$L_j^+\in [u_{j+1},u_{j+2}]$ and $L_k^-\in [u_{k-3},u_{k-2}]$ such that
\begin{equation*}

        S[t_{a-1},L_j^+]\cap S[L_j^++1,t_a]=\emptyset,
        \qquad
        S[t_{b-1},L_k^-]\cap S[L_k^-+1,t_b]=\emptyset .
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, $L_j^+$ and $L_k^-$ are local cut times for the full macro blocks
$I_a=[t_{a-1},t_a]$ and $I_b=[t_{b-1},t_b]$, respectively.
Then
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\exists (j,k)\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{RW}}:\widetilde A_{j,k}^c\bigr)
\le C\frac{(\log\log n)^{C_0}}{\log n}.
\end{equation}

[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2609.03403, 'Hyperpositive functions, sector bounded functions and a trace formula'] Let $T>0$ be such that $(T^{-1}+tT)>0$ and $F$ and $\sigma$ be related by \eqref{repre-321-11}. Then,
          \[
\det\sigma(z)\not\equiv0\quad\iff\quad \det (I_m-F(z)T)\not\equiv 0.
            \]
            When this condition is in force, one can extend $F$ to $\Omega(\sigma)$ (defined by \eqref{omega-g} with $G=\sigma$) by
            \begin{equation}
              F(-\overline{z})^*=-(I_m-F(z)T)^{-1}(F(z)+T)
          \end{equation}
  With $F$ so extended, formula \eqref{isolate-1} holds in $\Omega(\sigma)$. Denoting by $\mathfrak H_{ext}(F)$ the reproducing kernel space with reproducing kernel $K_{T,t}(z,w)$
  extended to $\Omega(\sigma)$, the map
\[
  f\mapsto (T^{-1}+tT)^{1/2}f
\]
is unitary from $\mathcal H_{ext}(\sigma)$ onto  $\mathfrak H_{ext}(F)$.
title: Proposition 22 of arXiv:2609.03403

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2609.02808, 'Minimizers of Laplace eigenvalues under a lower curvature bound'] Let $k\ge2$ and let $(g_n)\subset\Cc$ satisfy
$\Area(\Sph^2,g_n)\to0$. Then
\begin{equation}
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\lambda_k(\Sph^2,g_n)
\ge k(k+1)>\lambda_k(\Sph^2).
\end{equation}
Consequently, no minimizing sequence for $f_k$ collapses.

body:
[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\lambda>0$, and $p\geq 1$, and let, for all $j\geq 0$, $u^j$ be defined by~\eqref{eq:autonomous poisson}. Suppose there exists $M\geq 1$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $y\in\T^d,$
\[\|\nabla^n f^j_y\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq M 2^{(n-\alpha-d/p)j}.\]
Then 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the $u^j$ are mutually independent with $\E u^j =0$,
\item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite spatial range of dependence $2^{-j}$,
\item and there exists a constant $C(d)>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$ and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq CM(\lambda+p)2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate}
Letting $U:=\sum_{j= 0}^\infty u^j$, we further have that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] if for all $j\geq 0$ and $y\in\T^d$, $\nabla\cdot f^j_y=0$, then $\nabla\cdot U=0$,
    \item[(ii)] if there exists $r\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$
    \begin{equation}
    \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\T^d\\d_{\T^d}(x,y)\leq 2^{-(j+2)}}}\bigg\|\frac{d\mu^j_{y,x}(z)}{dz}\bigg\|_{L^\infty(\R^d)}\leq Cr^j e^{\lambda j},
    \end{equation}
    then it almost surely holds that for all $\alpha'<\alpha$
    \[\lim_{\eps\rightarrow 0} \eps^{-\alpha'd}|Z_\eps|=0,\]
    where $Z_\eps$ is defined as in~\eqref{eq:zero sets}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.05931

$$q_\mu(x)\geq C\sqrt{s}\,e^{-\Lambda_\mu^*(x)},\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}(K).$$

body: [Definition def:polyhom-germ-comp of arXiv:2609.00698, 'Kinetic Wedge Layers and Diffusive Limit of Neutron Transport in Polygonal Domains'] Let $\sigma\in\mathbb R$. An $X$-valued $F$ has a finite polyhomogeneous germ through degree $\sigma$ if $F(s)=\sum_{(\lambda,b)\in I_\sigma}s^\lambda(\ln s)^bF_{\lambda,b}+\mathcal R_\sigma(s)$ with $I_\sigma\subset\{(\lambda,b):\lambda<\sigma,\ b\in\mathbb N_0\}$ finite, $F_{\lambda,b}\in X$ and $\mathcal R_\sigma\in\mathcal C^{q,\gamma}_{\sigma,B}(0,\ell_{\mathrm{vtx}};X)$ for the stated $q,\gamma,B$. Terms with equal $\lambda$ group into a polynomial in $\ln s$, and two germs are identified when their displayed coefficients agree, equivalently when their difference lies in that residual class at degree $\sigma$.

The inequality $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\|f\|_p$, $\frac1p+\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\le p\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\|\hat f\|_\infty\le\|f\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\mathbb T$, $L^p\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\mathbb T$ with $\sum_n|\hat f(n)|^q=\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\|\hat f\|_{\ell^{p'}}\le C\|f\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\hat f\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\|f\|_{p'}\le\|\hat f\|_p$ for $1\le p\le2$. (iv) On $\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\big)^{d/2}\|f\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\mathbb T$ and $\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] When flipping a biased coin, with the probabilities being
$$P({\rm heads})=p\quad,\quad P({\rm tails})=1-p$$
with $p\in[0,1]$, your winning law, for heads, is the following probability measure,
$$b_p=(1-p)\delta_0+p\delta_1$$
called Bernoulli law of parameter $p\in[0,1]$.

body:
[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2506.15159, 'Conditional central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] For $W$ and $Y=\t E$ in \cref{20001}, 
    
    
    
    
    we have (recall \cref{eq:Mlpm})
    \begin{align}
       M_{0,\pm}(W,\t E)&=\t p\,\t q +R_{0,\pm},\\
     M_{1,+}(W,\t E)&=-\lambda \left( \alpha_+ W+R_{1,+}\right),\notag\\
      M_{1,-}(W,\t E)&=-\lambda \left( \alpha_- W+R_{1,-}\right),\notag\\
      M_{2,\pm}(W,\t E)&=\lambda(1+R_{2,\pm}),\notag
    \end{align}
where $\lambda=(2(1-2\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}\t q))/N$, $\Delta W=O_r(n^{-1}),$
\begin{align*}
     a_+=&\frac{\t p-2\t q^2\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_l s_l\t p^{e_l-1}}{1-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}}, \quad a_{-}=\frac{\t q-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_l s_l\t p^{e_l}}{1-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}},
     \\
     R_{0,\pm}=&O_{r}(n^{-1}),\quad R_{1,+}=O_{r}(n^{\frac{1}{2}}),\quad R_{1,-}=O_{r}(n^{\frac{1}{2}}),\quad
     R_{1,+}+R_{1,-}=O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
    \t R_{1,+}=&R_{1,+}-\E R_{1,+}=O(n^{-\frac{1}{2}})\t E+O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
    \t R_{1,-}=&R_{1,-}-\E R_{1,-}=O(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}) \t E+O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
     R_{2,+}=&O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\quad R_{2,-}=O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}).
\end{align*}
Hereafter, for convenience, we use $O_{r}(h)$ in an unconventional way to denote some random variable $X$ such that the $L^r$ norm $\|X/h\|_r\leq C_r$ for any given $r\geq 1$ and a constant $C_r$ depending only on $r$ and the subset $B$ of the subcritical region considered in \cref{thm:twostar}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 16 of arXiv:2603.26936, 'Sharp Riemannian heat kernel estimates on the cut locus and the Parabolic Anderson model'] Let $\alpha\in \left(\frac{d-2}{2},\frac{d}{2}\right)$ and $C$ be the constant from Theorem \ref{thm: L1 bd}. Recall the definition of $R^n$ from \eqref{quotient bound by G f}, and define a sequence of functions $k^n$ on $\R_+$ by \begin{align*}
        k^n(s):=&k^n_L(s)+k^n_S(s),\quad\text{where}\\
        k^n_L(s):=&\sup_{x,x'\in M}\iint_{M^2}  [G^{[n]}_s(x,z)+1][G^{[n]}_s(x',z')+1]\bm{d}(z,z')^{2\alpha-d}m(dz)m(dz'),\\
        k^n_S(s):=&\sup_{t\geq 2s}\sup_{x_0,x,x_0',x'\in M}\iint_{M^2}R^n_{t,x_0,x,x_0',x'}(s,z,z')\bm{d}(z,z')^{2\alpha-d}m(dz)m(dz').
    \end{align*}
    For a constant $C_M$ independent of $n$, these satisfy
    \[k^n(s)\leq C_M(1+s^{\frac{2\alpha-d}{2}}).\]
    Then, define iteratively another sequence of functions $h_n$ on $\R_+$ by \[ h_0(t)=1,\quad h_{n+1}(t):=\int_0^t h_n(t-s)k^n(s)ds.\]
    For all $n\geq 0$, $h_n$ is non-negative and non-decreasing. Furthermore, for all $n\geq 1$ and $x_0,x,x_0',x'\in M$, we have \[ \mathcal{L}_n(t,x_0,x,x_0',x')\leq (2C)^n[G^{[[n+1]}_t(d(x_0,x))+1][G^{[n+1]}_t(d(x_0',x'))+1]h_n(t).\]

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.11801, 'A non-local singular non-linear Fokker-Planck PDE'] Let $h$ be a vector-valued function
  in $C_TC_b^{2}(\R^d)$, $\eta_0\in L^1\cap
C_b^3(\R^d)$ be a non-negative function. 
 Let $\eta\in C_T\shc^{\beta}$ be the unique solution in the sense of  Definition   \ref{def:WsolFP}, 
ensured by Theorem~\ref{thm:exunlinFP}, 
to 
\begin{equation}
   \partial_t \eta =\frac12\Delta \eta -{\rm div}(\eta(s)h(s)),\ \eta(0)=\eta_0.
   \end{equation}
   Then 
    $\eta(t) \ge 0$
   and  $\|\eta(t)\|_{L^1}=
   \|\eta_0\|_{L^1}$,
   for all $t\in[0,T]$.

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0007-C006 v1; audits w667:PASS. For 0<epsilon<1/2 and 0<p<1, F=(1-p)Uniform[0,epsilon]+p Uniform[1-epsilon,1] is n-CM for every integer n>=ceil(2/epsilon). Two possible high-label counts are coupled to conditional upper/lower interval tilts. Bayes weights restore the original uniforms, and the established joint monotone-density criterion gives a constant-sum coupling in each label-count state. This is a special nonsymmetric disconnected-support family, not general D0007.

0<p<1
n integer >=ceil(2/epsilon)
Wang-Wang joint monotone-density criterion as cited at survey Section 2.2(e)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9e0ae1df27dcabbbb04579f088cec4b4ecf68418160f55e5e678e32b83b3c6e1","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9e/9e0ae1df27dcabbbb04579f088cec4b4ecf68418160f55e5e678e32b83b3c6e1.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:ee315ecb56d1ad5e56ba8feed309dfa55095c5eab85af324e2035d4700c6cf23","bundle_entry_key":"two-uniform","bundle_id":"population.finite-uniform-mixtures-counted-monotone-tilts-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; constant-sum couplings","draft":"w662/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.complete_mixability:two-separated-uniforms-eventual-complete-mixability-w662","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# D0007-C006 v1: Two separated equal-width uniforms are eventually completely mixable
Status: proof (unaudited). Uses the Wang-Wang monotone-density joint mixability theorem; special case only. Novelty not asserted.

For 0<epsilon<1/2 and 0<p<1, let F=(1-p)Uniform[0,epsilon]+p Uniform[1-epsilon,1]. Then F is n-CM for every integer n>=ceil(2/epsilon), regardless of p. This covers a nonsymmetric disconnected-support family where the global density-floor theorem is unavailable.

External theorem used exactly: Wang-Wang joint monotone-density criterion, quoted in Wang arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(e), equation (7), p.9, citing Wang and Wang, Joint Mixability, doi:10.1287/moor.2015.0755. If all n laws have increasing densities (or all have decreasing densities) on finite essential supports [a_i,b_i], with means mu_i, they are jointly mixable iff sum a_i+max_i(b_i-a_i)<=sum mu_i<=sum b_i-max_i(b_i-a_i). We use only this established theorem, not a new proof of it.

1. Put q=np. When q is integer, D0007-C005 gives a complete mix directly. Otherwise write k=floor(q), theta=q-k in (0,1), and w=1-theta. Let K=k with probability w and K=k+1 with probability theta, so E[K]=np. Think of K as the high-interval label count.

2. The probabilities of the K=k state conditional on a uniformly selected coordinate's low/high label must be

    t_L=(n-k)w/[n(1-p)],  t_H=k w/(np).

Both belong to [0,1]. Indeed the complementary probabilities are (n-k-1)theta/[n(1-p)] and (k+1)theta/(np), respectively, and each pair sums to one. If t_H=0 or t_L=1, the absent conditional label need not be defined; the present counterpart is just uniform.

3. On a component interval [a,a+epsilon], and for 0<t<1, define U^+_t=Uniform[a+(1-t)epsilon,a+epsilon] and U^-_t=Uniform[a,a+(1-t)epsilon]. Then t U^+_t+(1-t)U^-_t=Uniform[a,a+epsilon]. Relative to the full uniform center, their means are shifted by +(1-t)epsilon/2 and -t epsilon/2. The first lies at the upper end, the second at the lower end.

For each label j=L,H with t=t_j, conditional on K=k use distribution

    (1-tau) Uniform_j + tau U^+_t,

and conditional on K=k+1 use

    (1-tau) Uniform_j + tau U^-_t,

where tau in [0,1) is chosen below. The first has an increasing step density on the full component interval; the second a decreasing step density there. Their t/(1-t) mixture restores the full uniform marginal for that label. For t=0 use full uniform in the K=k+1 state; for t=1 use full uniform in the K=k state; the other state has no such label. The formulas for present means and densities follow by this convention.

4. Conditional on K=k the unperturbed sum of means is k(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2. The target is n mu=q(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2, so the required positive shift is theta(1-epsilon). The maximum shift coefficient at tau=1 is

    M=epsilon/2 * [(n-k)(1-t_L)+k(1-t_H)]
     =epsilon*theta/2 * [n - (1-theta)theta/(n p(1-p))].

To verify the second identity, (n-k)^2/[n(1-p)]+k^2/(np)=n+theta^2/[n p(1-p)]. Substituting the t values gives the displayed expression.

The correction d=(1-theta)theta/[n p(1-p)] is at most one. Indeed put l=n-k-1>=0. Since q=k+theta and n-q=l+(1-theta),

    q(n-q)-n theta(1-theta)
       =k*l+k*(1-theta)^2+l*theta^2 >=0.

Because n p(1-p)=q(n-q)/n, this proves d<=1. Consequently M>=epsilon*theta*(n-1)/2. Since n>=2/epsilon, epsilon*(n-1)/2>=1-epsilon/2>1-epsilon. Thus M>theta(1-epsilon), and

    tau=theta(1-epsilon)/M

belongs to (0,1). Conditional on K=k the perturbed sum of means equals n mu.

5. Conditional on K=k+1 its sum of means also equals n mu. Here is the exact averaging argument: the label-conditioned t mixtures restore both original component uniforms, and P(high)=E[K]/n=p, so a uniformly permuted coordinate has unconditional marginal F. Thus the unconditional expected total is n mu. The K=k state's total mean was just set equal to n mu; since the other state has positive probability theta, its total mean must also be n mu. This calculation concerns means only and does not assume a constant-sum coupling before it is built.

6. Joint mixes exist in each state. All conditional densities in the k state are increasing; all in the k+1 state are decreasing. Their essential interval widths are epsilon, since tau<1 keeps a positive uniform part. For a state with s high labels, the sum of support left endpoints is s(1-epsilon), and the sum of right endpoints is s(1-epsilon)+n epsilon. The monotone-density theorem requires the target to lie between s(1-epsilon)+epsilon and s(1-epsilon)+(n-1)epsilon.

For s=k its displacement above the unperturbed center is theta(1-epsilon); for s=k+1 the displacement below center is (1-theta)(1-epsilon). Both are <=1-epsilon. Since n>=2/epsilon,

    (n/2-1)epsilon >=1-epsilon.

Thus the target satisfies both support-mean inequalities in each state. The established theorem supplies a coupling of those n conditional laws with sum n mu almost surely.

7. Select the state K, use its joint mix, and uniformly permute all n coordinates. The sum is n mu in both states. The conditional label mixture from Steps 2-3 ensures every full marginal is exactly F. Therefore F is n-CM.

Scope and hardest piece: this proves a finite threshold for the indicated two equal-width uniform intervals. It neither claims the count condition of D0007-C005 is sufficient at smaller n nor solves arbitrary bounded absolutely continuous laws. An extension would need conditional tilts for multiple unequal components or general densities while preserving common centers and a provable joint-mixability criterion.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:0df680289ae3866f840c1c2c0b022a8ac78164e1513eb114ff06ff5ab5f9dcf7","revision_digest":"sha256:5af8171075ee1e63ae62330e2a97b663c5b46b1da03f8dd5c9ba9f3ceda29455","source_id":"own-work:w662:D0007-C006:v1","source_revision":"v1 2026-10-14","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary 2 (Derivative of the propagated functional) of arXiv:2608.03412, 'A McKean--Vlasov semigroup and its application to a martingale representation problem'] Assume {\rm \Cref{assum:main,assum:G}}. Then, for every $0\le t\le s\le T$, the map
\[
m\longmapsto \Gr(s,t,m)=G(\mu^{t,m}_s)
\]
admits a differentiable linear functional derivative. More precisely, for
$m\in\Pc(\R^d)$ and $x\in\R^d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_x\delta_m\Gr(s,t,m)(x)
&=
\E\Big[
\bigl(J^{t,m}_s\bigr)^\top
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(S^{t,m}_s)
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s, U=x
\Big]
\\
&\quad+
\E\Big[
\bigl(\overline J^{t,m}_s\bigr)^\top
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(\overline S^{t,m}_s)
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s, U=x
\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, for every $h\in\R^d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_x\delta_m\Gr(s,t,m)(x)\cdot h
&=
\E\Big[
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(S^{t,m}_s)
\cdot J^{t,m}_s h
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s,\ U=x
\Big]
\\
&\quad+
\E\Big[
\nabla_x\delta_mG(\mu^{t,m}_s)(\overline S^{t,m}_s)
\cdot \overline J^{t,m}_s h
\,\Big|\,\Gc_s,\ U=x
\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]

$$
\mathbb{E}[e^{itZ}]=\exp(-\sigma^\alpha|t|^\alpha)\text{ for all } t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$ Let $D_n(\alpha)=(d_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$ be a squared random matrix with i.i.d. entries, each entry has the law $n^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}Z$. Then there is a countable set $\mathcal{A}\subset(0,2)$ such that for all $\alpha\in(0,2)\setminus\mathcal{A}$, we have
$$\mathbb{P}(n\xi
\sigma_{min}(D_n(\alpha))\leq r)=1-\exp(-\frac{r^2}{2}-r)+\mathcal{O}_r(n^{-c})
$$ for some $c>0$, where $\xi$ is a constant depending only on $\alpha$ defined in [louvaris2022universality], eq. (1.4). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def-extension of probability space of arXiv:2505.24043, 'Weak solutions of Navier-Stokes Equation with purely discontinuous L\'evy Noise'] We say that a system $
\bigl(\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}, \pi  \bigr)$,
where
$
\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}=\bigl( \tilde{\Omega}, \tilde{\mathscr{F}}, \tilde{\mathbb{P}}, \tilde{\mathbb{F}}  \bigr)
$
is a filtered probability space,  with  $\tilde{\mathbb{F}}=(\tilde{\mathscr{F}}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ , and $
\pi\colon  \tilde{\Omega} \to \Omega
$
is a map,  is an extension of a
filtered probability space
$
\bigl( {\Omega}, {\mathscr{F}}, {\mathbb{P}}, {\mathbb{F}} \bigr), \mbox{ where } {\mathbb{F}}=({\mathscr{F}}_t)_{t\geq 0} ,
$
if and only if  the following four conditions are satisfied
\begin{trivlist}
\item[(i)] $\pi$ is $\tilde{\mathscr{F}}/{\mathscr{F}}$-measurable;
\item[(ii)] $\pi$ is $\tilde{\mathscr{F}}_t/{\mathscr{F}}_t$-measurable for every $t\geq 0$,
\item[(iii)] $\mathbb{P}=\tilde{\mathbb{P}} \circ \pi^{-1}$,
\item[(iv)] for every $ {\mathscr{F}}$-measurable and $ {\mathbb{P}}$-a.s.\ bounded, function  $X\colon  \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, and every $t\geq 0$, the following equality holds
\[
\tilde{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[ \tilde{X}\vert \tilde{\mathscr{F}}_t \bigr]=
\mathbb{E}\bigl[ {X}\vert {\mathscr{F}}_t \bigr] \circ \pi, \;\; \tilde{\mathbb{P}} \mbox{-a.s.}
\]
where
\[
\tilde{X}\coloneqq X \circ \pi \;\;\; :\tilde{\Omega} \to \mathbb{R}.
\]
\end{trivlist}

[Proposition lem:alternativeGradient of arXiv:2609.03094, 'Discrete Gromov--Wasserstein Duality: Algorithms and Isomorphism Testing'] For any $u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, let $x^{\star}_u$ be the unique solution of the regularized quadratic program $\min_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\frac 12 x^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}_1^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}_1x-u^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}_0x -\varepsilon \mathsf{H}(x)\right\}$. Then, $x^{\star}_u$ coincides with $x^{\star}_{(u,v^{\star}(u))}$, the unique solution of $\min_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left(\mathrm{B}_1^{\intercal} v^{\star}(u)-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal}x-\varepsilon \mathsf{H}(x)\right\}$, where $v^{\star}(u)$ is the unique solution of the strongly concave maximization problem 
    \begin{equation}
    
        \sup_{v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}} f_{u}(v)\coloneqq-\frac 12 \|v\|^2+\min_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left(\mathrm{B}_1^{\intercal} v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal}x-\varepsilon \mathsf{H}(x)\right\}.

Suppose $L \uparrow \infty$ as $t \to \infty$, and let $w_t$ denote either $v_t$ or $v_{t,L}$ for all $t$. If $\nu \in \sP_K^{\text{step}}$ satisfies Condition \ref{initialprofilecond}, then  
\[
	\mu_{t/K}^{\nu_L} \circ w_t^{-1}(A)  \sim (c_\nu/K) \mu_{t/K}^{L} \circ w_t^{-1}(A) , \qquad t \to \infty.
\]

Convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$. Let $W>0$ and let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$. Then $\hat f\in L^1$, so $f$ has a (unique) continuous representative $f(x)=\int_{-W}^{W}\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\xi}d\xi$, and for that representative $$f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f\!\left(\frac{n}{2W}\right)\operatorname{sinc}(2Wx-n),\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(t)=\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{\pi t},$$ the series converging in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\mathbb R$. Moreover $\sum_n|f(n/2W)|^2=2W\|f\|_2^2$, so the samples determine $f$ isometrically. The sampling rate $2W$ (the Nyquist rate) is critical: functions bandlimited to $[-W,W]$ are in general not determined by samples at a slower rate, and the theorem's conclusion uses $f\in L^2$ - the distributionally bandlimited function $\sin(2\pi Wx)$ has all samples $f(n/2W)=0$ without being zero, and it is excluded only because it is not in $L^2$.

the Fourier transform vanishes a.e. outside [-W,W] (bandlimited)
the identity is for the continuous representative of f, at the sample rate 2W

[Theorem Theorem~\ref{thm:design}, informal of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] For every sufficiently regular compactly supported law $\mu_{*}$ and every positive
weight $f$, the free diffusion
$\mathrm{d} X_{t}=b_{*}(X_{t})\mathrm{d} t+f(X_{t})\mathrm{d} S_{t}\,f(X_{t})$ with the explicit drift
$b_{*}=-f^{2}H(f^{2}\mu_{*})$ has $\mu_{*}$ as its stationary spectral law. When the
associated potential is convex, this diffusion is the Wasserstein gradient flow of a
strictly displacement-convex energy, so it relaxes to $\mu_{*}$ exponentially fast and
carries a reverse-time SDE and a trainable score; in particular the Marchenko--Pastur
law, the canonical covariance spectrum, is realised as such an equilibrium. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemme prbr of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] Let $g$ be an analytic continuation of the Laplace transform of $f$ such that there exists a point $\alpha_0$ and an angle $\delta \in\left[0, \frac{1}{2} \pi\right)$ such that $g(z)$ is analytic on the set $\mathcal{G}_\delta$.
Suppose that $g(z) \rightarrow 0$ as $|z| \rightarrow \infty$ for $z \in \mathcal{G}_\delta(\alpha)$,
and that there exist $a \in \mathbb{R}, \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and $c_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\lim _{\substack{z \rightarrow a \\ z \in \mathcal{G}_\delta(\alpha)}}(\alpha_0-z)^\lambda(g(z)-a)=c_0
$$
Then:
$$ f(x)  \underset{x \to \infty}{\sim} \frac{c_0}{\Gamma (\lambda)} x^{\lambda-1} e^{- \alpha_0 x}.  $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 1 (Increment Matrix Density) of arXiv:2606.25810, 'Spectral Collapse Under Geometric Alignment of Extreme Events'] Let \(Y(t) = (Y_1(t), \dots, Y_n(t))\) be a semimartingale. Define the predictable quadratic covariation matrix

\[
Q_n(t) = \left( \frac{d[Y_i, Y_j]_t}{dt} \right)_{1 \le i,j \le n},
\]

where \([Y_i, Y_j]_t\) denotes the quadratic covariation of \(Y_i\) and \(Y_j\). 

Throughout this paper, we work with the density form. For notational convenience, we write the informal shorthand

\[
Q_n = (dY_i dY_j)_{1 \le i,j \le n}
\]

to mean the same object.

The matrix \(Q_n(t)\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite for all \(t\).
title: Increment Matrix Density

[Proposition lemma:Itildeinvariantsetfoundaftercountablymanysteps of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, let $\underline{V}$ be an admissible sequence of open sets and let 
$C\subseteq \spt \mu$ be compact. For all $t\ge 0$, define compact sets $C_t^{\gamma}$ for
each ordinal number $\gamma$ as follows: 
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[i)] Set $C_t^0:=C$.
  \item[ii)] If $C_t^{\gamma}$ has been defined, set 
             $C_t^{\gamma+1}:=\JmuVt(C_t^{\gamma})$.
  \item[iii)] If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal and $C_t^{\gamma}$ has been defined for 
              every $\gamma<\lambda$, set 
        \[
        C_t^{\lambda}:=\bigcap_{\gamma<\lambda}C^{\gamma}_t.
        \]
\end{enumerate}        
Then there exists a countable ordinal $\beta_t$ for which $C_t^{\beta_t}$ is a fixed point of 
$\JmuVt$, i.e.,  $C_t^{\beta_t+1}=C_t^{\beta_t}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition lemma:Itildeinvariantsetfoundaftercountablymanysteps of arXiv:2506.10448

[Theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:Bernoulli_calY_representation}
The set $\{\hat{f}_k^r \mid r \in [0,1] \text{ and } k \in I^r \}$ is a basis for ${\rm aff}(\Sym(f))$. 

That is, for $f \in \Sym$, denoting 

$ R_f = \{ r \in [0,1] \mid \supp(f) \cap S^r \ne \emptyset \}, $ we have
\[ f = \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r , \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r = 1 . \]
\begin{proof}
The PMF $f$ is discrete, so its support is at most countable; therefore $R_f$ is at most countable. 
Write $f = \sum_{R_f} f\big\vert_{S^r}$ and for each $r \in R_f$ define $c_r = \sum_{z \in S^r} f(z)$. 
Then for each $r \in R_f$, $f_r = \frac{1}{c_r} f\big\vert_{S^r} \in \Sym$ by (lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers of the paper). 
Now apply the (lem:Bernoulli_calYr_representation of the paper) to each $f_r$ to find constants $\alpha_k^r[f_r]$; it is then obvious that $c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] = \alpha_k^r[f]$ for all $k$ and $r$. 

Thus we compute 
\[ 
f = \sum_{r \in R_f} c_r f_r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} c_r \alpha_k^r[f_r] \hat{f}_k^r 
= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r 
\]
as needed. 
Finally, 
\begin{align*} 
\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r 
&= \sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \bigg( \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \hat{f}_k^r(z) \bigg) \\
&= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} \bigg(\sum_{r \in R_f} \sum_{k \in I^r} \alpha_k^r \hat{f}_k^r(z)\bigg) 
= \sum_{z \in \supp(f)} f(z)
= 1 . \qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered theorem of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

[Theorem 16 of arXiv:2606.19115, 'Finite free perpetuities'] Let $(p_n)_{n\in \N}$ be a sequence of polynomials with $p_n\in \pols_n(\R_{\geq 0})$ and $\mu\in \MM(\R_{\geq 0})\backslash \{\delta_0\}$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The weak convergence: $\meas{p_n} \weak \mu$. 
\item For every $t\in (0,1-\mu(\{0\}))$ and every sequence $(k_n)_{n\in\N}$ with 
\[
1\leq k_n \leq n\quad\mbox{and}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{k_n}{n}=t,
\]
one has 
\begin{equation}

\lim_{\substack{n\to \infty}}\strans{p_n}{n}\left(-\frac{k_n}{n}\right)= S_\mu(-t),
\end{equation}
where $S_\mu$ is the $S$-transform of $\mu$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 16 of arXiv:2606.19115

PRIVATE STATUS NOTE from a bounded web search on 2026-09-07, not a re-read of the papers. Bourgade's ICM 2018 conjecture (0.2) for d = 1: bulk eigenvectors of N x N Hermitian band matrices with band width W are localised for W << N^{1/2} and delocalised with GUE statistics for W >> N^{1/2}. Yau and Yin (arXiv 2501.01718, 2025) proved, for W > N^{1/2+eps}, the local semicircle law down to scale N^{-1+eps}, simultaneous delocalisation of all bulk eigenvectors, quantum unique ergodicity and GUE bulk universality; arXiv 2508.05802 (2025) treats the localised side; together with Erdos-Riabov's delocalisation work the d = 1 transition is established. The d = 2 localisation side at fixed W (localisation length exp(W^2)) and the finite W_c in d = 3 remain open as far as the search found. A solver meeting the 1D conjecture should treat it as a theorem to cite, not a target.
Hermitian random band matrices, d = 1, subgaussian entries

values in Algorithm~\ref{alg:qshap-obl}:
\[
T_{1,i}[j]=T_{1,i'}[j],

T_{2,i}[j]=T_{2,i'}[j],
\qquad j=1,\ldots,p.
\]

[Defi 25 of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let $n=ml$. We define the \emph{fixed point set} $F_{n,l}:\S_n\rightarrow 2^{[n]}$ as follows. For $\sigma\in\S_n$, let
$$F_{n,l}(\sigma):=\{i\in [n]:\ \sigma(i)\equiv i \pmod m\}.$$
The function $F_{n,l}$ naturally descends to a well-defined function on $\sim_l\backslash\S_n$, which we still denote by $F_{n,l}$. We say that an element $\sigma\in\S_n$ is \emph{clustered} if $|F_{n,l}(\sigma)\cap T_{i,l}|\ge 2$ for some $1\le i\le m$.

[Definition def:coeff of arXiv:2604.23791, 'Finite-sample Borel--Cantelli inequalities under mixing conditions'] For sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal A,\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal F$,
\[
  \alpha(\mathcal A,\mathcal B):=\sup\bigl\{|\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)-\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)|:
  A\in\mathcal A,\,B\in\mathcal B\bigr\},
\]
\[
  \varphi(\mathcal A,\mathcal B):=\sup\bigl\{|\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)-\mathbb{P}(B)|:
  A\in\mathcal A,\,\mathbb{P}(A)>0,\,B\in\mathcal B\bigr\}.
\]
For the event sequence, set the \emph{ambient} coefficients
$\alpha_{A}(n):=\sup_{k\ge1}\alpha(\mathcal F_{1}^{k},
\mathcal F_{k+n}^{\infty})$ and
$\varphi_{A}(n):=\sup_{k\ge1}\varphi(\mathcal F_{1}^{k},
\mathcal F_{k+n}^{\infty})$, and, for a fixed finite horizon $N$, the
\emph{finite restricted} coefficients
\[
  \alpha_{N}(n):=\!\!\sup_{1\le k\le N}\!\!\alpha(\mathcal F_{1}^{k},\mathcal F_{k+n}^{N}),
  \qquad
  \varphi_{N}(n):=\!\!\sup_{1\le k\le N}\!\!\varphi(\mathcal F_{1}^{k},\mathcal F_{k+n}^{N}),
\]
where $\mathcal F_{a}^{N}$ is understood to be trivial when $a>N$.
title: Mixing coefficients

[Prop of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The pair $\smash{(\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*},1_+)}$ defines an idempotent algebra in $\textup{Pr}^S_T$, and hence also in $\CAT_T^\textup{$S$-cc}$. An $S$-cocomplete $T$-$\infty$-category ${\mathcal{C}}$ is a $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}$-module if and only if it is pointed.
    \begin{proof}
        By Corollary~(cor:Spc-S-T-*-pres of the paper), $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}$ is $S$-presentable. To see that it is idempotent and to characterize its modules, recall that $\smash{\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}}\simeq{{\Spc_*}\otimes\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T}}$ by Proposition~(prop:Spc*-levelwise-tensor of the paper). By [martiniwolf2022presentable]*{Proposition~2.6.3.7}, the functor ${-}\otimes\ul\Spc_S\colon\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}\to\textup{Pr}^{\textup{L}}_S$ can be upgraded to a strong symmetric monoidal functor; as $(\Spc_*,S^0)$ is an idempotent algebra [HA]*{Proposition 4.8.2.11}, so is its image $(\ul\Spc_{S,*},S^0)$. Lemma~(lemma:idempotent-restrict of the paper) then implies that also $\smash{(\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*},S^0)}$ is idempotent.

        Combining Lemma~(lemma:smash-module-internal-hom of the paper) with Proposition~(prop:univ-prop-*-cc-param of the paper) already shows that every pointed $S$-cocomplete $T$-$\infty$-category is a $\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}$-module. For the converse, it will suffice to show that $\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\text{$S$-cc}_T(\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*},{\mathcal{D}})$ is pointed for any $S$-cocomplete ${\mathcal{D}}$. By [CLL_Global]*{Corollary 4.1.10${}^{\textup{op}}$}, the full subcategory of $\ul{\textup{Fun}}_T(\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*}^{\textup{op}},{\mathcal{D}})$ spanned by the functors preserving the initial object is pointed; as $\ul{\textup{Fun}}^\text{$S$-cc}_T(\ul\Spc_{S\triangleright T,*},{\mathcal{D}})$ is a smaller subcategory still containing the initial object, it is then necessarily also pointed.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered prop of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

body: [Theorem thm:McCann of arXiv:2605.10491, 'Zero-couplings of infinite measures with cyclically monotone support and multivariate regu'] Let $P, Q \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, with $P$ vanishing on sets of Hausdorff dimension at most $d-1$. Own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and novelty assessment pending. Let P be any fixed target-independent latent probability law, and G a nonempty class of measurable maps into R^D, D>=1. Targets are supported on [-B,B]^D, B>0. Suppose each coordinate of the clipped maps Pi_B o g has subgraph VC dimension at most an integer V>=1. For 0<t<=2BD the clipped output laws have an external W1 t-cover with at most (12eBD/t)^(2DV) laws. Coordinate centers may come from different network parameters: their tuple need not be a realizable network, because the target packing lower bound must permit arbitrary law centers. If every family of <=2^S laws has minimax target error >=c(S+1)^(-alpha), then the original generator minimax error is at least c[2DV*log2(12eBD/t)+1]^(-alpha)-t. Thus error <=epsilon<=2BD requires 2DV*log2(12eBD/epsilon)+1 >=[c/(2epsilon)]^(1/alpha). For a standard fixed ReLU architecture with W total affine coefficient slots, U>=1 units and L>=1 layers, put Wprime=W+5, Uprime=U+2, Lprime=L+1 and V=ceil[Lprime+Lprime*Wprime*log2(4e*Lprime*Uprime*log2(2e*Lprime*Uprime))]. Bartlett-Harvey-Liaw-Mehrabian Theorem 6 (arXiv:1703.02930v3, p.4), applied to (z,s)->g_j(z)-s with an optional dummy unit, justifies this V without any bound on weight magnitudes or precision. Count every affine slot, including tied and fixed slots; no bound in terms of distinct shared slots alone is asserted. Clipping improves error to targets in the box. A finite union of A0 architectures adds log2(A0) to the cover bit budget. A target-dependent latent law or uncounted architecture choices are excluded. The proof uses an elementary Sauer counting and random-separation argument; no general-method novelty or matching optimal upper rate is asserted.
Fixed latent law; measurable maps; targets in a fixed box; finite coordinate subgraph dimension; arbitrary external law centers; complete architecture/slot accounting.

[Proposition prop:Gammajbounds of arXiv:2511.06321, 'Torus scaling limits and the plateau of the critical weakly coupled $|\varphi|^4$ model in'] Let $d \ge 3$,  $\eta \in [0,2)$ and $\vec{\textbf{a}} \in \operatorname{HB}_{\epsilon_p}$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon_p$. 
Then there exist covariance matrices $(\dot\Gamma_t : \Z^d \times \Z^d \rightarrow \R)_{t\ge 0}$ such that (equation eq:covdecmpZd of the paper) and the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
	\item (Symmetries) $\dot\Gamma_t : \Z^d \times \Z^d \rightarrow \R$ is a covariance matrix invariant under isometries,
	i.e., $\dot\Gamma_t \ge 0$ and $\dot\Gamma_t (E (x) , E(y)) = \dot\Gamma_t (x,y)$ for any isometry $E : \Z^d \rightarrow \Z^d$.
	\item (Finite range property) $\dot\Gamma_t$ has range $< t$ in the $\ell^1$-metric,  i.e.,  $\dot\Gamma_t (x,y) =0$ whenever $\norm{x-y}_{\ell^{1}} \ge t$. 
	\item (Upper bound) For each $k, k_x,k_y \ge 0$ with $k_x + k_y = k$,  
	\begin{align}
		\big\| \nabla_x^{k_x} \nabla_y^{k_y} \dot{\Gamma}_t (x,y) \big\|_{\ell^\infty (\Z^d \times \Z^d)} \le C_k \frac{t^{-d+1-\eta-k}\wedge 1}{1 + \textbf{a}^{(\emptyset)} t^{2\beta}}	 .  
	\end{align}
for some $j,L$-independent constant $C_k$.	
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:Gammajbounds of arXiv:2511.06321

Fix integers n,m>=1, real vectors x!=0 and a_1,...,a_m in R^n, and 0<beta<=1/2. Define gamma_beta(t)=|t| when |t|>beta, and gamma_beta(t)=t^2/(2 beta)+beta/2 when |t|<=beta. Put u_i=a_i^T z and v_i=a_i^T x. The smoothed amplitude-flow loss is F_beta(z)=(1/(2m))sum_i L_beta(u_i,v_i), where L_beta(u,v)=v^2(gamma_beta(u/v)-1)^2 for v!=0 and L_beta(u,0)=u^2. Since gamma_beta is even, the nonzero-v expression also equals v^2(gamma_beta(|u|/|v|)-1)^2. The loss is continuously differentiable. The source uses D_v h(z)=lim_{t down to0}(h(z+t v)-h(z))/t, when this limit exists, and D_v^2 F(z)=D_v(D_v F)(z). For C1 F this second derivative is lim_{t down to0}<grad F(z+t v)-grad F(z),v>/t. \(\beta>\beta_{\mathrm c,N}\), and every entry tends to infinity when

\(\beta=\beta_{\mathrm c,N}\), the crossing vector has the following
limits.  Put \(\tau=(\sqrt5-1)/2\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If \(N=3\), then
\[
  (x_m,y_m)\longrightarrow(\tau,0).
\]

\[
  (\phi_{1,m},\phi_{2,m},\theta_{1,m},\theta_{2,m})
  \longrightarrow

\]
where
\[
  \theta_*^5+2\theta_*^4=1,
  \qquad
  \phi_*=\frac1{\theta_*(1+\theta_*)}.
\]
\item If \(N\in\{6,9\}\), then
\[
  (X_m,Y_m)\longrightarrow(t_*,t_*),
  \qquad
  t_*=\tau^{1/d_N},
  \qquad
  d_N=\frac N3.
\]
\item If \(N=4k+\ell\notin\{3,5,6,9\}\), where
\(\ell\in\{1,2,3\}\), then
\[
  (X_m,Y_m)\longrightarrow(X_{*,N},Y_{*,N}),
\]
where \(Y_{*,N}\in(0,1)\) is the unique solution of
\[
  Y_{*,N}^{\,N}+2Y_{*,N}^{\,2k+2}=1
\]
and
\[
  X_{*,N}
  =
  \bigl(Y_{*,N}^{\,k}+Y_{*,N}^{\,3k+\ell-2}\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 12 (Drasin--Shea) of arXiv:2608.24616, '2608.24616'] Let $k$ be a nonnegative, nonzero measurable kernel, and let
\[
 \widehat k(z)=\int_0^\infty u^{-z}k(u)\,\frac{du}{u}
\]
have maximal interval of absolute convergence $(a,b)$, where
\[
 -\infty<a<0<b\leq+\infty.
\]
Assume that $\widehat k(x)\to\infty$ as $x\downarrow a$ and, if
$b<+\infty$, that $\widehat k(x)\to\infty$ as $x\uparrow b$.
Let $h:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be measurable, admit a locally bounded
extension to $[0,\infty)$, and have bounded increase or bounded decrease: for
some $x_0>0$, some finite
$A\geq0$, and some $C\in(0,\infty)$, respectively,
\[
 \frac{h(y)}{h(x)}\leq C\left(\frac yx\right)^A
 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 \frac{h(y)}{h(x)}\geq C^{-1}\left(\frac yx\right)^{-A},
 \qquad y\geq x\geq x_0.
\]
If $(k*_{M}h)(x)$ is finite for all sufficiently large $x$ and
\[
 \frac{(k*_{M}h)(x)}{h(x)}\longrightarrow\gamma\in(0,\infty),
\]
then, for some $\rho\in(a,b)$,
\[
 h\in\RV_\infty(\rho),\qquad \widehat k(\rho)=\gamma.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 (Local parabolic barrier on a ball) of arXiv:2606.03122, 'Propagation of support for super-Brownian motion with general branching mechanism'] Let $\Phi_0$ be  a spatially constant branching mechanism  satisfying  Condition \ref{con1} and $\Psi$ be another  branching mechanism  such that
$$
\Psi(x,u)\geq \Phi_0(u),
\qquad x\in\overline{B(x_0,R)},\quad u\geq0
$$
for $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $R>0$.
Set $\psi_{R,x_0}(x):=\psi_R(x-x_0)$ for $\psi_R$  defined in \eqref{definpsi}. Given $\theta>0$, let $u_\theta(x,t)$ be the
unique non-negative mild solution, locally bounded on each finite time interval, of
\begin{equation}
u_\theta(x,t)
=
P_x\left[
\int_0^t
\left\{
\theta\psi_{R,x_0}(W_s)
-
\Psi(W_s,u_\theta(W_s,t-s))
\right\}\dd s
\right]
\end{equation}
and let $u_{R,\Phi_0}$ denote the radial classical solution of \eqref{SBVP} in $B(0,R)$ associated with $\Phi_0$. Then, we have
\begin{equation}
u_\theta(x,t)\leq u_{R,\Phi_0}(|x-x_0|),
\qquad x\in B(x_0,R),\quad t\geq0 .
\end{equation}

[Theorem 3 (Variational formula for the logarithmic potential) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Fix  $k \ge 1$ integer,
$\alpha \in (0,\infty)$, and $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
For $u<\zeta_{-,\up{\alpha,\nu}}$,
set
\begin{equation}
    g_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS;u) := -\alpha u \Tr(\bS) + \alpha \int \log \det(\bI + \bT \bS) \nu(\de\bT) - \log|\det(\bS)| - k(\log \alpha +1 ).
\end{equation}
then we have (for $\cP_-$ defined as in Eq~\eqref{eq:P_def})
    \begin{equation}
  \Phi(u) := \int \log |\zeta - u| \, \mu_{\up{\alpha,\nu}}(\de \zeta) 
    =  \frac1k\inf_{\bS\in\cP_{-}} g_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS;u)\, .
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Variational formula for the logarithmic potential

[Lemma lem:thetastablefilt of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Let $\cA$ be an abelian category and $\theta\colon K_0(\cA)\to\bR$. 
Then $E\in\cA$ is $\theta$-semistable iff 
\begin{equation}
\langle\theta,\cF_\bullet\rangle\coloneqq \sum_{\alpha\in\bR}\alpha\theta\left(\cF_{\alpha}/\cF_{<\alpha}\right)\leq 0
\end{equation}
for all complete, finite $\bR$-filtrations $\cF_{\bullet}$ of $E$.
Moreover, $E$ is $\theta$-stable iff $E\neq 0$ and strict inequality holds in (equation eq:thetafilt of the paper) for all filtrations with at least two steps.

[Def 20 (Local groups) of arXiv:2608.30990, 'Convergence of symmetries: nilpotency, dimension, and perfectness'] A \emph{local group} is a pointed topological space $(G, e )$ equipped with an open set $\Omega \subset G \times G $ and continuous maps $m : \Omega \to G$ and $ ( \cdot ) ^{-1} : G \to G$ satisfying the following:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item For all $g \in G$, one has $(g,e), (e, g)\in \Omega$ and  
        \[ m( g , e)  = m(e  ,g) = g.\]
        \item For all $g \in G$, one has $(g,g^{-1}), (g^{-1}, g)\in \Omega$ and
        \[ m (g , g^{-1} )= m (g^{-1} , g ) = e .\]
        \item If $g,h,k \in G$ are such that $(g,h), (m(g , h ) , k), (h,k), (g,m (h , k)) \in \Omega$, then 
        \[    m   (m(g , h) , k) = m( g ,m (h , k)) .       \]
    \end{itemize}
    When no confusion arises, we denote the local group $(G,e , \Omega, m , ( \cdot  )^{-1} )$ simply by $G$.
title: Local groups

A Legendre fibration is a smooth fiber bundle $\pi: E \to M$ where $E$ is a contact manifold of dimension $2n+1$ and every fiber $\pi^{-1}(p)$ is a Legendre submanifold (an integral manifold of maximal dimension $n$ of the contact distribution). A Legendre immersion $i: L \to E$ projects via $\pi$ to a wavefront $\pi \circ i(L) \subset M$.
E is a contact (2n+1)-manifold
M is an (n+1)-dimensional base manifold
Fibers are Legendre submanifolds

body: In functional analysis, a field of mathematics, a key object of study is a normed space, which is a vector space equipped with a norm, which allows vectors to be measured. A standard normed space is the space $C([0,1],\mathbb {R})$ of continuous functions on the unit interval, $f:[0,1]\to \mathbb {R}$, which is equipped with the norm $\|f\|=\max _{x\in [0,1]}|f(x)|$, the maximum value of the function.

body:
[Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\alpha,L > 0$, $\fq \in [1,2]$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$. 
	Then, for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$,
	\begin{align}
		(\E \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu))^2
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\,,\\
	
		(\E \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\})))^2
		&\ge \bbW_2(\mu^\Ising(\cA_N),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))^2 - o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

\begin{proof}
	Abbreviate $X = \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)$.
	By Jensen's inequality, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq]^{2/\fq} 
		\le \E[X^2] 
		= (\E X)^2 + \E[(X-\E X)^2] \stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}}{=} (\E X)^2 + o_N(1)\,.
	\]
By convexity of $\bbW_\fq(\cdot,\cdot)^\fq$, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq] = \E [\bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)^\fq] \ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^\fq\,.
	\]
	Rearranging yields the first assertion \eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}.
	The second assertion
	\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound.ising} is proved in the same way, replacing $X$ with $J \equiv \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))$ in the above argument and using \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var.ising} from Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} in place of \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Definition 1 (Stopping times and overshoot event) of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] Let $\mathcal{H} \subset \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be a target set and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ a cutoff.  
Define
\[
T := \inf\{\, t \ge 0 : S_t \in \mathcal{H} \,\}, \qquad
\omega_N := \inf\{\, t \ge 0 : S_t > N \,\}, \qquad
A_N := \{\, \omega_N < T \,\},
\]
where $T$ is the first hitting time of the target set~$\mathcal{H}$,
$\omega_N$ is the first time the cumulative sum exceeds the cutoff~$N$,
and $A_N$ is the \emph{overshoot event}, corresponding to paths that cross~$N$
before reaching~$\mathcal{H}$.
title: Stopping times and overshoot event

body:
[Lemma 6 (Compact-time pathwise stability) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Fix $T<\infty$ and a compact set $K\subset\R^{3d}$.  Let $\calK$ be a compact
neighborhood of $K$, and let
\[
    \sigma_\delta:=\inf\left\{t\ge0:Z_t^\delta\notin\calK
    \text{ or } Z_t\notin\calK\right\}.
\]
If $Z_t^\delta$ and $Z_t$ start from the same point $z\in K$ and are coupled
by using the same Brownian motion $B$ in the $r$-coordinate, then, for every
$\eta>0$,
\[
    \sup_{z\in K}
    \Pbb_z\left(
        \sup_{0\le t\le T\wedge\sigma_\delta}\left|Z_t^\delta-Z_t\right|>\eta
    \right)
    \longrightarrow0
    \qquad\text{as }\delta\downarrow0.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{z\in K}
    \E_z\left[
        \sup_{0\le t\le T\wedge\sigma_\delta}
        \left|Z_t^\delta-Z_t\right|^2
    \right]
    \le C_{T,\calK}\delta .
\end{equation}
The same statement holds for the adjoint regularized processes.

[Proposition prop:vector-DE-variational-formula-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume the vector law is energy-admissible. Then
\begin{equation}
D_E(X)
=
\sup_{\substack{1<q<2\\ \rho(q)<1}}
\left(-\frac{2}{q}\log_2\rho(q)\right),
\end{equation}
with the empty supremum interpreted as \(0\). In particular,
\(
D_E(X)>0
\)
if and only if
\(
\rho(q)<1
\)
for some 
\(
q\in(1,2)
\).

Equivalently,
\(
D_E(X)>0
\)
if and only if 
\(
\rho(q)<\infty
\) for some \(q>1\).

[Definition def:explore-plus-spin-clusters of arXiv:2606.13147, 'Scaling limits of the single-curve interface and outermost loops in the planar random fiel'] Let $\mathcal C_0$ denote the plus spins cluster of $\mathcal P_0$ in $\Lambda_M.$
Then all the spins on $\partial_{\mathrm{ext}}\mathcal C_0\cap \Lambda_M$ are minus. Let $\mathscr C_0\subset 2^{\Lambda_M}$ denote all the possible choices of $\mathcal C_0$, i.e., $A\in\mathscr C_0$ if and only if 
$\mu^{\xi}(\mathcal C_0=A)>0.$
 Let $\mathscr F_0=\sigma\left(\{\mathcal C_0=A\}: A\in\mathscr C_0\right)$ denote the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal C_0.$ Recall that $\mathcal Y^{-}$ is the event that $\mathcal P_0$ is not plus-connected to $\mathcal P_1$ inside $\Lambda_M$, and  $\mathcal Y^{+}$ is the event that, for every $U\in \mathcal U$, the set $U$ is plus-connected to $\mathcal P_0$ inside $\Lambda_M$.
 Then we have $\mathcal Y^+,\mathcal Y^-\in\mathscr F_0$ since they are all decided by $\mathcal C_0.$
 Similarly, we can define $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathscr F_1$ to be the plus spins cluster of $\mathcal P_1$ in $\Lambda_M$ and the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal C_1$.

body: A metric space is a pair (X, d) where X is a set and d is a function from X x X to the real numbers satisfying, for all x, y, z in X: (i) d(x,y) >= 0, with d(x,y) = 0 if and only if x = y; (ii) symmetry, d(x,y) = d(y,x); (iii) the triangle inequality, d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z). The open ball of center x and radius r > 0 is B(x,r) = {y in X : d(x,y) < r}. The metric topology on X is the topology generated by the open balls as a basis: a set U is open exactly when for every point x of U some open ball B(x,r) is contained in U. Convergence of a sequence x_n to x means d(x_n, x) tends to 0.
title: Metric space
