[Definition of arXiv:2411.04590, 'Singular stochastic delay equations driven by fractional Brownian motion: Dynamics, longti'] Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a real Banach space. A strongly continuous semigroup of linear operators, or a $C_0$-semigroup, is a one-parameter family $\{T_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ of bounded linear operators on $\mathcal{B}$ that satisfies the following properties:
			
			\begin{enumerate}
				\item \textbf{Semigroup Property:} For all $t, s \geq 0$, we have
				\[
				T_{t+s} = T_t\circ T_s.
				\]
				\item \textbf{Identity at Zero:} The operator $T_0$ is the identity operator on $\mathcal{B}$, i.e.,
				\[
				T_0 = I.
				\]
				\item \textbf{Strong Continuity:} For every $x \in \mathcal{B}$, the map $t \mapsto T_t x$ is continuous from $[0, \infty)$ to $\mathcal{B}$.
			\end{enumerate}
			To every $C_0$-semigroup $\{T(t)\}_{t \geq 0}$ on a Banach space $\mathcal{B}$, we can associate an infinitesimal generator $L$ defined by
			
			\[
			{L} z = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{T(t) z - z}{t},
			\]
			
			for all $z \in \mathcal{D}(L)$. The domain of the generator $L$, denoted by $\mathcal{D}(L)$, is given by
			
			\[
			\mathcal{D}(L) = \left\{ \varphi \in \mathcal{B} \mid \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{T(t) \varphi - \varphi}{t} \text{ exists and is finite} \right\}.
			\]
			
			In other words, $\mathcal{D}(L)$ consists of all elements $\varphi \in \mathcal{B}$ for which the limit above exists. The generator $\mathcal{L}$ is a densely defined linear operator mapping $\mathcal{D}(L)$ into $\mathcal{B}$.

[Theorem thm: main 2 of arXiv:2607.20097, 'Phase transition for the asymptotic entropy of branching random walks on groups'] For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\{X_{n,k}\}_{k=1}^{\rho^n}$ be i.i.d. $G$-valued random variables with common law $X_{n,1} \sim \mu^{*n}$. Define the empirical measure
$$\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n(x) := \frac{1}{\rho^n}\sum_{k=1}^{\rho^n} \mathds1_{\{X_{n,k} = x\}}, \qquad x \in G,$$
and $H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)$ as in (equation eq:shannon-emp-distr of the paper) with $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n(x)$ instead of $\widehat{M}_n$.
If $\mu$ has  finite entropy and $\rho>1$, then the following holds. 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
\setlength\itemsep{0em}
    \item \textbf{Small-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho\leq \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)}{n}=\log\rho.$$
    \item  \textbf{Large-$\rho$ regime.} If $\rho> \mathsf{e}^{\textsf{h}(\mu)}$, then almost surely
    $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{H(\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_n)}{n} = \textsf{h}(\mu).$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Independent random walks

\[

\prod_{j\notin T}\tau_{b_j}(\omega)
\mathbf A',

\prod_{i\in S}\tau_{a_i}(\mathbf 1)

    There exists $R_0=R_0(Q,c)< \infty$
    such that for all $R \ge R_0$ the following holds.
    Assume $0 < c < Q/2$ and suppose $E'_x$ holds.

    such that the following hold.

        of $G^\nu \cap [-Q \log R, Q \log R]^d$ of Euclidean diameter at least $Q \log R$.
    \end{enumerate}

[Definition eq:critical-count-ceiling of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[definition]{def:critical-count-ceiling}
We say that the array satisfies \({\rm(CC)}_p\) if there are deterministic
finite numbers \(D_{N,p}\) such that, almost surely,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Crt}_N^J(\mathbb R)\le D_{N,p},
 \qquad
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log D_{N,p}\le\log(p-1).
\end{equation}
This is the exact counting input used by the localized upper bounds
below; it requires neither nondegeneracy nor absolute continuity.
Algebraic genericity is a convenient sufficient condition, with
\(D_{N,p}=2\{(p-1)^N-1\}/(p-2)\).

[Lemma symmeqa of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:Sr_restriction_of_symmetrizers_produces_symmetrizers}
Let $f \in \Sym$ and let $r > 0$ satisfy $\supp(f) \cap S^r \ne \emptyset$. 
Then 
\( g := (\frac{1}{c}) f \mathds{1}_{S^r} \in \Sym^r, \)
where $c = \sum_{z \in S^r} f(z)$. 
Moreover, if $c < 1$, then $\frac{f-cg}{1-c} \in \Sym$. 

\begin{proof}
Fix $r \in [0,\infty)$ and denote $ F_z = \{\pm z,-z\pm2,z\pm2\}$ for $z \in \mathbb{R}$. 
Writing one of $z = 2k - r$ (or $z = 2k + r$) for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, we have $-z = -2k+r$ (or $-z = -2k -r$); either way, $-z \in S^r$. 
Also, $z \in S^r$ implies $\{z \pm 2\} \subseteq S^r$ and $-z \in S^r$ implies $\{-z \pm 2\} \subseteq S^r$. 
Thus $z \in S^r$ if and only if $F_z \subseteq S^r$. 

Next, write $g = (\frac{1}{c}) f \mathds{1}_{S^r}$ and consider the symmetry equations 
\begin{align}
 q\varphi(z+2) + p\varphi(z) 	&= q\varphi(-z) + p\varphi(-z-2) \\
 q\varphi(z) + p\varphi(z-2)   	&= q\varphi(-z+2) + p\varphi(-z)  . 
\end{align}
Note that $\varphi$ is only evaluated at elements of $F_z$ in ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)). 
When $z \in S^r$, clearly $\varphi=f$ solves ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)); since both equations are linear and $g = \frac{1}{c}f$ on $F_z$, $g$ is also a solution. 
When $z \not\in S^r$, $g = 0$ on $F_z$ and solves ((symmeqa of the paper)-(symmeqb of the paper)) trivially. 
Thus $g \in \Sym$, and indeed $g \in \Sym^r$.

Finally, when 
$c < 1$, we have $(\frac{1}{1-c}) f \mathds{1}_{\mathbb{R} \setminus S^r} = \frac{f-cg}{1-c} \in \Sym$ by (lem:closure_under_subtraction of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition D:indexSpace of arXiv:2606.03079, 'Mean Field Limits for Stochastic, Underdamped Reactive Langevin Dynamics Models'] To describe the dynamics of $\nu_t$, we will sample vectors containing the indices of the specific substrate particles participating in a single $\ell$-type reaction from the substrate index space
$$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=(\mathbb{N} \backslash\{0\})^{|\alpha^{(\ell)}|}.
$$
For the allowable reactions considered in this work, we label the elements of $\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}$ according to their species types:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $\varnothing \rightarrow \cdots$
    $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\varnothing.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_j \rightarrow \cdots$
    $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{i_1^{(j)}\in\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\}\}.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_j + S_k \rightarrow \cdots$ with $j<k$
        $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{(i_1^{(j)},i_1^{(k)})\in (\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\})^2\}.
$$
    \item For $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $2S_j \rightarrow \cdots$
           $$
\mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}=\{(i_1^{(j)},i_2^{(j)})\in (\mathbb{N}\backslash\{0\})^2\}.
$$
\end{enumerate}
We write a particular sampled set of substrate indices $\bm{i}\in \mathbb{I}^{(\ell)}$ as
$$
\bm{i}=\bigl(i_{1}^{(1)}, \cdots, i_{\alpha_{\ell 1}}^{(1)}, \cdots, i_{1}^{(J)}, \cdots, i_{\alpha_{\ell J}}^{(J)}\bigr).
$$

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] Fix $k\in\{1,2,\dots\}$, $T>0$, and $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0$.
Assume \r{m0}, \r{m-monotone}, and \r{m-int-k}, and suppose that
$(u_0,v_0,u_-,f)$ satisfies the regularity and compatibility conditions of
order $k$ in Definition~\ref{def:compatibility}, for this value of
$\varepsilon$. Then \r{full_eq}, with $u(0)=u_0$, $u_t(0)=v_0$, the
prescribed prehistory $u_-$, and the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary
condition, has a unique weak solution. This solution is strong and satisfies
\[
\partial_t^j u\in C\bigl([0,T];H^{k+1-j}(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)\bigr),
\quad 0\leq j\leq k,\qquad
\partial_t^{k+1}u\in C\bigl([0,T];L^2(\Omega)\bigr).
\]
Moreover, $\partial_t^j u(0+)=U_j$ for $0\leq j\leq k+1$; hence the
forward and prehistory jets agree through order $k$. 
The solution depends continuously on the data in these spaces.

body: [Lemma g has two turning points of arXiv:2411.10296, 'Parking on a random rooted binary tree'] Let $\alpha > 2 - \sqrt{2}$. Then $g$ has two turning points, $t_1$ and $t_2$, which satisfy $0 < t_1 < t_2 < 1$. Both $t_1$ and 1 are roots of $g$, and $t_1$ is the point at which $G$ switches branches. Furthermore, $g$ is monotonically decreasing on $(0, t_1)$, increasing on $(t_1, t_2)$, and decreasing on $(t_2, 1)$.
title: Lemma g has two turning points of arXiv:2411.10296

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] A Markov chain (with transition matrix $P$) is called {\bf transitive} if for each pair of states $(x,y)\in \Omega^2$, there is a bijection $\xi_{(x,y)}: \Omega\to \Omega$ such that,
\[\xi(x) = y\]
and,
\[P(z,w)=P(\xi(z),\xi(w)),\quad \forall z,w\in \Omega\]

[Lemma thm_rel_energy_est of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold and $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$, $\mathscr{F}$, $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$, $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$, 
	$(u,\psi ,q)  $ be a weak  martingale solution to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper) with initial value 
	$u_0 \in L^2(\mathbb{T}^3; \mathbb{R}^3)$ divergence-free and $\psi_0\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^3)$ non-negative. Assume additionally that, on the same stochastic basis, there exists a local strong solution $(V,\Phi)$ to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper) until a stopping time $\tau>0$. Then it holds
	\begin{align}\begin{split}&
			\mathcal{E}( u_t,\psi^+_t | V_t,\Phi_t ) \,=\, 	\mathcal{E}( u_0,\psi_0  | V_0,\Phi_0 ) \,+\, \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} |u_t|^2 + (\psi_t^+)^2- |u_0|^2 - \psi_0^2\,\mathrm{d} x 
			\\&\qquad  +\, 2 \int_0^t  
			\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \nabla_{\mathrm{sym}} V:  \nabla_{\mathrm{sym}}  u + \nabla  \psi \cdot  \nabla \Phi 	\,\mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} s  \,-\,
			\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}  \frac{\psi}{\Phi} \bigl(
			|\nabla \Phi|^2+|\nabla_\mathrm{sym} V|^2
			\bigr)\,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} s \,-\, \int_{[0,t] \times \mathbb{T}^3}     \Phi   \,\mathrm{d} q
			\\&\qquad + \,  \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}   u \cdot      (( V \cdot \nabla)  V )-  \nabla   V:  u\otimes u \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s \,  + \, \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\psi V\cdot \nabla \Phi -\nabla \Phi \cdot (\psi u ) \,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} s,
	\end{split}\end{align}
	for all $t\in [0,T \wedge \tau)$,
	$\mathbb{P}$-almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: It\^o expansion of the relative energy

[Theorem 23 of arXiv:2609.03098, 'Standing waves for Schr\"odinger equations with Kato class potentials and $L^\infty$-bound'] {\em (See \cite[Ch. I, Th. 11.1]{rybakowski})}
Assume that a $C_0$ semigroup $\{T(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$ of bounded linear operators on a Banach space $X$ is hyperbolic (see, e.g., \cite[Def. V.1.14]{Engel}). If the dimension $\dim X_u=k$ of the unstable subspace $X_u$ \footnote{\ The unstable space $X_u$ is equal to $\ker P$, where $P$ is the spectral projection corresponding to $\{\lambda\in\sigma(T(t_0))\mid |\lambda|<1\}$ for some $t_0>0$.} is finite, then $\Phi\colon [0,+\infty) \times X\to X$, given by $\Phi(t,x):=T(t)x$, is a semiflow on $X$, $\{ 0\}$ is the maximal bounded invariant set with respect to $\Phi$, $(\Phi, \{ 0 \})\in {\mathcal I}(X)$ and $h(\Phi, \{ 0\})=\Sigma^k$ where $\Sigma^k=[(S^k, \overline s)]$  is the homotopy type of the pointed $k$-dimensional sphere.\hfill $\square$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 23 of arXiv:2609.03098

body:
[Theorem 20 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $\emptyset \ne \Omega \subset \RR^d$ be an arbitrary bounded domain.
Let $A_1,A_2\in \{B,F\}$.
Let $s_1,s_2\in \RR$ and let $0<p_1,q_1,p_2,q_2 \le \infty$ (with $p_i<\infty$ if $A_i=F$).
Assume that 
\begin{equation*}
   s_1 > s_2 
   \quad \text{and} \quad
    s_1 - \frac{1}{p_1} > s_2 -\frac{1}{p_2}.
\end{equation*}
Let $\SC$ denote the unit ball of $S^{s_1}_{p_1,q_1}A_1(\Omega)$
and let $\XX= S^{s_2}_{p_2,q_2}A_2(\Omega)$, endowed with the \mbox{(quasi-)}\allowbreak metric
induced by $\norm{\cdot\mid S^{s_2}_{p_2,q_2}A_2(\Omega)}$.
Then $\md(\SC)=\frac{1}{s_1-s_2}$ and there exists a Borel probability measure
on $\XX$ that is critical for $\SC$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 20 of arXiv:2608.30549

[Theorem thm:conc_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t \geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$, let
$\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper) with 
ergodic (time-independent) mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t]$, and
let $\nu \ll \mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu \in L^2(\mu)$. 
Then for all $t > 0$ and
$a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\bigl[-t I^\rho(\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] + a)\bigr],
  
\end{align}
where the Cram\'er transform
\begin{align}
I^\rho(s) \equiv \sup_{k \in \mathbb{R}}\bigl[k s - \Lambda^\rho(k)\bigr],

\end{align}
is defined as the Legendre conjugate of the principal eigenvalue $\Lambda^\rho(k)$~(equation eq:Lambda_rho_dirichlet of the paper).

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2603.28226, '2603.28226'] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:stein-gundy}. Let $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\ge0$. Then one can write
\[
 f=g_{\theta}+h_{\theta}+k_{\theta}
\]
where $g_{\theta}$ and $h_{\theta}$ satisfy the same estimates as in Theorem~\ref{thm:stein-gundy}\textup{(a)--(b)}, and
\begin{equation}

 0\le k_{\theta}\le(1+\theta)\lambda\quad\text{a.s.},
 \qquad
 \|k_{\theta}\|_1\le \|f\|_1,
 \qquad
 \|k_{\theta}\|_2^2\le(1+\theta)\lambda\|f\|_1.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
\[
 k_{\theta}=k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}+k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta},
\]
where
\[
 k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\gamma_j\mathbf1_{\{s_{\theta}\ge j\}},
 \qquad
 k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\mathbf1_{\{s_{\theta}\ge j\}},
\]
and
\[
 0\le k^{\mathrm{st}}_{\theta}\le \lambda,
 \qquad
 0\le k^{\mathrm{pr}}_{\theta}\le \theta\lambda
 \quad\text{a.s.}

[Proposition 40 (Coefficient-map transfer) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Assume $\kappa_r(\Phi)<\infty$ and that $\Phi$ maps finite-rank operators to
finite-rank operators.  Let
$K\in\cK_m^{\mathrm{alg}}$, and let $\Phi_\#K$ be obtained by applying
$\Phi$ to every deterministic coefficient of $K$.  Then
\begin{equation}

 \norm{\Flat_S(\Phi_\#K)}_{\Sch_r}
 \le\kappa_r(\Phi)\norm{\Flat_S(K)}_{\Sch_r}
\end{equation}
for every cut.  Hence
\[
 \Prof_{m,r}(\Phi_\#K)\le\kappa_r(\Phi)\Prof_{m,r}(K).
\]
For $1\le r<\infty$, $\Phi_\#$ therefore extends uniquely to a bounded map
between the corresponding simultaneous profile completions.

body:
[Corollary cor:hilbert-strata of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq1$, $k\geq2$, and a field $K$.  Recall the open normalized
exponent-shape simplex
\[
 \mathcal S_k=
 \{x\in\mathbb R^k:0=x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_k=1\}
\]
and put
\[
 N_h(x)=\left|\{u\cdot x:u\in\mathcal U_{h,k}\}\right|.
\]
For every $n\in\mathcal R(h,k)$, the locus
\[
 \mathcal H_{h,k}(n)=\{x\in\mathcal S_k:N_h(x)=n\}
\]
is a finite disjoint union of relatively open rational polytopes, and
\begin{equation}
 \max\{\dim P:P\text{ is a cell of }\mathcal H_{h,k}(n)\}
 =k-2-r_{h,k}(n).
\end{equation}
For rational $x\in\mathcal S_k$, choose $D\geq1$ with
$Dx\in\mathbb Z^k$ and let $C_x\subset\mathbb P^{k-1}$ be the projective
monomial curve defined by the kernel of
\[
 K[X_1,\ldots,X_k]\longrightarrow K[s,t],
 \qquad X_i\longmapsto s^{D(1-x_i)}t^{Dx_i}.
\]
The kernel is independent of the choice of $D$, and
\[
 H_{C_x}(h)=N_h(x).
\]
Consequently, $r_{h,k}(n)$ is exactly the codimension in exponent-shape
space of the largest stratum with degree-$h$ Hilbert value $n$.
If $h\geq2$, $k\geq3$, and $A_q$ is uniform in $\binom{[q]}k$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(|hA_q|=n)
 =k!c_{h,k,n}q^{-r_{h,k}(n)}
  +O_{h,k}(q^{-r_{h,k}(n)-1}),
\end{equation}
and hence the same integer has the four equivalent descriptions
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 r_{h,k}(n)
 =k-\deg F^{(k)}_{h,n}
 =\operatorname{codim}_{\mathcal S_k}\mathcal H_{h,k}(n)
 =-\lim_{q\to\infty}
   \frac{\log\mathbb P(|hA_q|=n)}{\log q}.}
\end{equation}
Here the codimension of a finite polyhedral union means the codimension of
its largest-dimensional cell.

body: Hurwitz's theorem is often quoted as 'a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is zero-free'. Three hypotheses carry that conclusion. (1) Connectedness of the domain. On U = D(0,1) union D(3,1) put f_n = 1/n on the first disk and f_n = 1 on the second; each f_n is holomorphic and zero-free on U and f_n converges locally uniformly, but the limit is 0 on one component and 1 on the other: neither zero-free nor identically zero. The correct statement is the dichotomy component by component. (2) The degenerate alternative cannot be dropped even on a connected domain: f_n(z) = exp(z)/n is zero-free on C and converges locally uniformly to the identically zero function. Likewise the injectivity version must allow constants: f_n(z) = z/n is injective on D and converges to the constant 0. (3) Holomorphy, not just real analyticity: on the real line f_n(x) = x^2 + 1/n has no real zeros and converges uniformly on compacts to x^2, which has a zero; the complex statement survives because the complex zeros ±i/sqrt(n) move to 0. (4) The counting form requires that the boundary circle avoid the zeros of the limit: f_n(z) = z - 1 + 1/n has one zero in the unit disk for every n, while f_n(z) = z - 1 - 1/n has none, and both converge to z - 1, whose only zero sits on the circle |z| = 1. Never conclude equal zero counts from a circle through a zero of the limit.
title: Pitfall: Hurwitz's theorem needs connectedness, holomorphy, and allows the degenerate limit

slowly varying functions. Then
\[
\sum_{\substack{1\le s,t\le n\\s\ne t}}
s^{-d}\ell(s)t^{-d}\ell(t)|t-s|^{-\beta}L(|t-s|)
\sim
n^{2-2d-\beta}\ell(n)^2L(n)I_{\beta,d},
\]
where
\(
I_{\beta,d}:=
\int_0^1\int_0^1x^{-d}y^{-d}|x-y|^{-\beta}\,dx\,dy<\infty .
\)

Their parameters are alpha=ell/d, kappa=k/d and tau=n/d^2, where ell is context length, k is the number of Gaussian tasks drawn once into a fixed pool, and n is the number of training contexts. Section III.E equation (18), printed p.11, predicts, in the additional joint limit alpha,tau -> infinity with fixed c_*=alpha/tau>0, that the task-generalization gap g_task=e_ICL-e_IDG equals (1-kappa)[1+rho*c_*/(1+rho)] for kappa<1 and 0 for kappa>1. Here rho>=0 is the label-noise variance. The displayed equation omits kappa=1. Section III.D equation (17) instead studies alpha -> infinity at fixed tau and gives a ridgeless ICL-error divergence boundary kappa<=min(tau,1). Preserve the different limit orders. The source explicitly discloses heuristic steps in Section III.B p.8 and the SI opening p.18. Record the final learning-curve asymptotics as qualified predictions, not as a fully rigorous theorem. body:
[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] Supposing Assumption~\ref{as:growth} and \(b\) has sub-linear growth
  in its radial direction, i.e. there exists some \(\delta > 0\) such that
  \begin{equation}
    \<x, b(x)\> \lesssim \|x\|(1 + \|x\|)^{1 - \delta},\qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
  \end{equation}
  Then, the unique global solution \((x_t)\) of the branched RDE~\eqref{eq:bRDE} satisfies
  \[\sup_{s \in [0, t]}\|x_s\| \lesssim \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\gamma; [0, t]}^\eta\]
  for any \(t \in [0, T]\) where
  \(\eta := (N^2 - N + 1)\left(\left(\frac{1}{\delta} + \frac{N + 1}{(1 - \delta)\lambda}\right) 
    \vee \left(\frac{1}{\delta} + \frac{1}{(1 - \delta)(1 - \theta)\gamma} - 1\right)\right)\)
  and \(\lambda := (1 - \theta + \kappa)\gamma\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 27 of arXiv:2606.09904

body:
[Proposition prop:fdd of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that the BPVE $(X_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies conditions (C1)--(C3) and for $k \geq 0, \ell \geq 0$ let 
$0 < t_{-k} < t_{-k+1} < \ldots < t_{-1} < t_0 = 1 < t_{1} < 
\ldots < t_{\ell} < \infty$, and $x_i \in \mathbb{N}$, $i = -k, \ldots, \ell$. 
Then
\[
\begin{split}
& \lim_{n \to \infty}
\mathbf{P} ( X_{A(n t_i)} = x_i, i= -k, \ldots,  \ell | 
X_{A(n)} > 0) \\
& = \mathbf{P}_{t_{-k}} ( U(t_i) = x_i, i= -k, \ldots, \ell | U(1) > 0),
\end{split}
\]
where $\mathbf{P}_{t_{-k}}$ denotes the law of $(U(t))_{t \geq t_{-k}}$ with 
initial distribution $U(t_{-k}) \sim \textrm{Geom}(\tfrac{2}{2+\nu})$.
title: Proposition prop:fdd of arXiv:2412.03325

[Definition 50 (Fractional Sobolev spaces) of arXiv:2605.14630, '2605.14630'] For $s\geqs0$, the \emph{fractional Sobolev space} $H^s(\Lambda)$ is the 
space of functions $f\in \H = L^2(\Lambda)$ such that 
\begin{equation}
 
 \norm{f}_{H^s}^2 := \sum_{k\in\Z^d} \lambda_k^s \abs{\hat f(k)}^2 < \infty\;.
\end{equation} 
In particular, $H^0(\Lambda) = L^2(\Lambda)$. For $s<0$, $H^s(\Lambda)$ is 
the closure of $L^2(\Lambda)$ under the norm \eqref{eq:Sobolev_norm}.

body:
[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] Let $\omega \in C([0,T], \Rr^d)\cap Q^\pi([0, T], \mathbb{R}^d)$ and $f\in C^2_b(\mathbb{R}^d, \Rr)$. Then the following limit change of variable formula holds
$$
f(\omega(T)) = f(\omega(0)) + \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega + \frac{1}{2}[\nabla f(\omega), \omega]_\pi(T).
$$
where the integral $ \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega$ is defined as the limit of left Riemann sums along the sequence of partitions $(\pi_n)_{n\geq 1}$:
\[
 \int_0^T \nabla f(\omega)d^\pi\omega:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{\pi_n} \nabla f(\omega(t^n_k))\cdot \left(\omega(t^n_{k+1}) - \omega(t^n_k)\right).
\]

body: Definition 4 (Edge type). Let G = (V, E, R, tau, w) be a base graph (Definition 1), where each node v in V carries a representational payload P_v as in Definition 2. The relation-type set R partitions into six pairwise-disjoint classes, R = R_causal U R_contain U R_temp U R_assoc U R_epist U R_spatial, each defined by an independent structural test below. For each edge e = (u, v) in E, the assigned type tau(e) in R belongs to exactly one class. A particular graph may employ only a subset; belief-graph and working-memory instantiations specify which classes appear in R_B and R_{W_t}. The six classes are: 1. Causal (R_causal). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_causal asserts that node u produces, enables, probabilistically raises, or inhibits the occurrence of node v, independent of the payload types of u and v: R_causal = {r_causes, r_enables, r_inhibits, r_counterfactual}. Causal edges are antisymmetric: (u, v) in E_{R_causal} implies (v, u) not in E_{R_causal}. Acyclicity over R_causal is a structural forbidden pattern in S. When u is a distinguished agent node, an optional attribution tag a(u, v) in V records whose causal model the edge belongs to, e.g. 'agent a believes u causes v'. 2. Containment (R_contain). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_contain asserts that v's existence or identity is nested inside u's scope, characterized by an existential-dependency test: (u, v) in E_{R_contain} iff removing u from G requires removing v as well. R_contain = {r_is-a, r_part-of, r_instance-of, r_role-of}. When v carries a graph payload G_v (Definition 2, item 5) or a structured perceptual payload (item 4), its internal subgraph is linked to v via r_part-of edges. Containment is transitive and irreflexive; a directed cycle over R_contain is a forbidden pattern in S. 3. Temporal (R_temp). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_temp encodes ordering of nodes across time via a node timestamp function theta_V : V -> R (distinct from the working-memory time index t) such that (u, v) in E_{R_temp} implies theta_V(u) <= theta_V(v): R_temp = {r_before, r_after, r_during, r_next}. Here r_before and r_after are mutually exclusive on the same ordered pair (a predicate incompatibility in F); r_next is the sequential successor used in action-sequence and planning subgraphs. 4. Associative (R_assoc). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_assoc encodes statistical co-occurrence or spreading-activation linkage with no stronger typed commitment: R_assoc = {r_related-to, r_co-occurs-with, r_similar-to}. Associative edges are undirected, represented as symmetric pairs (u, v), (v, u) in E with equal weights w(u, v) = w(v, u). This is the default class: any relation not warranting a stronger typed commitment from classes 1-3 or 5-6 defaults here. 5. Evidential (R_epist). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_epist encodes inferential, evidential, or evaluative support between propositional or evaluative nodes: R_epist = {r_supports, r_contradicts, r_derived-from, r_supersedes}. Valence and deontic force are carried as signed edge weights on r_supports and r_contradicts edges (extending w to R on R_epist when needed); an obligation is an r_supports edge with |w(u, v)| = 1 directed at a norm node, and a prohibition is the corresponding r_contradicts edge. Here r_contradicts induces a conflict pair in (F, S); r_supersedes is generated by belief-update operators when a node is revised rather than deleted. 6. Spatial (R_spatial). An edge (u, v) with tau(u, v) in R_spatial encodes geometric relations, restricted to node pairs where at least one endpoint carries a perceptual or structured perceptual payload (Definition 2, items 3-4): R_spatial = {r_above, r_below, r_left-of, r_right-of, r_near, r_affords}. The sub-type r_affords links a body-schema node u to a perceptual node v, encoding a sensorimotor affordance relation. For any edge class R_k, write E_{R_k} = {(u, v) in E | tau(u, v) in R_k} for the induced edge set. For a subgraph Q of B, the restriction E_{R_k}(Q) = E_{R_k} intersected with (V_Q x V_Q) denotes the edges of that class internal to Q.

[Proposition prop:approximation of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a compact $0<d$-doubling space of diameter at-most $1$; then, there are constants
$
    0<C_d<\infty
$\footnote{Depending only on $(X,\rho,\mathfrak{m})$.}, such that: for every $2\le N \in \mathbb{N}$ there are $\{x_n\}_{n=1}^N\subseteq X$ so that: for every $f\in\mathcal F_{1:d}$, the parameter vector
$
    \theta_f
\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \big((f(x_n),x_n,1)\big)_{n=1}^N
$
satisfies
\begin{equation}

    \|f-\hat{f}_{\theta_f}\|_{C(X)}
\le
    C_d\,N^{-1/d}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Defn 6 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] We define the empirical spin field as the following empirical signed measure:
$$\eta_N := \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{i=1}^N \sigma _i \delta_{i/N}.$$
    Further, for any function $f: [0,1]\to \R$, we define:
    $$\sigma_N(f) \coloneqq \int f \,\mathrm d \eta_N= \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{i=1}^N f\left(\frac{i}{N}\right)\sigma_i.$$
title: Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.12804

STATUS: proof (unaudited). For the Gaussian zero-bias width-n ReLU angle chain with fixed theta0 in (0,pi], every finite T admits C_(theta0,T),n0 with E|k theta_k-3pi|<=C_(theta0,T)[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)] for1<=k<=Tn, n>=n0. This holds for the hybrid regularized chain and for the exact chain killed at degeneracy and set to angle0. Consequently k_n theta_(k_n) converges to3pi in L1 whenever k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to0. Assumptions: Independent Gaussian rows and layers; zero-bias ReLU; fixed strictly positive initial angle. Reciprocal square-integrable martingale calculations are performed only for the C039 hybrid kernel, whose multiplier is bounded; bounded angle coupling transfers the conclusion to the exact chain. The angle transition uses n independent row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h iid standard Gaussians, independent across layers, and the angle between the resulting vectors. Kill at zero norm or zero angle. For the hybrid kernel use a fixed small concentration box for (mean(x^2+y^2),mean((x-y)^2)/theta^2,mean(x^2-y^2)/theta) at small theta, and ordinary Gram averages at larger theta, each centered at its expectation; self-loop on failure. Limit: Unaudited proof and dependencies. Constants need not remain bounded as theta0 tends to0. This does not assert finite raw exact reciprocal moments or the terminal weak-bias rate.
Independent Gaussian rows and layers; zero-bias ReLU; fixed strictly positive initial angle. Reciprocal square-integrable martingale calculations are performed only for the C039 hybrid kernel, whose multiplier is bounded; bounded angle coupling transfers the conclusion to the exact chain.

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
Use C039's global hybrid normalized/ordinary Gram regularization. Its
reciprocal U=1/(n theta) is finite; no raw exact-chain reciprocal mean is
used. Fix theta0 in (0,pi] and T<infinity. Constants may depend on theta0,T.
Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2).

## C040: quantitative mesoscopic angular law

For either the hybrid chain or the exact chain killed at degeneracy,

    E|k theta_k-1/a|
          <= C_(theta0,T)[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)],
                         1<=k<=floor(Tn), n sufficiently large. (1)

The exact angle is defined to be zero after killing. Consequently
k_n theta_(k_n) -> 3pi in L1 whenever k_n -> infinity and k_n/n -> 0.
The constants are not uniform as theta0 decreases to zero.

### Global reciprocal estimates for the hybrid chain

For all theta in (0,pi], with u=1/(n theta), its one-step multiplier
R=U_next/u=theta/theta_next satisfies

    E[R^q] <= 1+C_q(theta+1/n), q=1,2,
    E[(R-1)^2] <= C(theta^2+1/n),                  (2)
    |E(U_next-u)-(a+2u)/n|
                   <= C[theta/n+1/n^2+u/n^(3/2)]. (3)

To check (2), the multiplier and its coordinate derivatives are uniformly
bounded on each hybrid good box, and equal one off it. Sample-average
Taylor expansion gives E R^q=(theta/F(theta))^q+O_q(1/n), while the
Lipschitz estimate gives E|R-theta/F(theta)|^2<=C/n. The deterministic
ratio theta/F(theta)=1+O(theta) uniformly on (0,pi], proving (2).

For small theta the same centered Taylor expansion through order two
has third-absolute-moment remainder O(n^(-3/2)), uniformly in theta.
The covariance-Hessian contraction for R at theta=0 is2 (C032), its
variation is O(theta), and its deterministic term is
theta/F(theta)=1+a theta+O(theta^2). Hence

    E R=1+a theta+2/n
                    +O(theta^2+theta/n+n^(-3/2)).

Multiplication by u and u*theta=1/n proves (3) on that range. On the
remaining compact angle interval, u<=C/n; bounded multipliers imply
an O(1/n) error, which is bounded by C theta/n since theta is bounded
below there. Thus (3) holds globally. None of these estimates takes
the expectation of an unregularized reciprocal.

Let m_q(j)=E U_j^q. From (2),

    m_1(j+1)<=(1+C/n)m_1(j)+C/n,
    m_2(j+1)<=(1+C/n)m_2(j)+(C/n)m_1(j).

Since U0=1/(n theta0), summing these two recurrences in that order gives

    E U_j<=C_(theta0,T)(j+1)/n,
    E U_j^2<=C_(theta0,T)(j+1)^2/n^2,
                                          0<=j<=Tn.            (4)

The second estimate includes the initial square and the sum of the first
estimate divided by n. Equation (2) also gives

    E[(U_(j+1)-U_j)^2 | U_j,theta_j]
                                      <=C(U_j^2/n+1/n^2).      (5)

### Martingale tracking and inversion

Decompose U_k-U0 into its conditional mean increments and the square-
integrable martingale M_k. Orthogonality of martingale increments and
(4)-(5) imply

    ||M_k||_2 <= C[sqrt(k^3/n^3)+sqrt(k)/n].                    (6)

Using (3), (4), and the global p=2 angle bound from C039, Minkowski gives

    ||U_k-U0-a k/n-M_k||_2
       <= (2/n)sum_(j<k)||U_j||_2
          +C/n sum_(j<k)||theta_j||_2+Ck/n^2
          +C/n^(3/2)sum_(j<k)||U_j||_2
       <= C[k(k+1)/n^2+log(k+1)/n+k/n^2
                                      +k(k+1)/n^(5/2)].        (7)

Thus with Z_k=nU_k/k,

    ||Z_k-a||_2<=C[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)], 1<=k<=Tn.              (8)

Here log(k+1)/k<=C/sqrt(k), k/n<=sqrt(T)*sqrt(k/n), and the initial
nU0/k term is O_(theta0)(1/k). These justify the simplification in (8).

Now Y_k=k theta_k=1/Z_k. C039 with p=2 gives a uniform bound E Y_k^2<=C_T.
On {Z_k>=a/2}, |Y_k-1/a|<=2|Z_k-a|/a^2. On the complementary event,
Chebyshev bounds its probability by4||Z_k-a||_2^2/a^2. Cauchy-Schwarz
and the uniform second moment of Y_k bound its contribution to the L1
error by C||Z_k-a||_2 (if this norm is large, the same inequality follows
by increasing C). This proves (1) for the hybrid chain.

Couple the exact chain with it through time k as in C039. The discrepancy
probability is Ck exp(-cn). Both angles lie in [0,pi], so the additional
L1 error in k theta_k is at most Ck^2 exp(-cn). For k<=Tn this is absorbed
by C_(T)/sqrt(k). This proves (1) for the exact chain.

## C041: the network's weighted singular occupation coefficient

Let P_s be the semigroup of dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)V dW, V0=0, and
f(u)=1-exp(-u). Fix t>0, N=floor(nt), t_n=N/n, and

    h_(n,k)(u)=D P_(t_n-k/n)f(u), 1<=k<N,
    D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t)].

For both the hybrid chain and the exact chain with the alive indicator,

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E[theta_k h_(n,k)(U_k);alive]
                            =(D_t/a) log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1).   (9)

For the hybrid chain, with C=B-A^2/2 from C033,

    (1/n^2)sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E[(C P_(t_n-k/n)f)(U_k)]
                    =D_t log(n)/(2pi n)+O_(theta0,t)(1/n).     (10)

This is an occupation calculation on actual chain states, not yet a
telescoped weak-error formula for the terminal observable.

Proof. The affine solution V_v^u=V_v^0+uJ_v, J_v=exp(v+sqrt(2)W_v),
gives bounded first and second initial-value derivatives of P_v f,
uniformly for 0<=v<=t and u>=0. The time derivative of D P_v f is bounded
as in C034: (Af)' is bounded and E J_v is finite. Therefore

    |h_(n,k)(u)-D_(t_n)|<=C_t(k/n+u).                         (11)

On alive states theta_k U_k=1/n. C039 gives E theta_k<=C/(k+1), so

    E[theta_k |h_(n,k)(U_k)-D_(t_n)|;alive]<=C_t/n.

Its sum is O_t(1). From (1),

    |E theta_k-1/(ak)|<=C[k^(-3/2)+1/sqrt(nk)],

whose sum from1 toN-1 is bounded by C_(theta0,t). Consequently
sum E theta_k=(1/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1). Combining these facts and
|D_(t_n)-D_t|<=C_t/n proves (9). The killed exact chain has the same
estimates and the identity theta*U=1/n only on alive states, as required.

The singular drift term in C is b/u. In (10) its contribution is b/n
times (9), giving (b/a)D_t log(n)/n. The remaining terms are

    (8u+a/5) D P_v f+(4u^2-3au/5) D^2 P_v f.

Their expected absolute values are uniformly bounded using the bounded
derivatives and (4) through time t_n. Their n^-2 sum is therefore O(1/n).
Finally b/a=1/(2pi), proving (10).

The remaining global weak-rate step is a semigroup telescoping identity
whose accumulated local errors are O(1/n) for this unbounded reciprocal
state space and whose initial-layer contribution is also O(1/n).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:5dd8c87ca1986234f07df8c27b9999283f4a603a2d3d51680b9b8e5c4bf453e5","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C040:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Sharp relaxation exponent for local tree rotations and triangulation flips structural attempt Result: A canonical-path construction that first rotates every tree to one fixed comb has exponential congestion, even if each route is short. Let N be the number of states and use uniform stationary mass1/N. Routing the all-pairs demand pi(x)*pi(y) through that comb sends total order1 flow through a vertex whose total stationary transition capacity is1/N. Some incident edge therefore has load-to-capacity ratio at least order N. For triangulations N is a Catalan number of order4^n/n^(3/2). Check: The total capacity through the chosen vertex is sum_y pi(v)P(v,y)=1/N. Pairs not starting or ending there have total demand(1-1/N)^2 and must cross it in the proposed construction. Summing their edge loads gives the claimed bottleneck independently of path length. Obstruction: A proof needs routes or transport flows distributed over many intermediate shapes. The comb normal form is useful for irreducibility but cannot furnish the conjectured polynomial relaxation bound.

body:
Let X=(X_1,...,X_n) be a fixed finite tuple of bounded selfadjoint elements in a finite von Neumann algebra with faithful normal tracial state tau(1)=1. In a free extension, let S_1,...,S_n be centered semicircular elements with tau(S_j^2)=1, such that the algebra generated by X and the individual algebras generated by the S_j are freely independent. For a tuple Y, let Phi_star(Y) be conjugate-variable free Fisher information, the sum of squared L2 norms of its conjugate variables, with value +infinity if they do not all exist. Voiculescu defines non-microstates free entropy relative to C by chi_star(X)=(1/2)*integral_0^infinity [n/(1+t)-Phi_star(X_1+sqrt(t)*S_1,...,X_n+sqrt(t)*S_n)]dt+(n/2)*log(2*pi*e), using the improper-integral convention of the source. Logarithms are natural and the semicircular variance parameter is t. The integrand uses Phi_star, the sum of squared L2 norms of the conjugate variables. The notation chi_star distinguishes this construction from microstates free entropy chi; equality for arbitrary tuples is not asserted here. This card records the definition and its normalization, not a matrix mutual-information limit or an entropy differentiability theorem.
Fixed finite bounded selfadjoint tuple in a normalized tracial von Neumann setting.
Standard variance-one semicircular perturbations are mutually free and free from the input tuple.
Phi_star is conjugate-variable free Fisher information; logarithms are natural.

[Proposition 16 (The uniform-grid fixed-rate optimum is within-group flatness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Writing $E=\sum_k v_k^2$ for the total energy over coordinate magnitudes $v_k$,
the objective \eqref{eq:fixedrate-D}, which is the group-maximum objective of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii) rederived from the quantizer's own step rule, satisfies
\[
D_{\mathrm{fr}}=\sum_g M_g^2 \;\ge\; \frac1G\sum_k v_k^2 \;=\; \frac{E}{G},
\]
with equality iff every group is internally \emph{uniform}. Thus, at fixed $E$, $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$
is minimized precisely by driving every within-group crest factor to its floor;
the \emph{across}-group energy profile is irrelevant once each group is internally
balanced. No within-group concentration step lowers $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$, and any such step that
raises a group's peak $M_g$ raises it strictly; $D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, with equality
when every group's mass sits on a single coordinate.

[Corollary of arXiv:2608.07042, 'Limit Points of Reflow with Minibatch Optimal Transport'] Let $(\gamma_n)_n$ be generated by Algorithm~(alg:minibatch_OT_rec_grad of the paper) and $(n_k)_k$ a subsequence such that $(\gamma_{n_k})_k$ converges (weakly) to a limit point $\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu_0,\mu_1)$. Denote by $\mu_t$ and $\mu_{t,n}$ the corresponding interpolations (equation eq:def_mu_t of the paper). Assume that there exists $t\in(0,1)$ such that $\mu_{t,n_k}$ is absolutely continuous for all $k$ and fulfills that $1/\mu_{t,n_k}\rightharpoonup 1/\mu_t$ 
weakly in $L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Then $\gamma$ is an optimal transport plan between $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$.

body: The fundamental group pi_1(X, x0) of a topological space X at a basepoint x0 is the set of homotopy classes of loops based at x0, with concatenation as the group operation, constant loop as identity, and reversal as inverse. For path-connected X the isomorphism class is basepoint-independent. pi_1 is a homotopy invariant and a functor: continuous maps induce homomorphisms.
title: Fundamental Group

For each $(z,\theta,m)\in\mathcal Z\times\Theta\times\mathcal M$, define
\[
g_{z,\theta,m}(x)
:=
m+\ell\bigl(f(z,x,\theta)-m\bigr),
\]
and let
\[
\mathcal G
:=
\bigl\{
g_{z,\theta,m}
:\,
(z,\theta,m)\in\mathcal Z\times\Theta\times\mathcal M
\bigr\}.
\]
Then $\mathcal G$ is $\P$-Glivenko--Cantelli. In particular,
\[

\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g_{z,\theta,m}(X_i)-\E_\P[g_{z,\theta,m}(X)]
\right|
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z,\ \theta\in\Theta}
\left|
\rho^{\widehat{\mathbb P}_n}\!\big(f(z;X,\theta)\big)
-\rho^{\mathbb P}\!\big(f(z;X,\theta)\big)
\right|
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0.
\]

body: Dominated convergence theorem: if measurable functions f_n converge pointwise almost everywhere to f on a measure space, and |f_n| <= g almost everywhere for a single integrable g, then f is integrable, the integrals of f_n converge to the integral of f, and in fact f_n converges to f in L^1. Domination is essential: f_n = n on (0, 1/n) converges pointwise to 0 while the integrals stay 1.
title: Dominated convergence theorem

[Theorem th:log-normality-SHF of arXiv:2511.08479, '\Large From disordered systems to the Critical 2D Stochastic Heat Flow'] For a Euclidean ball $B(x,\delta) := \big\{y \in \mathbb{R}^2 \colon \ |y-x| < \delta \big\}$, denote the uniform distribution over it by
${\ensuremath{\mathcal U}} _{B(x,\delta)}(\cdot) := \frac{1}{\pi \delta^2} \, \mathrm{1}_{B(x,\delta)}(\cdot)$.
Then for any $t > 0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$, the following convergence in distribution holds:
\begin{equation}
	\forall \varrho \in (0,\infty) \colon \qquad
	\mathscr{Z}_{t}^{\vartheta} \big({\ensuremath{\mathcal U}} _{B(x,\sqrt{e^{\varrho \vartheta}})}\big)
	\ \xrightarrow[\ \vartheta \to -\infty \ ]{d} \
	e^{{\ensuremath{\mathcal N}} (0,\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2}
	\qquad \text{with } \sigma^2 = \log(1+\varrho) \,.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem th:log-normality-SHF of arXiv:2511.08479

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2604.08127, 'Asymptotics of Brownian occupation measures \\ with unusually large intersections'] A sequence $\widetilde{\mu}^{\otimes p}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_1^{\otimes p}$ converges to $\{ \widetilde{\alpha}_i^{\otimes p} \}$ in $(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}^{\otimes p}, \mathbf{D}^{\otimes p})$ if there exists a decomposition
    \[
    \mu_n^{\otimes p} = \sum_{i \in I} \alpha_{i, n}^{\otimes p} + \beta_n^{\otimes p}
    \]
    and points $x_{i, n} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\alpha_{i, n}^j \ast \delta_{x_i^n} \to \alpha_i^j$ weakly for all $i \in I$ and  $j = 1 , \dots , p$,
        \item $\beta_n^j$ \emph{totally disintegrates}, i.e., $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^d} \beta_n^j (B(x, R)) = 0$ for any finite $R > 0$.
        \item Distinct sequences are \emph{widely separated}, i.e., $\lim_{n \to \infty} |x_{i_1}^n - x_{i_2}^n| = \infty$ for any $i_1 \ne i_2$.
    \end{enumerate}
    As a consequence, the inclusion $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_1 \hookrightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal{X}}_{\le 1}^{\otimes p}$ is a continuous injection and $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_1$ is a dense subset of $\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}_{\le 1}^{\otimes p}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 24 of arXiv:2604.08127

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] Let $X$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold and $D$ a reduced simple normal crossing divisor on $X$.
    Assume that $K_X+D$ is nef.
    Then the following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $c_2(\Omega^1_X(\log D))=0 \text{ in } H^{2,2}(X,\mathbb{R})$.
        \item $\Omega^1_X(\log D)$ is nef and $\nd(K_X+D)\leq1$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 6 of arXiv:2609.01965

[Proposition prop:couplefronts of arXiv:2607.08914, 'Linear spreading speed in non-monotone population models'] There are constants $c,C \in (0,\infty)$ such that for every
  $\ell,\rho \in \mathbb{N}$ with
  $(\ell - \rho L_\mathrm{bl})/(2R ) \ge T_\mathrm{bl}+ (2\rho +1) T_\mathrm{bl}/\tilde v$
  and every
  $\eta_0^1, \eta_0^2$ satisfying
  \begin{align*}
    &\abs{ W(\eta^1_0 )\cap B^\mathrm{bl}_\rho(0) }\ge p_\nu V_\rho /2,
    \\&\abs{W(\eta_0^2)} \ge p_\nu V_\rho/2
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad\eta_0^2(x) = 0 \text{ for all }x > -\ell,
  \end{align*}
  there is a coupling $ P_{\eta_0^1,\eta_0^2}$ of processes $\eta^1$, $\eta^2$
  started from $\eta_0^1$, $\eta_0^2$, respectively, such that
  \begin{equation*}
    P_{\eta_0^1,\eta_0^2}\big(M^1_k \ge M^2_k \text{ for all } k\ge 0\big)
    \ge 1 - 2 C e^{-c \rho}
    - C \sqrt{\ell-\rho L_\mathrm{bl}}\,e^{ -c \sqrt{\ell -\rho L_\mathrm{bl}}}.
  \end{equation*}

[Definition 18 (Exponential factor of i.i.d. (EFIID)) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider the setting of Definition~\ref{def:FIID}.
   A FIID is called an \emph{exponential factor of i.i.d.}\ (EFIID) with tails $(c,C)$ for constants $c,C\in(0,\infty)$ if for any $u\in V$,
   there exists a connected local set $\calL_u=\calL_u(X)\ni u$ such that:
   \begin{itemize}
    \item The value of $\phi(X)_u$ is measurable with respect to $X|_{\calL_u}$,
    \item We have $\P[\{|\calL_u|\geq n\}]\leq C e^{-cn}$ for any $n\in\Z_{\geq 0}$.
   \end{itemize}

 \cap L_{T_0}^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{-1/2-\betasum-\kappa}.
\]
\item For every $a\in\mathfrak C$,
\[
 \Gamma_a^{\chi,\rho}\in C_{T_0}\mathcal C^{-\beta_{\Gamma,a}-\kappa}
 \cap L_{T_0}^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{-\beta_{\Gamma,a}-\kappa}.
\]
\item For $(a;b,b)\in\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}}$,
\[
 \mathcal D^{a;b}\in\mathcal L\bigl(
 E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma},L_{T_0}^\infty B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1}\bigr),
\]
and for every $(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L$,
\[
 \mathcal B^{a;b,c}\in\mathcal L\bigl(
 E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma},L_{T_0}^1B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1}\bigr).
\]
Define
\begin{equation}
 T^{a;b,c}:=
 \begin{cases}
  \mathcal D^{a;b}+\mathcal B^{a;b,b},
    &(a;b,c)=(a;b,b)\in\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}},\\
  \mathcal B^{a;b,c},
    &(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{off}}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 T^{a;b,c}\in\mathcal L(E_{T_0}^{2,\sigma},C_{T_0}H^{s_2-1})
 \qquad ((a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L).
\]
All these operators are causal, their restrictions are understood through
Lemma~\ref{lem:time-extension-causality}, and
\begin{align}
 &\sup_{I\subset[0,T_0]}
 \Bigg[
 \sum_{(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L}
 \|T_I^{a;b,c}\|_{E_{I,0}^{2,\sigma}\to C_IH^{s_2-1}}\notag\\
 &\hspace{35mm}+
 \sum_{(a;b,b)\in\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}}}
 \|\mathcal D_I^{a;b}\|_{E_{I,0}^{2,\sigma}\to
 L^\infty(I;B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1})}
 \Bigg]<\infty.
\end{align}
\item Define
\begin{equation}
 \omega_{\mathrm{cen},\Xi}(h):=
 \sum_{(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L}
 \sup_{\substack{I\subset[0,T_0]\text{ interval}\\ |I|\le h}}
 \|\mathcal B_I^{a;b,c}\|_{\mathcal L(
 E_{I,0}^{2,\sigma},L^1(I;B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1}))}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \omega_{\mathrm{cen},\Xi}(h)\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(h\downarrow0),
\end{equation}
and, separately,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L}
 \|\mathcal B^{a;b,c}_{[0,T]}\|_{\mathcal L(
 E_T^{2,\sigma},L_T^1B_{2,\infty}^{\sigma-1})}
 \longrightarrow0
 \qquad(T\downarrow0).
\end{equation}
The first limit is used on translated zero-history intervals; the second is
used for the fixed-point construction from prescribed Cauchy data.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:IorderedRandom of arXiv:2606.24465, 'History estimation in random recursive trees:\\Pointwise approach via iterated Jordan cent'] Fix some $v \geq 1$ and let $I$ be a function acting in the space of  recursive trees and returning a subset of vertices of $[v]$, such that for any recursive tree $\mathrm{t}$ of size $n\geq v$,

    \begin{itemize}
        \item for any permutation $\tau$ of $I(\mathrm{t})$, the tree $\mathrm{t}^{\tau}$ is recursive and $I(\mathrm{t}^{\tau})=I(\mathrm{t})$;
        \item for $\mathrm{t}_v$, the subtree of $\mathrm{t}$ spanned by vertices in $[v]$, $I(\mathrm{t}_v)=I(\mathrm{t})$. 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for any label-invariant estimator $\widehat{\sigma}$ and any set $\mathcal{I}$ in the image of $I$ with $i,v \in \mathcal{I}$,

    $$
     \widehat{\sigma}\left(v,T_n\right)\mid I(T_n)=\mathcal{I} \quad 
     \overset{\mathcal{L}}{=} \quad 
     \widehat{\sigma}\left(i,T_n\right)\mid  I(T_n)=\mathcal{I}.
     $$

[Corollary 4 (Certified finite-direction radial reconstruction for $1<\beta<2$) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] Assume
\[
m\ge2,
\qquad
1<\beta<2.
\]
Fix
\[
0\le\varepsilon<1
\quad\text{such that}\quad
1\le k=\lfloor(m+1)\varepsilon\rfloor\le m.
\]
Let $c$ be the common center from Corollary~\ref{cor:power} and define the explicit constants
\[
\mu_{-j},r_j,H_j,D_{ij},M_j,\lambda_j,\ell_j,L
\]
as above.  Then
\[
\operatorname{Lip}(R_j)\le\ell_j,
\qquad
\operatorname{Lip}(R_\varepsilon)\le L,
\]
where Lipschitz constants on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ are taken in chord distance.

Let
\[
\mathcal U=\{u_\ell\}_{\ell=1}^N\subset\mathbb S^{d-1}
\]
be a nonempty finite directional set.  Assume certified radial intervals
\[
a_\ell\le R_\varepsilon(u_\ell)\le b_\ell,
\qquad
b_\ell-a_\ell\le\delta.
\]
Define
\[
\underline R(u)
=
\max\left\{
0,
\max_\ell\left[a_\ell-L\|u-u_\ell\|\right]
\right\},
\]
and
\[
\overline R(u)
=
\min_\ell\left[b_\ell+L\|u-u_\ell\|\right].
\]
Then
\[
\underline R(u)\le R_\varepsilon(u)\le\overline R(u)
\qquad\forall u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}.
\]
Let
\[
h_{\mathcal U}
=
\sup_{u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}
\min_\ell\|u-u_\ell\|.
\]
Then
\[
\|\overline R-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Define
\[
\underline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\underline R(u)\},
\]
and
\[
\overline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\overline R(u)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\underline\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^\varepsilon\subseteq\overline\Gamma.
\]
Moreover,
\[
d_H(\underline\Gamma,\Gamma^\varepsilon)
\le
\|R_\varepsilon-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U},
\]
\[
d_H(\Gamma^\varepsilon,\overline\Gamma)
\le
\|\overline R-R_\varepsilon\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U},
\]
and directly
\[
d_H(\underline\Gamma,\overline\Gamma)
\le
\|\overline R-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U}.
\]

[Theorem 2 (Microscopic second-moment universality) of arXiv:2608.27641, 'Hard-Edge Determinant Fields and Second-Moment Universality for Random Matrix Ratios'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:matrix-atoms}, the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item The rescaled spectrum converges to the infinite complex Ginibre process:
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\qquad
\text{in }\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbb{C}\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\sqrt{n}R_{n,1},
\ldots,
\sqrt{n}R_{n,k}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1,\ldots,R_k
\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\frac{R_{n,n}}{\sqrt{n}},
\ldots,
\frac{R_{n,n-k+1}}{\sqrt{n}}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1^{-1},\ldots,R_k^{-1}
\right).
\]

\item In particular,
\[
\sqrt{n}\rho_{\min}\left(M_n\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1,
\qquad
\frac{\rho_{\max}\left(M_n\right)}{\sqrt{n}}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1^{-1}.
\]

\item If \(D\subset\mathbb{C}\) is a bounded Borel set whose boundary has zero planar Lebesgue measure, then
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n\left(D\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

More explicitly, let
\(\left(\Gamma_j\right)_{j\geq 1}\) be independent random variables satisfying
\[
\Gamma_j\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(j,1\right).
\]
The Kostlan representation gives the equality in distribution of unordered point configurations
\[
\left\{
\left|Z\right|^2:
Z\in\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\right\}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\left\{
\Gamma_j:
j\geq 1
\right\};
\]
see \citet[Theorem~4.7.3 and Section~7.2]{HoughKrishnapurPeresVirag2009}.
Consequently, \(\left(R_1,\ldots,R_k\right)\) are the first \(k\) order statistics of
\[
\left\{
\sqrt{\Gamma_j}:
j\geq 1
\right\}.
\]

For \(a>0\), let
\[
D_a:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\left|z\right|\leq a\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D_a\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}I_j\left(a\right),
\]
where the variables \(\left(I_j\left(a\right)\right)_{j\geq 1}\) are independent and
\[
I_j\left(a\right)
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(p_j\left(a\right)\right),
\qquad
p_j\left(a\right)
=
\Pr\left(\Gamma_j\leq a^2\right)
=
1-e^{-a^2}
\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}
\frac{a^{2\ell}}{\ell!}.
\]

body:
[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Let $M$ be a compact metrizable group 
and let $\eta: \wt B \to B$ be a Lipschitz $M$-principal bundle. 
Let $\rho: M \to {\rm GL}_d(\bb C)$ be a continuous linear representation for some integer $d \geq 1$.  
Let $G$ be a locally compact second countable topological group acting continuously on $\wt B$ by Lipschitz continuous homeomorphisms, 
and assume that the actions of $M$ and $G$ commute with each other. 
Then, for any $g \in G$ and $\varphi \in C^0_{\rho}(\wt B, \bb C^d)$, we have 
\begin{align*}
s_{g \varphi} = g s_{\varphi}. 
\end{align*}

body:
[Lemma le:law-restriction of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider a reversible Markov jump process $(X,T)$ on the
  finite graph $G$. Assume that it starts in
  $\rho\in J$, has the reversible measure $\pi$ with 
  $\pi_i>0$ for all $i\in\Lambda$, and that the  
  jump rates are given by $q_{ij}=C_{ij}/\pi_i$ for $i,j\in\Lambda$. 
  Then, the processes $(X^{\neq},T^{\neq})$ and $(X^J,T^J)$ are
  again reversible Markov jump processes with rates $q^{\neq}$ and $q^J$, weights
  $C^{\neq}$ and $C^J$, transition probabilities $p^{\neq}$ and $p^J$, and
  reversible measures $\pi$ and $\pi|_J$, respectively. Applying both
  transformations successively, $(X^{J\neq},T^{J\neq})$ is also a reversible Markov jump process
  with rates $q^{J\neq}$, weights $C^{J\neq}$, transition probabilities $p^{J\neq}$, and
  reversible measure $\pi|_J$. 
  In particular, the restriction $X^{J\neq}$ of $X$ to $J$ with self-loops removed
  with starting point $X_0=\rho\in J$ has the same law as
  a random walk on the complete graph over $J$ endowed with the weights $C^{J\neq}$.
  In other words, $Q_{\rho}^{C,\Lambda}(X^{J\neq}\in\cdot)=Q_{\rho}^{C^{J\neq},J}$.

[Defn of arXiv:2512.12796, 'Symmetrization and the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Problem'] For $u\in L^{p}(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ the $\emph{Gagliardo seminorm}$
of $u$ is defined by the quantity
\[
[u]_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb{S}^{1})}:=\begin{cases}
{\displaystyle \left(\iint_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{\vert u(e^{\xi i})-u(e^{\sigma i})\vert^{p}}{\vert e^{\xi i}-e^{\sigma i}\vert^{1+sp}}d\xi d\sigma\right)^{\frac{1}{p}},} & 1\le p<+\infty,\\[1.2em]
{\displaystyle \text{ess sup}_{\xi\not=\sigma\in(-\pi,\pi)}\frac{\vert u(e^{\xi i})-u(e^{\sigma i})\vert}{\vert e^{\xi i}-e^{\sigma i}\vert^{s}},} & p=+\infty.
\end{cases}
\]
$[\cdot]_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb{S}^{1})}$ is a seminorm (it assigns the
magnitude zero to constant functions for example). The periodic $\emph{fractional Sobolev space}$
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb{S}^{1})$ is defined by 
\[
W^{s,p}(\mathbb{S}^{1}):=\Big\{ u\in L^{p}(\mathbb{S}^{1}),\,\,[u]_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb{S}^{1})}<+\infty\Big\},
\]
endowed with the norm 
\[

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The binary and ternary harmonic measures of the Cantor set are mutually singular (October 2026). For the middle-thirds Cantor set E and an integer b >= 2, the coding tree of E in base b has as vertices the b-adic intervals meeting E; simple random walk on it is transient, and the law of its limiting end pushed forward to E is a probability measure nu_b (nu_3 is the Cantor measure). Lyons and Peres (Probability on Trees and Networks, Question 16.7) asked whether nu_2 and nu_3 are mutually singular; the paper proves they are. The proof compares conditional splits of the two measures on dyadic cells through Hellinger affinities: at the dyadic cell [4/128, 5/128], whose intersection with E is the ternary cylinder [8/243, 9/243], the Cantor measure splits evenly while the harmonic measure, computed as an electrical current, gives the left half more than 0.507 of the mass, and a Fourier argument based on Stewart's theorem on digit changes in bases 2 and 3 shows that non-singularity would contradict the summability of the Hellinger losses. Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file verify the numerical values. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/cantor-harmonic-codings-singular (commit 228666ba76c4). Not refereed.
title: The binary and ternary harmonic measures of the Cantor set are mutually singular, answering Lyons-Peres Question 16.7 (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/cantor-harmonic-codings-singular)

body: In Riemannian geometry, the Cheeger isoperimetric constant of a compact Riemannian manifold M is a positive real number h(M) defined in terms of the minimal area of a hypersurface that divides M into two disjoint pieces. In 1971, Jeff Cheeger proved an inequality that related the first nontrivial eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on M to h(M). In 1982, Peter Buser proved a reverse version of this inequality, and the two inequalities put together are sometimes called the Cheeger-Buser inequality. These inequalities were highly influential not only in Riemannian geometry and global analysis, but also in the theory of Markov chains and in graph theory, where they have inspired the analogous Cheeger constant of a graph and the notion of conductance.
title: Cheeger constant

body:
[Definition upper and lower incomplete gamma functions of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] For $s>0$, $x>0$, $\Gamma(s,x):=\int_x^{+\infty} t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the upper incomplete gamma function, and $\gamma(s,x):=\int_0^x t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the lower incomplete gamma function. For $s>0$ they satisfy $\Gamma(s)=\gamma(s,x)+\Gamma(s,x)$, where $\Gamma(s)$ is the well-known gamma function with domain $s>0$. The above additive relation tells us that for $s>0$,$$\sup_{x>0}\gamma(s,x)=\sup_{x>0}\Gamma(s,x)=\Gamma(s).$$
        If $s=0,$ the additive relation fails due to $\gamma(0,x)$ being undefined. However, we have $\Gamma(0,x)=-\text{Ei}(-x)$, where $\text{Ei}(z):=-\int_{-z}^{+\infty} \frac{e^{-t}}{t}dt$ is the exponential integral function. 
        The following asymptotic results follow from elementary calculus arguments.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item For $s>0$, $\gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\downarrow 0}x^{s}.$
            \item For $s\geq 0$, $\Gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\uparrow+\infty}e^{-x}$.
            \item $-\text{Ei}(-x)\sim_{x\downarrow0}-\ln(x)$.
        \end{enumerate}
title: Some non-elementary functions

[Thm 1231219 of arXiv:2606.29143, 'Comonotonic and moment matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables'] Let $A = (a_1, ..., a_m)^{'}$ and $Q = (q_1, ..., q_m)^{'}$ be two numerical vectors with $\min(a_1, ..., a_m) \geq 0, \max(a_1, ..., a_m) > 0$ and $0 = q_0 < q_1 < q_2 < ... < q_m = 1$. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable and $X_{A, Q}$ the step-weighted version of $X$ associated with the numerical vectors $A$ and $Q$. Then it holds that 
\begin{itemize} 
\item $F_{X_{A, Q}}(x)  = G_{A, Q}(F_X(x)) \,\, \text{for any} \,\, x \in \mathbb{R}$, 
\item $F_{X_{A, Q}}^{-1}(p) = F_X^{-1}(G^{-1}_{A, Q}(p))$ for any $p \in (0, 1)$, 
 \item $F_{X_{A, Q}}^{-1+}(p) = F_X^{-1+}(G^{-1+}_{A, Q}(p))$ for any $p \in (0, 1)$,

[Lemma lem:robust-concentration of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Suppose that $Z_i \in \RR, i\le n$ are i.i.d. samples drawn from a distribution such that $\EE[|Z_i|^k] < \infty $ for some $k\ge 2$.  
Let $\mu = \EE[Z_i]$ be the mean of the distribution.  
Consider the truncated empirical mean $\hat \mu_M   = n^{-1} \sum_{i\le n} \cT_M(Z_i)$, where $\cT_M(z) = \max\{\min\{z,M\}, -M\}$ is the truncation operator at level $M>0$. 
Then with $M = \Big((k-1) \EE[|Z|^k] \cdot \sqrt{4\log(2/\delta) / n }\Big)^{ 1/k} $, it holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ that  
\begin{align}
    |\hat \mu_M - \mu| &\le  \Big(2\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{n}}\Big)^{\frac{k-1}{k }} \,   \frac{k\EE[|Z_i|^k ]^{1/k}}{(k-1)^{1-1/k}}.   
\end{align}
title: Robust concentration

[Definition def:egu of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$ be a gamble space, and $X:\Omega\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ a variable.
  Then the \emph{upper game-theoretic expectation of $X$}, with respect to $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$, is given by the following equivalent definitions (see Proposition~(prop:egu-equiv-defs of the paper)).
  \begin{align}
    \overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X
    &:= \inf_{Z\in\mathcal{Z}} \sup_{\omega\in\Omega} X(\omega) - Z(\omega)
      
    \\
    &\phantom{:}= \inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb{R} \mid \exists Z\in\mathcal{Z} \text{ s.t. } Z + \alpha > X\}~.
      
  \end{align}
  We define the \emph{lower game-theoretic expectation of $X$}, with respect to $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$ by $\underline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X := - \overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}}(-X)$.
  When $\overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X = \underline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X$, we write $\textsf{\textbf{E}} X := \overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X = \underline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X$.
title: Game-theoretic upper expectation

[Lem 88 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\mu \in \cP_2(\bbR_{\ge 0})$, the preimage
    \[
        \sym^{-1}(\mu) \equiv \Big\{
            \tilde \mu \in \cP_2(\bbR) : \sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu
        \Big\}
    \]
    is compact with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly closed. Therefore, it suffices to show that any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ has a $\bbW_2$-convergent subsequence. The collection of measures $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly tight, since we have 
	\[
	\tilde{\mu}([-K,K])
	=\mu([0,K]) 
	\stackrel{K\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1\,,
	\]
uniformly over all $\tilde{\mu}\in \sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
    By Prohorov's theorem, any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ must have a subsequence $(\tilde \mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ that converges weakly to some measure $\tilde{\mu}$, which is also clearly in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
By Skorokhod's theorem, we have can find random variables $X_n,X$ such that $X_n$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}_{n_j}$, $X$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}$, and $X_n$ converges to $X$ almost surely as $n\to\infty$. Then, for any finite $M$, we have
	\[
	\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} \le M
	\Big]
	\le \E\Big[\max\Big\{(X_n-X)^2
	; (2M)^2
	\Big\}
	\Big] \stackrel{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 0
	\]
by the bounded convergence theorem. On the other hand,	since $|X_n|$ and $|X|$ are distributed as samples from $\mu$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	&\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} 
		> M
	\Big]
	\le 2\Big\{
	\E[(X_n)^2;|X_n|>M]
	+\E[X^2;|X|>M]\Big\} \\
	&\qquad= 4 \E[X^2;|X|>M]
	\le o_M(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
By sending $M\to\infty$ we conclude $\tilde \mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \tilde \mu$ in $\bbW_2$, from which the compactness claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 88 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Define a {\bf Rook's Walk Birth-Death} (denoted RWBD) Markov chain over the state space $\Omega_* = \{0,\dots , d\}$ with a transition from $X_t \in \Omega_*$ to $X_{t+1}\in \Omega_*$ governed by parameter $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ as follows:
  \[X_{t+1}=\begin{cases}
   X_t, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}] \\
   X_t-1, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t-1} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}]\\
   X_t+1, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t+1} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}] \\
  \end{cases}\]
  where $Y_1\in \Omega$ follows from $Y_0\in \Omega$ according to the Rook's Walk with parameters $n,d$ where $\Omega$ is the state space of said Rook's Walk.

\end{equation}

body:
Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon unbiased selection influence objective. Let X have a specified probability law. For fixed p>=1, let H be a deterministic symmetric positive-definite p-by-p matrix, Q a deterministic symmetric positive-semidefinite p-by-p matrix, and G(X) a measurable positive-semidefinite p-by-p matrix. Define Z(X)=Tr(G(X) H^(-1) Q H^(-1)), and assume E Z(X)<infinity. A nonnegative randomized selection weight S is unbiased when E[S|X]=1 almost surely. Its retention probability is pi(X)=P(S>0|X), and a fixed mean retention budget is E pi(X)=gamma. Define the influence objective J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)], allowing infinity. An inverse-probability scheme draws I conditional on X as Bernoulli(pi(X)), and sets S=I/pi(X), for measurable pi(X)>0; then it is unbiased and J(S)=E[Z(X)/pi(X)]. In the source statistical application, G is the conditional score outer-product matrix and H is the population risk Hessian. Sharp two-quantile variance lower bound

Let X be a real square-integrable random variable. Suppose a < b, p,q > 0, P(X <= a) >= p, and P(X >= b) >= q. Necessarily p+q <= 1. Then

    Var(X) >= [pq/(p+q)] (b-a)^2.

Proof. Write mu=E X. If mu lies in [a,b], the two disjoint events give
Var(X) >= p(mu-a)^2 + q(b-mu)^2. Completing the square gives the claimed lower bound. If mu<a, the right event alone gives Var(X) >= q(b-mu)^2 >= q(b-a)^2, which is at least the claimed expression. The case mu>b is symmetric. Equality is attained by masses p at a, q at b, and 1-p-q at (pa+qb)/(p+q). The mean of this three-atom law is that middle location, so the computed variance is exactly the lower bound. This proves sharpness. No claim about independence of lattice events is used.

Consequence. If (X_n-m_n)/a_n converges in law to a nondegenerate Z, choose continuity points u<v for which P(Z<=u)>0 and P(Z>=v)>0. Convergence supplies fixed positive lower bounds p,q on the corresponding probabilities for large n. Thus Var(X_n)>=c a_n^2. This direction needs no fourth-moment bound.

If additionally T(0,x) is square-integrable (for example iid Exp(1)), L1 gives Var(T(0,x))>=c log ||x|| for sufficiently large ||x||. \begin{itemize}
	\item[8.] removing all blue faces sent to the edge $e$ by $\psi$ does not disconnect the dual graph of $m$.
\end{itemize} 

We denote by $\mathcal{N}\mathcal{P}\mathcal{M}(\ell,K)$ the set of non-separable planar embedded maps with boundary $\ell$ and plaquette assignment $K$.
For a non-balanced pair $(\ell,K)$, we define $\mathcal{N}\mathcal{P}\mathcal{M}(\ell,K)=\emptyset$.

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] \begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)]	Let $\eta\in (0,2]$, and $y^{(\eta)}:=y\textbf{1}_{\eta\in[1,2]}$. For any $p\in (d/\eta\vee 1,\infty]$, there is a constant $C=C(p,d,\eta)>0$ such that for all $f\in \mH_{\eta,p}(\mR^d)$,
		\begin{equation}
			\| \sup_{y\neq 0}|y|^{-\eta}|f(\cdot+y)-f(\cdot)-y^{(\eta)}\cdot \nabla f(\cdot) \|_p\leq C\| f\|_{\mH_{\eta,p}(\mR^d)},
		\end{equation}
		where we adopt the convention $\nabla f =0$ when $\eta\in (0,1)$.
		\item[(ii)] For any $p\in (d,\infty]$, there is a constant $C=C(p,d)>0$ such that for all $f\in \mH_{1,p}(\mR^d)$,
		\be
		\| \sup_{y\neq 0}|y|^{-1}|f(\cdot+y)-f(\cdot)|\|_p\leq C\| f\|_{\mH_{1,p}(\mR^d)}.
		\ee 
		\item[(iii)] For any $\delta,\gamma\in (0,1]$ and $p\in (d/\delta\vee d/\gamma,\infty]$, there is a constant $C=C(p,d,\delta,\gamma)>0$ such that for all $f\in \mH_{\delta+\gamma,p}(\mR^d)$,
		\be 
		\|\sup_{z,w\neq 0}|w|^{-\delta}|z|^{-\gamma}|(f(\cdot+z+w)-f(\cdot+z))-(f(\cdot+w)-f(\cdot))|\|_p\leq C\| f\|_{\mH_{\delta+\gamma,p}(\mR^d)}.
		\ee
	\end{enumerate}

\[
\Lambda_a(\theta)
=

=
\frac{(a-1)(a+3)}{8\pi a(a+1)}.
\]

body: Burnside's lemma, sometimes also called Burnside's counting theorem, the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma, or the orbit-counting theorem, is a result in group theory that is often useful in taking account of symmetry when counting mathematical objects. It was discovered by Augustin Louis Cauchy and Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, and became well known after William Burnside quoted it. The result enumerates orbits of a symmetry group acting on some objects: that is, it counts distinct objects, considering objects symmetric to each other as the same; or counting distinct objects up to a symmetry equivalence relation; or counting only objects in canonical form. For example, in describing possible organic compounds of certain type, one considers them up to spatial rotation symmetry: different rotated drawings of a given molecule are chemically identical.
title: Burnside's lemma

body: [Proposition 3.3 of arXiv:2304.14793, 'Learning Graph Neural Networks using Exact Compression'] Let 𝐿be a GNN composed of𝑑∈N layers,𝑑≥1. If cr𝑑(𝐺)(𝑣) = cr𝑑(𝐻)(𝑤) then 𝐿(𝐺)(𝑣) = 𝐿(𝐻)(𝑤). As a consequence, if S is a hypothesis space consisting of GNNs of at most 𝑑layers and cr𝑑(𝐺)(𝑣) = cr𝑑(𝐻)(𝑤) then (𝐺, 𝑣) ∼S (𝐻,𝑤). In other words, 𝑑-layer GNNs cannot distinguish nodes that are assigned the same color by 𝑑steps of color refinement.

[Corollary prop:actionclassification_perfectfits of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(M\) be a closed, orientable 3-manifold and \(\varphi\) be an almost pseudo-Anosov flow without perfect fits and not conjugate to suspension Anosov flow.
Let \(g\in \pi_{1}(M)\) act on \(P_{\varphi}\) by deck transformation.
Then, exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(g\) fix a regular point in \(P_{\varphi}\)
\item \(g\) fix a singular point \(p\) in \(P_{\varphi^{\natural}}\) and hence all the vertices of blown-up tree associated to \(p\) in \(P_{\varphi}\).
\item \(g\) acts hyperbolically on \(\partial P_{\varphi}\) with one fixed point attracting and the other repelling.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary prop:actionclassification_perfectfits of arXiv:2608.30973

[Prop weighted-tree-small-smin of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be a real weighted bipartite graph. Suppose $G$ contains a
\hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m$-matching rooted tree}}}, witnessed by a root $j_\star$ and sets
$\mathcal K_i$, $i\in I_\star=N_G(j_\star)$. 
Define the third left layer
\[
\mathcal L_{\rm out}:=
\bigcup_{i\in I_\star}
\bigcup_{j\in\mathcal K_i}
\left(N_G(j)\setminus I_\star\right),
\]
and define its maximum weight by
\[
A_{\rm out}:=
\max\left\{
|M_{\ell,j}|:
i\in I_\star,\ j\in\mathcal K_i,\ \ell\in N_G(j)\setminus I_\star
\right\},
\]
with the convention $A_{\rm out}=0$ if the set is empty. Then
\[
s_{\min}(M)\le
\frac{A_{\rm out}}{m}\sqrt{|\mathcal L_{\rm out}|}.
\]

[Definition 12 (Entropy solution) of arXiv:2609.00867, '2609.00867'] For \(T>0\), a symmetric probability density
\(F^N\in L^\infty(0,T;L^1(\mathbb R^{3N}))\) is an entropy solution on \([0,T]\)
if it solves \eqref{eq:first-order-coulomb-fokker-planck} in the sense of
distributions and satisfies
\[
 \sup_{0\le t\le T}\frac1N
 \int\sum_{i=1}^N(1+|x_i|^2)F^N(t,X^{1:N})\dd X^{1:N}<\infty,
\]
and, for almost every \(t\in[0,T]\),
\begin{align}
 &\int F^N(t)\log\frac{F^N(t)}{G_N}\dd X^{1:N}
 +\frac1\beta\int_0^t\!\int F^N(r)
   \left|\nabla\log\frac{F^N(r)}{G_N}\right|^2
   \dd X^{1:N}\dd r                                                \notag\\

body:
[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ admits a well-defined decomposition into primitive languages:
\begin{align*}
  H = \Big[\Big(\C_1^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_1^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_1\Big]
  \circ \cdots \circ
  \Big[
    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_m
  \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_H(z) = \left(1-p\right)^m \left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
It holds for all $i$ that
\[
  \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{z(1-p)/m} \quad \text{and} \quad
  \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{zp/m} \quad \text{and} \quad 
  \phi_{\C_i}(z) = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}.
\]
Apply Proposition \ref{thm:shuffling} to find
\[
  \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(z)
  = \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) \,
    \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{z/m},
\]
then take the Laplace--Borel transform:
\[
  \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(x)
  = \int_0^\infty e^{xt/m}\, e^{-t} \, dt
  = \int_0^\infty e^{-\left(1-x/m\right)t} \, dt
  = \frac{1}{1-x/m}, \quad 0 < x < 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant0}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{1-z/m}
  = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n
  = (1-p) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n,
\]
so by introducing the $n!$ terms,
\[
  \hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
  = (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(z/m)^n}{n!}
  = (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right).
\]
We find $\hat\phi_H(z) = \prod_i 
\hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
= (1-p)^m\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 8 of arXiv:2605.14206

\begin{equation}
 P(u_i)=F(u_i)\qquad(1\le i\le m).
\end{equation}

[Proposition 11 (I-MMSE representation of measurement-force energy) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Under the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{thm:posterior-tweedie}, let
$\widehat m_\gamma(Y_\gamma)=\E[X_0\mid Y_\gamma]$ and
$\widehat m_\gamma^R(Y_\gamma,R)=\E[X_0\mid Y_\gamma,R]$.  Then, for
$\gamma>0$ (and by right differentiation at $\gamma=0$),
\begin{equation}

\frac{\dd}{\dd\gamma}\mathcal M_\gamma
=
\frac12\E\big\|
\widehat m_\gamma^R(Y_\gamma,R)-\widehat m_\gamma(Y_\gamma)
\big\|^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}

\mathcal M_\gamma
=
\frac12\int_0^\gamma
\E\big\|
\widehat m_u^R(Y_u,R)-\widehat m_u(Y_u)
\big\|^2\,\dd u.
\end{equation}
At $\gamma_t=a_t^2/\Delta_t$,
\begin{equation}

\E\|g_t(X_t,R)\|^2
=
\left.
\frac{2a_t^2}{\Delta_t^2}
\frac{\dd}{\dd\gamma}\mathcal M_\gamma
\right|_{\gamma=\gamma_t}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then Theorem~(thm:dichotomy of the paper) holds after replacing the OBABO kernel by the kernel of the splitting $\dagger$, the definition of $s$ in (equation eq:hbparamsintro of the paper) by $s_\dagger$, and the stability condition $h<2/\sqrt\kappa$ by $0<s_\dagger<2(1+\beta)/\kappa$, and, for OABAO, with the time window in (equation eq:cyclemetaintro of the paper) replaced by $0\le n\le\lfloor\tfrac1{32}e^{c_0R^2}\rfloor$.

[Defn Slices of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\bm{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k}$ for $0 \leq k \leq n-1$. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The \textbf{(right) $\bm{t}$-slice of $A$} is defined as
    $$Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A \coloneqq \left(\mathbb{R}^{k} \times \{\bm{t}\}\right) \cap A.$$
    It can be naturally identified with a subset of $\mathbb{R}^k$.
        \item The set of \textbf{transversally interior points} in the (right) $\bm{t}$-slice $Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A$, denoted by $Sl^\circ_{\vert\bm{t}} A$, is the set of $\bm s \in Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A$ such that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ satisfying 
        $$\{\bm{s}\} \times (\bm{t}-\bm{\varepsilon}, \bm{t} +\bm{\varepsilon}) \subset A.$$
    \end{itemize}

body: In combinatorics, the inclusion–exclusion principle is a counting technique which generalizes the familiar method of obtaining the number of elements in the union of two finite sets; symbolically expressed as where A and B are two finite sets and |S| indicates the cardinality of a set S. The formula expresses the fact that the sum of the sizes of the two sets may be too large since some elements may be counted twice. The double-counted elements are those in the intersection of the two sets and the count is corrected by subtracting the size of the intersection.
title: Inclusion–exclusion principle

body:
[Corollary 4 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Let $B$ be a compact metric space and let $\pi: E \to B$ be a 
Lipschitz vector bundle of dimension $d$ over $B$. 
Let $G$ be a locally compact group acting on $E$ by an isometric Lipschitz bundle action
and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $G$. 
Assume that there exists a constant $\alpha >0$ such that $\bb E ({\rm Lip}_E(g_1)^{\alpha} ) < \infty$ 
and that the pair $(G, \mu)$ satisfies the contraction property \eqref{contraction-property-on-B} on $B$. 
Then, for each $b \in B$, there exists a continuous linear map $\zeta_b: \bf \Gamma^{0}(E) \to \pi^{-1} (b)$
such that, for any section $s \in \bf \Gamma^{0}(E)$, we have  
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} P_{\mu}^k s(b)  \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}  \zeta_b(s). 
\end{align*}
Moreover, this convergence holds uniformly over $b \in B$.
title: Corollary 4 of arXiv:2607.19873
