AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Square Haar-signal MI/log-energy calibration, proof unaudited. Let A_n be deterministic nonnegative diagonal n by n profiles with bounded operator norms and ||A_n||_F^2/n->a2; S_n=L_n A_n R_n^T has independent real Haar frames. For independent Z_n with iid N(0,1/n) entries and fixed s>=0, suppose the empirical singular law of Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n converges in expected squared W2 to a compact bounded-density law eta_s. Then I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2 converges to Sigma(sym eta_s)-Sigma(semicircle_1). Limit existence follows from exact real-SVD density normalization, the bounded-density quantile-box lemma017 and spectral Lipschitz continuity of the finite spherical integral; no asymptotic spherical-integral theorem or prior MI-limit existence is assumed. This conditional lemma does not identify eta_s or establish C1 regularity. The method is standard; novelty unestablished.
Real square matrices and independent Haar left/right frames.
Uniformly bounded deterministic input operator norms and convergent normalized squared Frobenius norms.
Fixed nonnegative SNR and iid Gaussian noise variance 1/n.
Expected squared spectral W2 convergence to a deterministic compact bounded-density law.
Unaudited quantile lemma017 and standard square Gaussian Marchenko-Pastur/W2 limit.
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3698d63405aa1563fc5c1a1dcd5b3725c8c4f9b68c4c2ce77af702250bdfb8aa","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/36/3698d63405aa1563fc5c1a1dcd5b3725c8c4f9b68c4c2ce77af702250bdfb8aa.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:26ccb837dbba6c98e5cddc0e0c215c36f68708f1bc45cd1754c64b87d2b36f37","bundle_entry_key":"square-haar-mi-log-energy-calibration-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-square-calibration-and-oracle-gap-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:square-haar-mi-log-energy-calibration-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Square Haar-signal mutual information from its observation spectral law

Target 2 supporting lemma; proof draft, unaudited. This pays a specific
step in the open square reference-differentiability route. It does not
identify the observation law as a free convolution or prove smoothness.
The general normalization method is standard; novelty is unestablished.

## Statement and conventions

Let A_n be deterministic nonnegative diagonal n by n matrices with
uniformly bounded operator norm and n^(-1)||A_n||_F^2 -> a_2. Let L_n,R_n
be independent Haar orthogonal matrices, S_n=L_n A_n R_n^T. Independently,
Z_n has iid N(0,1/n) entries. Fix s>=0 and observe Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n.
Suppose the empirical positive singular-value law eta_{Y_n} satisfies

    E W2(eta_{Y_n},eta_s)^2 -> 0,                    (A)

for a deterministic compactly supported law eta_s on [0,infinity) with a
bounded Lebesgue density. Write sym(eta) for its symmetric reflection
average and Sigma(rho)=double integral log|x-y| rho(dx)rho(dy). Then

    lim I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2
        = Sigma(sym(eta_s)) - Sigma(sigma_1),         (B)

where sigma_1 is the centered semicircle law of variance one.
Both energies on the right are finite. Importantly, existence of the MI
limit is a conclusion here, not an additional spherical-integral theorem
or a previously assumed MI-limit premise.

## Exact finite identities and the real Jacobian

For deterministic matrices D,T put

    J_n(D,T)=n^(-2) log integral exp(n tr(D R T^T L^T)) dL dR.

Normalized Haar measures are used. The integrand is positive. Orthogonal
invariance makes J depend only on singular values. Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |J_n(D,T)-J_n(D,T')| <= ||D||_F ||T-T'||_F/n.     (1)

Indeed bound the change of the exponent uniformly in both frames, then
bound the ratio of integrals in both directions. After optimal singular
alignment and D=sqrt(s)A_n, this becomes

    |J_n(D,T)-J_n(D,T')|
       <= sqrt(s a_{2,n}) W2(eta_T,eta_T'),           (2)

where a_{2,n}=||A_n||_F^2/n. Also |J_n(D,T)|<=||D||_F||T||_F/n, from
the same bound relative to T'=0.

The Gaussian mixture density of Y is a constant times
exp[-n(||Y||_F^2+s||A_n||_F^2)/2+n^2 J_n(sqrt(s)A_n,Y)]. The real square
SVD Jacobian is a constant times product_{i<j}|y_j^2-y_i^2| on ordered
positive singular values; there is no extra power of y_i when rows and
columns are equal. Thus their exact density is

    p_n(y)=C_n exp(n^2[-(m_2(eta_y)+s a_{2,n})/2
                             +J_n(sqrt(s)A_n,diag y)+V_n(y)]),          (3)
    V_n(y)=n^(-2) sum_{i<j}log|y_j^2-y_i^2|.

C_n is independent of A_n and s. It includes the Gaussian normalizing
constant and the angular Jacobian and may depend on n. The relevant real
rectangular Jacobian, with first power of the Vandermonde and the factor
product y_i^(p-m), is explicitly displayed in arXiv:2203.07752,
Section 2.1 equation (15); here p=m=n. This is not the complex/unitary
Jacobian, whose Vandermonde power differs.

Taking expected log conditional likelihood divided by marginal likelihood
gives the exact information identity

    i_n(s):=I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2
             =s a_{2,n}-E J_n(sqrt(s)A_n,Y_n).        (4)

In detail E||Y||_F^2=s||A_n||_F^2+n and E||Z||_F^2=n; substituting the
two Gaussian densities yields (4). Thus no asymptotic differentiation is
used. The variables have finite second moments, so the likelihood and
J expectations are integrable by (1).

## High-probability bounded chamber and moments

There exists a fixed R such that P(||Y_n||op<=R)->1. To see this without a
sharp spectral-edge theorem, take 1/4-nets of both unit spheres of size at
most 9^n. Bilinear approximation bounds ||Z||op by twice the largest net
bilinear form. Each has law N(0,1/n), so

    P(||Z||op>K)<=2 exp(n(2 log 9-K^2/8)).

Choose K=8 and add sqrt(s) sup||A_n||op. Enlarge R if necessary beyond
the compact support of eta_s. By (A), with probability tending to one the
profile is in any prescribed W2 neighborhood of eta_s and in [0,R].
Moreover m_2(eta_s)=1+s a_2. Indeed (A) implies convergence of expected
second moments: |sqrt(m_2(eta_{Y_n}))-sqrt(m_2(eta_s))|<=W2, and the
expectation of m_2(eta_{Y_n}) is exactly 1+s a_{2,n}.

## Calibrating C_n with pure Gaussian noise

For A_n=0 the observation law is the square Ginibre singular law, converging
in expected W2 to the quarter-circle law eta_0; its symmetrization is
sigma_1. This is the standard square Marchenko-Pastur limit, also a
special case of the Gaussian spectral convergence used in claim 008.
The elementary Gaussian net bound above supplies the bounded chamber.

Claim017, proofs/quantile_vandermonde_boxes.md, supplies three facts for
every compact bounded-density eta: V_n at midpoint quantiles tends to
Sigma(sym eta); boxes of radius 1/(4Cn^3) about those quantiles have
log volume o(n^2) and uniform matching lower energy; and V_n has a uniform
matching upper bound on a small weak neighborhood within [0,R].

Put c_n=n^(-2)log C_n and E_0=Sigma(sigma_1). In (3) with A=0, J=0.
On a high-probability bounded spectral neighborhood of eta_0, for every
epsilon>0 and large n the exponent other than c_n is at most
-1/2+E_0+epsilon. Its volume is at most R^n. Hence

    1-o(1)<=R^n exp(n^2[c_n-1/2+E_0+epsilon]),

and liminf c_n>=1/2-E_0. On the small quantile box the same exponent is
at least -1/2+E_0-epsilon. Integrating there gives

    1>=exp(n^2[c_n-1/2+E_0-epsilon]+o(n^2)),

so limsup c_n<=1/2-E_0. Therefore

    c_n -> c=1/2-Sigma(sigma_1).                     (5)

This pays the leading angular and Gaussian constants without an
unjustified differential-entropy limit or a Stirling formula convention.

## Normalization identifies all subsequential information limits

Let q_n be the midpoint-quantile profile of eta_s, and put
K_n=J_n(sqrt(s)A_n,diag q_n). By the absolute bound after (2), K_n is a
bounded real sequence. Choose any convergent subsequence K_n->K. By (A),
deterministic quantile W2 convergence and (2),

    E|J_n(sqrt(s)A_n,Y_n)-K_n| -> 0.                 (6)

On bounded profiles in a sufficiently small W2 neighborhood of eta_s,
the quadratic term and J in (3) are uniformly close to their limits, by
(2); the energy has the uniform upper bound from claim017. Thus the
high-probability-neighborhood argument used for (5) gives

    0 <= c -(m_2(eta_s)+s a_2)/2 +K+Sigma(sym eta_s).

Conversely, throughout the tiny boxes about q_n, the quadratic and J
terms converge uniformly and the Vandermonde has the matching lower
bound. Integrating these subexponential-volume boxes in (3) gives the
opposite inequality. Therefore equality holds, and

    K=s a_2+Sigma(sigma_1)-Sigma(sym eta_s),          (7)

using m_2(eta_s)=1+s a_2 and (5). Every convergent subsequence of the
bounded K_n has this same limit; hence the full sequence converges.
Equations (4),(6),(7) prove (B).

## What remains before applying this to T287

The analytic proof above assumes (A) and the bounded density of eta_s.
For square bounded input profiles, the intended primary free-probability
input identifies sym(eta_s) as dilation_sqrt(s)(sym eta_input) free-plus
sigma_1, and gives its bounded density. That source applicability and the
expected-W2 upgrade must be attached explicitly before claiming a T287
consequence from this lemma. The Gaussian-factor reference must also be
transferred to fixed bounded profiles using the existing spectral/entropy
coupling, with its unaudited dependencies retained.

Even after those steps, proving that the right side is C1 for every s>0
requires the free entropy derivative with justified positive-noise
regularity. Formula (B) alone does not order derivatives, prove any
fixed-SNR MMSE conclusion at a corner, or close full Target 2.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:f91ebbe6b88f8d0da76d7a95800245ceda66ac687a4f50d4d4c01642933be55d","revision_digest":"sha256:641a5706f52a48c7a2e83e5a3bd94be4cb9bc14e692933bd1e0c64d0351d89c0","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:square-haar-mi-log-energy-calibration-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-019 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

such that   $X^\frozen(q_*)$ is equidistributed as $Y^\frozen(q_*)$, and

	\[

Likewise with the processes $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}$ and $X^{\frozen,\Ising}$.
 
\begin{proof}
First, $\vY^\frozen$ is close to 
$\hvY^\frozen(t)= \vY^\frozen(t-\sss)+\xxx$ because $\sss$ and $\xxx$ are both small: $\xxx$ is sampled from the spatial kernel $\sphi$ (Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}), so $\|\xxx\|_\infty \le\sep$. Meanwhile $\sss$ is sampled from the temporal kernel $\tphi$ (Definition~\ref{d:t.smooth}), so $|\sss| \le\tep$. We can apply  the bound \eqref{e:Y.I.Kolmogorov} from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov} for increments of $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$, and the bound from Proposition~\ref{p:Y.notI.second.quenched}
for increments of $Y^{\frozen,\RomII}$, $Y^{\frozen,\RomIII}$, and $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}$. By Fatou's lemma, in the $N\to\infty$ limit we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE\bigg[\Big\| \vY^\frozen(t)-\hvY^\frozen(t)\Big\|^2\bigg]
	\le O(\sep)+ L^{O(1)}
	 \tep\,.
	\]
Next recall that $Y^\frozen$ is the coordinate sum \eqref{e:Y.plus}, and 
recall that $\iY^\frozen$ is the coordinate sum  \eqref{e:iY.plus}.
Meanwhile, $\iX^\frozen$ solves the SDE \eqref{e:iX.sde}. By Proposition~\ref{p:fokker.planck},
$\iY^\frozen(t)$ and $\iX^\frozen(t)$ have the same marginal law for all $t$. We finally compare $\iX^\frozen$ to the solution $X^\frozen$ of the SDE \eqref{e:actual.sde}. By Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}\ref{c:reg.in.limit.a},  the coefficients are uniformly bounded by
$(\frac{\trK L}{\sep})^{O(1)}$. 
By Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.vs.actual.coeffs},
the coefficients of the two SDEs
are close:
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\Big|\tF(t,y)-\iF(t,y)
	\Big|
	: y\in\R, t\in[q_*,1]\setminus\oJ
	\bigg\}
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \tep^{1/2}\,.
	\] 
Since for any $x,y\ge0$ we have $|x^{1/2}-y^{1/2}| \le |x-y|^{1/2}$, we immediately deduce a bound on $\tF^{1/2}-\iF^{1/2}$.
Lemma~\ref{l:gronwall} then implies the existence of a coupling under which
	\[
	\bE\bigg[ \Big( X^\frozen(t)-\iX^\frozen(t)\Big)^2\bigg]
	\le
	C\bigg( \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	\bigg) \tep^{1/2}
	\]
for all $q_*\le t\le 1$. Combining the above bounds gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 60 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] Let $\Sigma = \Sigma_{g,p}$ with $g\geqslant 2$ and $p\geqslant 1$. 
        Let 
        $s\in \{\pm 1\}^p$ and $n\in \big\{\chi(\Sigma) + p_+(s) ,\dots, -\chi(\Sigma) - p_-(s)\big\}$, and let $[\rho]\in X^s_n$. 
        Assume that there is a separating simple closed curve $\gamma$ 
        that satisfies the following conditions:
        \begin{enumerate}[(1)]

            \item $\rho(\gamma)$ is elliptic of infinite order.

            
            \item $\gamma$ separates $\Sigma$ into a surface $\Sigma_1$ with positive genus and a pair of pants $\Sigma_2$, where $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ contains peripheral elements $c_1$ and $c_2$ of $\pi_1(\Sigma)$ that map to negative parabolic elements.

            
        \end{enumerate}
        
        Assume further that there is a decomposition $\mathcal{P}\in \pgd$ whose complement $\Sigma\setminus \mathcal{P}$ contains 
        \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
            \item 
            a one-holed torus $T$ in $\Sigma_1$ where $e\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(T)}\big)\in \{-1,0\}$,

            \item a pair of pants $P$ in $\Sigma_1$ where $e\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(P)}\big) = -1$ and $s\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(P)}\big) = (0,0,0)$ or $(0,-1,0)$,

            
            \item a pair of pants $P$ in $\Sigma_1$ where $e\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(P)}\big) = 0$, $s\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(P)}\big) = (0,0,0)$ or $(0,+1,0)$, and $\rho|_{\pi_1(P)}$ is non-abelian, or

            \item a pair of pants $P$ in $\Sigma_1$ where $\gamma$ is represented by one of its boundary components, and $e\big(\rho|_{\pi_1(P\cup_\gamma \Sigma_2)}\big) = -1$.
        \end{enumerate}
        
        Then there is a non-separating simple closed curve that maps to an elliptic element.
title: Lemma 60 of arXiv:2609.02065

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2607.18862, 'Tamed Euler Schemes for Singular SDEs with Multiplicative L\'{e}vy Noise'] Let $p,p_1,p_2$ be real number in $(1,\infty)$ and let $\theta\in (0,1]$.
	
	(i) Assume that $p_1,p_2\geq p$ and the indices satisfy the condition $\frac{1}{p}\leq \frac{1}{p_1}+\frac{1}{p_2}<\frac{1}{p}+\frac{\theta}{d}$. Then the pointwise multiplication is a continuous bilinear map
	\ce 
	\mH_{\theta,p_1}(\mR^d)\times \mH_{\theta,p_2}(\mR^d)\to \mH_{\theta,p}(\mR^d).
	\de 
	
	(ii) Assume that $p_1\geq p,p_2\geq p_1^*$,  and the indices fulfill $\frac{1}{p}\leq \frac{1}{p_1}+\frac{1}{p_2}<\frac{1}{p}+\frac{\theta}{d}$. Then the pointwise multiplication is a continuous bilinear map 
	\ce 
	\mH_{-\theta,p_1}(\mR^d)\times \mH_{-\theta,p_2}(\mR^d)\to \mH_{-\theta,p}(\mR^d).
	\de 
	
	(iii) Let $g$ be a bounded measurable function such that its gradient $\nabla g$ belongs to $ L_{p_0}(\mR^d)$ for some $p_0\in (d,\infty)$. Let $f\in \mH_{1,p^*}(\mR^d)$, $h\in \mH_{-1,p}(\mR^d)$, and suppose  $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{p_0}<1$. Then the product $fg$ belongs to $\mH_{1,p^*}(\mR^d)$, $gh$ belongs to $\mH_{-1,p}(\mR^d)$ and he following inequalities hold:
	\ce 
	\|fg\|_{\mH_{1,p^*}(\mR^d)}&\lesssim &(\|g\|_{\infty}+\|\nabla g\|_{p_0})\|f\|_{\mH_{1,p^*}(\mR^d)},\\
	\|gh\|_{\mH_{-1,p}(\mR^d)}&\lesssim &(\|g\|_{\infty}+\|\nabla g\|_{p_0})\|h\|_{\mH_{-1,p}(\mR^d)}.
	\de (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 26 of arXiv:2607.18862

[Theorem thm:imag of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $N=2M$. For every real $\theta$ the matrix $U_\theta:=W_{i\theta}=e^{i\theta K}$
is real orthogonal, $U_\theta\in\SO(N,\mathbb{R})$, and therefore also unitary,
$U_\theta\in\UU(N)$. Equivalently, the imaginary slice is the Schr\"odinger
evolution

\[
U_\theta=e^{-i\thetaH_{\mathrm{NUO}}},\qquad H_{\mathrm{NUO}}:=-K=-\sigma^y\otimes A=H_{\mathrm{NUO}}^{*},
\]

generated by the Hermitian Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{NUO}}$. The genuine quantum density
$\sigma_\theta:=U_\theta\sigma_0U_\theta^{*}$, which is Hermitian, positive, and
unit-trace, obeys the ordinary von Neumann equation

\[
\dfrac{d\sigma_\theta}{d\theta}=-i[H_{\mathrm{NUO}},\sigma_\theta].
\]

[Lemma prop: f' and f'' of arXiv:2505.05921, 'Limit Theorems for step reinforced random walks\\ with regularly varying memory'] {}
    Let $f$ be the regularly varying function defined in (equation eq: RV f of the paper). Then we have, for all large enough $x$,
     $$f'(x)={(\alpha+ \zeta(\log x))} \frac{f(x)}{x} \quad \text{and} \quad f''(x)=\left\{(\alpha+ \zeta(\log x))(\alpha-1+ \zeta(\log x))+ \zeta'(\log x) \right\} \frac{f(x)}{x^2}.$$
    Further, the functions $|f'|$ and $|f''|$ are regularly varying of indices $\alpha-1$ and $\alpha-2$ respectively, except when $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ and $\zeta$ is identically zero. If $\alpha=0$ and $\zeta$ is the zero function, then $f'$ and $f''$ both are identically zero functions. If $\alpha=1$ and $\zeta$ is the zero function, then $f''$ is the identically zero function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma prop: f' and f'' of arXiv:2505.05921

		\end{equation}

body:
[Lemma lem:nice-form of arXiv:2607.00800, 'Brownian motion in Minkowski normed spaces'] Let $1\leq i, j \leq d$, $z\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $t>0$.
    Then
    \[
    a_{ij}\bigl(x,f^z_Q(t)\bigr) = \frac 1 2 \partial_{ij}Q^*\bigl(\nabla Q(z-x)\bigr),\quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{z\},
    \]
    and $a_{ij}(z,f^z_Q(t)) = \frac{1}{2}\delta_{ij}$, i.e.,
    \begin{equation}
        a_{ij}\bigl(x,f^z_Q(t)\bigr) = \frac{1}{2} A_{ij}(z-x), \quad b_i\bigl(x,f^z_Q(t)\bigr) = -\frac{1}{2} B_i(z-x),
    \end{equation}
    where $A$ and $B$ are as in Lemma (lem:structure of the paper).
    Moreover, $(t,x) \mapsto a_{ij}(x,f^z_Q(t))$ is bounded on $(0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R}^d$.
title: Properties of $a_{ij},b_i$

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2604.24664, 'Absolute continuity of Rosenblatt measures'] Let $\alpha > 0$ and $f \in L^1([0, T])$. The \emph{left} and \emph{right  Riemann--Liouville fractional integrals of $f$ of order $\alpha$} are defined by
	\begin{align*}
		(I^\alpha_{0+} f)(x) &= \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^x (x-y)^{\alpha-1} f(y) \d{y},
		\\
		(I^\alpha_{T-} f)(x') &= \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_{x'}^{T} (y-x')^{\alpha-1} f(y) \d{y},
	\end{align*}
	respectively, for almost all $x,x' \in [0, T]$.

O(N^{-4}).
\]

body:
[Defn of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S = \langle L, \leq, \top, \bot, \Box, \boxtimes\rangle$ be an APS and let $x \in L$. 
    \begin{enumerate}  
        \item $x$ is \emph{provable} in $S$ if $\top \leq x$.
        \item $x$ is \emph{refutable} in $S$ if $x \leq \bot$.
        \item $S$ is \emph{inconsistent} if $\top \leq \bot$. 
        Otherwise, $S$ is \emph{consistent}.
         \item $x$ is a \emph{G\"odelian fixed point} of $S$ if $x = \boxtimes x$. 
   \end{enumerate}
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'

body: [Corollary 3.9 of arXiv:2603.27659, 'Operator Norm Bounds for Multi-leg Matrix Tensors and Applications to Random Matrix Theory'] Let $m,k,N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $k\geq m+1$, and let $\sigma\in\mathcal{P}([m])$. Then $\displaystyle\max_{\|A_{1}\|,\ldots,\|A_{m}\|\leq 1}\left|\left(\mathrm{Tr}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathrm{Tr}_{\gamma}\otimes\ldots\otimes\mathrm{Tr}_{\gamma}\right)\left(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\right)\right|=N^{R(\sigma)+k-1}.$

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a twice differentiable function $f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$, we have
$$f(x+t)\simeq f(x)+f'(x)t+\frac{<f''(x)t,t>}{2}$$
with $f'(x)\in M_{1\times N}(\mathbb R)$ being a row vector, and with $f''(x)\in M_N(\mathbb R)$, given by 
$$f''(x)=\left(\frac{d^2f}{dx_idx_j}\right)_{ij}(x)$$
being the Hessian matrix of $f$, at the point $x\in\mathbb R^N$.

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The spectrum of an operator $T\in B(H)$ is the set
$$\sigma(T)=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb C\Big|T-\lambda\not\in B(H)^{-1}\right\}$$
where $B(H)^{-1}\subset B(H)$ is the set of invertible operators.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For critical planar percolation on Z^2 or the triangular lattice, let alpha_k(r,R) be the probability of k disjoint arms of prescribed colours, at least one of each colour (polychromatic), crossing the annulus from radius r to radius R. Quasi-multiplicativity: there are constants 0 < c <= C < infinity depending only on k such that c alpha_k(r,r') alpha_k(r',R) <= alpha_k(r,R) <= C alpha_k(r,r') alpha_k(r',R) for all r <= r' <= R (Kesten 1987; Nolin 2008 for a complete account). It follows from RSW crossing estimates, FKG and the separation-of-arms lemma; it holds for polychromatic arm events of every k and, with a separate argument, for the monochromatic one-arm event; monochromatic k-arm events for k >= 2 need extra care. Consequence: alpha_k(1,R) is comparable to the product over dyadic scales of the one-scale factors alpha_k(2^j, 2^{j+1}), each bounded between constants. It does NOT give the existence of an exponent: that needs the one-scale factors to have a Cesaro-convergent logarithm, which on the triangular lattice comes from SLE(6) and on Z^2 is open (only the universal exponents, the 5-arm exponent 2 and the half-plane 2- and 3-arm exponents 1 and 2, are known there). Typical failure: Treating quasi-multiplicativity as exact multiplicativity, dropping the universal constants, when telescoping the estimate across many scales to compute an exponent; the accumulated multiplicative error, while bounded at each step, need not be negligible over a growing number of scales, and applying the estimate to arm counts or configurations outside the range covered by the underlying construction, without re-deriving the necessary cross-scale independence, is a further common overreach. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Nolin, 2008, Electronic Journal of Probability; Schramm and Steif, 2010, Annals of Mathematics.
RSW crossing estimates and FKG at the critical point
Polychromatic arm events (or the monochromatic one-arm event)
Planarity and the separation-of-arms lemma
title: Technique: Quasi-Multiplicativity of Arm Events

[Proposition 95 (Measurable lifetimes and compatibility across compact sets) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $K_n=\overline{B(0,n)}$ and fix deterministic adapted localization pairs
$(\chi_n,\rho_n)$ for $(K_n,1)$.  On the common probability-one event on which
all dyadic approximating tuples are defined, there are measurable random variables
$\tau_n>0$ such that $\tau_{n+1}\le\tau_n$ and the localized fixed points for
$(\chi_n,\rho_n)$ form a strongly measurable solution on $[0,\tau_n)$ in the
sense of Definition~\ref{def:random-interval-solution}.  The solutions and
nonlinear sources for different $n$ agree on overlaps and therefore form a
compatible family of local solutions in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:compatible-local-solutions}.  For an arbitrary compact $K$, set
\begin{equation}
 n(K):=\min\{n:K\subset B(0,n)\},\qquad
 (\chi_K^\circ,\rho_K^\circ):=(\chi_{n(K)},\rho_{n(K)}),\qquad
 \tau_K:=\tau_{n(K)}.
\end{equation}
Then $K_1\subset K_2$ implies $\tau_{K_1}\ge\tau_{K_2}$.  Every other pair
$(\chi,\rho)$ adapted to $(K,1)$ has a measurable existence time
$\tau_K^{\chi,\rho}>0$, obtained by the same formula below, and its solution
agrees with the solution obtained from the fixed localization pair on every interval
$[0,T]$ with $T<\tau_K\wedge\tau_K^{\chi,\rho}$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2b801d6baaa7d812bf2e3847626892c4c78362122a5c68dd22f2f8a880715184","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2b/2b801d6baaa7d812bf2e3847626892c4c78362122a5c68dd22f2f8a880715184.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:ce68577967eae23a669baeb497b6bc053d3548e1f4c8fb816633162c8469ccf7","bundle_entry_key":"t362-common-hessian-optimizer","bundle_id":"population.t362-global-step-and-li-kappa-001","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; finite-sum SGD","draft":"w732/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-global-constant-step-optimizer","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T362 target 1: global constant-step minimization

Status: derivation completed below; exact checks and prior-art comparison are logged separately before submission. The existing row's rr_exact.py is taken as settled ground for the fixed-step recursion. The extension here concerns global minimization, which its grid and local ternary search do not certify. No novelty beyond the named target is asserted.

## Instance and exact polynomial

Let n >= 2, K >= 1, 0 < mu <= L. Let

    f_i(x,y) = mu*x^2/2 + L*y^2/2 + b_i*x + c_i*y,

where sum b_i = sum c_i = 0. Set s_mu = (sum b_i^2)/n and s_L = (sum c_i^2)/n. Initial coordinates are deterministic u_mu=x0, u_L=y0. Each epoch uses a new independent uniform permutation. The same permutation acts on both coordinates; their noise need not be independent. The objective is a sum of coordinate squares, so no cross moment is needed.

For h in {mu,L}, set a_h=1-h*eta and

    V_h(eta) = s_h/(n-1) * sum_{0<=i<j<n} (a_h^i-a_h^j)^2,
    G_K(z) = sum_{r=0}^{K-1} z^r.

The settled scalar recursion gives the following polynomial, with no removable singularities:

    P_K(eta) = sum_h h/2 * [u_h^2*a_h^(2*n*K)
                        + eta^2*V_h(eta)*G_K(a_h^(2*n))].                 (1)

Here sums over h denote the two indexed coordinates j=1,2 with h_1=mu and h_2=L, not a set of distinct curvature values. When mu=L both coordinate contributions are still included. The labels s_mu,u_mu and s_L,u_L distinguish the two coordinates even then.

The pairwise expression follows from
sum_{i<j}(w_i-w_j)^2 = n*sum_i w_i^2 - (sum_i w_i)^2.
This is a polynomial of degree at most 2*n*K. It is valid for every real eta, including eta=0, eta=1/h and eta=2/h. For eta>=0 it is precisely E[F(X_K)-F*].

For any specified closed admissible interval [0,H], the exact global optimum is

    min {P_K(r): r in {0,H} union {r in (0,H): P_K'(r)=0}}.             (2)

If P_K' is identically zero, every step is optimal. Otherwise the set is finite. With rational inputs, (2) is an exact algebraic specification, computable by rational Sturm isolation and algebraic comparison. It is not a claim of an elementary formula for roots of arbitrary degree. For the open interval (0,H), discard endpoints for attainment but retain them when calculating the infimum. Endpoint-only minimizers must be reported as an infimum rather than an attained minimum.

For eta>=0 without an upper cap, a nonconstant P_K is coercive: it is a nonnegative polynomial on the whole real line, since (1) is a sum of squares times sums of even powers. A nonconstant globally nonnegative polynomial has even degree with positive leading coefficient. Thus the same formula with candidate 0 and all positive critical roots gives a global minimum. A constant polynomial is treated separately.

## Named target extension: optimized asymptotic, fixed instance

Assume x0 != 0 and s_mu+s_L > 0. Keep n, mu, L, x0, y0, s_mu, s_L fixed as K tends to infinity, and put T=n*K. Let eta_T be any global minimizer over eta>=0. The argument also applies to minimizers over [0,H] for any fixed H>0. Define

    D = n*(n+1)*(mu^2*s_mu+L^2*s_L)/(48*mu^3) > 0.

Conclusion:

    mu*T*eta_T / log(T) -> 3/2,
    min_eta P_K(eta) ~ (27/8)*D*log(T)^3/T^3.                         (3)

For noise only on the flat coordinate, the leading coefficient has no L dependence. For noise on the stiff coordinate it contains L^2/mu^2 when factored in units 1/mu. The quantifiers keep kappa fixed: (3) does not settle a bound uniform in kappa, nor the row's general last-iterate obstruction.

### Derivation

All constants implicit in O and o below may depend on the fixed instance; none is asserted uniform in n or kappa.

1. Write a_h^i = 1-i*h*eta+O(eta^2), a finite polynomial expansion. Thus

       V_h(eta) = [s_h*h^2*n^2*(n+1)/12]*eta^2 + O(eta^3).

   Indeed sum_{i<j}(i-j)^2 = n*sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i^2 - (sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i)^2
   = n^2*(n^2-1)/12, and division by n-1 gives the coefficient. The identity follows by expanding both finite sums; no asymptotic interchange is involved.

2. For 0<eta<1/L, 0<a_h<1, so 1-a_h^(2*n)>0. Define

       B_h(eta)= (h/2)*eta^2*V_h(eta)/(1-a_h^(2*n)).

   Since 1-a_h^(2*n)=2*n*h*eta+O(eta^2), division is legitimate for positive eta sufficiently small, and

       B_h(eta)= [s_h*h^2*n*(n+1)/48]*eta^3 + O(eta^4).

   If s_h=0 this expression is identically zero. For eta in this range, (1) is exactly the sum of the deterministic transients and B_h(eta)*(1-a_h^(2*T)).

3. Set eta_c=3*log(T)/(2*mu*T). For large T this belongs to (0,1/L). The elementary inequality 1-z<=exp(-z) gives
   a_mu^(2*T)<=T^-3 and a_L^(2*T)<=T^(-3*L/mu)<=T^-3. Thus the total transient at eta_c is O(T^-3). Summing step 2 over coordinates gives

       P_K(eta_c) <= [(27/8)*D+o(1)]*log(T)^3/T^3.                 (4)

   In particular the optimum tends to zero. Existence of a global minimizer follows from polynomial coercivity; here the noise is nonzero, so the polynomial is not constant. On a fixed closed bounded interval it follows from continuity. Eventually a minimizer is not eta=0 since P_K(0)>=mu*x0^2/2>0.

4. Choose a coordinate h with s_h>0. Its final-epoch variance term in (1) is at least h*eta^2*V_h(eta)/2 because G_K(a_h^(2*n))>=1 for every real eta. The pair (0,1) gives

       V_h(eta)>=s_h*h^2*eta^2/(n-1),
       P_K(eta)>=s_h*h^3*eta^4/[2*(n-1)].

   Applying this to the vanishing optimum proves eta_T->0. Thus all later uses of a geometric denominator occur in (0,1/L).

5. Put t_T=mu*T*eta_T. If t_T had a bounded subsequence, then eta_T=O(1/T) there and

       2*T*log(1-mu*eta_T)=-2*t_T+O(T*eta_T^2)=-2*t_T+o(1).

   The flat-coordinate deterministic error mu*x0^2*a_mu^(2*T)/2 would stay bounded away from zero on that subsequence, contradicting step 3. Therefore t_T->infinity. For either h, a_h^(2*T)<=exp(-2*(h/mu)*t_T)->0. Since sum_h B_h(eta)=[mu^3*D+o(1)]*eta^3 with D>0, eventually

       P_K(eta_T)>=(mu^3*D/2)*eta_T^3.

   Together with (4), this implies t_T=O(log T).

6. Hence T*eta_T^2=O(log(T)^2/T)=o(1). With A=mu*x0^2/2>0, the flat transient is A*exp(-2*t_T+o(1)). Bound it above by (4), take logarithms, and obtain

       t_T >= (3/2)*log T - (3/2)*log log T - O(1).               (5)

   The variance contribution at any minimizer is now

       sum_h B_h(eta_T)*(1-a_h^(2*T))=(D+o(1))*t_T^3/T^3.        (6)

   All omitted transients are nonnegative. Combining (6) and (4) gives
   limsup t_T/log T <= 3/2, while (5) gives liminf >=3/2. Substituting the resulting limit into (6) gives a lower bound with leading coefficient (27/8)*D; (4) supplies the matching upper bound. This proves (3).

For a fixed capped interval [0,H], the candidate eta_c is eventually admissible, and every argument applies unchanged. For (0,H), eventual optimizers are interior because eta_T->0 and P_K(0)>0, so the same asymptotic holds.

## Scope and checks that can fail

- x0!=0 is used precisely in steps 5 and 6. If the slow coordinate has no initial displacement, the slowest active transient can instead be the L direction and the leading optimized constant changes. The stated conclusion does not cover that case.
- Nonzero variance is used for D>0, coercivity via noise, and steps 4 and 5. With zero variance an exactly tuned step may annihilate a deterministic coordinate, so this argument is inapplicable.
- Fresh independent permutations justify summing epoch variances through G_K. A fixed permutation reused each epoch gives correlated noise and a different recursion.
- Correlation between coordinates is allowed; F has no mixed quadratic term, so no cross-coordinate covariance is used.
- Fixed n and kappa are essential to every Taylor remainder above. This result does not infer uniform kappa bounds from fixed-instance limits.
- Finite-K minimizers need not be unique. Every global minimizer obeys (3); the proof never assumes unimodality or a unique critical point.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b365549f1ce43f643362d67f0505c62a6eaee982ceb911ce8d3902524e7b43ae","revision_digest":"sha256:64433b6c579697e38fea8e9213c34167b32467d7d2d3f68a5207a07df176f8f7","source_id":"own-work:w732:T362:C001:v1","source_revision":"C001-v1-reviewer-PASS; reviewer urn:mb-agent:7a4f9e38007c2a28; T362-w732-C001 v1; proof sha256 7ae6d255596fb33690d720434c8915f7b1c329702bbed58c28be6bc2e959c604","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

\msF_2 &= z^3 y + z^2 (\delta x s + \varepsilon x t + g_4) + z (\alpha s^2 + \beta t^2 + \gamma s t + w g_2 + g_6) \\
&\hspace{6cm} + w^2 + w h_4 + g_8,
\end{split}
\]
where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \varepsilon \in \mbC$, $f_2, f_6, g_2, g_4 \in \mbC [x, y]$ and $g_6, g_8, h_4 \in (x, y) \subset \mbC [x, y, s, t]$ with $g_6, g_8 \in (x^2, y)$.

body:
[Lemma 11 (Immediate crossing when $r\ne0$) of arXiv:2607.19752, 'Weak Equilibrium Measures and Capacity--Hitting Identities\\ for the Hypoelliptic Third-Or'] Let $\rho$ be one of the signed defining functions in
Definition~\ref{def:signed-boundary-functions}. Suppose that the limiting
forward or adjoint process starts from a boundary point
$z_0=(\theta_0,p_0,r_0)$ with $r_0\ne0$. Then, for every $\eta>0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pbb_{z_0}\left(
    \sup_{0<t\le\eta}\rho(Z_t)>0,\ 
    \inf_{0<t\le\eta}\rho(Z_t)<0
\right)=1,\\
&\Pbb_{z_0}^{*}\left(
    \sup_{0<t\le\eta}\rho(Z_t^*)>0,\ 
    \inf_{0<t\le\eta}\rho(Z_t^*)<0
\right)=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
For every fixed $\delta>0$, the same almost-sure immediate-crossing
statement holds for the corresponding regularized forward and adjoint
processes: for every $\eta>0$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pbb_{z_0}^{\delta}\left(
    \sup_{0<t\le\eta}\rho\left(Z_t^\delta\right)>0,\ 
    \inf_{0<t\le\eta}\rho\left(Z_t^\delta\right)<0
\right)=1,\\
&\Pbb_{z_0}^{\delta,*}\left(
    \sup_{0<t\le\eta}\rho\left(Z_t^{\delta,*}\right)>0,\ 
    \inf_{0<t\le\eta}\rho\left(Z_t^{\delta,*}\right)<0
\right)=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

body: [Theorem 2 of arXiv:2506.11799, 'Quenched limit for diffusive biased random walks in random environment'] Let us consider a random walk in random environment in dimension $d\ge2$ under conditions (S), (R) and $(T)_\gamma$. For $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$, define $\tilde \mathcal{L}^\rho_n$ from $\tilde X_1$ the same way as $\mathcal{L}^\rho_n$ from $X_1$.

$$
d(\mathcal{L}^\rho_n, \tilde \mathcal{L}^\rho_n) \stackrel{\mathbb P}{\to} 0,
$$
where $d$ is (any) metric metrizing the uniform-on-compact topology on functions from $\mathbb H^2_\uparrow \to \mathbb{R}$. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

[Cor:distinguished of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \(z\in \mathcal{C}_{2}(\varphi)\) and let \(D_{n}(z)\) be the set of regular closed orbits which is \(z\)-distinguished in at least \(n\) directions. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item each orbit in \(D_{1}(z)\) has a power which is isotoped into \(R_{\pm}\)-part of \(\mathrm{Guts}(z)\),
\item \(\#D_{2}(z)\leq\) the number of sutured annuli in \(\mathrm{Guts}(z)\),
\item \(\#D_{4}(z)\leq\) the number of 4-STs in \(\mathrm{Guts}(z)\).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Pro of arXiv:2412.10001, 'On the Markov transformation of Gaussian processes'] Consider $H \in ]0,1[$ and denote by $\mathcal{B}_H$ the fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H$, \textnormal{i.e.} ,\ the centered Gaussian measure with covariance function $K_H : (s,t) \in \mathbb{R}_+^* \times \mathbb{R}_+^* \mapsto \frac{1}{2}(|t|^{2H} + |s|^{2H} - |t-s|^{2H})$. The centered Gaussian measure $\mathcal{B}_H'$ with covariance matrix \[K_{H}' : (s,t) \in \mathbb{R}_+^* \times \mathbb{R}_+^*  \mapsto 
		\begin{cases}
			s^{H}t^H\mathds{1}_{s = t} + 0\mathds{1}_{s \neq t} & \text{if } H < 1/2  \\ \min(s,t) &\text{if } H=1/2 \\   s^{H}t^{H}& \text{if } H > 1/2 
		\end{cases} \] is the strong local Markov transform of $\mathcal{B}_H.$
title: Unnumbered pro of arXiv:2412.10001, 'On the Markov transformation of Gaussian processes'

[Lemma lem:conditional-transfer of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathbb F_t),\mathbb P)$ be a standard
stochastic basis carrying an $\mathbb F$-Brownian motion $W$, let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathbb F_0$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field, let
$b:\Omega\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be $\mathcal G$-measurable with
continuous paths, and let $X$ be a continuous non-negative
$\mathbb F$-adapted process with $\mathbb{E}[\sup_{t\le1}X_t]<\infty$ satisfying,
almost surely,
\begin{equation}
X_t=b(t)+\nu\int_0^tK(t-s)\sqrt{X_s}\,dW_s,
\qquad t\in[0,1].
\end{equation}
Let $(\mathbb P^\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}$ be a regular conditional
probability given $\mathcal G$.  Then for $\mathbb P$-almost every
$\omega$: under $\mathbb P^\omega$, the process $W$ is a Brownian motion
with respect to the filtration
$\mathbb F_t^\circ:=\sigma(b)\vee\sigma(X_r,W_r:r\le t)$;
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb P^\omega}[\sup_{t\le1}X_t]<\infty$; and $X$ is an integrable
solution in the sense of Definition~(def:integrable-solution of the paper) with
the deterministic input $f=b(\cdot,\omega)$.

body: [Theorem prelim_things_abt_rank_r_times of arXiv:2411.04795, 'Metastable Distributions of Semi-Markov Processes'] Let $0 \le  r < R, 1 \le  k \le M_r$. An n x n matrix A over a field is diagonalizable (similar to a diagonal matrix, A = P D P^{-1}) if and only if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently if and only if for every eigenvalue the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity and the characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over the field. In particular a matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

[Defn 6 of arXiv:2506.15341, '\bf Superpositions for General Conditional Mckean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations'] A family of $\sP_1(\sM_1(\hR^d)))$-valued process $(\bP_t^Y)_{t\in[0,T]}$  is called a solution to the conditional Fokker-Planck equation (\ref{FP for nonlinear Zakai}), if, 

\ms
(i) $(\bP_t^Y)_{t\in[0,T]}\in \hL^2_{\hF^Y}(\Omega_0;  \hC([0,T],\sP_1(\sM_1(\hR^d))))$; and 

\ms
(ii) for any  $k$-cylindrical test function $F(\cd)$ defined by (\ref{Fn}), the equation (\ref{CFPeq}), or equivalently (\ref{FP for nonlinear Zakai}), holds. 

In particular, the solution $(\bP_t^Y)$ is called ``regular" if for some $p>1$ and $\hQ^0$-a.s., the following integrability condition holds: 
\bea

&&\Phi(T):=\int_0^T \int_{\sM(\hR^d)}\Big[ \|b(t,\cd, Y_t ,\bm)\|_{L^1(|\bn|)}^p+\|\sigma\sigma^{\ts}(t,\cd, Y_t,\bm)\|_{L^1(|\bn|)}^p\\
&&\qq\qq\qq+\|\rho(t,\cd, Y_t,\bm)\|_{L^1(|\bn|)}^{2p}+\|h(t,\cd, Y_t,\bm)\|_{L^1(|\bn|)}^{2p}\Big] \bP^Y_t(d\bn)dt<\infty, \nonumber
\eea  
where $\bm=\bm(\bn)$ is defined by (\ref{bm}), and $\Phi(\cdot)$ is $\hF^Y$-adapted.
\qed

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model with ferromagnetic couplings J_xy >= 0, the random-current representation writes correlation functions as sums over integer-valued edge configurations n = (n_xy) weighted by prod_{xy} (beta J_xy)^{n_xy} / n_xy!, subject to a source condition specifying a subset A of vertices where the total current degree is odd (and even elsewhere); the two-point function <sigma_x sigma_y> is proportional to the sum of weights over currents with sources {x,y}, with higher correlations expressed via larger source sets. The switching lemma is the key combinatorial identity underlying this representation: summing over pairs of independent currents with sources A and B and comparing to pairs with sources determined by the symmetric difference of A and B allows swapping which edges are assigned to which current while preserving all parity constraints, reducing correlation inequalities such as the Griffiths and Lebowitz inequalities, and Aizenman's tree-graph inequality used in proving triviality of the phi^4 field theory scaling limit in dimension d>=4 (or d=4 with logarithmic corrections), to purely combinatorial statements about current configurations. The representation does not extend beyond the Ising model or closely related models admitting an analogous high-temperature expansion, and it requires ferromagnetic couplings for the current weights to be nonnegative and hence probabilistically interpretable. Typical failure: Attempting to apply the random-current representation and switching lemma to models with mixed-sign (non-ferromagnetic) couplings, where the current weights are no longer nonnegative and the entire probabilistic interpretation, along with any downstream FKG-type consequences, breaks down; a further common error is misidentifying the source-set parity condition when composing several currents, which silently produces an identity for a different correlation function than intended. Canonical reference: Griffiths, Hurst and Sherman, 1970, Journal of Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, 1982, Communications in Mathematical Physics.

&&
(\mscrX_{\F_p})^{\dR}
  \arrow[dl,"\nu_{\mscrX_{\F_p}}"]
\\
&
\mscrX_{\F_p}.
&
\end{tikzcd}
\]

[Thm functional-thm of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Under (fass1 of the paper)--(fass3 of the paper), $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is stochastically persistent in the sense that for all $\delta > 0$ there are $0 < b < B < \infty$ such that for any nonnegative initial condition $\phi \in \mathcal{M}_+$, 
    $$
    \liminf_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T}m(\{t \leq T \mid b \leq \min_{i \leq n} (X_i)_t \leq \max_{i \leq n} (X_i)_t \leq B\}) \geq 1 - \delta
    $$ 
    almost surely, where $m=m_T$ denotes the Lebesgue measure on $[0, T]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm functional-thm of arXiv:2601.19145

[Proposition 34 (Conditional exponential representation) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] Conditionally on $Y_N^\gamma(n)$, the fitnesses
$\{F_{N,x}^\gamma(n):x\in\Lambda_N\}$ are independent, and
$F_{N,x}^\gamma(n)$ has the exponential distribution conditioned to lie
above $Y_{N,x}^\gamma(n)$. Consequently, for distinct
$x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\Lambda_N$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_k\geq0$,
\[
        \mathbb{P}(F_{N,x_j}^\gamma(n)\leq z_j,\ 1\leq j\leq k)
        =
        \mathbb{E}\left[
        \prod_{j=1}^kH_{Y_{N,x_j}^\gamma(n)}(z_j)
        \right].
\]

[Proposition 55 (Hilbert-space realization and covariance subtraction) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $\mathcal G_a:=\widehat{\mathfrak H}_a$ be the real Gaussian Hilbert
space in \eqref{eq:hermitian-gaussian-hilbert-space}.  Fix either a finite
spectral cutoff $\lambda=\Lambda$ or the uncut state $\lambda=\infty$, set
$m_\infty=1$, and put
\[
 S_b:=\mathsf S_{b,N,s}^{(m_\lambda)}:
 \mathcal G_b\to\mathcal A_N,
 \qquad
 S_c:=\mathsf S_{c,L,t}^{(m_\lambda)}:
 \mathcal G_c\to\mathcal C_{1,L}.
\]
For
\[
 \mathbf H_{t,s}^{\sharp,\lambda}(F,G,f,g)
 :=\mathbf H_{t,s}(S_bF,S_cG,f,g),
\]
the four pulled-back flattenings, with the superscript $\lambda$ suppressed,
have the directions
\begin{align}
 F_1^\sharp&:\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c\otimes_2\mathcal C_{0,Q}
       \longrightarrow\mathcal E_M,
 &F_1^\sharp&=F_1(S_b\otimes S_c\otimes I_Q),
 \\
 F_2^\sharp&:\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c\otimes_2\mathcal E_M
       \longrightarrow\mathcal C_{0,Q},
 &F_2^\sharp&=F_2(S_b\otimes S_c\otimes I_M),
 \\
 F_3^\sharp&:\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal C_{0,Q}
       \longrightarrow\mathcal G_c\otimes_2\mathcal E_M,
 &F_3^\sharp&=(S_c^*\otimes I_M)F_3(S_b\otimes I_Q),
 \\
 F_4^\sharp&:\mathcal G_c\otimes_2\mathcal C_{0,Q}
       \longrightarrow\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal E_M,
 &F_4^\sharp&=(S_b^*\otimes I_M)F_4(S_c\otimes I_Q).
 
\end{align}
Here $I_Q$ and $I_M$ are the identities on the input and output shell
spaces.  Each factorization contains one copy of $S_b$ and one copy of $S_c$.
When $\lambda=\Lambda$, \eqref{eq:single-shell-factor-after-pullback} gives the
finite-cutoff stochastic multipliers
\begin{equation}
 \rho_N(\ell)\rho_L(r)m_\Lambda(\ell)m_\Lambda(r).
\end{equation}

Assume now that $b=c$.  Testing the covariance of the two finite-cutoff
synthesis maps against the deterministic kernel gives
\begin{align}
 &\widetilde\rho_N(\ell)\widetilde\rho_L(r)
 (2\pi)^3\delta(\ell+r)
 \rho_N(\ell)\rho_L(r)m_\Lambda(\ell)m_\Lambda(r)
 \sigma_b(\ell;s,t)\notag\\
 &\qquad=(2\pi)^3\delta(\ell+r)
 \rho_N(\ell)\rho_L(r)m_\Lambda(\ell)m_\Lambda(r)
 \sigma_b(\ell;s,t).
 
\end{align}
After imposing $r=-\ell$ and using evenness, its scalar shell factor is
\begin{equation}
 \rho_N(\ell)\rho_L(-\ell)m_\Lambda(\ell)^2
 \sigma_b(\ell;s,t).
\end{equation}
On a same-shell summand $L=N$, this becomes
\begin{equation}
 \rho_N(\ell)^2m_\Lambda(\ell)^2\sigma_b(\ell;s,t).
\end{equation}
This is the covariance term in Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-color-split} and,
after finite-overlap shell reindexing, the factor in
\eqref{eq:localized-contraction-kernel}.

Let $P$ be a finite-rank orthogonal projection on the common Gaussian space
$\mathcal G_b$.  Choose an orthonormal basis
$(e_\mu)_{\mu=1}^{d_P}$ of $P\mathcal G_b$ and define the finite compressed
covariance contraction by
\begin{equation}
 D_P:=\sum_{\mu=1}^{d_P} H_{e_\mu,e_\mu}^{\sharp,\lambda},
 \qquad
 \langle H_{F,G}^{\sharp,\lambda}f,g\rangle
 :=\mathbf H_{t,s}(S_bF,S_cG,f,g).
\end{equation}
The sum is basis independent and equals the covariance of the two
$P$-compressed first chaoses.  Wick centering subtracts $D_P$ at finite rank.
For the dyadic block, \eqref{eq:same-color-shell-contraction} is treated
separately, and Gaussian completion is applied to the centered tensor.

[Proposition propclass of arXiv:2411.04238, 'Holomorphic jump-diffusions'] Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^d$ be an open set.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item{\textbf{Cauchy integral formula}} 
 (Theorem 1.3.3 in [SC:05])

    
     Let $f:U\to \mathbb C$ be a holomorphic function and fix $z_0\in U$ and $R\in (0,\infty)^d$ such that   $\overline{P_R^d(z_0)}\subseteq U$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
     D^\alpha f(z_0)=\frac{\alpha!}{(2\pi i)^d}\int_{T^d_{R}(z_0)} \frac{f(w)} {(z_0-w)^{\alpha +1}}   dw,
    \end{align*}
    where $\alpha+1:=(\alpha_1+1,\ldots,\alpha_d+1)$, and 
    $$|D^\alpha f(z_0)|\leq \frac {\alpha!}{R^\alpha}\|f|_{T_R^d(z_0)}\|_\infty.$$

    
    \item{\textbf{Taylor expansion}} (Corollary 1.5.9 in [SC:05])
    
    Let $f:U\to \mathbb R$ be a holomorphic functions and fix $z_0\in U$ and $R\in (0,\infty]^d$ such that   $\overline{P_R^d(z_0)}\subseteq U$. Then 
\begin{equation}
        f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in \mathbb{N}^d_0}\frac 1 {\alpha!}D^\alpha f(z_0)(z-z_0)^\alpha,
    \qquad \text{for all }z\in P_R^d(z_0).
\end{equation}
By~(class:it1 of the paper) and Example~1.5.7 in [SC:05], for $R\in (0,\infty)^d$  the reminder's term can be bounded as follows
\begin{align*}
\Big|\sum_{|\alpha|\geq k+1}\frac 1 {\alpha!}D^\alpha f(z_0)(z-z_0)^\alpha\Big|
\leq\|f|_{T_R^d(z_0)}\|_\infty\prod_{i=1}^d\frac 1 {1-\frac{|z_i-z_{0i}|}{R_i}}\sum_{|\alpha|= k+1}\frac{|z-z_0|^\alpha}{R^\alpha}.
        \end{align*}
 \item{\textbf{Identity theorem}} (Conclusion 1.2.12.2 in [SC:05]) Let $f:U\rightarrow\mathbb C$ be a holomorphic function. If $U$ is connected and $f=0$ on some open set $E\subseteq U$, then $f(z)=0$ for all $z\in U$. For $d=1$ the set $E$ is just required to have an accumulation point in $U$.
    \item {\textbf{Vitali-Porter theorem}} (Exercise 1.4.37 in [SC:05]) 
    
    Fix an open subset $E\subseteq U$ and consider a sequence $\{f_n\}_n$ of holomorphic functions $f_n:U\to \mathbb C$.
    Suppose that $\{f_n\}_n$ is a locally bounded sequence (uniformly bounded on every compact set of the domain of definition) and  
    \begin{equation}
    f(z):=\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(z)
    \end{equation} exists for all $z\in E$. Then the limit in (equation eqn7 of the paper) is well defined for each $z\in U$, the resulting map $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, and the convergence holds locally uniformly. For $d=1$ the set $E$ is just required to have an accumulation point in $U$ (see p.44 [S:93]).

    \item{\textbf{Goursat's theorem}} (Theorem 1.1 in [SS:10])
    
    Fix $d=1$ and let $\triangle\subseteq U$ be a triangle whose interior is contained in $U$. If $f:U\to \mathbb C$ is holomorphic then
    $$\int_\triangle f(z) dz=0.$$
    \item{\textbf{Morera's theorem}} (Theorem 5.1 in [SS:10])
    
    Fix $d=1,R\in (0,\infty)$,   $a\in \mathbb C$, and let $f:P^1_R(a)\to \mathbb C$ be a continuous map. If for any triangle $\triangle\subset P^1_R(a)$ it holds
    $$\int_\triangle f(z) dz=0,$$
    then $f$ is holomorphic.
    \item{\textbf{Hartogs' theorem}} (see p.28 in [S:92])
    
    Let $f:U\to \mathbb C$ be a partially holomorphic function, meaning that it is holomorphic in each variable  while the other variables are held constant. Then $f$ is holomorphic.
    \item {\textbf{Weierstrass' theorem}} (Theorem 1.4.20 in [SC:05]).

    
     $H(U,\mathbb C)$ is a closed subspace of $C(U,\mathbb C)$ with respect to the locally uniform convergence. Moreover, for every $\alpha\in \mathbb{N}_0^d$ the linear operator
$D^\alpha:H(U,\mathbb C)\to H(U,\mathbb C)$ 
is continuous.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm: orthogonal simplex of arXiv:2505.09839, '\textbf{Density Frankl–Rödl on the Sphere}'] Fix an integer \( k \geq 2 \). For any measurable set \( A \subseteq {\mathbb{S}^{n-1} } \), the probability that a tuple \( (v_1, \cdots, v_k) \) drawn uniformly at random from \( \Delta_k(n,0) \) lies entirely in \( A \) is at least
\[
\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{(x_1, \cdots, x_k) \in \Delta_k(n,0)}(x_1 \in A, \cdots, x_k \in A) \geq \Omega_k\left(\sigma(A)^k-C_k \exp(-cn^{1/3})\sigma(A)^{k-1}\right),
\]
where \(c > 0 \) is a universal constant and $C_k$ is a constant depending only on $k$.

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.21014, 'The stochastic Cahn--Hilliard equation in critical spaces'] Let $d=4$ and suppose that the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:localWP_weakened} hold. Moreover, let $u_0\in L^0_{\F_0}(\Omega;H^1(\sO))$ and $T>0$. Let $(u,\sigma)$ be the unique maximal solution to \eqref{eq:SCHtorus} and $\mu$ the associated chemical potential from Definition~\ref{def:chemPotential}. Then the following three estimates hold a.s.\ for a.e.\ $0\le s <\sigma \land T$
    \begin{align}
        \|\Delta u(s)\|_{L^2}^2  & \le \|\mu(s)\|_{L^2}^2 + 2\| \grad u(s)\|_{L^2}^2 , \\
         \|u^2(s)\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2 & \lesssim
        \|u(s)\|^3_{H^1}
        \left(\|\Delta u(s)\|_{L^2}^2
        +\|u(s)\|^2_{H^1}  \right)
        \left( \|\grad \Delta u(s)\|_{L^2}
        +\|u(s)\|_{H^1}\right),
         \\
        \|\mu(s)\|_{L^2}^4 & \lesssim \|\nabla\mu(s)\|_{L^2}^2 \left(\|u(s)\|_{H^1}^6 + 1\right) + 1
        + \|u(s)\|_{H^1}^{12}. 
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma asymptotics of arXiv:2607.22156, 'A random matrix approach to lamplighter groups'] Let $C$ be a test-graph whose underlying graph is a cycle of length $c$ and $L$ be a test-graph whose underlying graph is a line of length $l$. Let $V_N$ be a uniform random permutation matrix. By a direct computation, one has
	       \begin{align*}
		      \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Tr}^{0}(C(V_{N}))\right]&=N\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{U}_{N}\in\mathrm{Cyc}_{c})=1,\\
            \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Tr}^{0}(L(V_{N}))\right]&=N\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{U}_{N}\in\mathrm{Cyc}_{\geq l})=N(1-\frac{l-1}{N}),
	       \end{align*}
        where $\mathcal{U}_{N}$ is a uniform random variable on $\{1,\cdots,N\}$ and the notations $\mathcal{U}_{N}\in\mathrm{Cyc}_{c}$ and $\mathcal{U}_{N}\in\mathrm{Cyc}_{\geq l}$ correspond to "$U_{N}$ belongs to a cycle of length $c$ of $V_{N}$" and "$U_{N}$ belongs to a cycle of length at least $l$ of $V_{N}$" respectively. 

        Moreover, if a test-graph $T$ has an underlying graph which is not a cycle nor a directed line, then, $\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Tr}^{0}(T(V_{N}))\right]=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma asymptotics of arXiv:2607.22156

body:
[Lem 74 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have 
\begin{align*}\sM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\svii}(\alpha,q_0)\,,\\
\sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
\end{align*}
    
\begin{proof} 
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\GREATdefn\\
	\SPRdefn\\
	\PRFFOURdefn\\
	\PRFTWOdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
The $\svi$ and $\svii$ classes differ only in the condition on the function $p$: the $\svi$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.2}, while the $\svii$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.4}. The $\sxii$ 
and $\sx$ classes also differ only in the condition on the function $p$: the $\sxii$ 
class satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}, while the $\sx$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}.

    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Then $\mu$ is of the form $\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0)$ for some $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Since $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.2}, it is concave.

    Let $\epsilon_0 > 0$ be arbitrary. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:approximate-p-by-C2} 
     (applied with $\epsilon_0,L_0$ in place of $\epsilon,L$), there exists sufficiently large $L_0 = L_0(\epsilon_0)$ and concave $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ such that $1/L_0 \le \tilde p(q_0) \le \epsilon_0$ and $\|\tilde p\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L_0$ (i.e. satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.4}, as required of the $\svii$ class) and $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 \le \epsilon_0$.

By condition~\ref{it:4.3}, we have
$\mu \in \cM(q_0;p,f)$ for budget function
 $f(t) = (\E w_t)^2 / \alpha$.
    Proposition~\ref{p:continuity.in.p} then implies the existence of 
    \[
        \tilde\mu \in \cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)
        \subseteq \cM^{\svii}(\alpha,q_0;\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)
    \]
    with $\bbW_2(\mu,\tilde \mu)^2 \le 6(1+1/\alpha) \cdot \epsilon_0 \equiv (\tilde\epsilon_0)^2$.
    We have thus shown that for any $\epsilon_0 > 0$ there exists $L_0 = L_0(\epsilon_0)$ such that
    \[
        \cM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon_0}\Big(\cM^{\svii}(\alpha,q_0;\epsilon,L_0,\tilde \epsilon_0)\Big)\,.
    \]
Consequently, for $\hat\epsilon_0 = \epsilon_0 + \tilde\epsilon_0$, we have
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon_0}\Big(\cM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) 
        \subseteq \cB_{\hat\epsilon_0}\Big(
        \cM^{\svii}(\alpha,q_0;\epsilon,L_0,\hat \epsilon_0)
        \Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking unions and intersections of the above, in the order specified by Definition~\ref{d:measure.classes}, gives the first assertion $\sM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\svii}(\alpha,q_0)$.

    The proof of the remaining inclusion $\sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0)$ is very similar. We consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)$, realized by controls $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)$, so that $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}. 
    For arbitrary $\epsilon > 0$,  Lemma~\ref{l:approximate-p-by-C2} 
    implies the existence of sufficiently large $L = L(\epsilon)$ and $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ such that $1/L \le \tilde p(q_0) \le \epsilon$ and $\|\tilde p\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1}, as required of the $\sx$ class) and $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 \le \epsilon$.
    Arguing as above shows that for $\tilde\epsilon^2 \equiv 6(1+1/\alpha) \cdot \epsilon$,
    \[
        \cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}(\cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\tilde\epsilon))\,,
    \]
    which implies the result similarly to above.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma spectral_lower_bound_of_escape_probability of arXiv:2512.06640, 'Existence and sharpness of the phase transition for the frog model on transitive graphs'] Let $(G,W)$ be a non-amenable electrical network as above with spectral radius $\rho$. Assume that $W$ is weight-locally finite.
  Let $A \subseteq G$ be a non-empty subset, and let $\pi_{A}(\cdot) := \pi(\cdot) / \pi(A)$ be the normalized restriction of $\pi$ to $A$.
  Also for a discrete-time random walk $X$, let $T^+_A := \inf \{n \ge 1: X(n) \in A \}$ be the \textbf{positive hitting time} of $A$.
  Then,
  \begin{align}
    \mathbb P_{\pi_A} \left( T^+_A = \infty \right) := \sum _{x \in A}\pi_{A}(x) \mathbb P_{x}(T^+_A = \infty) \geq 1 - \rho.
  \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma spectral_lower_bound_of_escape_probability of arXiv:2512.06640

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The central moments of $c_{mp}$ are given by the formulae
$$M_1'=0$$
$$M_2'=\frac{m(1-p)}{p^2}$$
$$M_3'=\frac{m(1-p)(2-p)}{p^3}$$
$$M_4'=\frac{m(1-p)((3m+6)(1-p)+p^2)}{p^4}$$
$$\vdots$$
with the computation in general being possible by recurrence.

body:
[Proposition prop:HXZ of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $M^T$ be square-integrable compensated point-process martingales on
$[0,1]$, with predictable brackets
\[
 d\langle M^T\rangle_t=q_t^T\,dt,
\]
and assume that the jumps of the renormalized martingales vanish in
probability uniformly on $[0,1]$.  Let
\[
I_t^T=\int_0^t K_T(t-s)\,dM_s^T.
\]
Suppose that for some $\eta>0$,
\begin{equation}
\sup_T\int_0^\infty |K_T(u+h)-K_T(u)|^2\,du
\le C h^\eta,
\qquad h\in(0,1],
\end{equation}
and that, for some $p>1/\eta$,
\begin{equation}
\sup_T\mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t\in[0,1]} |q_t^T|^p\right]<\infty .
\end{equation}
Then $(I^T)_T$ is tight in $D([0,1])$, and every limit point is continuous.
Equivalently, $(I^T)_T$ is $C$-tight.

body:
[Prop intro-bridge of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G_k$ be a sequence of weighted bipartite graphs with $k$ left vertices,
$n_k$ right vertices, average right support-degree $O(1)$, average nonzero
weight magnitude at most $1$, $n_k/k\to\infty$, and \hyperref[def:local-sparse-four-cycle-incidence]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{local sparse four-cycle incidence}}}{}. Let $r_k$
satisfy $k/r_k=O(1)$. Then, for a uniform right sample $\Omega_k$ of size $r_k$, with
probability $1-o(1)$ one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G_k[\Omega_k]$ has an isolated sampled right vertex;
\item $G_k[\Omega_k]$ has two degree-one sampled right vertices with the same
left neighbor;
\item $G_k[\Omega_k]$ contains a \hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m_k$-matching rooted tree}}} inside a
$C_4$-free subgraph of bounded maximum right degree, with nonzero weights
bounded by a constant depending only on the average-degree bound, where
\[
m_k\to\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:miss_rate_fixed_N of arXiv:2412.00279, 'Optimal local storage policy based on stochastic intensities and its large scale behavior'] Let $p_N^{\pm}=p_N\pm\frac{1}{N}$ where $p_N=1-\frac{C}{N-1}$. Let $\varphi_N^{\pm}$ be the probability distribution function of the random variable $\widehat{\theta}_N^{\pm}:=\widehat{Q}_N\left(p_N^{\pm}\right)$ under the probability ${\rm P}$. Then the miss rate is bounded from above and below by
\begin{equation}
\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \lambda G_0\left(\frac{\theta}{\lambda}\right)\varphi_N^-(d\theta) L_N(d\lambda)
\leqslant \frac{m_{\mathcal{C}^*}^{(N)} }{N}\leqslant \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \lambda G_0\left(\frac{\theta}{\lambda}\right)\varphi_N^+(d\theta) L_N(d\lambda).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theo lichlap of arXiv:2608.25865, 'Instability of Böhm's Einstein metrics'] In the basis $(e_0,e_i,e_\alpha)$, the Lichnerowicz Laplacian of the tensor $T=a(t)dt^2+\phi(t)f(t)^2g^k+\psi(t)h(t)^2g^l\in \mathscr{T}^G_{TT}(M)$ (where $M=S^{k+1}\times S^l$ or $S^{k+l+1}$) is diagonal, with
\begin{align*}
  (\Delta_L T)_{00}&=-a''(t)-Ha'(t)+2k\left(\frac{f'^2}{f^2}-\frac{f''}{f}\right)(a(t)-\phi(t))+2l\left(\frac{h'^2}{h^2}-\frac{h''}{h}\right)(a(t)-\psi(t)),
\\
  (\Delta_L T)_{ii}&=-\phi''(t)-H\phi'(t)-2\left(\frac{f'^2}{f^2}-\frac{f''}{f}\right)(a(t)-\phi(t))+2\frac{f'h'}{fh}l(\psi(t)-\phi(t)),
\\
  (\Delta_L T)_{\alpha\alpha}&=-\psi''(t)-H\psi'(t)-2\left(\frac{h'^2}{h^2}-\frac{h''}{h}\right)(a(t)-\psi(t))+2\frac{f'h'}{fh}k(\phi(t)-\psi(t)),
\end{align*}
where $\displaystyle H=k\frac{f'}{f}+l\frac{h'}{h}$.

[Definition 13 (\normalfont Hierarchical-star structure) of arXiv:2604.24684, 'Waning Immunity Fails to Restore a Positive Epidemic Threshold on Power--Law Networks'] We say that a graph $G=(V,E)$ \emph{contains a $( k_1 ,k_2)$--hierarchical-star} if there
exist distinct vertices
\[
v,\; u_1,\ldots,u_{\lceil k_1\rceil},\; w_{i,1},\ldots,w_{i,\lceil k_2\rceil}\qquad (i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil)
\]
such that the following edges are present:
\begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (a)}]
\item $v$ is adjacent to $u_i$ for every $i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil$;
\item for each $i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil$, the vertex $u_i$ is adjacent to $w_{i,1},\ldots,w_{i,\lceil k_2\rceil}$.
\end{enumerate}
The spanning subgraph on these vertices consisting \emph{only} of the edges
\[
\big\{\{v,u_i\}: i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil\big\}\ \cup\ \big\{\{u_i,w_{i,j}\}: i=1,\ldots,\lceil k_1\rceil,\ j=1,\ldots,\lceil k_2\rceil\big\}
\]
is called a \emph{$(k_1,k_2)$--hierarchical-star}, with center $v$, first-layer vertices $\{u_i\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil}$, and
second-layer vertices $\{w_{i,j}\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil,\,j\le \lceil k_2\rceil}$.
We denote this designated subgraph by $\mathrm{HStar}(v;\{u_i\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil};\{w_{i,j}\}_{i\le \lceil k_1\rceil,\,j\le \lceil k_2\rceil})$.
title: \normalfont Hierarchical-star structure

\|F(u)\|_{\mathcal{W}_T} \le C_1 T^{\theta_1} \|u\|_{\mathcal{W}_T}^2 + C_2 T^{\theta_2} (1 + \|u\|_{\mathcal{W}_T}),

where $\theta_1 = \frac{\alpha(1-2\nu)}{2}$ and $\theta_2 = \min\left\{\frac{(2-\nu)\alpha}{2}, \frac{\alpha(1-\nu)}{2}\right\} > 0$.

[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] Let \((M^{n},g)\), \(n\geq3\), be a closed, connected, locally
conformally flat manifold satisfying
\(\mathrm{Sc}_{g}\geq n(n-1)\). Assume that $\pi_1(M)$ is infinite. Let
\(\mathrm{dev}\colon(\widetilde M,\tilde g)\to (S^n,g_{st})\)
denote a developing map, where \(\tilde g\) is the lifted metric. Then
there exists \(x\in\widetilde M\) such that
\(\mathrm{Lip}_{x}(\mathrm{dev})>1\).

[Definition def_one of arXiv:2608.08532, 'Constrained Maximum Weight Paths in Random Geometric Graphs'] For deterministic sequences~\(l_n,s_n,w_n \geq 0,\) we say that~\(\Pi\) is a~\((l_n,q_n,w_n)-\)path in~\(G\) if:\\
\((i)\)~\(\Pi\) contains at most~\(l_n\) edges and has~\(O_1\) and~\(O_2\) as endvertices,\\
\((ii)\) The Euclidean length of each edge in~\(\Pi\) is at least~\(q_n;\) i.e.,
\[\min_{0 \leq i \leq t-1} d(X_{v_i},X_{v_{i+1}}) \geq q_n\] and\\
\((iii)\) The weight of each edge in~\(\Pi\) is at least~\(w_n;\) i.e.,
\[\min_{0 \leq i \leq t-1} W(v_i,v_{i+1}) \geq w_n.\]
We define~\[W(\Pi) := \sum_{i=1}^{t-1}W(v_i,v_{i+1})\] to be the weight of~\(\Pi.\)

body:
Own work draft; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. For an equal-weight centered equilateral three-Gaussian teacher with known covariance I_d and original radius R>=1, ordinary unaugmented empirical DDPM GD on centered mean parameters from centered Gaussian factor initialization achieves noisy mean Frobenius error a epsilon up to permutation with probability at least 7/20-eta>1/3 for eta<=1/100. At the inverse-polynomial noisy radius a of C08, a polynomial number of iid DDPM sample/noise pairs suffices; physical unit-step iteration count is O(a^(-2) log d+a^(-4) log(C/epsilon)). Uniform rescaled gradient error zeta=c a^2 epsilon gives a controlled angular floor O(zeta/a^2), rather than exact finite-sample convergence. Student means are M=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T with V=sqrt(2/3)U^T and U the unit equilateral vertex matrix; Z_0 has iid N(0,1/d) entries. A sufficient sample choice is n=ceil(B^80), B=C_0(d+1/a+1/zeta+1/eta+1)^2 for a sufficiently large absolute C_0. The centroid is imposed to be zero and radius is known; arbitrary triangles and finite-precision complexity remain open.
d>=2, R>=1 known
true centered equilateral triangle in an unknown plane
equal weights 1/3 and known common covariance I_d
centered mean parameterization throughout
a inverse polynomial in d as in C08 with sufficiently small absolute constant
OU tau=a/R and sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2
iid original data and independent Gaussian DDPM noise; initialization independent of all pairs
0<epsilon<1, 0<eta<=1/100
exact empirical gradients, physical unit step, real arithmetic including score exponentials

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:eff8a3c12bf8b61692949a4612a1c89f574447289a791fad4e379b81394ac8d6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ef/eff8a3c12bf8b61692949a4612a1c89f574447289a791fad4e379b81394ac8d6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:db4315b575d251e8436b83b02ffb4957ac7546b6d5a9b968b916c9f8a8fc957c","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c09","bundle_id":"population.t309-ordinary-empirical-centered-equilateral-random-init-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-centered-equilateral-empirical-random-initialization","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Own work draft; proof (unaudited), T309-w721-C09 v2, Target 2.

# Ordinary empirical DDPM GD: the centered equilateral random-initialization case

This builds on unaudited C07 v2 and C08 v2. It replaces the population gradient by the ordinary empirical gradient, without orbit augmentation. It does not solve the unrestricted K=3 target. The centroid is constrained to zero, weights and covariance are known, radius is known, and the true triangle is equilateral. No novelty or bit-complexity claim is made.

## 1. Statement and objective

Let the original teacher be (1/3)sum_j N(R E u_j,I_d), d>=2, R>=1 known, E^T E=I_2 and u_j the unit equilateral vertices. Choose a at the inverse-polynomial-in-d scale of C08, with its absolute constant reduced as needed below. Set tau=a/R and sigma=sqrt(1-tau^2)>=1/2. Draw n iid pairs (X_i,Y_i), where X_i is an original teacher sample and Y_i~N(0,I_d) independently. Put W_i=tau X_i+sigma Y_i. The loss is the usual single-time empirical DDPM objective

    Lhat(Z)=(1/n)sum_i ||s_{M(Z)}(W_i)+Y_i/sigma||^2,
    M(Z)=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T,

where V=sqrt(2/3)U^T, as in C07. This is Eq. (5) with the Eq. (9) mixture-score student. Initialization has iid N(0,1/d) entries in Z_0 and is independent of these pairs.

For each 0<epsilon<1 and 0<eta<=1/100, there is an n polynomial in d,1/a,1/epsilon,1/eta such that physical unit-step GD on the centered parameters satisfies

    min_pi ||M_T-M_teacher,pi||_F<=a epsilon          (1)

with probability at least 7/20-eta, after

    T=O(a^(-2)log d+a^(-4)log(C/epsilon)).             (2)

In particular the success probability exceeds 1/3. Both sample count and real-arithmetic work are polynomial in d,1/epsilon,1/eta because a is inverse polynomial in d. Arithmetic evaluations of the score and its gradient, including exponentials, are counted here; no finite-precision runtime theorem is asserted. Rescaling the means by R/a gives original mean error R epsilon and hence TV at most R epsilon/2 after matching, by Gaussian KL and Pinsker. For a prescribed original-law error, choose epsilon accordingly. There is no claim of exact convergence for a fixed finite sample.

## 2. Polynomial uniform gradient approximation

Write F_a(Z) for the population excess score risk in C07. The conditional-expectation identity for DDPM gives E grad Lhat=grad F_a; the difference between their population losses is constant in Z. Define the rescaled fields

    f_a(Z)=-a^(-4)grad_Z F_a(Z),
    fhat(Z)=-a^(-4)grad_Z Lhat(Z).

For each 0<zeta<1, a polynomial n suffices for

    sup_{||Z||_F<=5} ||fhat(Z)-f_a(Z)||_F<=zeta       (3)

with probability at least 1-eta. Here are explicit deliberately loose polynomial choices and a proof.

Take B=C_0(d+a^(-1)+zeta^(-1)+eta^(-1)+1)^2 and n=ceil(B^80), with C_0 an absolute sufficiently large constant. A pair is safe when ||W||,||Y||<=B. Marginally W is a three-component unit-covariance Gaussian mixture with means of norm a; Y is standard Gaussian. Their correlation is irrelevant to the union bound. For a standard d-Gaussian G, direct Gaussian integration gives E exp(||G||^2/4)=2^(d/2). Markov, B>=2a, and a union bound yield unsafe probability at most C exp(-c B^2), provided B^2 exceeds a sufficiently large constant times d.

Uniformly on the model ball and safe pairs, the rescaled per-pair gradient and its Z Lipschitz constant are bounded by C B^12. To verify a polynomial envelope, let b_M(w)=sum_j p_j(w)m_j be the posterior mean correction in s_M=-w+b_M. Since ||m_j||<=C a, the residual norm is at most C B. The first Z derivative of b has operator norm at most C a(1+aB+a^2); differentiating the logits once introduces a(w-m_j). A second derivative has a bound C a^2(1+B)^3. These follow by differentiating the three softmax weights, whose values lie in [0,1]. The gradient of a squared residual is twice the score Jacobian adjoint applied to the residual; its Hessian is twice the Jacobian square plus twice the residual paired with the score Hessian. Multiplying their bounds by a^(-4), and using B>=1/a, gives the stated looser B^12 bound in Frobenius/operator norm. These bounds do not introduce an exponential of a logit or an unbounded number of components.

Multiply the per-pair field by the safe-pair indicator for the purpose of the proof only. The truncated expectation differs from f_a by at most zeta/10 uniformly on the ball. Indeed the same derivative formulas give a fixed polynomial envelope in ||W||+||Y||, multiplied by a^(-4). Its second moment is bounded by a fixed polynomial in d and 1/a. Cauchy--Schwarz and the unsafe probability bound give polynomial(d,1/a)*exp(-cB^2), which is below zeta/10 for the stated B and large C_0. The algorithm itself does not truncate: with probability at least 1-eta/4 all n pairs are safe, since n exp(-cB^2)<=eta/4.

Choose a model net of mesh zeta/(100 C B^12) in the radius-5 ball of R^(2d), and a 1/2-net of the unit sphere in the same space. The elementary disjoint-ball packing argument bounds the two cardinalities by (1+C B^12/zeta)^(2d) and 5^(2d). Their combined logarithm is at most C d log B<=C B^2. At each model and direction net point the truncated scalar field is bounded by C B^12. For independent bounded scalars in [-G,G],

    P(|sample mean-expectation|>u)<=2exp(-n u^2/(2G^2)).

For clarity, this bound can be proved directly: the second derivative of the log moment-generating function is a tilted variance, bounded by G^2 for a variable in [-G,G]. Integrating twice from zero bounds the centered log MGF by t^2 G^2/2. Chernoff optimization for the independent sum and the two signs gives the displayed inequality. No Gaussianity of the gradient is assumed.

Apply this at tolerance a small constant times zeta and union bound over both nets. Since zeta>=1/B and n>=B^80, the tail exponent is at least cB^54, dominating the net logarithm and log(1/eta). The direction net converts scalar to vector bounds with factor at most two. The model Lipschitz bound extends to the whole ball, with error at most zeta/10. Adding the truncated-expectation bias and the all-samples-safe event proves (3), after allocating the failure probabilities below eta. All estimates hold at once over parameters, so no independence between later GD iterates and the samples is needed.

## 3. Entry still has polynomial cost

On (3), the empirical unit-step update is

    Z_{k+1}=Z_k+gamma[f(Z_k)+R_a(Z_k)+e(Z_k)],
    gamma=2a^2/3, ||R_a||<=C a^2, ||e||<=zeta,

where f=(P-ZZ^T)Z. C07's stopped flow comparison on its logarithmic rescaled entry interval now gives error at most

    C(a^2+zeta)exp(76(S+1)).

Set zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon, with c_* small, and reduce the absolute constant in C07's choice of a. This comparison is then still at most rho/4. The same norm-4 initialization event, tube entry and angular error transfer apply to the empirical trajectory. In particular the good surrogate-flow angle event in C08 has probability at least 7/20. It is not claimed that the empirical objective is rotation invariant.

## 4. Stable recurrences with persistent error

Use C08's branch, subspace L, normalized radius r, normal error w, and nearest-sector-minimum angle alpha. As long as the trajectory is in the tube, (3) and the normal contraction imply

    ||w_{k+1}||<=(1-c gamma)||w_k||+gamma zeta,
    ||w_k||<=C rho exp(-c gamma k)+C zeta.             (4)

The exact population tangent correction remains quadratic in w, by C08's self-adjoint Hessian and invariant-subspace argument. The empirical field adds at most zeta directly. Thus the angular error from the restricted map is bounded by the sum of a transient term Cgamma rho^2 exp(-c gamma k) and a persistent term Cgamma zeta, since zeta^2<=zeta. The transient has total sum at most C rho^2; choose the fixed rho to make this at most delta/8, where delta=pi/24.

The persistent term cannot simply be summed over all time. Instead, near a sector boundary at angular margin in [delta/2,3delta/4], the restricted map moves inward by at least c gamma a^2 delta. Choosing zeta<=c' a^2 makes that inward drift dominate its persistent perturbation. A precise moving barrier is b_k=3delta/4 minus the partial sum of the transient error bounds; it stays above 5delta/8. The restricted boundary-distance map is increasing and moves b_k inward by the stated amount. Subtracting the persistent perturbation still leaves at least b_k, and subtracting the current transient leaves at least b_{k+1}. Induction therefore keeps the margin at least delta/2. This closes the angular barrier without incorrectly claiming a summable persistent error.

The radial annulus also remains invariant: its leading field (1-r^2)r has fixed inward margins at 0.9 and 1.1, and its perturbations are bounded by C(a^2+||w||^2+zeta). Choose the constants small, exactly as in C08. This and (4) close the tube induction simultaneously.

Within the sector, the angle recurrence is

    alpha_{k+1}<=(1-c gamma a^2)alpha_k
                      +Cgamma rho^2 exp(-c' gamma k)
                      +Cgamma zeta.

Its geometric-series solution is

    alpha_k<=C exp(-c'' gamma a^2 k)+C zeta/a^2.       (5)

The first convolution is bounded uniformly because its forcing decays on the faster normal scale. The constant forcing has exactly the slow-rate denominator a^2; it is not being discarded.

Writing b=r-1, C08's radial estimate now reads

    |b_{k+1}|<=(1-c gamma)|b_k|
                      +Cgamma a^2 alpha_k^2
                      +Cgamma ||w_k||^2+Cgamma zeta.

Using (4),(5) and zeta<=a^2 gives

    |b_k|+alpha_k+||w_k||
       <=C exp(-c_1 gamma a^2 k)+C_1 zeta/a^2.        (6)

For example the persistent radial contribution is bounded by C(zeta+zeta^2/a^2), at most C'zeta; angular error is the larger floor. Choose c_* in zeta=c_* a^2 epsilon to make the last term of (6) a small enough multiple of epsilon. The factor-to-means isometry then proves (1) after the time in (2).

## 5. Probability, scope, and review

The surrogate initialization-and-angle event has probability at least 7/20 and uniform empirical control fails with probability at most eta. A union bound gives success at least 7/20-eta. No conditional independence or product of success probabilities is required. With eta<=1/100 this is at least 17/50>1/3.

This supplies a candidate polynomial empirical result for the centered equilateral case, with enormous polynomial exponents. It removes orbit augmentation and a known teacher plane from C04. It does not release the centroid constraint, identify an unknown radius, allow unequal weights, or resolve general well-separated K=3 mixtures. In particular C06's anisotropic high-noise local minimum remains an obstruction to a naive generalization.

The least trusted steps for review are the global polynomial gradient envelope and net extension in Section 2, the moving angular barrier with persistent error, and closure of the radial/normal tube. There is no computer-assisted bound here: this is an analytic argument using explicit polynomial domination. No training run, numerical concentration estimate, Lean certificate, or reviewer PASS is offered. Work as d->infinity with integers N=N(d)->infinity and M=M(d)>=1. Let (X_d,nu_d) and (Omega_d,tau_d) be probability spaces and sigma_d in L2(nu_d times tau_d). Use its singular expansion sigma_d(x,theta)=sum_j sqrt(mu_j) psi_j(x) phi_j(theta), with ordered nonnegative mu_j, sum_j mu_j<infinity, positive mu_(M+1) and positive denominators in the displayed tail conditions, and orthonormal families psi_j in L2(nu_d), phi_j in L2(tau_d). Let D_d be the closed span of the psi_j and P_<=M its orthogonal projection onto the first M modes. Define the feature kernel U_d(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu_d sigma_d(x,theta)sigma_d(x,thetaprime), its spectral tail U_>r=sum_(j>r) mu_j phi_j phi_j^T, and kappa_r=sum_(j>r)mu_j>0 for each cutoff used. Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau_d and let K_ij=U_d(theta_i,theta_j). All stochastic rates below are as d->infinity. (H) There is one sequence u(d)>=M(d) such that, for every fixed real q>=1, all g in span{phi_1,...,phi_u} satisfy ||g||_(L2q(tau_d))<=C_q||g||_(L2(tau_d)), with C_q independent of d and g. (E) For the same u there is a fixed delta_E>0 such that N^(2+delta_E)<=kappa_u^2/sum_(j>u)mu_j^2 eventually. (Dupper) For every epsilon>0, max_i U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M=O_P(N^epsilon). (Dlower) For every epsilon>0, min_i U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M=Omega_P(N^(-epsilon)), where Omega_P means that the reciprocal divided by N^epsilon is stochastically bounded. (Sa) There is a fixed delta_a>0 with N^(1+delta_a)<=kappa_M/mu_(M+1) eventually. (Sb) There is a fixed delta_b>0 with M<=N^(1-delta_b) and kappa_M/mu_M<=N^(1-delta_b) eventually. Assumption6 consists of H,E,Dupper,Dlower; Assumption7 consists of Sa,Sb. Results using only some clauses retain exactly their listed subsets. The divergence N(d)->infinity is explicit here as the asymptotic feature-count regime. No coordinate independence of the vector (phi_j(theta)) is imposed.
